React Mastery

React is a library for building a user interface out of small pieces called components. You describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React works out what to change on the page. This course teaches what React actually does with your components, starting from the smallest piece. It covers what JSX turns into (JSX is the HTML-like syntax you write components in), why a piece of state belongs to a position on the screen rather than to your component, and reconciliation (how React compares the old screen with the new one), measured rather than described. Then Effects as a way to keep React in step with something outside it, the Rules of React as the conditions React depends on rather than etiquette, the React Compiler's real output, transitions and Suspense (two ways of controlling when the screen updates) as one scheduling story, streaming server rendering, and Server Components with the data they send printed out.

How to use this course

  • This course is the last step of the web front end. It assumes the JavaScript and TypeScript courses: closures, the event loop, modules and the type layer are used here without being taught again. What this course adds is what React does with your components. Knowing that is the difference between guessing why something re-rendered (ran again and redrew) and being able to say why.
  • Everything here was run against the installed release. Every example was executed against React 19.3.0. JSX was compiled, components were rendered to real markup, the lint rules (automatic checks that flag suspicious code) were run from the plugin the project actually installs, and the compiler's output is printed rather than paraphrased. The 19.3 additions are taught with their behaviour measured: <ViewTransition> and addTransitionType (§12.10), transitions that render independently (§12.11), react-dom's browser() (§16.9) and Fragment refs (§7.9). Where 19.3 changed something 19.2.8 did, both results are shown. Where the documentation describes an API the stable release does not export, as with the two taint APIs, the course says so at the point it teaches them.
  • The authority is react.dev and the package itself. The syllabus was derived from the complete react.dev Learn and Reference sitemap, all 179 pages, fetched on 2026-09-24 for the 19.3 update. It was then checked against what the installed react and react-dom really export. Where the two disagreed, the package won.
  • The course moves from the model outward. It is built in five parts:
    • §1–§4: components, rendering and reconciliation, state and context (a way to pass data deep into the tree).
    • §5–§9: the Rules of React, Effects, the escape hatches (the tools for stepping outside React's model), custom hooks and DOM events.
    • §10–§15: performance, the React Compiler, concurrent rendering (React pausing and resuming work so the page stays responsive), Suspense, error handling and Actions (React's built-in way to run a submission and track its progress).
    • §16–§17: server rendering, hydration (the browser taking over HTML the server produced) and streaming, then Server Components and Server Functions.
    • §18 covers TypeScript, testing and class components, and §19 builds one complete feature and measures it.
  • Each section has numbered subsections, runnable examples with their real output, and exercises with worked solutions. The render counts and markup in the examples are measurements. If yours differ, the difference is information. It is usually a missing key, a new object in a dependency array, or Strict Mode doing its job (Strict Mode is a development setting that deliberately runs some code twice to expose bugs).

You need Node and a React 19 project. Check both before starting:

node --version             # v24 or newer
npm ls react react-dom     # both 19.3.x in the project you are working in

Versions every example in this course was produced against: React 19.3.0 · react-dom 19.3.0 · eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 · babel-plugin-react-compiler 1.0.0 · Node 24. The view-transition results were also checked in Chromium 151 against the browser's real View Transition API.

What you are actually learning

Not a catalogue of hooks. Five ideas, each of which explains a whole family of bugs:

  1. Three stages, held apart. A component is a function. An element is the inert object that function returns, a description of what should be on screen. A DOM node is the real thing in the page, which React eventually produces. "The component rendered" and "the DOM changed" are different claims, and nearly every confusing bug lives in the gap between them (§1–§2).
  2. State belongs to a position. State (data a component remembers between renders) lives in a slot of the render tree, not in your component. That is why wrapping a component in a different element resets it, why two branches of a ternary can share state, and why key={index} hands one item's state to another item's data the moment a list is reordered (§2–§4).
  3. Effects synchronise with something outside React. Think of an Effect as "start" and "stop", not "mount" and "unmount" (appearing on and disappearing from the screen). Its dependency array (the list of values that decide when it re-runs) is derived from what the setup reads. And there is a longer list of Effects you should not write at all (§6). That list is one of the highest-value ideas in the course.
  4. Rendering is scheduled, not just executed. Transitions keep the old interface interactive while the new one is prepared. Suspense boundaries are the units in which content is revealed. Both are one scheduling story rather than two features (§12–§13). The compiler takes over the memoisation (caching a result so it is not recomputed) you used to write by hand (§11).
  5. Two environments. A Server Component runs only on the server: its code never reaches the browser, only its output does. And every Server Function is a public endpoint (a URL anyone can call), so it must authenticate, authorise and validate its own arguments (§16–§17).

By the end you should be able to:

  • predict what re-renders and why;
  • choose a state shape that cannot contradict itself;
  • write an Effect only when there is an external system to synchronise with;
  • place server and client boundaries as a design decision;
  • and, when React surprises you, find out what it did by asking the installed package rather than an article.
SECTION 1

Components, JSX and the Element Tree

React is a library that does two jobs. First, you describe what a user interface should look like, given some data. Then React makes the real interface on the page match that description. Everything in this course follows from that one sentence. Almost every difficulty people have with React comes from treating its two halves as one.

  • Describing is your job. It happens in ordinary JavaScript functions.
  • Making the interface match is React's job. It happens later, and your code does not do it.

So the first thing to get straight is the shape of the pipeline, the chain of steps from your code to the screen. You write components, which are functions. Calling one produces elements, which are plain objects that do nothing by themselves. React reads a tree of those objects and compares it with the tree it built last time. Then it makes the smallest set of changes to the DOM (the browser's live model of the page) that makes the page agree. That is three stages, with three different kinds of thing, and it is worth keeping their names apart from day one: a component is a function, an element is a value, and a DOM node is a thing on the screen.

You write
A component — a function taking one object of props and returning a description. It is called by React, never by you.
Calling it makes
An element — a frozen plain object {$$typeof, type, key, props}. It describes a thing; it is not the thing, and creating one does nothing.
React produces
A DOM node — or an HTML string on a server, or a native view. The element tree is the same either way; only the renderer differs.

The most common beginner complaint is "my component isn't updating". It is nearly always a mix-up between the second and third rows. The function did run, but the element it returned was identical to the previous one, so React correctly did nothing. Keeping the three stages apart turns that from a mystery into something you can diagnose.

This section builds the pipeline from the bottom. It takes its time over JSX on purpose. JSX is the part everyone learns first and understands last: it looks like HTML, but it is not HTML. Knowing exactly what it compiles into (what plain JavaScript the build tool turns it into) removes a whole class of surprises about children, keys, whitespace and booleans. Everything here is checked against React 19.2.8 by running it.

1.1 A Component Is a Function That Returns a Description

A React component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns something React can render. That is the whole definition. There is no base class to extend, no registration step, and no special framework object passed in. That is why you can test a component as an ordinary function, and why "just call it and look at what comes back" is a legitimate way to debug one.

function Greeting({ name }) {
  return <p>Hello, {name}!</p>;
}

const description = Greeting({ name: 'Ada' });
console.log(typeof description);
console.log(description.type, JSON.stringify(description.props));

object
p {"children":["Hello, ","Ada","!"]}

Two things in that output deserve attention, and one of them is a trap.

The first: calling Greeting returned a plain object, not a string of HTML and not a DOM node. Nothing was rendered. The function is pure in the ordinary sense: same input, same output, and nothing else changes. §5 turns that from an observation into a formal rule.

The second: the capital letter is not a convention you may ignore. In JSX, a lowercase tag name compiles to the string 'p', and a capitalised one compiles to the identifier Greeting (a reference to your function). Write <greeting /> and React will faithfully ask the DOM for an element called greeting. It gets a HTMLUnknownElement and renders nothing useful. There is no error, because from React's point of view you asked for an unfamiliar HTML tag, and that is a legal thing to want.

function Card() { return <b>real</b>; }

console.log(JSON.stringify((<Card />).type === Card));
console.log(JSON.stringify((<card />).type));

true
"card"

That is the whole mechanism behind the capitalisation rule. type is either a string naming a host element (a built-in tag such as p) or a reference to your function. There is nothing more to it. Once you have seen the two type values side by side, the rule stops looking arbitrary.

The capitalisation style itself has a name, PascalCase (every word starts with a capital), and the file should use the same convention. A component may return an element, a string, a number, null, an array of any of those, or a fragment (a wrapper that adds nothing to the page). It may not return two elements side by side without wrapping them, because a function returns one value. That limit comes from JavaScript, not from React, and it is the reason fragments exist at all.

A function component and a react element are the two words to keep separate for the rest of the course. When a later section says "the component re-rendered", it means React called the function again. When it says "the element changed", it means the returned object differs from the previous one. Those are different claims with different consequences.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: PascalCase.

1.2 JSX Is Syntax, Not Semantics

JSX is a syntax extension: a shorthand, handled by the compiler, for function calls. It is not part of JavaScript, no browser runs it, and it has no meaning of its own. Every piece of JSX turns into exact JavaScript (the technical word is desugaring), and every rule that feels arbitrary is a consequence of that translation.

There are exactly three rules, and each one follows from "this becomes a function call".

Return a single root element. A return statement returns one value, and each JSX element is one value. Two sibling elements would be two values, which is not a thing a return can do. Wrapping them in a <div> fixes it by making one value; wrapping them in <>…</> fixes it without adding a DOM node.

Close all the tags. In HTML, some elements are void (they never have an end tag, like <br>) and some end tags are optional. JSX has neither idea, because it is not an HTML parser. It is a compiler, and it needs to know exactly where a node's children begin and end. <br> is a syntax error; <br /> is fine. HTML's rule that <li> may be left unclosed does not carry over into JSX.

Most attributes are camelCase. A camelCase attribute (written likeThis, with no dashes) becomes a key of a props object, and React uses the props object to set DOM properties, the names JavaScript uses for an element's settings. class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so React uses the className prop, matching the DOM property of the same name. for is also reserved, so it is htmlFor. tabindex becomes tabIndex, onclick becomes onClick, stroke-width becomes strokeWidth. The exceptions are data-* and aria-*, which keep their dashes precisely because they are not DOM properties. They are attributes looked up by their string name, so there is no camelCase spelling to match.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

const field = (
  <>
    <label htmlFor="q" className="lbl">Query</label>
    <input id="q" tabIndex={2} aria-describedby="hint" data-testid="q" />
  </>
);
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(field));

<label for="q" class="lbl">Query</label><input id="q" tabindex="2" aria-describedby="hint" data-testid="q"/>

The rendered output shows the round trip: you write the property name, and React writes the attribute name. htmlFor came out as for, className as class, tabIndex as tabindex, and the dashed pair came out unchanged. React is not inventing an alternative HTML here. It is writing to the DOM the way JavaScript normally addresses the DOM.

Note the self-closing <input …/> in the output. That is the renderer writing out a void element, not JSX leaking through; §16 covers what the server renderer does and does not put in its output.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: single root element, close all the tags, camelCase attribute and the className prop.

1.3 What JSX Compiles To: the Automatic Runtime

The desugaring is worth seeing rather than describing, because the details settle three later arguments at once. Compile a file of JSX and read the JavaScript that comes out.

// input.tsx
const two = <ul><li>a</li><li>b</li></ul>;
const one = <ul><li>a</li></ul>;
const keyed = <li key="k" id="i">x</li>;
export { one, two, keyed };

Compiled with tsc --jsx react-jsx, that file becomes this JavaScript:

import { jsx as _jsx, jsxs as _jsxs } from "react/jsx-runtime";
// input.tsx
const two = _jsxs("ul", { children: [_jsx("li", { children: "a" }), _jsx("li", { children: "b" })] });
const one = _jsx("ul", { children: _jsx("li", { children: "a" }) });
const keyed = _jsx("li", { id: "i", children: "x" }, "k");
export { one, two, keyed };

Four facts are visible in it.

The import is injected for you. This is the automatic jsx runtime, introduced in React 17 and now the default everywhere. The compiler adds import … from "react/jsx-runtime" itself, which is why a modern React file does not need import React from 'react' at the top. Files written before 2021 have that import because the old transform compiled to React.createElement(...), and therefore needed React to be in scope. If you see that import in new code, it is harmless and unnecessary. The jsxImportSource option points the injected import somewhere other than react. Every CSS-in-JS library, and every tool other than React that uses JSX, relies on it.

Children are a prop. The output contains { children: "a" }: there is no separate channel for children. <p>hi</p> and <p children="hi" /> compile to the same call. That is why children behaves like any other prop, and why a component can accept it, ignore it, wrap it or pass it on.

A single child is not an array. one has children: _jsx(...), while two has children: [ …, … ]. This is the most common surprise in code that inspects children by hand, and §1.9 is about the helpers that exist because of it.

key is not a prop. In keyed, id went into the props object, but key became a third argument. That is why props.key is undefined inside a component, and why the linter warns if you read it. key is a message to React about identity, used up before your function ever runs. §1.8 is about what it is for.

The two functions differ in only one way: jsxs promises a list of children that is known at compile time. That is an optimisation, since React can skip a check when the compiler has already proved the array's shape. You never call either by hand, but recognising them in a stack trace or a bundle is worth the thirty seconds it took to read this.

To have in hand before moving on: createElement(, automatic JSX runtime, jsxImportSource and react-jsx.

1.4 The Element Object

A react element is a plain object. It is worth printing one. "React is fast because it uses a virtual DOM" is a sentence people repeat without ever having looked at what the virtual DOM is made of.

const el = <p className="lead" id="x">Hi</p>;

console.log(Object.keys(el).join(','));
console.log(String(el.$$typeof));
console.log(JSON.stringify({ type: el.type, key: el.key, props: el.props }));
console.log(Object.isFrozen(el), Object.isFrozen(el.props));

$$typeof,type,key,props,_owner,_store
Symbol(react.transitional.element)
{"type":"p","key":null,"props":{"className":"lead","id":"x","children":"Hi"}}
true true

Four measured facts, each of which contradicts something widely written.

$$typeof is Symbol(react.transitional.element), not Symbol(react.element). The name changed with React 19, and older articles still quote the old one. The purpose has not changed. It is a symbol, symbols do not survive JSON.parse, and so a server that controls a JSON response cannot forge an element. That is a deliberate defence against someone injecting a React element through data a user supplied.

The element is frozen, and so are its props, in the development build. Changing el.props.className throws an error in strict mode and silently does nothing otherwise. This is React enforcing §5's rule that props are immutable, rather than merely asking you not to change them.

The development and production builds differ. In production the same element has the keys $$typeof,type,key,ref,props, and it is not frozen. Freezing costs time and catches a mistake you were meant to fix during development, and _owner/_store are debugging fields with no use in production. Two consequences follow. A bug that only appears in your production bundle may be a mutation that development was silently preventing. And any code that reads _owner is reading a field that will not be there.

There is no DOM in this object, and no work has happened. type, key and props: that is the entire virtual DOM. What makes React fast is not that this object is clever. It is that this object is cheap: cheap enough to build the whole tree again on every update and compare it with the old one, which is what §2 is about.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: props are immutable.

1.5 Props Are the Arguments

Props are the single object React passes to your component. Everything you can do with a JavaScript object you can do with props, and everything you cannot do to a frozen object you cannot do to props.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Badge({ label, tone = 'neutral', ...rest }) {
  return <span className={`badge badge--${tone}`} {...rest}>{label}</span>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Badge label="new" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Badge label="late" tone="warn" title="overdue" />));

<span class="badge badge--neutral">new</span>
<span class="badge badge--warn" title="overdue">late</span>

Destructuring props in the parameter list (unpacking them into named variables) is the normal style. It gives you two things besides brevity. The component's signature becomes a readable list of what it accepts. And a default value for a prop is written with ordinary JavaScript default-parameter syntax, not a React feature. Note carefully that a default parameter applies for undefined and not for null. Passing tone={null} gives you badge--null, which is a real bug people spend an afternoon on.

The jsx spread, {...rest}, is the second half of the pattern. You collect the props you did not name and spread them onto the underlying element. That is how a component stays useful without listing every HTML attribute someone might want. It is also how a component accidentally becomes unusable. Spreading rest before className would let a caller silently wipe out the component's own styling, and spreading it after means the caller can never add to it. Which order you choose is a design decision, not a detail. Decide it on purpose; §1.10 comes back to it.

Props flow in one direction: a parent passes them down, and a child cannot change them. Not "should not": cannot, because the object is frozen. When a child needs to affect its parent, the parent passes down a function, and calling it is the child's only way to send something upward. That one-way design is what makes a React tree traceable. To find out why a value is what it is, you walk up the tree, and there is exactly one path.

In summary, the vocabulary here is destructuring props, default value for a prop and JSX spread.

1.6 children, and What Counts as a Child

The children prop is a prop like any other, but the values it can hold follow rules worth memorising, because the answer to "why did nothing render?" is nearly always here.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<p>{null}{undefined}{false}{true}{0}{''}{NaN}</p>));

<p>0NaN</p>

null, undefined, false, true and the empty string render nothing at all. 0 renders 0. NaN renders NaN. That is the complete rule, and the last two are where the bugs live:

  • {count && <List/>} renders a literal 0 when count is 0, which is the most-reported React surprise in existence;
  • {price * qty} on bad input renders the string NaN into your page instead of failing.

Objects are the one thing that causes an error rather than silently rendering nothing:

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

try { renderToStaticMarkup(<p>{{ a: 1 }}</p>); }
catch (e) { console.log(e.message.split('\n')[0]); }

Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {a}). If you meant to render a collection of children, use an array instead.

That message is worth recognising on sight. In practice it means one of three things:

  • you forgot a property access ({user} instead of {user.name});
  • you rendered a Date or a Map;
  • or you rendered a promise, which usually means an async function component in a place that does not support one.

Arrays, by contrast, are rendered one element at a time, and nested arrays are flattened for you:

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<ul>{[<li key="1">1</li>, [<li key="2">2</li>]]}</ul>));

const name = 'Ada';
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<p>Hello, {name}! You have {2 + 3} messages</p>));

<ul><li>1</li><li>2</li></ul>
<p>Hello, Ada! You have 5 messages</p>

The second line is worth a note because it changed. Older React put <!-- --> comment separators between neighbouring pieces of text in server output, so that hydration could tell where one text node ended and the next began. React 19's renderer does not: the output is exactly <p>Hello, Ada! You have 5 messages</p>. Any test or snapshot that contains those comments was written against an older version.

Curly braces in JSX are the general mechanism here. A JSX expression is anything between them: { opens a JavaScript expression anywhere a child or an attribute value may go. It must be an expression (something that produces a value), not a statement. {if (x) …} is a syntax error, which is why §1.7 exists. And the double curlies you see in style={{ color: 'red' }} are not special syntax at all: the outer pair opens an expression, and the inner pair is an object literal.

What to carry forward from this subsection: JSX expression, curly braces in JSX, double curlies and children prop.

1.7 Conditional Rendering

Because JSX holds expressions, every conditional in React is an ordinary JavaScript expression. Choosing between the forms is about readability, not about what each one can do.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Item({ text, done, count }) {
  if (!text) return null;                    // early return: nothing to show
  return (
    <li>
      {/* ternary: pick between two renderings of the same slot */}
      {done ? <s>{text}</s> : text}
      {/* logical AND: render something, or nothing */}
      {count > 0 && <b> ({count})</b>}
    </li>
  );
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Item text="milk" done={false} count={2} />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Item text="eggs" done={true} count={0} />));
console.log(JSON.stringify(renderToStaticMarkup(<Item text="" done={false} count={1} />)));

<li>milk<b> (2)</b></li>
<li><s>eggs</s></li>
""

Three forms, three jobs:

  • Returning null from a component renders nothing. It is the right answer when the whole component has nothing to show. Note that React still calls the function and still keeps the component in the tree, which matters for state (§2.7).
  • The ternary operator in jsx picks between two renderings of the same spot.
  • The logical and operator in jsx renders something or nothing.

The && form has the sharp edge already met in §1.6, and it is worth stating as a rule: && is safe only when its left side is a boolean. count && <b/> with count === 0 renders 0. items.length && <List/> with an empty array renders 0. Write count > 0 && or items.length > 0 &&, or use a ternary with an explicit null. The lint rules cannot catch this, because rendering 0 is a legitimate thing to want.

A detail that bites when a comment or a second expression shares a line: whitespace between two expressions on the same line is a text child, and whitespace spanning a line break is not. JSX throws away the spaces at the start and end of a line, and drops lines that contain only whitespace. But it keeps the spaces that sit between things on one line. That is why the comments above are on their own lines instead of after the expressions they describe.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

const a = 'x', b = 'y';
console.log(JSON.stringify(renderToStaticMarkup(<p>{a}   {b}</p>)));
console.log(JSON.stringify(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <p>
    {a}
    {b}
  </p>
)));

"<p>x   y</p>"
"<p>xy</p>"

Same two expressions, different output, and the only difference is a line break. Put a {/* comment */} after an expression on the same line and you have silently added the spaces before it to the page.

Once the branching goes past two cases, take it out of JSX entirely: assign elements to variables, or return early. JSX has no switch, and three nested ternaries produce something nobody can review.

The terms above, gathered: ternary operator in JSX, logical AND operator in JSX and returning null.

1.8 Lists and the key Prop

Rendering lists is done with map, returning one element per item. The interesting half is the key prop, which is the most misunderstood thing in React and the one worth spending real time on.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

const rows = [{ id: 'a1', text: 'alpha' }, { id: 'b2', text: 'beta' }];

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<ul>{rows.map(r => <li key={r.id}>{r.text}</li>)}</ul>));
console.log((<li key="a1">x</li>).key, JSON.stringify((<li key="a1">x</li>).props));

<ul><li>alpha</li><li>beta</li></ul>
a1 {"children":"x"}

Notice again that key does not appear in props. It is not data for your component. It answers a question React asks itself: when I compare this list with the list from last time, which new item is the same item as which old one?

Without keys, React matches children by position. Position is a fine answer when the list never changes. It is the wrong answer the moment items are inserted, removed or reordered. React will then conclude that the item that is now first is the item that was first, and reuse its DOM node and its state for different data. This is why index as a key is a bug rather than a shortcut. key={i} gives you exactly the matching by position you would have got with no key at all, dressed up to silence the warning.

The rules of keys are short:

Stable
The same item gets the same key on every render. A key generated during render — Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID() — recreates every node every time, which is the opposite of what keys are for.
Unique among siblings
Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally. Two lists on the same page may both use key 1; two items in the same list may not.
From the data
A database id, a filename, a slug — something that identifies the item independently of where it currently sits. Generating a key from data is the whole job.

If the data really has no id, make one when the item is created, not when it is rendered, and store it with the item. A key invented during render is not an identity.

When one item needs to produce several sibling nodes, the key goes on a keyed fragment. This is the one case where the <>…</> shorthand will not do: the shorthand takes no attributes, so you need the explicit <Fragment key={…}> form.

import { Fragment } from 'react';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

const defs = [{ id: 1, t: 'DOM', d: 'the page' }, { id: 2, t: 'JSX', d: 'the syntax' }];

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <dl>{defs.map(x => (
    <Fragment key={x.id}><dt>{x.t}</dt><dd>{x.d}</dd></Fragment>
  ))}</dl>
));
console.log(String((<></>).type));

<dl><dt>DOM</dt><dd>the page</dd><dt>JSX</dt><dd>the syntax</dd></dl>
Symbol(react.fragment)

The fragment shorthand <></> and <Fragment></Fragment> produce the same type: a symbol React recognises as "render my children and add nothing". §2 shows what keys actually do when React compares trees; this subsection is about writing them correctly, and the payoff comes there.

One line each, for reference: rendering lists, index as a key, keys must be unique among siblings, rules of keys, generating a key from data, fragment shorthand and keyed fragment.

1.9 The Children Helpers and cloneElement

Because a single child is not an array (§1.3), code that wants to inspect or transform props.children cannot just call .map on it. React ships five helpers for that, all on the Children object. They are worth knowing mainly so you can recognise the pattern in a library, and so you know why the modern advice is to avoid them.

import { Children } from 'react';

const items = ['a', 'b'];
const kids = <>{items.map(i => <li key={i}>{i}</li>)}<li>c</li></>;
const arr = Children.toArray(kids.props.children);

console.log(Children.count(kids.props.children));
console.log(arr.map(c => c.key).join(' '));

3
.0:$a .0:$b .1

Children.count( counted three, not two, even though children holds an array of two things, one of which is itself an array of two. The helpers walk into nested arrays and flatten them, which is exactly what makes them different from props.children.length.

Children.toArray( produced the keys .0:$a, .0:$b and .1. That prefix is how React keeps keys unique when several lists are merged into one children slot: .0 and .1 are positions in the outer array, and $a is your key. It also explains a real failure. If you pass a Children.toArray result back into a new list, the keys change, so state tied to those children resets.

Children.map(, Children.forEach( and Children.only( complete the set. The first two loop over the children with the same flattening. only checks that there is exactly one child and returns it, throwing an error otherwise.

cloneElement( is the other half of this older toolkit. It produces a copy of an element with merged props:

import { cloneElement, isValidElement } from 'react';

const base = <b key="k1" className="a" title="t">hi</b>;
const cloned = cloneElement(base, { className: 'b' });

console.log(cloned.key, JSON.stringify(cloned.props));
console.log(isValidElement(base), isValidElement('b'), isValidElement({ type: 'b' }));

k1 {"className":"b","title":"t","children":"hi"}
true false false

The key survives, title survives, and className is replaced: a shallow merge, which combines only the top level of the props. isValidElement( answers whether a value is a React element at all, and its second and third results show it doing real work. A string is not an element, and neither is an object that merely looks like one, because the check is on that $$typeof symbol from §1.4.

Both of these are legacy APIs in the sense that they solve a problem better solved another way. A component that clones its children to inject props is a component whose contract is invisible: the caller cannot see what they will receive, TypeScript cannot check it, and adding a wrapper <div> around the children breaks it silently. Context (§4) or an explicit render prop (§1.10) does the same job in a way the reader and the compiler can both follow. Know these five; reach for them rarely.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: isValidElement(, cloneElement(, Children.count(, Children.map(, Children.toArray(, Children.only(, Children.forEach( and legacy API.

1.10 Composition: children, Slots and Render Props

React has no dependency-injection system, no mixins and no directives (features other frameworks use to share behaviour). It has one way to combine components: passing values as props, including elements and functions. The three named patterns below are all that same mechanism, used from different angles.

Passing JSX as children is the default. A component that takes children can wrap content without knowing what that content is.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Panel({ title, children }) {
  return <section className="panel"><h2>{title}</h2><div>{children}</div></section>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <Panel title="Stats"><p>one</p><p>two</p></Panel>
));

<section class="panel"><h2>Stats</h2><div><p>one</p><p>two</p></div></section>

Slots are the same idea with more than one opening. When a layout needs a header and a footer, pass elements as ordinary named props, instead of trying to sort one children array into groups.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Dialog({ heading, body, actions }) {
  return (
    <div className="dialog">
      <header>{heading}</header>
      <div className="body">{body}</div>
      <footer>{actions}</footer>
    </div>
  );
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <Dialog heading={<h2>Delete?</h2>} body={<p>This cannot be undone.</p>}
          actions={<><button>Cancel</button><button>Delete</button></>} />
));

<div class="dialog"><header><h2>Delete?</h2></header><div class="body"><p>This cannot be undone.</p></div><footer><button>Cancel</button><button>Delete</button></footer></div>

Elements are values (§1.4), so putting one in a prop is not a trick. It is the same thing as putting a number in a prop.

A render prop reverses the direction. Instead of the parent handing the child finished markup, the child hands the parent some data, and the parent decides what to render with it. It is a function passed as a prop and called during render.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function List({ items, renderItem }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((it, i) => <li key={it.id}>{renderItem(it, i)}</li>)}</ul>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <List items={[{ id: 1, n: 'a' }, { id: 2, n: 'b' }]}
        renderItem={(it, i) => <span>{i}: {it.n}</span>} />
));

<ul><li><span>0: a</span></li><li><span>1: b</span></li></ul>

Render props were once the standard way to share logic that holds state between components. Custom hooks (§8) replaced them entirely for that job. What they are still the right answer for is sharing rendering decisions: for example, a table that owns sorting and paging but not what a cell looks like. When you see a render prop in modern code, ask one question. Is it sharing behaviour? Then it wants to be a hook. Is it sharing layout? Then it is fine where it is.

Component composition is the umbrella term for all of this, and the practical rule it leads to is: prefer passing an element over passing the data needed to build one. A <Layout sidebar={<Nav/>} /> cannot be broken by Layout changing its mind about how a nav is built, because Layout never knew.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: passing JSX as children and component composition.

1.11 Importing and Exporting Components

Components are values in modules, so importing and exporting components is ordinary ES module work. The conventions matter more here than elsewhere, though, because tools read them.

Nesting components, defining one inside another, is the one arrangement to avoid. The inner one becomes a new component type on every render (§2.4), so its state resets each time. Declare each component at the top level of its module.

One component per file is the norm, exported as the default, with the file named after the component. A file may export several related components. When it does, give them all names rather than mixing a default with several named exports. A default export has no name of its own, so every file that imports it may spell it differently. That inconsistency makes a codebase hard to search. It also makes stack traces and DevTools unhelpful: React takes a component's display name from the function's name, and an anonymous arrow function assigned to a default export has none.

// Button.jsx  — named, so the name survives into stack traces and DevTools
export function Button({ children }) { return <button>{children}</button>; }
export default Button;

// avoid: the component is anonymous, and DevTools will show "Anonymous"
// export default ({ children }) => <button>{children}</button>;

function Button() and const Button = () => … are equivalent to React. The only difference that matters is hoisting (a function declaration can be used before the line that defines it), and by convention a component file declares things before it uses them.

Where to split a component is a judgement call, and size is not the useful test. Split when a piece of the tree has its own state, its own props contract, or its own reason to change. A 200-line component that renders one coherent thing with no internal state is easier to read than five components that only exist because someone had a line limit.

To have in hand before moving on: nesting components.

1.12 Your UI as a Tree: Render Tree and Module Dependency Tree

Two different trees describe a React application, and they have different shapes. Confusing them is behind a whole family of "why is this re-rendering?" and "why is my bundle so big?" questions.

The render tree is what React builds while the app runs: which component rendered which. State, context and reconciliation all work on this tree. It changes as the app runs: a conditional branch adds or removes a whole subtree. And a component's position in it decides whether its state survives an update (§2.7).

The module dependency tree is what the bundler builds at build time: which file imports which. It never changes while the app runs. It includes files that render nothing (utilities, constants). It decides how large your bundle is and what lazy() can split off into a separate file (§13).

Render tree — runtime
Built by React, one node per rendered component.
  • Changes as state and props change
  • A component appears once per place it is rendered
  • Decides re-renders, context lookup, state identity
  • Read it in React DevTools' Components tab
Module dependency tree — build time
Built by the bundler, one node per file.
  • Fixed once the build runs
  • A file appears once no matter how often it renders
  • Decides bundle size and code-splitting boundaries
  • Read it in a bundle analyser

A component that appears once in the module tree may appear two hundred times in the render tree. A module that is enormous may render nothing. When someone says "move this component up the tree", ask which tree they mean. The answer is nearly always the render tree, and nearly always about state.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: Components tab and code-splitting.

1.13 Thinking in React

The five steps below are React's own recommended process for turning a design into components. Follow them literally the first several times, because each one is a decision that is expensive to undo later.

Step 1 — breaking the UI into a component hierarchy. Draw boxes around every piece of the design and name them. The useful principle is the same one that applies to functions: a component should do one thing. If it grows, split it. Where the design's structure and the data's structure agree, follow both. Where they disagree, follow the data, because the data is what will change.

Step 2 — build a static version. Build the whole thing with props and no state at all. This is deliberately boring and deliberately fast, and it separates two hard problems: what does it look like and how does it change. Trying to solve both at once is why first attempts sprawl.

Step 3 — find the minimal but complete representation of UI state. Go through every piece of data and ask three questions:

  • Does it stay the same over time? Then it is not state.
  • Is it passed in from a parent? Then it is not state.
  • Can you compute it from other state or props? Then it is definitely not state.

What survives all three is the minimal representation of ui state. §3.5 explains why keeping it minimal is about correctness, not tidiness.

Step 4 — identify where state should live. For each piece of state, find every component that renders something depending on it. Find their closest common parent, and put the state there, or higher if there is a natural owner above. This is lifting state up (§3.7). Doing it on purpose at design time is far cheaper than discovering it when a second component needs the value.

Step 5 — add inverse data flow. Children need to change state that lives above them, and they do it by calling functions passed down as props. There is no other way. Inverse data flow is the name for that pattern. Its cost is writing the handler in the parent and passing it down. What it buys you is a tree where every value has exactly one source.

The result is a design where data flows in one direction and each piece of state has one owner. Everything the rest of this course adds (effects, context, reducers, transitions, server components) is built on top of that shape, and none of it repairs a design that got step 3 wrong.

In summary, the vocabulary here is breaking the UI into a component hierarchy, static version and minimal representation of UI state.

What This Section Established

React's pipeline has three stages and three kinds of value: a component is a function you write, an element is an inert frozen object it returns, and a DOM node is what React eventually produces. "The component rendered" and "the DOM changed" are different claims.

JSX is syntax with an exact desugaring, and the desugaring answers the questions. Children are a prop, so a single child is not an array. key is a third argument, so it never reaches your component. The import is injected by the compiler, which is why import React is no longer needed. Attributes become DOM properties, which is why they are camelCase — except data-* and aria-*, which are not properties.

The rendering rules for children are worth memorising because they fail silently: null, undefined, false, true and '' render nothing, 0 and NaN render themselves, objects throw, and arrays flatten. That is the whole reason count && <X/> is a bug and count > 0 && <X/> is not.

Keys are identity, not order. They must be stable, unique among siblings, and derived from the data — and key={index} is exactly the positional matching that having no key gives you.

Composition is one mechanism — props holding values, which may be elements or functions — wearing three names: children, slots and render props. And two trees describe an app: the render tree, which decides state and re-renders, and the module dependency tree, which decides bundle size.

Exercises

1. Read the desugaring. Without running anything, write out what each of these compiles to under the automatic runtime, including which of jsx/jsxs is used and where key ends up: <img src={u} alt="" />; <Row key={id} n={1}><Cell/></Row>; <><A/><B/></>; <p>{a} and {b}</p>. Then check yourself by compiling them. For the last one, say how many entries props.children holds and why.

2. Make the silent failures visible. Write one component that demonstrates all five ways a child can render nothing, and one that demonstrates both ways a child renders something you did not intend. For the second, give the two-character fix for each and explain why no lint rule can catch them.

3. Keys under mutation. Given [{id:'a'},{id:'b'},{id:'c'}] rendered with key={item.id} and with key={index}, write down for each of the following what React concludes about identity: prepending an item, removing the middle item, and reversing the list. Then say which of the three is harmless with index keys and why.

4. Convert a clone to a contract. Take a <Toolbar> that uses Children.map and cloneElement to inject a size prop into each child button. Rewrite it twice — once with an explicit render prop, once with a size prop the caller passes down themselves — and state one thing each rewrite makes possible that the original did not.

5. Two trees. Sketch the render tree and the module dependency tree for an app where App imports Page, Page imports Card and formatDate, and Page renders three Cards inside a conditional that is currently false. Give the node count of each tree, and name one question each tree answers that the other cannot.

Solution

1. The desugaring.

_jsx("img", { src: u, alt: "" })
_jsx(Row, { n: 1, children: _jsx(Cell, {}) }, id)
_jsxs(Fragment, { children: [_jsx(A, {}), _jsx(B, {})] })
_jsxs("p", { children: [a, " and ", b] })

jsxs is used whenever the compiler can see a statically known list of two or more children; jsx otherwise. key is never in props — it is the third argument, which is why Row receives only { n, children }.

The last one holds three entries: a, the literal string " and ", and b. The literal text between two expressions is a child in its own right, which is why adjacent text and expressions produce an array rather than a concatenated string.

2. The silent failures.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Nothing() {
  return <p>{null}{undefined}{false}{true}{''}</p>;   // five ways to render nothing
}

function Oops({ count, price, qty }) {
  return <p>{count && 'has items'}{price * qty}</p>;  // renders 0, and NaN
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Nothing />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Oops count={0} price={undefined} qty={2} />));

<p></p>
<p>0NaN</p>

The fixes are count > 0 && and a guard such as Number.isFinite(total) ? total : '—'. No lint rule can catch either, because rendering the number 0 and rendering the string NaN are both legitimate things to want; the rule would have to know your intent.

3. Keys under mutation.

                     key={item.id}                     key={index}
prepend      a,b,c keep identity; new node    every item shifts: 'a' now
             is inserted at the front         has key 1, so React treats it
                                              as the old 'b' and reuses its
                                              DOM node and state

remove mid   'b' is unmounted; a and c        'c' inherits index 1, so React
             keep their nodes                 treats it as the old 'b';
                                              the last node is unmounted

reverse      React reorders the existing      React concludes nothing moved
             nodes; state follows each item   and rewrites the text of every
                                              node; state stays at its position

Only appending is harmless with index keys — an appended item gets a fresh index and no existing item's index changes. That is the precise condition under which key={index} is defensible: a list that is append-only and never reordered, filtered or deleted from.

4. Clone to contract.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

// render prop: the toolbar hands out `size`, the caller decides what to build
function ToolbarRP({ size = 'sm', renderButtons }) {
  return <div className="toolbar">{renderButtons(size)}</div>;
}

// explicit props: the toolbar owns layout only
function ToolbarEx({ children }) {
  return <div className="toolbar">{children}</div>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <ToolbarRP renderButtons={size => <><button className={size}>a</button><button className={size}>b</button></>} />
));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <ToolbarEx><button className="sm">a</button><span>not a button</span></ToolbarEx>
));

<div class="toolbar"><button class="sm">a</button><button class="sm">b</button></div>
<div class="toolbar"><button class="sm">a</button><span>not a button</span></div>

The render prop makes the contract visible and typed — the caller can see that a size arrives, and TypeScript checks it. The explicit-prop version makes it possible to wrap children in anything — a <span>, a tooltip, a <div> — without the toolbar silently failing to find its buttons, which is exactly what Children.map plus cloneElement breaks on.

5. Two trees.

Render tree (runtime, conditional false)     Module dependency tree (build)
  App                                          App.jsx
    Page                                         Page.jsx
                                                   Card.jsx
  2 nodes                                          formatDate.js
                                                 4 nodes

With the conditional true the render tree grows to five nodes — App, Page, and three separate Card nodes — while the module tree stays at four, because Card.jsx is imported once no matter how many times it renders. formatDate.js never appears in the render tree at all.

The render tree alone answers "which components will re-render when this state changes, and where does this context come from". The module tree alone answers "what is in my bundle, and where can I split it". Neither can answer the other's question.

SECTION 2

Rendering, Reconciliation and Keys

§1 ended with a tree of objects that do nothing by themselves. This section is about what React does with that tree. It is the section that decides whether the rest of the course feels like a set of rules to memorise or a set of consequences you can work out.

It matters because almost every question a working React developer actually asks is a question about this machinery:

  • Why did this re-render?
  • Why did my input lose focus?
  • Why did the state of the wrong row change?
  • Why is my animation restarting?

Answered from folklore, each one is a separate mystery with its own superstition attached. Answered from the model, they are the same three or four facts applied to different situations.

The model is small. React re-renders by calling your functions again and comparing the elements they return with the elements from last time. This comparison is called reconciliation. It matches old to new by position and by type, keys included (a key is a label you give an item so React can recognise it). Where the match succeeds, React keeps the existing DOM node and the existing state, and changes only what differs. Where it fails, React throws the old subtree away, state and all, and builds a new one. That is essentially all of it. Everything below makes that sentence precise enough to predict behaviour.

Every claim in this section was measured by running React 19.3.0 against a real DOM and counting: renders, DOM mutations (changes to the page), and what survived.

2.1 Three Steps: Trigger, Render, Commit

An update in React happens in three separate steps, and they happen at different times.

Trigger
Something asks for a render: the initial render via createRoot(…).render(…), or a state update in a component already on screen. Nothing has happened yet — the request is queued.
Render
React calls your component functions and walks down through everything they return, building a new element tree. No DOM is touched. This phase must be pure, and it can be paused, restarted or abandoned (§12).
Commit
React applies the differences to the DOM, synchronously and all at once. Then layout effects run, the browser paints, and passive effects run after that.

This separation is not an implementation detail you can ignore, because the two phases follow different rules.

  • The render phase is where React calls your components. It may run more than once for a single update, may run for a tree that is never committed, and runs twice on purpose in development (§2.13).
  • The commit phase happens exactly once per committed update. It is where the world outside React, the real page, finally changes.

The ordering is observable:

import { useState, useEffect, useLayoutEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Child({ n }) {
  log.push('render Child ' + n);
  useLayoutEffect(() => { log.push('layout effect ' + n); });
  useEffect(() => { log.push('passive effect ' + n); });
  return <span>{n}</span>;
}
function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  log.push('render App ' + n);
  globalThis.bump = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <p><Child n={n} /></p>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log(log.join(' | '));

log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.bump(); });
console.log(log.join(' | '));

render App 0 | render Child 0 | layout effect 0 | passive effect 0
render App 1 | render Child 1 | layout effect 1 | passive effect 1

Parents render before children, because React cannot know what a child is until the parent has returned it. Layout effects run inside the commit, before the browser gets a chance to paint the screen. Passive effects (ordinary useEffect) run after. §6 and §7 cover what belongs in each. The point here is only that the commit separates them, and that everything labelled render happened before anything touched the page.

What to carry forward from this subsection: initial render and createRoot(.

2.2 The Render Phase: React Calls Your Function

"Rendering" in React means React calls your component function. It does not mean anything appeared on screen. This is the most useful vocabulary correction there is. "My component re-rendered" and "the DOM changed" are different events, and mixing them up makes performance work impossible.

Trigger a render happens in exactly two ways:

  • the initial render, when a root is created and rendered into a DOM node;
  • a state update, in a component that is already on screen.

There is no third way. Props changing is not a trigger in itself: what happened is that a parent re-rendered, and that produced the new props.

React then walks down the tree. It calls the component and looks at what it returned. For every component element in that output it calls that component too, and so on, until only host elements (built-in tags such as div) and text are left. That repetition is why a state update near the root can call a hundred functions.

And it does that by default, for the whole subtree, regardless of whether props changed:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let appRenders = 0, childRenders = 0;
function Child({ n }) { childRenders++; return <span>{n}</span>; }
function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  const [other, setOther] = useState(0);
  appRenders++;
  globalThis.setN = setN; globalThis.setOther = setOther;
  return <p><Child n={n} /><i>{other}</i></p>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });

appRenders = childRenders = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setN(0); });      // same value as before
console.log('set to the same value  -> App:', appRenders, 'Child:', childRenders);
appRenders = childRenders = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setOther(1); });  // state Child does not use
console.log('unrelated state change -> App:', appRenders, 'Child:', childRenders);

set to the same value  -> App: 0 Child: 0
unrelated state change -> App: 1 Child: 1

The second line is the important one, and it surprises people. Child was called again even though n did not change and its element was identical in structure. React does not compare props to decide whether to call a child. It calls the child, gets an element, and compares that. Skipping the call is an optimisation you opt into (memo, §10.4) or something the compiler does for you (§11). It is never the default.

The first line is the other half, and it is a real bail-out (React stopping early), not just a fast render. Setting state to a value that is Object.is-equal to the current one caused zero calls to either function. React compares the new state with the old before scheduling anything, and if they match it stops. Note the subtle consequence. Calling a state setter with the same value costs nothing. Calling it with a new object that happens to hold the same data is not free, because Object.is compares references (whether it is the same object), not contents.

The terms above, gathered: trigger a render.

2.3 The Commit Phase: the Minimum DOM Operations

After the render phase produces a new tree, React commits. The rule it follows is worth stating exactly: React does not touch the dom when the output is unchanged. That is not a vague "React is efficient". It is a specific claim, which you can test, about which nodes get written to.

Watch it with a MutationObserver, a browser API that reports every change the DOM actually receives:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Row({ n, tone }) {
  return <li className={tone}><b>label</b> <span>{n}</span></li>;
}
function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  const [tone, setTone] = useState('warm');
  globalThis.setN = setN; globalThis.setTone = setTone;
  return <ul><Row n={n} tone={tone} /></ul>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });

const seen = [];
new window.MutationObserver(recs => {
  for (const r of recs) seen.push(r.type === 'characterData'
    ? 'text -> ' + r.target.nodeValue : r.type + ' ' + (r.attributeName ?? ''));
}).observe(box, { subtree: true, childList: true, attributes: true, characterData: true });

await act(async () => { globalThis.setN(1); });
console.log('changing n:   ', JSON.stringify(seen));
seen.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setTone('cool'); });
console.log('changing tone:', JSON.stringify(seen));

changing n:    ["text -> 1"]
changing tone: ["attributes class"]

One mutation each. Changing n rewrote a single text node: the <li>, the <b>, the <span> and the whitespace were all left alone. Changing tone set one attribute. Both times the entire Row function ran again and produced a whole new element tree, and the DOM received one write.

This is the trade React makes, and it is worth naming: re-running your code is cheap, and touching the DOM is expensive. Building a few thousand small frozen objects and comparing them costs microseconds. Making the browser recalculate the layout costs milliseconds. React spends the cheap resource to save the expensive one. It is also why the performance advice in §10 is about avoiding renders you did not need, not about avoiding DOM writes: React has already kept those to a minimum.

One line each, for reference: React does not touch the DOM when the output is unchanged.

2.4 Reconciliation: Matching Old to New

Reconciliation is the algorithm that decides, for each position in the new tree, whether there is a matching node in the old tree. It is the heart of the whole library. It is built on two rules, both chosen for speed rather than for a perfect result.

Different type ⇒ new tree
If the type at a position differs — 'div' vs 'p', Login vs Home — React does not try to find what the two have in common. It unmounts the whole old subtree and mounts a new one.
Same type ⇒ update in place
Same type means the same node. The DOM node is kept, its attributes are patched to match, its state is kept, and React recurses into the children.
Children match by key, else by position
Within a list of children, a key — when present — identifies which old child a new child corresponds to. With no key, the match is the index in the list.

A general algorithm for comparing two trees is O(n³): its work grows with the cube of the number of nodes. These two shortcuts bring it down to O(n), growing only in step with the number of nodes. The price is being wrong in cases React considers rare. Moving a subtree under a different type of parent really does throw it away, even though a human can see it is "the same" component. That is not a bug to work around. It is the deal, and the rest of this section is about living with it on purpose.

Diffing is the common name for the comparison, and virtual dom for the tree being compared, although neither term appears in React's own API. Both are fine as vocabulary as long as they do not become magic. The virtual DOM is the pile of {type, key, props} objects from §1.4, and diffing is the two rules above.

2.5 State Is Tied to a Position, Not to a Component

Here is the fact that explains more confusing React bugs than any other, and it is worth reading twice: state does not belong to your component function. It belongs to a position in the render tree.

React keeps state in its own tree, alongside the element tree, filed by where each component sits. When the new tree has the same component type at the same position, that state is handed to the new render. When it does not, that state is thrown away.

Three experiments in one, measured:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter({ label }) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis['inc_' + label] = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <span>{label}:{n} </span>;
}
function App() {
  const [swap, setSwap] = useState(false);
  const [k, setK] = useState('a');
  globalThis.setSwap = setSwap; globalThis.setK = setK;
  return (
    <div>
      {swap ? <p><Counter label="wrapped" /></p> : <div><Counter label="wrapped" /></div>}
      <Counter key={k} label="keyed" />
    </div>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.inc_wrapped(); globalThis.inc_wrapped();
                        globalThis.inc_keyed(); });
console.log('after clicking     :', box.textContent.trim());
await act(async () => { globalThis.setSwap(true); });     // <div> wrapper becomes <p>
console.log('after div -> p     :', box.textContent.trim());
await act(async () => { globalThis.setK('b'); });         // key changes
console.log('after key a -> b   :', box.textContent.trim());

after clicking     : wrapped:2 keyed:1
after div -> p     : wrapped:0 keyed:1
after key a -> b   : wrapped:0 keyed:0

Read the second line carefully. Counter is the same component, rendered with the same props, in the same place in your source code — and its state reset to zero. All that changed is that its parent element went from <div> to <p>. React saw a different type at that position, applied rule one, and destroyed the subtree including the counter's state.

That is different components at the same position resets state, and its mirror image is same component at the same position preserves state. Both are about position, and neither is about how your source code is laid out. Two <Counter/> calls written in different branches of a ternary are the same position if they land in the same slot of the same parent. That is why this example keeps its state instead of resetting it:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter({ tone }) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.inc = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <span>{tone}:{n}</span>;
}
function App() {
  const [alt, setAlt] = useState(false);
  globalThis.setAlt = setAlt;
  return <div>{alt ? <Counter tone="B" /> : <Counter tone="A" />}</div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.inc(); globalThis.inc(); globalThis.inc(); });
console.log('before switching branch:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.setAlt(true); });
console.log('after switching branch :', box.textContent);

before switching branch: A:3
after switching branch : B:3

Two branches of a ternary that look different, one shared position, one preserved counter. When people say "React kept my old form values after I switched tabs", this is why. It is not a bug: it is rule two working exactly as designed.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: same component at the same position preserves state and different components at the same position resets state.

2.6 Preserving and Resetting State with a key

Preserving and resetting state is therefore one decision, not two. State is tied to position, and a key changes what React considers "the same" child. So resetting state with a key is the supported way to say this is a different thing now, start fresh.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Draft({ id }) {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  globalThis.typeInto = s => setText(s);
  return <span>[{id}: {text || '(empty)'}]</span>;
}
function Editor({ keyed }) {
  const [id, setId] = useState('note-1');
  globalThis.openNote = next => setId(next);
  return <div>{keyed ? <Draft key={id} id={id} /> : <Draft id={id} />}</div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const keyed of [true, false]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Editor keyed={keyed} />); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.typeInto('unsaved text'); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.openNote('note-2'); });
  console.log(keyed ? 'with key={id}:' : 'without a key:', box.textContent);
}

with key={id}: [note-2: (empty)]
without a key: [note-2: unsaved text]

The second line is the bug this pattern prevents. Without the key, opening note 2 showed note 1's unsaved text, because React saw the same component at the same position and handed over the old state. key={id} states the intent in one attribute: identity follows the note, not the slot. It is nearly always the right fix for "the form did not clear".

Two cautions.

  • A key change remounts: every effect in that subtree is torn down and re-run, and every DOM node is rebuilt. That is cheap for a form, but not free for a large subtree.
  • A key on a component whose identity did not change is the mirror-image bug. key={Math.random()} remounts on every single render, and is a common cause of inputs that lose focus while you type.

2.7 Preserving State for Removed Components

The consequence of §2.5 is uncomfortable: if a component is removed from the tree, its state is gone. Closing a panel and opening it again gives you a fresh panel. For the ordinary case React has no built-in "keep this around while hidden", and there are three real answers.

Render it always, hide it with CSS. The component stays in the tree, so its state stays. This is cheap and correct for a small subtree. It is wasteful for a large one, because it keeps rendering and keeps its DOM nodes alive.

Lift the state up. Move the state to a parent that is not being removed, and pass it down. The panel no longer holds state, and its data outlives it. This is the standard answer, and it works with everything else in the course.

Persist it outside React, in localStorage, a URL parameter or a store. This is the right answer when the state should survive more than closing a panel, such as a page reload.

React 19 adds a fourth answer for the case where hiding is what you actually mean: <Activity>. It renders a subtree in hidden mode, which removes its effects but keeps its state and its DOM. It is covered in §12.9, because its interesting properties are about scheduling. It is mentioned here so that the list of answers is complete rather than three-quarters complete.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: hidden mode.

2.8 Keys During Reconciliation

§1.8 gave the rules for writing keys. Here is what keys do, which is the half that makes the rules easy to remember.

When React reconciles a list of children, it builds a map from each key to its old child, then walks through the new children.

  • A new child whose key is in the map is the same child. React updates it in place and, if its position moved, moves the DOM node instead of recreating it.
  • A new child whose key is not in the map is mounted (created fresh).
  • An old key that no new child claims is unmounted (removed).

With no keys, the position is the key. So adding an item at the front shifts every match by one:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Field({ name }) {
  const [v, setV] = useState(name);           // initial value only
  globalThis['set_' + name] = setV;
  return <b>{v} </b>;
}
function List({ keyed }) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(['b', 'c']);
  globalThis.prepend = () => setItems(xs => ['a', ...xs]);
  return <div>{items.map((it, i) =>
    keyed ? <Field key={it} name={it} /> : <Field key={i} name={it} />)}</div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const keyed of [true, false]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<List keyed={keyed} />); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.set_b('EDITED'); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.prepend(); });
  console.log((keyed ? 'key={item}:' : 'key={index}:'), box.textContent.trim());
}

key={item}: a EDITED c
key={index}: EDITED c c

With stable keys, the edit stayed with the item it belonged to, and a fresh field appeared at the front. With index keys, React concluded that the item now at index 0 is the item that used to be at index 0. So the edited state stayed at position 0 and the name prop changed underneath it, while the item at index 2 mounted fresh and took 'c' again. The list is wrong in a way that no error reports, and that only shows up when state or DOM focus is involved.

This is why key={index} is a decision, not just a way to quiet the linter. It is correct exactly when items are only ever added at the end, and the list is never reordered, filtered or deleted from.

2.9 Batching

Automatic batching is React grouping several state updates into a single render. It is not an optimisation you switch on; it is simply how updates work.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { flushSync } from 'react-dom';

let renders = 0;
function App() {
  const [a, setA] = useState(0);
  const [b, setB] = useState(0);
  renders++;
  globalThis.both = () => { setA(x => x + 1); setB(x => x + 1); };
  globalThis.afterAwait = async () => {
    await Promise.resolve(); setA(x => x + 10); setB(x => x + 10);
  };
  globalThis.flushed = () => {
    flushSync(() => setA(x => x + 100)); setB(x => x + 100);
  };
  return <span>{a},{b}</span>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });

renders = 0; await act(async () => { globalThis.both(); });
console.log('two updates in one handler ->', renders, 'render:', box.textContent);
renders = 0; await act(async () => { await globalThis.afterAwait(); });
console.log('two updates after an await ->', renders, 'render:', box.textContent);
renders = 0; await act(async () => { globalThis.flushed(); });
console.log('flushSync then an update   ->', renders, 'renders:', box.textContent);

two updates in one handler -> 1 render: 1,1
two updates after an await -> 1 render: 11,11
flushSync then an update   -> 2 renders: 111,111

The middle line is the one that changed in React 18, and that older writing gets wrong. Before automatic batching, only updates inside React event handlers were batched. Updates in a promise callback, a setTimeout or a native event listener each caused their own render. Now everything is batched, everywhere. A component that relied on seeing the in-between state was relying on a bug.

Batching is also why §3.4's rule about updater functions matters. Inside one batch, calling setA(a + 1) twice gives you a + 1, because both calls captured the same a. Calling setA(x => x + 1) twice gives you a + 2, because the second call receives the first one's result.

unstable_batchedUpdates still exists in react-dom for libraries that needed to force batching before React 18. In an application it is dead weight: the behaviour it provided is now the default.

To have in hand before moving on: unstable_batchedUpdates and updater function.

2.10 flushSync, and When Breaking Batching Is Right

flushSync( forces React to render and commit the updates in its callback right away, before it returns. The third line of the previous example shows the cost: two renders and two commits instead of one.

It exists for the cases where you must read the DOM after an update but before the browser paints. Examples: measuring a newly added row so you can scroll to it, focusing an element that only exists after the update, printing a page, or handing a freshly rendered node to a library that is not React. In every one of those cases, the alternative is reading a DOM that has not been written yet.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { flushSync } from 'react-dom';

function List() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(['a']);
  globalThis.addNaive = () => {
    setItems(xs => [...xs, 'x']);
    globalThis.naiveCount = document.querySelectorAll('li').length;
  };
  globalThis.addFlushed = () => {
    flushSync(() => setItems(xs => [...xs, 'y']));
    globalThis.flushedCount = document.querySelectorAll('li').length;
  };
  return <ul>{items.map(i => <li key={i}>{i}</li>)}</ul>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<List />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.addNaive(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.addFlushed(); });
console.log('read after setState :', globalThis.naiveCount, 'items in the DOM');
console.log('read after flushSync:', globalThis.flushedCount, 'items in the DOM');

read after setState : 1 items in the DOM
read after flushSync: 3 items in the DOM

The naive version measured the DOM as it was before its own update: one item, because the second had not been committed yet. The flushSync version saw all three.

Use it for that and nothing else. flushSync takes a subtree out of every scheduling benefit in §12. The update cannot be interrupted, cannot be batched with anything else, and blocks the main thread until it commits. React logs a warning if you call it during a render or an effect, because "commit right now, in the middle of a commit" has no correct meaning.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: flushSync(.

2.11 What the Tree Is Made Of: Fiber

The element tree from §1 is thrown away and rebuilt on every render. The tree React keeps between renders is a different structure. Its name is worth knowing, because it appears in every profile and every stack trace: a fiber.

A fiber is an object React changes over time, one per component instance and one per host element. It holds what an element cannot:

  • the state hooks for that position;
  • the memoised (saved) props from the last render;
  • a reference to the actual DOM node;
  • the list of effects;
  • and pointers to its parent, its first child and its next sibling.

It is the position that §2.5 keeps talking about, made concrete.

Two consequences are worth carrying forward.

  • The fiber tree is a linked list (each node points to the next) rather than a recursive structure. That is what makes the render phase interruptible: React can stop after any fiber, hand control back to the browser, and resume from that pointer later. That ability is the entire foundation of §12.
  • "Component instance" is a meaningful idea in React even though components are functions. The fiber is the instance. It is created on mount and destroyed on unmount, and your state lives on it.

You never touch fibers directly, and any library that does depends on internals that have changed before and will change again. Knowing the word is enough to read a flame graph (a profiler chart of where time went).

2.12 State as a Snapshot

The last idea in this section is the one that makes §3 and §6 manageable, so it is worth stating precisely here and coming back to twice.

State as a snapshot is the name for it. Each time React calls your component, it produces a snapshot: the props, the state and every variable computed from them are fixed for that call, and never change afterwards. The function returns, the values it closed over keep the values they had, and nothing later reaches back to update them. A later render is a different call with different values: a new snapshot, sharing nothing with the old one except the position in the tree.

That is why this prints what it prints:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.click = () => {
    setN(n + 1);
    setN(n + 1);
    setN(n + 1);
    console.log('inside the handler, n is still', n);
  };
  return <span>{n}</span>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.click(); });
console.log('after three setN(n + 1) calls:', box.textContent);

inside the handler, n is still 0
after three setN(n + 1) calls: 1
