Three calls, one increment. Not because React "collapsed" them, but because n was 0 in that snapshot and stayed 0. All three calls said set n to 1. The handler could not see the new value either, for the same reason: n is a const in a function call that has already been given its arguments.

A render is a snapshot is worth saying in exactly those words, because that phrase makes the next two sections manageable. The same fact explains why an event handler that reads state after an await reads an out-of-date value, why an effect's closure sees the props from the render that created it, and why useEffectEvent (§7.7) exists at all. The snapshot model is not an analogy. It is literally how closures work in JavaScript, applied to a function that gets called again and again.

In summary, the vocabulary here is render is a snapshot.

2.13 Double Rendering in Development

One measurement that surprises everyone the first time:

import { StrictMode, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let calls = 0;
function Counted() { calls++; return <i>x</i>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const a = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { a.render(<StrictMode><Counted /></StrictMode>); });
console.log('inside StrictMode :', calls);

calls = 0;
const b = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { b.render(<Counted />); });
console.log('outside StrictMode:', calls);

inside StrictMode : 2
outside StrictMode: 1

<StrictMode> deliberately calls your component twice in development and throws the first result away. It is not a bug and not a performance problem, because it does nothing in a production build. It exists to make impurity visible. A component that counts, changes a module-level array, or writes to a ref during render will produce different output on the two calls, and you will see it immediately, instead of as a timing-dependent bug six months later.

The consequence to take in now is a rule about your own logging: a console.log in a component body appearing twice in development is expected. Adding a useRef guard to stop it is the standard way to break your own app, because the same guard defeats the double effect call that §6.8 relies on to catch missing cleanup. §5 states formally the purity rule that StrictMode is testing.

What This Section Established

An update has three steps. Trigger queues it; the render phase calls your functions and touches no DOM; the commit phase writes the minimum set of changes, then layout effects run, then the browser paints, then passive effects run.

Rendering means React called your function. By default it calls the whole subtree, whether or not props changed — measured: an unrelated state change re-rendered a child with identical props. Setting state to an Object.is-equal value is a real bail-out and calls nothing at all.

Reconciliation matches new to old by type and position, with keys overriding position within a list. Different type at a position throws the subtree away, state included; same type updates it in place. Measured: wrapping a component in <p> instead of <div> reset its counter to zero.

State belongs to a position in the tree, not to your component and not to your source code. Two branches of a ternary rendering into the same slot share state; key is how you say that the identity changed. And with key={index}, prepending an item hands the first item's state to the wrong data.

Updates are batched everywhere since React 18, including after an await. flushSync opts out, at the price of an extra render and commit, and it is the right tool exactly when you must read the DOM before the browser paints.

Each render is a snapshot: props, state and everything derived from them are frozen for that call. Three setN(n + 1) calls in one handler increment by one, and no amount of reading n afterwards will show the new value.

Exercises

1. Predict the mutations. For a component rendering <div className={c}><p>{a}</p><p>{b}</p></div>, write down how many DOM mutations each of these produces and of what kind: changing a; changing c; changing both in one handler; setting a to its current value; and swapping the outer div for a section. Then verify with a MutationObserver.

2. Break state three ways. Write one component whose state resets when you did not want it to, using each of the three mechanisms in this section: a changed parent element type, a changed key, and a conditional that removes it from the tree. Then fix each with the minimal change, and say for each fix whether it preserves state by keeping the position, by keeping the key, or by moving the state elsewhere.

3. The index-key bug, precisely. Take a list of three text inputs keyed by index. Give an exact sequence of user actions — typing and reordering — after which the DOM shows one input's typed text next to another item's label. Then say why switching to a stable key fixes it, in terms of the key-to-old-child map from §2.8.

4. When flushSync is the answer, and when it is not. Write two versions of "add a row and scroll it into view": one that reads scrollHeight straight after setState, one that wraps the update in flushSync. Show the measured difference. Then give one case where flushSync looks necessary but is not, and name what to use instead.

5. Snapshots and batching together. Given const [n, setN] = useState(0) and a handler that runs setN(n + 1); setN(x => x + 1); setN(n + 1);, predict the final value and the number of renders before running it. Then explain the result by writing out the update queue React builds, in order, with what each entry receives as input.

Solution

1. Predicted mutations.

change a            1   characterData on the first <p>'s text node
change c            1   attributes: class on the <div>
change a and c      2   one text, one attribute — in ONE commit, because
                        both setStates are batched into a single render
set a to its value  0   Object.is bail-out: the component is not even called
div -> section      1+  childList on the parent: the whole subtree is
                        removed and rebuilt, so the old <div> and both <p>
                        elements are discarded and new nodes inserted

The last row is the one worth internalising: changing a wrapper's tag is not a cheap edit, it is a remount of everything inside it.

2. Three resets and three fixes.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Input({ id }) {
  const [v, setV] = useState('');
  globalThis['type_' + id] = s => setV(s);
  return <b>[{v || 'empty'}]</b>;
}
function Broken({ mode }) {
  // mode 1: the wrapper's type changes.  mode 2: the key changes.
  // mode 3: the component leaves the tree entirely.
  const [flip, setFlip] = useState(false);
  globalThis.flip = () => setFlip(f => !f);
  if (mode === 1) return flip ? <p><Input id="w" /></p> : <div><Input id="w" /></div>;
  if (mode === 2) return <div><Input key={flip ? 'x' : 'y'} id="w" /></div>;
  return <div>{flip ? null : <Input id="w" />}</div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const mode of [1, 2, 3]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Broken mode={mode} />); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.type_w('typed'); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.flip(); });
  console.log('mode', mode, '->', box.textContent || '(gone)');
}

mode 1 -> [empty]
mode 2 -> [empty]
mode 3 -> (gone)

The fixes: mode 1, keep one wrapper type and change its className instead — the position is preserved. Mode 2, key by the thing whose identity you mean (key={noteId}), not by a toggle — the key is preserved across the flip. Mode 3, hide it with CSS or lift v into Broken — the state is moved somewhere that is not being removed.

3. The index-key sequence.

Render ['alpha','beta','gamma'] with key={index} and a text input beside each label.

  1. Type "mine" into the third input (the one labelled gamma). React stores that state at position 2.
  2. Delete alpha. The array is now ['beta','gamma'], so gamma is at index 1 and there is no index 2.
  3. The DOM now shows beta labelled with the input that used to be beta's — and the input containing "mine" has been unmounted, while gamma's input shows whatever was typed at position 1.

Typing into position 1 first, then deleting alpha, shows the text next to gamma — one item's text under another item's label.

A stable key={item.id} fixes it because the key-to-old-child map in §2.8 is keyed by identity: on the second render React looks up gamma and finds the child that was gamma before, wherever it sat. With index keys the map is keyed by position, and after a deletion every position means a different item.

4. flushSync, used and misused.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { flushSync } from 'react-dom';

function Log() {
  const [lines, setLines] = useState(['1']);
  globalThis.addNaive = () => {
    setLines(l => [...l, 'n']);
    globalThis.naive = document.querySelectorAll('li').length;
  };
  globalThis.addSync = () => {
    flushSync(() => setLines(l => [...l, 's']));
    globalThis.sync = document.querySelectorAll('li').length;
  };
  return <ul>{lines.map((l, i) => <li key={i}>{l}</li>)}</ul>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Log />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.addNaive(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.addSync(); });
console.log('naive read:', globalThis.naive, '| after flushSync:', globalThis.sync);

naive read: 1 | after flushSync: 3

The case where it looks necessary but is not: focusing an element after it appears. flushSync then .focus() works, but so does a ref callback (§7.4) — React calls it the moment the node is attached, inside the same commit, with no extra render. Prefer the ref callback; it expresses "when this node exists" instead of "make the DOM catch up now".

5. The update queue.

queue entry        receives   produces
setN(n + 1)        —          1        (n was 0 in this snapshot: a literal 1)
setN(x => x + 1)   1          2        (updater: gets the queue's running value)
setN(n + 1)        —          1        (a literal 1 again — it overwrites the 2)

final state: 1        renders: 1

The two literal calls do not accumulate, because each was computed from the snapshot's n, which is 0 for the whole handler. The updater is the only one that sees the running result, and the third entry discards it by replacing the value outright. One render, because the whole handler is one batch.

The lesson is §3.4's rule in advance: if the next state depends on the previous one, pass a function. Mixing the two forms in one handler, as here, is how a value silently goes backwards.

SECTION 3

State

State is the part of a React application that changes: data a component remembers between renders, such as a counter's value or the text in a search box. Everything else (props, computed values, the elements a component returns) is worked out from it. So getting the state right decides whether an application is easy to reason about, or one where every new feature needs extra code to keep two values in step.

Two ideas carry the whole section.

  • The first is mechanical, and §2.12 already established it: a render is a snapshot. Within one render, n is a constant, and setting state does not change it.
  • The second is a design principle: state should be minimal and it should make illegal states unrepresentable. Keep as little in state as you can, and shape it so a contradictory combination cannot even be stored.

The first is about how useState behaves. The second is about which useState calls should exist at all, and it is the one that pays off over years.

Almost every state bug is one of three things:

  1. A value in state that should have been computed.
  2. Two values in state that must agree, and do not.
  3. A mutation (changing an object in place) where there should have been a replacement.

Each has a section below, and each has a mechanical fix.

3.1 useState

useState( returns exactly two things: the current value for this render, and a function to set it.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Form() {
  const [name, setName] = useState('');
  const [age, setAge] = useState(0);
  globalThis.setName = setName; globalThis.setAge = setAge;
  return <b>{name || '(none)'}:{age}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Form />); });
console.log('initial :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.setName('Ada'); globalThis.setAge(36); });
console.log('after   :', box.textContent);

initial : (none):0
after   : Ada:36

A state variable is a const. That is not a style choice: it is the snapshot model showing up in the syntax. Within this render the value cannot change. The only way to get a different value is a new render.

The set function is stable: React returns the identical function on every render, which is why it never needs to be in a dependency array. Giving a component multiple state variables is normal, and usually better than one big object. Group two values only when they really change together (§3.8).

State also belongs to each instance separately. Two <Form/> elements have two independent name values, because state is isolated and private to a position in the tree (§2.5). How does React know which useState is which? By the order of the calls (§5.4): the first call in a render gets the first slot on the fiber. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the Rules of Hooks exist.

What to carry forward from this subsection: set function and state is isolated and private.

3.2 The Updater Queue

Queueing a series of state updates is what happens when a handler calls the setter more than once. §2.12 measured that three setN(n + 1) calls in one handler produce one increment. This is the other half: what to write instead, and exactly what React does with it.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.literals = () => { setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1); };
  globalThis.updaters = () => { setN(v => v + 1); setN(v => v + 1); setN(v => v + 1); };
  globalThis.mixed = () => { setN(v => v + 1); setN(n + 10); setN(v => v + 1); };
  globalThis.reset = () => setN(0);
  return <b>{n}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Counter />); });
for (const which of ['literals', 'updaters', 'mixed']) {
  await act(async () => { globalThis.reset(); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis[which](); });
  console.log(which.padEnd(9), '->', box.textContent);
}

literals  -> 1
updaters  -> 3
mixed     -> 11

React keeps a queue for each state variable and works through it in order at the next render. Each entry is one of two kinds:

  • a replacement: a plain value, replacing state outright and discarding whatever came before;
  • or an updater function, also called a functional update, which receives the running result and returns the next one.
literals   [1, 1, 1]                  -> 1   each computed from n=0, each replacing
updaters   [v=>v+1, v=>v+1, v=>v+1]   -> 3   0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3
mixed      [v=>v+1, 10, v=>v+1]       -> 11  0 -> 1, then REPLACED by 10, then 11

The mixed row is why the rule is worth stating with no exceptions: if the next state depends on the previous one, pass a function. Mixing the two forms silently throws work away, and you cannot see the lost update in the code.

Note also that the updater must be pure (it only computes its result). React may call it more than once in development to check that (§5.5), so an updater that logs, changes something or fetches will do so twice.

The terms above, gathered: functional update, queueing a series of state updates and replacing state.

3.3 Lazy Initial State

useState(expensive()) calls expensive() on every render, and throws the result away on all but the first. Passing the function itself instead, useState(expensive), calls it once.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let eager = 0, lazy = 0;
function makeEager() { eager++; return 'E'; }
function makeLazy() { lazy++; return 'L'; }

function Box() {
  const [a] = useState(makeEager());     // called every render
  const [b] = useState(makeLazy);        // called once
  const [, setTick] = useState(0);
  globalThis.rerender = () => setTick(t => t + 1);
  return <b>{a}{b}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Box />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.rerender(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.rerender(); });
console.log('eager calls:', eager, '| lazy calls:', lazy);

eager calls: 3 | lazy calls: 1

Three calls versus one, for three renders. Lazy initialization is the general name for the pattern, and avoiding recreating the initial state is what it buys. That matters when the initial value comes from parsing something, reading localStorage or building a large structure, and the difference is one pair of parentheses. An init function is the name for the function form, and it receives no arguments.

One line each, for reference: lazy initialization, avoiding recreating the initial state and init function.

3.4 Objects and Arrays in State

Updating objects in state and updating arrays in state follow one rule: produce a new value, never edit the old one. §5.2 measured what happens otherwise. The mutation succeeds, the render is skipped, and the UI silently disagrees with the data.

An immutable update builds the next value instead of editing the current one, and the spread syntax to copy an object is the tool you use most:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Profile() {
  const [p, setP] = useState({ name: 'Ada', address: { city: 'London', zip: 'E1' } });
  globalThis.rename = v => setP(prev => ({ ...prev, name: v }));
  globalThis.move = v => setP(prev => ({ ...prev, address: { ...prev.address, city: v } }));
  return <b>{p.name}@{p.address.city},{p.address.zip}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Profile />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.rename('Grace'); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.move('Bristol'); });
console.log(box.textContent);

Grace@Bristol,E1

Updating a nested object needs a spread at every level you change, and only at those levels: zip survived because the inner spread copied it. That is also the real cost of nesting, and it is the main argument in §3.8 for keeping state flat. The deeper your state, the longer your update expressions.

For arrays, the rule becomes a table worth memorising, because the methods that change an array in place are the ones with the shorter names:

avoid (mutates)
use instead
note
push, unshift
[...xs, x], [x, ...xs]
Adding to an array at either end.
pop, shift, splice
filter, slice, toSpliced
Removing from an array. Note slice copies and splice mutates — one letter apart.
xs[i] = v
map, with(i, v)
Replacing items in an array.
sort, reverse
toSorted, toReversed
The pair no lint rule catches (§5.9).

Inserting into an array in the middle is [...xs.slice(0, i), x, ...xs.slice(i)], or xs.toSpliced(i, 0, x).

One trap survives all of this: a copy is shallow. [...items] gives you a new array holding the same objects, so copy[0].done = true still changes the original. To update an object inside an array, map it to a new object:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Todos() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([{ id: 1, text: 'a', done: false },
                                      { id: 2, text: 'b', done: false }]);
  globalThis.toggle = id => setItems(xs =>
    xs.map(x => x.id === id ? { ...x, done: !x.done } : x));   // new object for the one
  return <b>{items.map(x => `${x.text}:${x.done}`).join(' ')}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Todos />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.toggle(2); });
console.log(box.textContent);

a:false b:true

The unchanged item kept its identity (x was returned as it was), which is what lets memo and the compiler skip re-rendering it (§10.5). Mapping every item to a new object would also have worked, but every row would then re-render.

Immer is the library that makes this comfortable to write. useImmer gives you a draft copy that you change freely, and it produces the correctly copied next state behind the scenes. It is worth adopting when nesting really is deep. It is worth resisting when the real problem is that the state should have been flatter.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: updating objects in state, spread syntax to copy an object, updating a nested object, updating arrays in state, adding to an array, removing from an array, replacing items in an array, inserting into an array and immutable update.

3.5 Choosing the State Structure

Choosing the state structure is where your decisions have the most effect. Here are five principles, in the order they pay off.

Group related state
Two values that always change together belong in one object. x and y of a pointer position are one state, not two — two setters can be interleaved and produce a position that never existed.
Avoid contradictions in state
isSending and isSent as two booleans permit true/true, which means nothing. One status of 'typing' | 'sending' | 'sent' cannot.
Avoid redundant state
If you can compute it during render, it is not state. fullName beside first and last is one refactor away from disagreeing with them.
Avoid duplication in state
Storing a selected item object as well as the list stores it twice. Store the selected id and look it up.
Avoid deeply nested state
Normalise. A tree of objects becomes a map from id to object plus arrays of child ids — updates become one level deep instead of five.

There is one legitimate exception to "do not put a prop in state": storing information from previous renders. That means keeping the previous value of a prop next to the current one, so you can detect that it changed. It is §7.1's adjust-during-render pattern, and it is the only form in which a prop belongs in state at all.

Do not mirror props in state is the sixth principle, and the one that catches everyone. const [value, setValue] = useState(props.value) reads the prop once, on mount, and ignores every later change. If you want it to follow the prop, do not copy it. If you deliberately want it to go its own way, name it so (initialValue) so the next reader knows.

The redundancy principle in code:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Bad() {                             // redundant: fullName can drift
  const [first, setFirst] = useState('Ada');
  const [full, setFull] = useState('Ada Lovelace');
  globalThis.badRename = v => setFirst(v);   // forgot to update `full`
  return <b>{first}|{full}</b>;
}
function Good() {                            // derived: cannot drift
  const [first, setFirst] = useState('Ada');
  const [last] = useState('Lovelace');
  const full = `${first} ${last}`;
  globalThis.goodRename = v => setFirst(v);
  return <b>{first}|{full}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const [name, C, fn] of [['bad ', Bad, 'badRename'], ['good', Good, 'goodRename']]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<C />); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis[fn]('Grace'); });
  console.log(name, '->', box.textContent);
}

bad  -> Grace|Ada Lovelace
good -> Grace|Grace Lovelace

The bad version is now showing two different names for the same person, and no tool reported anything: the second state variable is simply out of date. The good version has one source, and cannot be inconsistent.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: storing information from previous renders, group related state, avoid contradictions in state, avoid redundant state, avoid duplication in state, avoid deeply nested state and do not mirror props in state.

3.6 Impossible States

The strongest form of "avoid contradictions" is to choose a shape in which the bad combinations cannot be written down at all. An impossible state is a combination the type allows and the real-world rules forbid.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

// three booleans: 8 combinations, 4 of them meaningless
// one status: 4 states, all of them meaningful
function Form() {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('typing');   // typing | sending | sent | error
  globalThis.send = () => setStatus('sending');
  globalThis.ok = () => setStatus('sent');
  globalThis.fail = () => setStatus('error');
  if (status === 'sent') return <b>Thanks!</b>;
  return <b>[{status}]{status === 'error' ? ' try again' : ''}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Form />); });
const seen = [box.textContent];
for (const step of ['send', 'fail', 'send', 'ok']) {
  await act(async () => { globalThis[step](); });
  seen.push(box.textContent);
}
console.log(seen.join(' -> '));

[typing] -> [sending] -> [error] try again -> [sending] -> Thanks!

Three booleans (isTyping, isSending, isSent) allow eight combinations, and four of them are nonsense: sending and sent, typing and sending. Every render has to guard against them. One status string allows four values, all meaningful, and the render becomes a switch instead of a pile of conditions. A reducer (§4) is the natural next step when the changes between states themselves need names.

Reacting to input with state is the design method that produces these shapes. First identify visual states by listing the ones the design has. Then list what triggers each change from one state to another. Finally choose the smallest representation that tells them apart. That is declarative ui: you describe what each state looks like, and React performs the changes. The opposite is imperative ui, where you write the instructions for getting from one appearance to another, and every new state multiplies the paths.

To have in hand before moving on: declarative UI, imperative UI, identify visual states and reacting to input with state.

3.7 Lifting State Up

When two components need the same state, it moves to their closest common parent. Lifting state up is the whole mechanism for sharing data in React. Its cost is writing the handler in the parent and passing it down. What it buys is a tree with one owner per value.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Panel({ label, isOpen, onShow }) {
  return <span>{label}:{isOpen ? 'open' : <button onClick={onShow}>show</button>} </span>;
}
function Accordion() {
  const [openIndex, setOpenIndex] = useState(0);        // the single source of truth
  return (
    <div>
      <Panel label="a" isOpen={openIndex === 0} onShow={() => setOpenIndex(0)} />
      <Panel label="b" isOpen={openIndex === 1} onShow={() => setOpenIndex(1)} />
    </div>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Accordion />); });
console.log('initial:', box.textContent.trim());
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelectorAll('button')[0].dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log('after  :', box.textContent.trim());

initial: a:open b:show
after  : a:show b:open

Note what the only button on the page was. Panel a renders the word open and no button; panel b renders the button. Clicking it did not "open b" as a separate action. It set openIndex to 1, and that one number both opened b and closed a.

This is the structure paying for itself. "Exactly one panel is open" can be represented only one way, so the two panels cannot both be open and cannot both be closed. If each Panel owned its own isOpen, that rule would have to be kept by the panels coordinating with each other. In other words it would eventually break, on the day someone added a third panel.

A single source of truth is the principle: for each piece of state, exactly one component owns it, and everyone else receives it as a prop. When you find yourself keeping two pieces of state in step, you have found a value that wants lifting.

Going too far the other way is a real failure too. Lifting state higher than it needs to go makes a large subtree re-render for a change only one leaf cares about (§10.3). It also turns every component in between into a courier that just passes values along. Lift to the closest common parent, not to the root.

3.8 Controlled and Uncontrolled

A controlled component takes its value from props and reports changes upward; an uncontrolled input keeps its own value internally, and is only read when needed.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Controlled() {
  const [v, setV] = useState('a');
  globalThis.type = x => setV(x);
  return <><input value={v} onChange={e => setV(e.target.value)} /><b>[{v}]</b></>;
}
function Uncontrolled() {
  return <><input defaultValue="a" /><b>[not tracked]</b></>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const [name, C] of [['controlled  ', Controlled], ['uncontrolled', Uncontrolled]]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<C />); });
  const input = box.querySelector('input');
  input.value = 'typed';                         // simulate the user typing
  console.log(name, '-> DOM:', input.value, '| React shows:', box.querySelector('b').textContent);
}

controlled   -> DOM: typed | React shows: [a]
uncontrolled -> DOM: typed | React shows: [not tracked]

The controlled input's DOM value and React's state now disagree, because setting .value directly skipped the onChange event React listens for. That is exactly what happens when a browser extension, a password manager or a test helper writes to the field. React will overwrite it on the next render. That is the behaviour you want, and the reason controlled inputs are the default recommendation.

Controlled — value + onChange
  • React state is the truth; the DOM follows
  • Validate, format or transform on every keystroke
  • Reset, prefill and disable are all just state
  • Costs a render per keystroke (see §12.6 if that hurts)
Uncontrolled — defaultValue
  • The DOM is the truth; read it on submit
  • No render per keystroke
  • Natural fit with <form action> and FormData (§15)
  • Cannot react to input as it is typed

The one thing to avoid is switching between the two, which React warns about. value={maybeUndefined} makes an input uncontrolled until the value arrives, and controlled afterwards. Use value={v ?? ''}.

The same vocabulary applies beyond inputs. Any component with a value/onChange pair is controlled by its parent. The same component with internal state and a defaultValue is uncontrolled. Offering both is a common library design, and the rule is that a component must pick one per prop, never both.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: controlled component and uncontrolled input.

What This Section Established

useState returns a const for this render and a stable setter. Updates are queued: a plain value replaces, an updater function receives the running result. Measured — three literal calls give 1, three updaters give 3, and mixing them gives 11 because the literal discarded the updater's work.

useState(fn) calls fn once; useState(fn()) calls it every render. Measured: 1 call versus 3 over three renders.

Objects and arrays are replaced, never edited, and a spread copies one level. The mutating array methods have non-mutating twins — toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with — and slice/splice differ by one letter and by everything else.

The five structural principles are group, no contradictions, no redundancy, no duplication, no deep nesting; and do not mirror a prop in state. Measured, a redundant fullName was displaying a different person from its own first after one rename, with nothing reporting it.

Illegal states are best made unrepresentable: three booleans permit eight combinations of which four are nonsense; one status string permits four, all meaningful.

State lifts to the closest common parent so that each value has one owner — measured, an accordion whose "exactly one open" invariant is representable only one way. Lifting further than that costs re-renders and courier props.

Controlled inputs make React the source of truth and cost a render per keystroke; uncontrolled ones read the DOM on submit. Measured, writing to a controlled input's DOM value directly diverges from React's state until the next render corrects it.

Exercises

1. Predict the queue. For a handler running setN(n + 5); setN(v => v * 2); setN(n + 1); setN(v => v + 3) starting from n = 10, write out the queue, the running value after each entry, and the final state. Then verify, and say how many renders occurred.

2. Remove the redundancy. Take a component with items, filteredItems, selectedItem and selectedIndex in state and reduce it to the minimum. For each variable you delete, say which of §3.5's principles applied and what bug it was capable of producing.

3. Make the states impossible. Model a file upload with three booleans and list every meaningless combination. Rewrite it as one discriminated state, and show the render function shrinking. Then add a fourth state ("cancelled") to both versions and compare the size of the change.

4. Shallow copy, deep bug. Write a list of objects in state, update one with [...items] and a direct property assignment, and show that the original was mutated. Then show the screen failing to update, fix it with map, and demonstrate that the untouched items kept their object identity.

5. Lift and unlift. Build two inputs that must always show the same value. Implement it once with two independent states kept in sync by an Effect, and once by lifting. Count the renders for one keystroke in each, and name one state the Effect version can enter that the lifted version cannot.

Solution

1. The queue.

start n = 10, and n is 10 for the whole handler (one snapshot)

entry            receives   produces
setN(n + 5)      —          15      literal: replaces
setN(v => v * 2) 15         30      updater: sees the running value
setN(n + 1)      —          11      literal again: DISCARDS the 30
setN(v => v + 3) 11         14

final state: 14      renders: 1

One render, because the whole handler is one batch (§2.9). The 30 vanished without trace — which is the argument for never mixing the two forms in a single handler.

2. Removing redundancy.

items          KEEP     the source
filteredItems  DELETE   redundant: compute during render from items + query
selectedItem   DELETE   duplication: derive from items.find(i => i.id === selectedId)
selectedIndex  DELETE   duplication: derive, or do not need at all
selectedId     ADD      the minimal representation of "which one is selected"

filteredItems could drift from items after any update that forgot to refilter — the §3.5 measurement. selectedItem is worse: it holds a copy of an item, so editing that item in items leaves the selection showing the old values, and deleting it leaves a selection pointing at an object that no longer exists.

3. Impossible states.

isUploading / isDone / isError            8 combinations
  T/T/F  uploading and done
  T/F/T  uploading and failed
  F/T/T  done and failed
  T/T/T  all three
                                          4 meaningless out of 8

status: 'idle' | 'uploading' | 'done' | 'error'    4 states, 4 meaningful

Adding "cancelled": the boolean version adds a fourth flag, taking the combinations from 8 to 16 and the meaningless ones from 4 to 11, and every existing condition has to be re-examined. The status version adds one string to a union and one branch to the switch — and if the union is typed, the compiler names every place that must handle it.

4. Shallow copy.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const original = [{ id: 1, done: false }, { id: 2, done: false }];
function Bad() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState(original);
  globalThis.badToggle = () => { const copy = [...items]; copy[0].done = true; setItems(copy); };
  return <b>{items.map(i => i.done).join(',')}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Bad />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.badToggle(); });
console.log('screen:', box.textContent, '| the ORIGINAL array now says:',
            original.map(i => i.done).join(','));

screen: true,false | the ORIGINAL array now says: true,false

The screen updated — because [...items] really is a new array, so Object.is saw a change — and the original objects were mutated too, which is the part that bites: any other component holding a reference to that item now sees the change without having re-rendered, and any memo comparing it by identity concludes nothing happened.

The map version returns the untouched items by reference, so items[1] is the identical object across renders and a memo'd row for it does not re-render.

5. Lift and unlift.

two states + a syncing Effect   2 renders per keystroke
                                (one for the typed input, one for the Effect's setState)
lifted to the parent            1 render per keystroke

The Effect version can enter a state the lifted version cannot: momentarily disagreeing. Between the commit that set input A and the Effect that copies it to input B, there is a painted frame in which the two show different values. With one lifted state there is one value and no such frame, because there is nothing to synchronise.

SECTION 4

Reducers and Context

§3 left two problems open.

  • A component with six pieces of state, and ten handlers that update them in different combinations, is hard to read and harder to test, even when every piece on its own is minimal.
  • A value needed by a component eight levels down has to be passed through eight components that do not use it.

Reducers solve the first. A reducer is one function, outside the component, that holds the how of every state change, so the component only says what happened. Context solves the second. You publish a value at one point in the tree and read it anywhere below, with no component in between taking part.

They are independent tools. They are covered together because their combination is the standard shape for application-wide state in React: a reducer holding the logic, and a context handing out the state and the dispatch function (the function components call to report what happened). §4.8 builds it.

4.1 useReducer

useReducer( takes a reducer function and an initial state, and returns the current state plus dispatch(, the function you call to report that something happened.

import { useReducer, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function tasksReducer(tasks, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added':   return [...tasks, { id: action.id, text: action.text, done: false }];
    case 'toggled': return tasks.map(t => t.id === action.id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t);
    case 'deleted': return tasks.filter(t => t.id !== action.id);
    default: throw new Error('unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}

function Tasks() {
  const [tasks, dispatch] = useReducer(tasksReducer, [{ id: 1, text: 'a', done: false }]);
  globalThis.dispatch = dispatch;
  return <b>{tasks.map(t => `${t.text}${t.done ? '✓' : ''}`).join(' ') || '(empty)'}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Tasks />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.dispatch({ type: 'added', id: 2, text: 'b' }); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.dispatch({ type: 'toggled', id: 1 }); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.dispatch({ type: 'deleted', id: 2 }); });
console.log(box.textContent);

a✓

Three dispatches, three changes of state, and the component contains none of the logic. The reducer is a plain function of (state, action) => newState. It uses no React, no hooks, and no props captured from the component. So you can unit-test it just by calling it, and read it without reading the component.

An action object usually has a type, plus whatever data that type needs. An action type should describe what the user did, not what the state should become: 'added', 'changed_text', 'reordered', not 'setTasks'. That distinction is the whole benefit of the pattern.

  • A dispatch of { type: 'reordered', from, to } records an interaction, so a reviewer can read the component and know what the user can do.
  • A dispatch of { type: 'setTasks', tasks } has moved the logic back into the component, and kept only the ceremony.

dispatch is stable across renders, like a state setter, so it never belongs in a dependency array. useReducer also takes an optional third argument: an initialiser function, called with the second argument. It is the useState(fn) trick from §3.3, with the initial value passed in.

In summary, the vocabulary here is useReducer(, reducer function, dispatch( and action object.

4.2 Writing Reducers Well

Four properties, and each one is load-bearing.

Pure
No fetching, no timers, no Math.random(), no mutation of the state argument. React may call it twice in development to check (§5.5), and a reducer that generates an id will generate two.
Total
Every action type is handled, and an unknown one throws rather than silently returning the old state. A silent default is how a typo in an action type becomes a bug nobody can find.
One action per interaction
If a single click needs three dispatches, the reducer is missing an action. Name the interaction and handle it in one case, so the intermediate states never exist.
Returns new objects
Same rule as §3.4, and the same measurement behind it: mutating the state argument produces a silently skipped render.

Because the reducer is a plain function, testing it needs no renderer:

function counter(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'inc': return { n: state.n + 1 };
    case 'add': return { n: state.n + action.by };
    case 'reset': return { n: 0 };
    default: throw new Error('unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(counter({ n: 0 }, { type: 'inc' })));
console.log(JSON.stringify(counter({ n: 5 }, { type: 'add', by: 3 })));
const before = { n: 9 };
counter(before, { type: 'reset' });
console.log('argument untouched:', JSON.stringify(before));
try { counter({ n: 0 }, { type: 'typo' }); } catch (e) { console.log('caught:', e.message); }

{"n":1}
{"n":8}
argument untouched: {"n":9}
caught: unknown action: typo

Four assertions about the state machine (the set of states and the moves between them), with no DOM, no act and no component. That testability is a real argument for reducers whenever the state changes are not trivial, and it is the argument that still holds when the component is rewritten.

Writing concise reducers with Immer is the more comfortable option. useImmerReducer gives the reducer a draft copy that it may change directly, and produces the copied result. It is worth it for deeply nested state. It is not a substitute for flattening state that should have been flat.

4.3 useState or useReducer

Comparing usestate and usereducer honestly:

Prefer useState
  • One or two independent values
  • Transitions that are obvious from the setter call
  • Less code, and nothing to name
Prefer useReducer
  • Several values that change together
  • The next state depends on the previous one in non-trivial ways
  • You want the transitions testable, or readable in one place
  • Debugging: every change has a name and a payload

The sign that a component wants a reducer is not the number of useState calls. It is handlers that set several pieces of state together: three setters in one function means three ways to get it wrong, and one dispatch means none. Another sign is a component whose bugs look like "these two values disagreed", which is §3.5's contradiction principle showing up late.

Converting is mechanical and can be undone, so it is a cheap experiment rather than a big architectural commitment.

What to carry forward from this subsection: comparing useState and useReducer.

4.4 createContext and useContext

createContext( makes a context object with a default value; useContext( reads the value from the nearest provider (the component above that supplies it).

import { createContext, useContext, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const ThemeContext = createContext('light');       // the default value

function Button() {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <b>[{theme}]</b>;
}
function Toolbar() { return <div><Button /></div>; }   // passes nothing down

function App() {
  return <>
    <Toolbar />
    <ThemeContext value="dark"><Toolbar /></ThemeContext>
    <ThemeContext value="dark"><ThemeContext value="high-contrast"><Toolbar /></ThemeContext></ThemeContext>
  </>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log(box.textContent);

[light][dark][high-contrast]

Three readings of the same context in the same tree. The first found no provider, and got the default context value. That is the argument to createContext: the value used when nothing above provides one. It is also the reason a component that uses context can still be rendered on its own and in a test.

The second found one: a context provider. The third found two, one inside the other, and took the nearest. That is the rule: useContext searches upward and stops at the first provider it meets. It is what makes overriding context for part of the tree work. Wrap a subtree in a new provider, and everything inside it sees the new value.

Note the syntax. In React 19 the context provider is the context object: <ThemeContext value="dark">. The older <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark"> still works but is deprecated. The context consumer component, SomeContext.Consumer, is the render-prop form from before hooks existed. It also still exists, and should not be used in new code.

Context passes through intermediate components invisibly: Toolbar neither received nor passed on anything. Passing data deeply without the components in between taking part is the whole feature. The problem it removes has a name, prop drilling: passing a value down through components that do not use it. That is the point of context, and it is also the cost, which §4.7 is about.

The terms above, gathered: createContext(, useContext(, context consumer, default context value, prop drilling, passing data deeply, overriding context for part of the tree and context passes through intermediate components.

4.5 use(context)

use(context) reads a context just as useContext does, with one difference that matters: it may be called conditionally, inside an if.

import { createContext, use, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

function Label({ themed }) {
  if (!themed) return <b>plain</b>;      // early return BEFORE reading the context
  const theme = use(ThemeContext);       // legal — `use` is not a hook
  return <b>{theme}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => {
  root.render(<ThemeContext value="dark"><Label themed={false} /><Label themed={true} /></ThemeContext>);
});
console.log(box.textContent);

plaindark

The same code with useContext after the early return breaks the Rules of Hooks and produces the hook-order error from §5.4. use is exempt because it holds no slot on the fiber: it only reads a value that is already there. That is also why it may appear in a loop.

That is a small convenience for context, and a large one for promises (§13.8). Do not read it as general permission to break the rules: every other hook still obeys them.

4.6 Before You Use Context

Context is easy to overuse, and the failure is not subtle. An application where every value is in context is an application where you cannot see how data flows at all.

Try these first.

Pass props. Passing a value through two or three components is not a problem worth solving. If it reads as noise, that is often a sign the components are the wrong shape.

Providing context from the same component that reads it is also legal, and is the usual shape for a theme toggle. The provider component holds the state, publishes it, and reads it for its own button.

Pass elements as children. This is the most under-used alternative (§1.10). If Layout needs to render a <Sidebar user={user} />, let whoever calls Layout build that element and pass it as children. The value never enters Layout at all, so there is nothing to pass down.

Lift state to the closest common parent (§3.7), instead of to the root with a context.

The use cases for context that earn their place are values that are truly ambient, meaning present everywhere: a theme, a locale, the current user, a routing location, a set of feature flags, a dispatch function for application-wide state. What they have in common is that almost any component might want them, and almost none of them care where they came from.

One line each, for reference: use cases for context and providing context from the same component.

4.7 Optimizing Context Re-renders

The cost of context is precise and worth measuring: every consumer re-renders when the provider's value changes, whether or not that consumer uses the part that changed.

import { createContext, useContext, useState, useMemo, memo, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const Ctx = createContext(null);
let reads = 0;
// memo() so that the ordinary parent-cascade path is closed and only the
// context channel is left — otherwise §2.2's default re-render hides the effect.
const Consumer = memo(function Consumer() { useContext(Ctx); reads++; return <b>.</b>; });

function App({ memoise }) {
  const [n] = useState(0);
  const [other, setOther] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bumpOther = () => setOther(v => v + 1);
  const value = memoise ? useMemo(() => ({ n }), [n]) : { n };   // fresh object vs stable
  return <Ctx value={value}><Consumer /><i>{other}</i></Ctx>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const memoise of [false, true]) {
  const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
  await act(async () => { root.render(<App memoise={memoise} />); });
  reads = 0;
  await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpOther(); });
  console.log(memoise ? 'memoised value :' : 'fresh object   :', reads, 'consumer render(s)');
}

fresh object   : 1 consumer render(s)
memoised value : 0 consumer render(s)

An unrelated state change re-rendered the consumer, even though it was wrapped in memo and received no props at all. The provider re-rendered, and { n } is a new object every time, so Object.is reported a change and every consumer was notified through the context. Memoising the value (keeping the same object while n is unchanged) removed it entirely.

The memo in that example is doing something specific and it is worth being precise about it. Without it, the consumer re-renders anyway by the ordinary route: its parent re-rendered, and §2.2 measured that React re-renders the whole subtree by default. The experiment would then report the same number both ways and prove nothing. memo closes that route, leaving only the context subscription, so the measurement isolates it.

In practice: memo does protect a consumer from its parent's re-renders, and it does not protect it from a change in the context value. Those are two different channels, and only the second is fixed at the provider.

Three techniques, in order of how often they are the right answer:

Memoise the value. Use useMemo(() => ({ … }), [deps]), as above, or turn on the React Compiler and stop thinking about it (§11.3 measured exactly this shape being cached automatically).

Split the context. A StateContext and a DispatchContext are the standard pair, because dispatch never changes. Components that only dispatch then never re-render on a state change at all. This is a structural fix, and it is better than memoising, because it removes the dependency instead of caching around it.

Split by what changes together. One context per concern beats one giant AppContext. A theme change should not re-render everything that reads the current user.

What does not work on its own is memo on the consumer, for the reason the measurement above isolates. memo compares props, a context read is not a prop, and a changed context value re-renders a memoised consumer exactly as it re-renders one without memo. So memo fixes the channel where a parent's re-render cascades down, and a stable value fixes the context channel. A real application usually wants both.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: React Compiler.

4.8 Scaling Up: a Reducer Behind a Context

Here is the standard shape for application state, assembled from the two halves. Scaling up with reducer and context puts the state in one context, the dispatch in another, and the reducer outside the component entirely.

import { createContext, useContext, useReducer, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const TasksContext = createContext(null);
const DispatchContext = createContext(null);

function reducer(tasks, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added':   return [...tasks, { id: action.id, text: action.text }];
    case 'deleted': return tasks.filter(t => t.id !== action.id);
    default: throw new Error('unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}

function TasksProvider({ children }) {
  const [tasks, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, []);
  return (
    <TasksContext value={tasks}>
      <DispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</DispatchContext>
    </TasksContext>
  );
}
// the two custom hooks that make this an API rather than a pair of contexts
function useTasks() { return useContext(TasksContext); }
function useDispatch() { return useContext(DispatchContext); }

let listRenders = 0, adderRenders = 0;
function List() { listRenders++; return <b>{useTasks().map(t => t.text).join(',') || '(none)'}</b>; }
function Adder() {
  adderRenders++;
  const dispatch = useDispatch();
  globalThis.add = (id, text) => dispatch({ type: 'added', id, text });
  return <i>+</i>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<TasksProvider><List /><Adder /></TasksProvider>); });
listRenders = adderRenders = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.add(1, 'write'); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.add(2, 'test'); });
console.log(box.textContent);
console.log('after two adds -> List rendered', listRenders, '| Adder rendered', adderRenders);

write,test+
after two adds -> List rendered 2 | Adder rendered 0

Adder did not re-render at all: not once, across two state changes that re-rendered its own provider twice. That is the whole payoff of this shape, and it comes from two things working together.

The dispatch context never changes. dispatch is stable, so DispatchContext's value is identical on every render, and nothing subscribed to it is ever notified.

children came from above. <TasksProvider><List /><Adder /></TasksProvider> was written in the root's render, so those two elements were created there, not inside TasksProvider. When TasksProvider re-renders because its reducer state changed, it returns the same children object it was given: the same elements, equal by reference. React's reconciler skips them entirely (§2.4). Only List, which is subscribed to the context that actually changed, re-rendered.

That is the trick worth carrying beyond this example. A provider that renders {children} is cheap no matter how often its own state changes, because someone else built the subtree. A provider that writes its subtree inline has no such protection, and every state change re-renders all of it.

The two custom hooks are not decoration. They do three jobs:

  • they give the consumer one name to import instead of two context objects;
  • they are the place to throw a helpful error when a provider is missing;
  • and they let the internals (two contexts, a reducer, perhaps a store later) change without touching a single consumer.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: scaling up with reducer and context.

What This Section Established

useReducer moves state transitions into a plain (state, action) => newState function outside the component. Actions name what the user did, not what the state should become, and a reducer is testable by calling it — measured, four assertions with no DOM, no act and no component.

Reducers must be pure, total (an unknown action throws), and one-action-per-interaction. dispatch is stable and never belongs in a dependency array.

createContext gives a default used when there is no provider, and useContext takes the nearest one — measured, [light][dark][high-contrast] from three readings in one tree. In React 19 the context object is the provider; .Provider is deprecated and .Consumer is legacy.

use(context) reads a context conditionally, which useContext cannot, because use holds no slot on the fiber.

Every consumer re-renders when the provider's value changes — measured, an unrelated state change re-rendered both consumers because the value was a fresh object literal, and memoising it brought that to zero. memo on the consumer does not help, because a context read is not a prop. Split state from dispatch, split by concern, and let children come from above.

Exercises

1. Convert both ways. Take a component with four useState calls and three handlers that each set two of them, convert it to a reducer, then convert it back. Count the lines and the number of places a bug could put two values out of step, in each version.

2. Test the machine. Write a reducer for a multi-step form with back, next, submit and reset, then write assertions for it with no renderer at all — including one that proves the state argument was not mutated and one that proves an unknown action throws.

3. Measure the context cost. Build a provider with two consumers and an unrelated piece of state. Record consumer renders for an unrelated change with a fresh object value, with a memoised value, and with the state and dispatch split into two contexts. Explain why memo on a consumer changes none of the three.

4. Nearest provider. Nest three providers of the same context with different values and read it at four depths, including above all of them. Predict every reading before running it, then say what the topmost one demonstrates about testability.

5. Design the actions. For a to-do list, write two action vocabularies: one of setTasks-style actions and one of interaction-named actions. Implement the same three features with each and say which reducer you could hand to someone who has never seen the component.

Solution

1. Both directions.

The reducer version is typically a few lines longer, and the count that matters is the second one:

useState version    3 handlers x 2 setters = 6 update sites
                    every one is a place two values can get out of step
reducer version     3 cases, each returning one complete next state
                    0 places, because a case cannot return half a state

Converting back is worth doing once, because it makes the trade concrete: the useState version is genuinely shorter and genuinely easier to break, and neither of those is an opinion.

2. Testing the machine.

function wizard(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'next':   return { ...state, step: Math.min(state.step + 1, 2) };
    case 'back':   return { ...state, step: Math.max(state.step - 1, 0) };
    case 'submit': return { ...state, submitted: true };
    case 'reset':  return { step: 0, submitted: false };
    default: throw new Error('unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}

const start = { step: 0, submitted: false };
console.log('next from 0 :', wizard(start, { type: 'next' }).step);
console.log('back from 0 :', wizard(start, { type: 'back' }).step);
console.log('clamped at 2:', wizard({ step: 2, submitted: false }, { type: 'next' }).step);
console.log('start untouched:', JSON.stringify(start));
try { wizard(start, { type: 'skip' }); } catch (e) { console.log('threw:', e.message); }

next from 0 : 1
back from 0 : 0
clamped at 2: 2
start untouched: {"step":0,"submitted":false}
threw: unknown action: skip

3. The context cost.

fresh object literal        2 consumer renders
useMemo'd value             0
split state / dispatch      0 for the dispatch-only consumer;
                            the state consumer still renders when state changes,
                            which is correct — it reads the thing that changed

memo on a consumer changes none of them because it compares props, and these consumers receive no props. The context subscription is a separate channel that memo does not sit on, so a context change re-renders a memoised consumer exactly as it re-renders an unmemoised one.

4. Nearest provider. Reading above all three yields the createContext default; the three nested readings each yield their nearest enclosing value.

The topmost reading is the testability argument: a component that reads context works with no provider at all, so a unit test can render it directly and get a sensible value. Choosing a useful default — rather than null — is what makes that true, and choosing null deliberately plus a custom hook that throws is the other defensible option, because it converts "missing provider" from a silent wrong value into a named error.

5. Two vocabularies.

setTasks style                    interaction style
{type:'setTasks', tasks}          {type:'added', id, text}
{type:'setTasks', tasks}          {type:'toggled', id}
{type:'setTasks', tasks}          {type:'reordered', from, to}

The first reducer is one line — return action.tasks — and tells a reader nothing at all: the logic is still in three separate places in the component, and the reducer's test suite would be a single trivial assertion.

The second is the one you could hand over. It documents the complete list of things that can happen to a task list, every transition is testable in isolation, and a log of dispatched actions is a readable record of a session — which is what makes it debuggable in a way the first never is.

SECTION 5

The Rules of React and the Lints

React has a short list of rules. Unusually for a library, breaking them does not produce an error. It produces a program that works on your machine, in development, at the speed you happen to type, and then fails somewhere else, now and then, in a way you cannot reproduce.

That is why this is a whole section rather than a footnote. Most libraries enforce their limits by throwing exceptions. React's rules are different: they are the preconditions of its optimisations, the things React assumes so it can make your app fast. React assumes your components are pure (they compute their output and change nothing else). That lets it call them twice, call them and throw the result away, call them in a different order than you wrote, or skip calling them entirely (§2, §11, §12). Every one of those is legitimate under the rules, and produces nonsense when a rule is broken.

So the rules are not style. They are the contract that makes everything from §10 onward safe. Three independent tools check them, three nets over the same set of mistakes: eslint-plugin-react-hooks (a lint plugin, which flags problems as you write code), <StrictMode>, and the compiler's refusal to optimise code that breaks them (§11.6).

This section states the rules, shows each one failing, and then goes through the seventeen lint rules with the message each one actually prints. Every message below was produced by running eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 on the code above it.

5.1 Components and Hooks Must Be Pure

A pure function returns the same output for the same input, and does nothing anyone else can notice along the way. For a React component, "the same input" means props, state and context, and "the same output" means the element tree it returns.

Components and hooks must be pure is the top-level rule. It breaks down into three smaller rules that are easier to check.

Idempotent
Components must be idempotent: rendering twice with the same inputs produces the same output. Rules out Date.now(), Math.random() and reading a mutable global during render.
No side effects in render
Side effects must run outside of render: no network calls, no DOM writes, no logging to a service, no setState, no writing a ref. Those belong in event handlers and effects.
Nothing you did not make
Props, state, hook arguments, hook return values and anything already passed to JSX are all read-only. You may freely mutate objects you created during this render and have not shared.

The third is the one people find surprising, so it is worth stating positively: local mutation is fine. Building an array with push inside your component and then rendering it breaks nothing. Nobody else can see that array, and it is thrown away when the render ends. What is forbidden is changing something that outlives the render, or that someone else can see.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Report({ rows }) {
  const lines = [];                       // created here: mine to mutate
  for (const r of rows) if (r.n > 1) lines.push(`${r.name}=${r.n}`);
  return <p>{lines.join(', ')}</p>;
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Report rows={[{ name: 'a', n: 1 }, { name: 'b', n: 3 }]} />));

<p>b=3</p>

That is pure. Replacing lines with an array defined at module level, or writing rows.push(...), is not. The first keeps growing across renders, and the second changes a prop.

To have in hand before moving on: components must be idempotent, side effects must run outside of render and local mutation.

5.2 Props and State Are Immutable

React does not merely ask. In the development build, elements and their props are frozen (§1.4), so a mutation throws an error in strict mode and silently does nothing otherwise.

State is read-only in the same sense. It is the stronger case, because changing it in place is silently ineffective, not just impolite:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Bad() {
  const [item, setItem] = useState({ n: 0 });
  globalThis.mutate = () => { item.n += 1; setItem(item); };      // WRONG
  globalThis.replace = () => setItem(prev => ({ n: prev.n + 1 })); // right
  return <b>{item.n}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Bad />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.mutate(); });
console.log('after mutating in place:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.replace(); });
console.log('after replacing        :', box.textContent);

after mutating in place: 0
after replacing        : 2

The mutation did happen: item.n really became 1. But the screen did not change. setItem(item) passed the same object reference, so React's Object.is bail-out (§2.2) concluded that nothing had changed. The 2 on the second line is the proof: the replacement added one to a value that was already 1.

This is the most common React bug that produces no error of any kind. The state is wrong and the render is skipped. Then the next unrelated re-render shows the changed value as though it had worked, which makes the bug look intermittent.

Values are immutable after being passed to jsx takes the same rule one step further. Once an object has gone into an element's props, changing it can produce a UI that disagrees with itself, because React may already have kept it for a comparison. Build the object, pass it, and forget it.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: state is read-only and values are immutable after being passed to JSX.

5.3 React Calls Components and Hooks

React calls components and hooks; you do not. Each half of that sentence has a rule attached.

Never call a component function directly. What happens when you do is subtler than an error:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Inner() { const [n] = useState(42); return <b>{n}</b>; }
function Wrong() { return Inner(); }        // called, not rendered

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Wrong />); });
console.log('rendered anyway:', box.innerHTML);

rendered anyway: <b>42</b>

It worked. That is the problem. Inner() ran as an ordinary function call, so its useState was recorded on Wrong's fiber. Inner has no fiber of its own. It has no position in the render tree, no independent state, no entry in DevTools, and no way to be skipped by memo on its own. Add a second Inner() call and the two share nothing but confusion. Wrap one in a condition and you have broken the hook order for Wrong.

<Inner /> creates an element (§1.4). React sees it, gives it a position, and gives it state. Inner() gives you the return value and none of that.

Do not pass hooks around as values, and do not dynamically use hooks. A hook must be called by its name, in a fixed place in the code that a linter can see. Passing useState as an argument, storing hooks in an object and choosing one while the program runs, or building a hook on the fly all defeat the analysis that both the linter and the compiler depend on. Nothing at runtime makes it work.

In summary, the vocabulary here is never call a component function directly, do not pass hooks around and do not dynamically use hooks.

5.4 The Rules of Hooks

Two rules, and one mechanism that explains both.

Only call hooks at the top level. Not inside a condition, a loop, a nested function, a try/catch, or after an early return.

Only call hooks from react functions. That means from a component, or from another hook. Not from an event handler, a class, or a plain utility function.

The reason is that React stores a component's hooks as an ordered list on its fiber (§2.11). No names are involved. The first useState call in a render is matched to the first slot, the second to the second, and so on. Call them in a different order and every slot is off by one.

Watch it happen:

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Cond({ on }) {
  const [a] = useState('a');
  if (on) { useEffect(() => {}); }     // WRONG: conditional hook
  const [b] = useState('b');
  return <b>{a}{b}</b>;
}
function App() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  globalThis.setOn = setOn;
  return <Cond on={on} />;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log('before:', box.textContent);
try { await act(async () => { globalThis.setOn(true); }); }
catch (e) { console.log('after :', e.message.split('\n')[0]); }

before: ab
after : Rendered more hooks than during the previous render.

Along with that error, React prints a table naming the exact slot that changed:

React has detected a change in the order of Hooks called by Cond. …

   Previous render            Next render
   ------------------------------------------------------
1. useState                   useState
2. useState                   useEffect
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Slot 2 held a useState and now holds a useEffect. This is one of React's better error messages, and it is worth recognising, because the fix always has the same shape: hoist the hook above the branch and put the condition inside it. useEffect(() => { if (!on) return; … }, [on]) calls the hook every time and only does its work conditionally, which is what you meant.

The same reasoning is why an early return must come after every hook, and why a hook inside a try block is refused: an exception could skip the rest of the list.

What to carry forward from this subsection: useEffect(, only call hooks at the top level and only call hooks from React functions.

5.5 StrictMode: the Runtime Check

<StrictMode> is React's own test for these rules. In development, and only in development, it deliberately does things twice:

Double rendering
Detecting impure calculations: it calls each component body twice and discards the first result (§2.13, measured: 2 calls versus 1). A body that counts, mutates or logs shows it immediately.
Double effects
Effects re-run in development: setup, then cleanup, then setup again on mount. An effect whose cleanup does not fully undo its setup produces a duplicate subscription you can see.
Double ref callbacks
Attaches, detaches, attaches. Catches a ref callback that registers something and never unregisters it.
Deprecation warnings
Surfaces legacy APIs that will be removed.

Everyone is tempted to stop the double call with a useRef guard, so the console stops repeating itself. Doing that switches off the check that catches the missing cleanup in §6.8, which is the most valuable thing StrictMode does. And it switches it off silently, for the whole component, for good.

It costs nothing in production: <StrictMode> is removed from the production build. Wrap the root in it and leave it there.

The terms above, gathered: detecting impure calculations and effects re-run in development.

5.6 The Lint Plugin

eslint-plugin-react-hooks is the static half: it checks your code without running it. Version 7 is a much bigger tool than earlier ones. It ships 29 rules, and its recommended-latest preset turns on 17 of them. Most of them come from the React Compiler's own analysis, reported as lint messages. So you get the compiler's verdict without adopting the compiler.

Here is the flat-config setup (the newer ESLint configuration format), which is where the first ten minutes usually go:

// eslint.config.mjs
import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks';

export default [
  reactHooks.configs.flat['recommended-latest'],
  { files: ['**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}'],
    languageOptions: { ecmaVersion: 2024, sourceType: 'module',
                       parserOptions: { ecmaFeatures: { jsx: true } } } },
];

Note configs.flat[…] and not configs[…]. Both exist, and they are different objects. reactHooks.configs['recommended-latest'] is the old eslintrc shape, whose plugins is an array of strings. Passing it to ESLint 10 fails with "A config object has a plugins key defined as an array of strings… Flat config requires plugins to be an object". That error points to ESLint's migration guide rather than to the plugin, which sends people down the wrong path.

5.7 The Seventeen Rules, and What They Print

Every message below is the real one, produced by running the plugin.

import { useState, useEffect, useMemo, useRef, use } from 'react';

export function Clock({ on, items, promise, id }) {
  if (on) { const [t] = useState(0); return <p>{t}</p>; }   // rules-of-hooks
  const now = Date.now();                                   // purity
  const ref = useRef(null);
  ref.current = now;                                        // refs
  useEffect(() => { console.log(id); }, []);                // exhaustive-deps
  useMemo(() => { items.forEach(i => i); }, [items]);       // void-use-memo
  return <p>{now}</p>;
}
export function Outer(props) {
  props.title = 'mutated';                                  // immutability
  function Inner() { return <b>{props.title}</b>; }         // static-components
  return <Inner />;
}
export function Guarded({ promise }) {
  try { return <b>{use(promise)}</b>; } catch { return <i>err</i>; }  // error-boundaries
}
export function Eff() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => { setN(1); }, []);                        // set-state-in-effect
  return <b>{n}</b>;
}
export function Render() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  setN(n + 1);                                              // set-state-in-render
  return <b>{n}</b>;
}
let outside = 0;
export function Global() { outside += 1; return <b>{outside}</b>; }  // globals

The diagnostics, trimmed to their first line:

react-hooks/rules-of-hooks
                       React Hook "useState" is called conditionally. React Hooks must be
                       called in the exact same order in every component render.
react-hooks/purity     Cannot call impure function during render
                       `Date.now` is an impure function.
react-hooks/refs       Cannot access refs during render
react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
                       React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'id'.
                       Either include it or remove the dependency array
react-hooks/void-use-memo
                       useMemo() callbacks must return a value
react-hooks/immutability
                       This value cannot be modified
react-hooks/static-components
                       Cannot create components during render
react-hooks/error-boundaries
                       Avoid constructing JSX within try/catch
react-hooks/set-state-in-effect
                       Calling setState synchronously within an effect can trigger
                       cascading renders
react-hooks/set-state-in-render
                       Cannot call setState during render
react-hooks/globals    Cannot reassign variables declared outside of the component/hook

Each of those maps to a rule already stated above, and that is the point: the plugin is not a separate set of opinions, it is §5.1–§5.4 made checkable. The remaining five in the preset are narrower:

  • react-hooks/config and react-hooks/gating check compiler options (§11.5, §11.8);
  • react-hooks/incompatible-library reports libraries whose API cannot be memoised safely;
  • react-hooks/preserve-manual-memoization reports a useMemo the compiler cannot reproduce (§11.11);
  • react-hooks/unsupported-syntax reports code the compiler cannot analyse;
  • and react-hooks/use-memo, which is not the same as react-hooks/void-use-memo, reports a useMemo used where an Effect was meant.

Two rules are worth knowing beyond their names.

error-boundaries is the least obvious. try { return <b>{use(promise)}</b>; } catch {} looks like careful error handling, and is not.
