A suspending component (one waiting for data) throws a promise, not an error, so the catch swallows the suspension and breaks Suspense entirely. Errors during render belong to error boundaries (§14), which are a different mechanism at a different level.

set-state-in-effect is the one that catches the most existing code. Calling setState directly in an effect means every mount renders twice. It is nearly always a sign of derived state that should have been computed during render instead (§7.2).

One line each, for reference: react-hooks/rules-of-hooks, react-hooks/static-components, react-hooks/unsupported-syntax, react-hooks/incompatible-library, react-hooks/globals, react-hooks/config, react-hooks/error-boundaries, react-hooks/use-memo, react-hooks/preserve-manual-memoization, react-hooks/purity, react-hooks/immutability, react-hooks/refs, react-hooks/set-state-in-effect, react-hooks/set-state-in-render and react-hooks/gating.

5.8 The Docs and the Plugin Disagree

Worth checking rather than trusting, because they do not match.

The React documentation lists seventeen recommended rules. The installed plugin's recommended-latest also turns on seventeen, and it is not the same seventeen.

import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks';

const preset = Object.keys(reactHooks.configs['recommended-latest'].rules)
  .map(r => r.replace('react-hooks/', '')).sort();
const documented = ['exhaustive-deps', 'rules-of-hooks', 'component-hook-factories', 'config',
  'error-boundaries', 'gating', 'globals', 'immutability', 'incompatible-library',
  'preserve-manual-memoization', 'purity', 'refs', 'set-state-in-effect',
  'set-state-in-render', 'static-components', 'unsupported-syntax', 'use-memo'].sort();

console.log('rules shipped by the plugin :', Object.keys(reactHooks.rules).length);
console.log('enabled by recommended-latest:', preset.length);
console.log('in the preset, not documented:', preset.filter(r => !documented.includes(r)));
console.log('documented, not in the preset:', documented.filter(r => !preset.includes(r)));

rules shipped by the plugin : 29
enabled by recommended-latest: 17
in the preset, not documented: [ 'void-use-memo' ]
documented, not in the preset: [ 'component-hook-factories' ]

void-use-memo is turned on, and is not on the documentation page at all. It is the rule that produced "useMemo() callbacks must return a value" above. component-hook-factories is documented as recommended but is not turned on, although it exists and you can switch it on by hand.

Neither gap is a crisis; the point is the habit. Read the preset from the installed package rather than from a page, in four lines, at the start of any project. The same four lines show you the twelve rules outside the preset, several of which are worth turning on deliberately.

5.9 What the Tools Miss

Three safety nets, and a hole that goes through all three. Measured on this machine, with the full recommended preset turned on and the compiler running:

// reported by react-hooks/immutability: "This value cannot be modified"
function Caught(props) { props.title = 'x'; return <b>{props.title}</b>; }

// reported by NOTHING — no lint finding, and the compiler compiles it
function Silent({ items }) { items.sort(); return <b>{items[0]}</b>; }

Property assignment on a prop is analysed. A method call that changes an array in place (sort, push, splice, reverse) on a destructured array prop is not caught by any of the seventeen rules. The React Compiler produces optimised code for it without complaint (§11.13).

This matters more than a curiosity, because items.sort() is the most common way a prop actually gets changed in real code. Someone wants a sorted list, sort is right there, and it sorts in place. The array belongs to the parent, so the parent's state is now silently reordered, and the parent will not re-render because nothing was set.

The habit that closes this hole costs a few characters: [...items].sort(), or items.toSorted() for the same thing in one call. toReversed, toSpliced and with are the forms of the other three that do not change the original.

Two more limits, stated plainly.

  • exhaustive-deps is a warning, not an error, in the recommended preset. There are legitimate cases where the array should not list everything, and making it an error in a large codebase produces hundreds of failures at once. Treat it as an error in new code, and fix the cause rather than silencing it (§7.6 is about how).
  • And none of the three tools knows what your code means. A component that is pure, obeys every hook rule and computes the wrong number passes everything.

What This Section Established

React's rules are the preconditions of its optimisations, which is why breaking them produces wrong behaviour rather than an error. Components and hooks must be pure: idempotent, free of side effects during render, and mutating nothing they did not create. Local mutation of an object you built this render is explicitly fine.

Mutating state in place is the quietest bug in React — measured, the mutation happened, the screen did not change, and the Object.is bail-out skipped the render entirely.

React calls your components. Calling one directly works, which is why it is dangerous: measured, Inner() rendered fine while registering its state on the caller's fiber, with no position in the tree, no independent state and no possibility of being memoised.

Hooks are stored as an ordered list with no names, so a conditional hook shifts every slot. Measured: React prints a previous-versus-next table naming the diverging slot and throws "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render." The fix is always to hoist the hook and move the condition inside it.

<StrictMode> double-invokes renders, effects and ref callbacks in development to make impurity and missing cleanup visible, and compiles away in production. Suppressing its repetition with a ref guard disables the most useful check it performs.

eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 ships 29 rules and enables 17, wired through configs.flat['recommended-latest'] — not configs['recommended-latest'], which is the eslintrc shape and fails on ESLint 10. Measured, the enabled seventeen are not the documented seventeen: void-use-memo is enabled and undocumented, component-hook-factories is documented and not enabled.

And the hole all three share: a mutating method call on a destructured array prop is reported by nothing and compiled without complaint. Copy before you sort.

Exercises

1. Make the silent bug loud. Write a component whose state is an object, mutate it in place, and show that the screen does not update. Then show the same mutation does take effect on the next unrelated re-render. Explain why that combination makes the bug look intermittent, and give the two-line fix.

2. Break the hook order deliberately. Produce React's previous-versus-next table by flipping a prop. Then fix it three different ways — hoist the hook, split the component, use a key — and say which fix you would choose for a component whose two branches share no state.

3. Call a component directly. Render <Inner/> and Inner() side by side, each with a useState counter, and demonstrate three differences: what DevTools shows, whether the two instances have independent state, and what happens when you wrap one in memo.

4. Audit your preset. Print the enabled rules from your installed plugin, diff them against the documentation page, and then enable one rule outside the preset. Run it over an existing codebase and report what it finds — and whether you agree with it.

5. Find the hole. Write four ways to mutate a prop: property assignment, a mutating array method on a destructured prop, the same method through props.x, and a mutation inside a callback. Run the linter and the compiler on all four, report exactly which are caught, and give the non-mutating rewrite of each.

Solution

1. The silent bug.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Silent() {
  const [item, setItem] = useState({ n: 0 });
  const [tick, setTick] = useState(0);
  globalThis.mutate = () => { item.n += 1; setItem(item); };
  globalThis.unrelated = () => setTick(t => t + 1);
  return <b>{item.n}/{tick}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Silent />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.mutate(); globalThis.mutate(); });
console.log('after two mutations   :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.unrelated(); });
console.log('after an unrelated set:', box.textContent);

after two mutations   : 0/0
after an unrelated set: 2/1

Two mutations changed nothing on screen, and then a completely unrelated state change made both appear at once. That is why it reads as intermittent: the value is correct in memory the whole time, and whether it is on screen depends on whether something else happened to re-render. The fix is setItem(prev => ({ ...prev, n: prev.n + 1 })) — a new object every time.

2. Three fixes for the hook order.

// hoist: the hook is unconditional, the behaviour is conditional
useEffect(() => { if (!on) return; subscribe(); }, [on]);

// split: two components, each with its own honest hook list
function Cond({ on }) { return on ? <WithEffect /> : <Plain />; }

// key: force a remount so the hook list is rebuilt from scratch
<Panel key={on ? 'on' : 'off'} on={on} />

For two branches that share no state, split is the right answer. Hoisting produces one component with a hook list that is half-unused in each branch and grows every time a branch does; the key trick forces a remount that is unnecessary if the branches were separate components to begin with. Splitting makes each component's hook list mean something.

3. Rendered versus called.

import { useState, memo, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); globalThis.inc = () => setN(n + 1); return <b>{n}</b>; }
function Rendered() { return <Counter />; }
function Called() { return Counter(); }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const [name, C] of [['<Counter/>', Rendered], ['Counter()', Called]]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<C />); });
  console.log(name, '->', box.innerHTML);
}

<Counter/> -> <b>0</b>
Counter() -> <b>0</b>

Identical output, three differences underneath. DevTools shows a Counter node in the first tree and only Called in the second — the component has vanished from the render tree. State in the second case lives on Called's fiber, so two Counter() calls in one component share a hook list and interleave their slots. And memo(Counter) does nothing in the second case: memo decides whether React calls the component, and here you called it yourself before React had any say.

4. Auditing the preset.

The diff on the installed 7.1.1 is void-use-memo enabled-but-undocumented and component-hook-factories documented-but-disabled. Enabling component-hook-factories over an existing codebase typically finds higher-order components that build a new component inside a render path — which is the §2.4 remount bug with a factory in front of it, and is worth fixing whether or not you adopt the compiler.

5. Four mutations.

// 1  property assignment            REPORTED  react-hooks/immutability
function A(props) { props.title = 'x'; return <b>{props.title}</b>; }
// 2  mutating method, destructured  NOT REPORTED by anything
function B({ items }) { items.sort(); return <b>{items[0]}</b>; }
// 3  mutating method via props      NOT REPORTED by anything
function C(props) { props.items.push('x'); return <b>{props.items.length}</b>; }
// 4  mutation inside a callback     NOT REPORTED by anything
function D({ items }) { return <b>{items.map(i => { i.seen = true; return i.n; })}</b>; }

Only the first is caught. The rewrites: A takes the value as a new prop or lifts the change to the owner; B becomes [...items].sort() or items.toSorted(); C becomes [...props.items, 'x'] built where the state lives; D maps to new objects — items.map(i => ({ ...i, seen: true })) — or, better, does not need seen at render time at all.

The pattern across all four: the fix is always to produce a new value rather than to edit an old one, and that is also the only version the compiler can safely optimise.

SECTION 6

Effects: the Synchronization Model

useEffect is the most misused API in React, and the misuse has a single cause. People learn it as "run this code after render", and then use it for everything that is not rendering. That description is accurate about when the code runs, but says nothing about what it is for. That is why it produces components with six effects that update each other in a chain.

Here is the accurate description. An Effect exists to synchronize a React component with an external system.

  • External means outside React's tree: a WebSocket, a browser API, a third-party widget, a subscription, an analytics service, the document title.
  • Synchronize means: whenever these values change, make the outside world match; and when this component goes away, undo it.

That definition is useful because it rules things out. Data derived from props or state is not an external system, so computing it does not need an Effect. Something that should happen when the user clicks is not synchronization, so it belongs in the event handler. §7.2 is the whole list of things people write Effects for that do not need one. It is a long list, long enough that the honest advice is: write the Effect last, after you have checked it is not one of those.

This section is about the Effects that survive that check, and about the model that makes them predictable. An Effect does not have a mount and an unmount (appearing on and leaving the screen). It has a start and a stop, and React may run that pair as many times as it likes.

6.1 Setup, Cleanup, Dependencies

An Effect is three things, and the shape is fixed.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Chat({ room }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    log.push(`connect ${room}`);                       // setup
    return () => { log.push(`disconnect ${room}`); };  // cleanup
  }, [room]);                                          // dependencies
  return <b>{room}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Chat room="general" />); });
console.log('mount:', log.join(' | '));

mount: connect general

An Effect has three parts:

  • The setup function starts the synchronization.
  • The cleanup function, which setup returns, stops it.
  • The dependency array lists every reactive value the setup reads.

The cleanup is not optional bookkeeping. It is half the definition. An Effect that connects without a way to disconnect, subscribes without unsubscribing, or starts a timer without clearing it is not a synchronization: it is a leak, something that keeps running after nobody needs it. Apply one test to every Effect you write: if React runs this setup twice in a row, does the cleanup in between make that harmless? If the answer is no, the Effect is wrong.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: setup function.

6.2 The Lifecycle Is Not Mount and Unmount

Class components had componentDidMount and componentWillUnmount (methods that ran when a component appeared and when it was removed). Thinking of useEffect as those two glued together causes most Effect bugs. The lifecycle of an effect is different. It starts synchronizing and stops synchronizing, possibly many times, and a component's mount and unmount are only two of the moments that can cause that.

Watch the whole lifecycle:

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Chat({ room }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    log.push(`connect ${room}`);
    return () => { log.push(`disconnect ${room}`); };
  }, [room]);
  return <b>{room}</b>;
}
function App() {
  const [room, setRoom] = useState('general');
  const [other, setOther] = useState(0);
  globalThis.setRoom = setRoom; globalThis.setOther = setOther;
  return <Chat room={room} />;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log('mount           :', log.join(' | ')); log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setOther(1); });
console.log('unrelated update:', log.join(' | ') || '(nothing)'); log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setRoom('random'); });
console.log('room changed    :', log.join(' | ')); log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { root.unmount(); });
console.log('unmount         :', log.join(' | '));

mount           : connect general
unrelated update: (nothing)
room changed    : disconnect general | connect random
unmount         : disconnect random

Four moments, three behaviours.

The four moments are:

  • On mount, setup runs.
  • On an unrelated re-render, nothing happens. Chat re-rendered, but room was unchanged, so React left the synchronization alone.
  • On a dependency change, cleanup runs with the old value, then setup runs with the new one, in that order: disconnect from general, then connect to random.
  • On unmount, cleanup runs.

The middle line deserves the emphasis. An Effect does not re-run on every render; it re-runs when its dependencies change. And the third line is the one that names the model. React did not "update" the connection: it stopped the old one and started a new one. There is no update step, and that is deliberate. An Effect only has to describe how to start and how to stop, never how to move from one state to another.

Cleanup on unmount is therefore only one of the four moments. The same cleanup runs on every dependency change too, and treating it as "the unmount handler" is exactly the misreading this subsection argues against. Notice also that the cleanup captured general, not random. Each cleanup belongs to the setup that created it, and sees that render's values (§2.12). That is what makes "disconnect from the room we were actually connected to" work, without you storing it anywhere.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: lifecycle of an effect.

To have in hand before moving on: cleanup on unmount.

6.3 Reactive Values and the Dependency Array

A reactive value is any value that can differ between renders: props, state, context, and anything computed from them inside the component body. The dependency array must contain every reactive value the setup function reads. Not the ones you think matter: all of them.

That rule is not a style preference and it is not up for negotiation, because the model above only makes sense with it. The Effect describes a synchronization for a particular set of values. If a value it uses changes and React does not know, the outside world is now synchronized to values that no longer exist. That is called a stale closure (a function still holding old values), and you cannot see it.

Three forms, three meanings:

[a, b]
Re-synchronize when a or b changes, compared with Object.is. The normal case.
[]
An empty dependency array: this Effect reads no reactive values, so it never needs to re-synchronize. It is a claim about the code, not a way to say "only on mount" — if the setup reads a prop, the array is a lie.
omitted
An omitted dependency array: re-synchronize after every render. Occasionally correct — a measurement that must happen each commit — and usually a bug that runs a fetch on every keystroke.

The distinction that ends the argument: you do not choose the dependencies, you derive them. The array follows mechanically from what the setup body reads. If you want a value out of the array, the fix is to change the code so the setup no longer reads it (§7.6 lists the ways). It is never to delete the entry and move on.

react-hooks/exhaustive-deps works out the array for you and reports any difference. It ships as a warning in the recommended preset (§5.6). That is a concession to existing codebases, not a statement that it is optional.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: empty dependency array and omitted dependency array.

6.4 Effects Fire Twice in Development

In development, under <StrictMode>, React deliberately runs setup, cleanup, setup on mount:

import { useEffect, act, StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Chat({ room }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    log.push(`connect ${room}`);
    return () => { log.push(`disconnect ${room}`); };
  }, [room]);
  return <b>{room}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<StrictMode><Chat room="general" /></StrictMode>); });
console.log(log.join(' | '));

connect general | disconnect general | connect general

This is not a bug and not a performance concern: it does nothing in production. It is a test, and it tests exactly one thing: that your cleanup fully undoes your setup. If connect-disconnect-connect leaves you with two connections, one leftover listener or a duplicated log entry, the Effect was broken. You would otherwise have found out when a user changed rooms twice.

The wrong response, and it is extremely common, is a ref guard:

// DO NOT DO THIS
const done = useRef(false);
useEffect(() => { if (done.current) return; done.current = true; connect(); }, []);

That hides the symptom and switches off the check for that component for good. It also breaks the Effect for real. After a genuine dependency change, the guard stops it from synchronizing again, so the component stays connected to the old room forever. If the double run causes a visible problem, the cleanup is missing: write it.

6.5 Connecting to an External System

The Effects that survive §7.2's filter almost all have one shape: acquire a resource, and return a function that releases it.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Ticker({ interval, onTick }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    log.push(`start ${interval}ms`);
    const id = setInterval(onTick, interval);
    return () => { clearInterval(id); log.push(`stop ${interval}ms`); };
  }, [interval, onTick]);
  return <b>{interval}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const noop = () => {};
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Ticker interval={100} onTick={noop} />); });
await act(async () => { root.render(<Ticker interval={250} onTick={noop} />); });
await act(async () => { root.unmount(); });
console.log(log.join(' | '));

start 100ms | stop 100ms | start 250ms | stop 250ms

Every interval that started was stopped, in order. The structure guarantees the pairing, so you do not have to remember it. The same shape covers the other cases:

Subscribing to browser events
addEventListener on window or document, cleanup removes it. For an element you own, use onClick instead — that is not an external system.
Controlling a non-react widget
A map, an editor, a chart library. Create it in setup, destroy it in cleanup, and use a second Effect with narrow dependencies to push prop changes into it.
Triggering an animation
Start it in setup, reset it in cleanup. Anything that must run before the browser paints belongs in useLayoutEffect (§7.8).
Sending analytics
A page-view on mount is a legitimate Effect. A click event is not — that is an event handler.
Not: initializing the application
Work that must happen once per app load belongs at module scope or before createRoot, not in a component's Effect where mounting twice will do it twice.

A single Effect should do a single thing. Two unrelated synchronizations in one Effect share a dependency array. That means each one re-runs when the other's inputs change: a live subscription torn down and rebuilt because an unrelated prop changed.

In summary, the vocabulary here is subscribing to browser events, controlling a non-React widget, triggering an animation, initializing the application and sending analytics.

6.6 Fetching in an Effect, and the Race Condition

Fetching data in an effect is the most common Effect, and the one with the sharpest edge. The edge is a race condition: two requests are in flight, and the slower one finishes last and overwrites the faster one's result.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const resolvers = new Map();
const fetchUser = id => new Promise(r => resolvers.set(id, r));

function Profile({ id, guard }) {
  const [name, setName] = useState('—');
  useEffect(() => {
    let stale = false;
    fetchUser(id).then(n => { if (!guard || !stale) setName(n); });
    return () => { stale = true; };
  }, [id, guard]);
  return <b>{name}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const guard of [false, true]) {
  resolvers.clear();
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Profile id={1} guard={guard} />); });
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Profile id={2} guard={guard} />); });
  // id 2 answers first, then the stale id 1 answers late
  await act(async () => { resolvers.get(2)('SECOND'); });
  await act(async () => { resolvers.get(1)('FIRST'); });
  console.log(guard ? 'with the stale flag   :' : 'without the stale flag:', box.textContent);
}

without the stale flag: FIRST
with the stale flag   : SECOND

Without the guard, the component ends up showing FIRST: the answer to a request for a user the interface stopped caring about two updates ago. The user sees the wrong profile, and nothing anywhere reports an error.

The fix is four lines, and it is always the same: a let stale = false in the setup, a check before every setState, and stale = true in the cleanup. Ignore stale responses is the name for it. Note that it is just the ordinary cleanup mechanism from §6.1 doing its ordinary job: the request is the resource, and cancelling it is the release.

AbortController is the stronger version. fetch(url, { signal }) in setup and controller.abort() in cleanup actually cancels the request instead of ignoring its answer, which also frees the connection. Use it when the request is expensive; use the flag when you cannot cancel.

Two things about this pattern are worth saying out loud rather than leaving implied.

  • It is the reason the double-invocation test in §6.4 matters: an unguarded fetch Effect passes casual testing, and fails exactly when the user is quick.
  • And it is a strong argument for not writing fetch Effects at all. A framework loader, a query library that supports Suspense, or a Server Component (§17) handles the race, the cache, removing duplicate requests and the error state. This four-line pattern addresses none of those. §7.2 makes the same argument at more length.

What to carry forward from this subsection: fetching data in an effect and ignore stale responses.

6.7 Each Render Has Its Own Effects

The snapshot model from §2.12 applies to Effects in full: each render has its own effects, which capture that render's props and state.

That single fact explains the behaviour people find most mysterious.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.inc = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  useEffect(() => {
    globalThis.readCurrent = () => `correct array saw n=${n}`;
  }, [n]);
  useEffect(() => {
    globalThis.readStale = () => `empty array saw n=${n}`;
  }, []);                                        // deliberately wrong array
  return <b>{n}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Counter />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.inc(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.inc(); });
console.log('on screen:', box.textContent);
console.log(globalThis.readCurrent());
console.log(globalThis.readStale());

on screen: 2
correct array saw n=2
empty array saw n=0

Both closures read the same variable n, in the same component, and they were called one line apart, yet they reported different values. The first Effect synchronized again on every change, so the closure it installed last came from the render where n was 2. The second declared [], a claim that it reads no reactive values. That claim was false, so React never re-ran it, and the closure it installed on the very first render is still in place, still seeing n = 0.

None of that is a React quirk. It is what a closure does. It is also why "just remove it from the array to stop the re-runs" is never the fix: the value does not stop being read, it stops being current.

6.8 When Effects Run, Relative to Everything Else

From §2.1, in order within one update: render, commit, layout effects, browser paint, passive effects. useEffect is the passive one, and where it sits has three consequences worth knowing.

An Effect never blocks the paint. Whatever it does, the user has already seen the new UI. That makes it the right place for a network request, and the wrong place for a DOM measurement whose result changes the layout, because the user would see the frame from before the measurement first. useLayoutEffect (§7.8) exists for the second case.

Effects run child-first. When a parent and a child both have Effects, the child's setup runs before the parent's. That is the same order as componentDidMount, and it is why a parent can rely on its children having synchronized by the time its own Effect runs.

Setting state in an Effect causes a second render. Sometimes that is exactly right. Usually it means the value should have been computed during render instead. react-hooks/set-state-in-effect reports the synchronous case with "Calling setState synchronously within an effect can trigger cascading renders" (§5.7), and §7.2 is about what to do instead.

6.9 Reading the Model Back

The whole section comes down to four questions, asked in order. They are worth learning as a checklist, because they catch nearly every Effect mistake before it is written.

Is there an external system?
If the answer is "no, I am computing something from props" — delete the Effect and compute it during render (§7.2).
Does it happen because of an event?
If it happens because the user clicked, it belongs in the handler. An Effect runs because the component is on screen, never because something was pressed.
What stops it?
Write the cleanup before you finish the setup. If nothing needs stopping, ask question one again — you may not have an external system.
What does the setup read?
Every reactive value goes in the array. If that makes it re-run too often, change the code, not the array (§7.6).

What This Section Established

An Effect synchronizes a component with an external system. That definition excludes most of what Effects are used for, and §7.2 is the list.

Its lifecycle is start and stop, not mount and unmount. Measured across four moments: setup on mount; nothing on an unrelated re-render; cleanup-with-the-old-value then setup-with-the-new on a dependency change; cleanup on unmount. There is no update path, only stop and start.

The dependency array is derived from what the setup reads, not chosen. [] is a claim that the setup reads no reactive value, and a false one produces a closure frozen at the first render — measured, two Effects in the same component reading the same n reported 2 and 0.

Development runs setup-cleanup-setup on mount to test that the cleanup undoes the setup. Measured: connect | disconnect | connect. A useRef guard silences the test and breaks re-synchronization at the same time.

Fetching in an Effect needs a stale flag. Measured: without one, a late response for the previous id overwrote the current one and the component displayed FIRST instead of SECOND, with no error anywhere.

Passive effects run after the browser paints, child before parent, and setting state in one causes a second render.

Exercises

1. Chart the lifecycle. Instrument an Effect with a logged setup and cleanup, then produce all four transitions: mount, an unrelated re-render, a dependency change, and unmount. Write down which value each cleanup closed over and explain why it is the old one rather than the new one.

2. Break it with an empty array. Write two Effects in one component that read the same state, one with a correct array and one with [], and show them reporting different values at the same moment. Then state what exhaustive-deps says about the second, and why deleting a dependency never removes the read.

3. Lose the race. Reproduce the stale-response bug with two requests that resolve out of order, then fix it twice — with a stale flag and with an AbortController. Say what the second gives you that the first does not, and one case where only the first is possible.

4. Defeat StrictMode, then repair it. Write an Effect that misbehaves under double invocation, "fix" it with a ref guard, and then demonstrate the second bug that the guard introduces by changing a dependency. Give the real fix.

5. Sort the list. For each of these, say whether it needs an Effect and where it belongs otherwise: updating the document title from a prop; sending a POST when a form is submitted; connecting to a chat room; computing a filtered list from a search box; logging a page view; resetting a form when the selected record changes; starting an animation when an item is added.

Solution

1. The lifecycle. Measured in §6.2: connect general / (nothing) / disconnect general | connect random / disconnect random.

Each cleanup closed over the old value because it was created by the setup that used that value. The cleanup returned from the general setup is a closure over that render's room, and React holds onto it until it needs to stop that synchronization. If cleanups saw the new value they would be unable to undo what was actually done — you would disconnect from a room you never joined.

2. The empty array. Measured in §6.7: timeout saw n=2 | stale saw n=0.

exhaustive-deps reports "React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'n'. Either include it or remove the dependency array". Deleting n from the array does not stop the setup from reading n; it stops React from re-running the setup when n changes, so the closure that reads it is never replaced. The read is in the code; the array only controls how often that code is re-created.

3. The race.

// stale flag: ignore the answer
useEffect(() => {
  let stale = false;
  fetchUser(id).then(u => { if (!stale) setUser(u); });
  return () => { stale = true; };
}, [id]);

// AbortController: cancel the request
useEffect(() => {
  const c = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/u/${id}`, { signal: c.signal }).then(r => r.json()).then(setUser)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') throw e; });
  return () => c.abort();
}, [id]);

The controller actually cancels: the connection is freed, the server can stop working, and on a slow network the browser's six-connections-per-host limit is not consumed by requests nobody wants. The flag only ignores the answer.

Only the flag is possible when the promise is not cancellable — a third-party SDK method, an IndexedDB read, a postMessage round trip. Note the .catch in the second: aborting rejects, and an unhandled AbortError in the console is the usual reason people abandon the approach.

4. Defeat and repair.

// misbehaves: two connections after the double invocation
useEffect(() => { connect(room); }, [room]);
// "fixed" with a guard: one connection, and it never changes room again
const done = useRef(false);
useEffect(() => { if (done.current) return; done.current = true; connect(room); }, [room]);
// real fix
useEffect(() => { const c = connect(room); return () => c.disconnect(); }, [room]);

The guard's second bug appears the moment room changes: the Effect re-runs, returns immediately, and the component stays connected to the previous room permanently. The symptom is "messages from the wrong channel", it does not reproduce on mount, and the guard makes it look like the connection code is fine.

5. Effect or not.

document title from a prop      Effect (the document is an external system)
POST on form submit             event handler / an Action (§15) — not an Effect
connect to a chat room          Effect, with a disconnect cleanup
filtered list from a search box NOT an Effect — compute it during render
log a page view                 Effect (mount), or the router's own navigation event
reset a form on record change   NOT an Effect — key the component by the record id (§2.6)
start an animation on add       Effect, or useLayoutEffect if it must not flash

The two "not"s are the two most common wrong Effects in existence, and both have a one-line replacement: a computation in the body, and a key.

SECTION 7

Escape Hatches: Refs, the DOM and Effect Events

React's model is that the UI is a function of state: you change data, and React works out the screen. React also owns the DOM, so your code does not change the page directly. Most of an application fits inside that model comfortably. Some of it does not, and pretending otherwise produces worse code than admitting it.

An escape hatch is an API for stepping outside the model on purpose. It lets you:

  • hold a value React does not track;
  • touch a DOM node directly;
  • read something that lives outside React's tree;
  • or do work before the browser paints the screen.

Each one is a small, well-defined hole in the model, and each comes with a rule about where it may be used.

The order here is deliberate. The section opens with the largest escape hatch of all, which is not writing an Effect. The most common reason people reach for a hatch is that they wrote an Effect they did not need, and then need another hatch to make it behave. §7.1 is that list. Everything after it is a genuine hole in the model.

7.1 You Might Not Need an Effect

You might not need an effect is the single highest-value idea in this course after §2.5. Two rules cover almost all of it:

If you can compute it during render, do not put it in state and do not synchronize it with an Effect.

If it happens because of a user interaction, put it in the event handler.

Here is the catalogue, with the replacement for each.

Deriving state from props
Calculating during render instead. const full = first + ' ' + last — no state, no Effect, no extra render, and it can never be stale.
An expensive derivation
Still during render, wrapped in useMemo if a profile says so — or nothing at all if the compiler is on (§11.11). Cache a calculation without effects.
Resetting state when a prop changes
A key on the component (§2.6). React remounts it and the state resets, with no Effect and no intermediate render showing the old value.
Adjusting state when a prop changes
Set it during render — React restarts the render immediately without painting the intermediate state. Rare and legitimate; see below.
Sharing logic between handlers
A plain function both handlers call. An Effect that watches for a flag one handler sets runs on every mount too, including after a reload.
Sending a POST on submit
The submit handler, or an Action (§15). It happens because the user pressed a button, not because the component is on screen.
A chain of computations
Effects that each set state another Effect watches. Compute everything you can during render and do the rest in the one handler that started it — a chain of n Effects is n extra renders and a fragile order.
Initializing the application
Module scope, or before createRoot. An Effect at the root runs twice in development and again if the root ever remounts.
Notifying parent components
Call the callback in the same handler that changed the state, so parent and child update in one pass. An Effect makes the parent render a frame later.

The adjust-during-render case is the one that looks illegal, and is not:

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let renders = 0;
function List({ items }) {
  const [prevItems, setPrevItems] = useState(items);
  const [selection, setSelection] = useState(null);
  renders++;
  if (items !== prevItems) {          // adjusting state during render
    setPrevItems(items);
    setSelection(null);
  }
  globalThis.select = v => setSelection(v);
  return <b>{String(selection)}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
const a = ['x'], b = ['y'];
await act(async () => { root.render(<List items={a} />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.select('chosen'); });
console.log('after selecting:', box.textContent);
renders = 0;
await act(async () => { root.render(<List items={b} />); });
console.log('after new items:', box.textContent, '| renders:', renders);

after selecting: chosen
after new items: null | renders: 2

React saw the setState during render, threw away the output, and ran the component again immediately. That is two render calls and one commit, and the browser never painted a frame showing the old selection against the new items. An Effect doing the same job would have committed the out-of-date frame first and then corrected it, which shows up as a visible flash.

This pattern is narrow, and its conditions are strict:

  • only set state of the same component;
  • only inside a condition that eventually becomes false;
  • and never for state that belongs to a child.

Outside those conditions, react-hooks/set-state-in-render reports it, correctly, as "Cannot call setState during render". Prefer a key when a key will do.

The terms above, gathered: calculating during render, cache a calculation without effects, resetting state when a prop changes, adjusting state when a prop changes, chain of computations and notifying parent components.

7.2 useRef: a Value React Does Not Track

useRef( gives you a box you can change, which persists across renders and does not cause a re-render when it changes.

import { useRef, useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let renders = 0;
function Counter() {
  const clicks = useRef(0);
  const [shown, setShown] = useState(0);
  renders++;
  globalThis.click = () => { clicks.current += 1; };
  globalThis.reveal = () => setShown(clicks.current);
  return <b>{shown}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Counter />); });
renders = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.click(); globalThis.click(); globalThis.click(); });
console.log('after 3 ref writes:', box.textContent, '| renders:', renders);
await act(async () => { globalThis.reveal(); });
console.log('after revealing   :', box.textContent, '| renders:', renders);

after 3 ref writes: 0 | renders: 0
after revealing   : 3 | renders: 1

Three writes, zero renders. The differences between refs and state come down to that one line, and the table below covers the rest. Refs are not reactive: that is the entire difference from state. It makes them right for a value the UI does not display, such as a timeout id, a previous value kept for comparison, a flag saying whether an animation has started, or a reference to an object from another library.

State
  • Changing it re-renders
  • Immutable: replace, never edit
  • Readable during render
  • For anything the user sees
Ref
  • Changing it does nothing
  • Mutable: ref.current = x is the API
  • Not readable or writable during render
  • For values that are not output

The third row is the rule that catches people: Do not read or write a ref during rendering. Reading one makes the render depend on a value React did not track, so two renders with identical inputs can produce different output. That breaks purity (§5.1). Under a transition, a render that is abandoned and re-run may also see a different value than the one that commits. react-hooks/refs reports both with "Cannot access refs during render". Read and write refs in event handlers and Effects, where render has already finished.

One exception is allowed: avoiding recreating the ref contents with if (ref.current === null) ref.current = expensiveThing(). That is a lazy initialisation that gives the same result however many times it runs, and looks identical from outside on every render. It is the documented way to avoid building an object on every render only to throw it away.

One line each, for reference: useRef(, do not read or write a ref during rendering and differences between refs and state.

7.3 Refs to DOM Nodes

Pass a ref to a host element, and React puts the DOM node in .current after the commit.

import { useRef, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Field() {
  const input = useRef(null);
  globalThis.readDuringRender = input.current;      // always null: not attached yet
  useEffect(() => { globalThis.readInEffect = input.current?.tagName; }, []);
  return <input ref={input} defaultValue="hi" />;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Field />); });
console.log('during render:', globalThis.readDuringRender);
console.log('in an effect :', globalThis.readInEffect);

during render: null
in an effect : INPUT

When react attaches the refs is during the commit: after the DOM is built, and before layout effects run. So a ref read during render is null on the first render, and holds the previous node on later ones. That is one more reason for the rule against reading refs during render.

Ref as a prop is a React 19 change worth knowing if you read any existing code. A function component can now accept ref in its props like any other prop:

function TextField({ ref, ...rest }) { return <input ref={ref} {...rest} />; }

Before 19 this required forwardRef(, which wrapped the component so React would pass it a second ref argument. forwardRef still works but is deprecated. New code takes ref as a prop, and a codemod (a tool that rewrites code automatically) converts the old form.

createRef( is the class-component ancestor of useRef. It makes a ref object with no memory across renders, which is why calling it in a function component produces a fresh ref every time. It appears only in class code (§18.9).

A ref callback is the other form: you pass a function instead of a ref object, and React calls it with the node when it attaches. React 19 added a really useful ability here: the callback may return a cleanup function, called when the node detaches:

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Item({ show }) {
  return show
    ? <b ref={node => { log.push('attach ' + node.tagName); return () => log.push('detach'); }}>x</b>
    : null;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Item show={true} />); });
await act(async () => { root.render(<Item show={false} />); });
console.log(log.join(' | '));

attach B | detach

That returned function is a ref cleanup function. Before it existed, React called a ref callback with null on detach, and every callback needed an if (node) branch. The cleanup form mirrors useEffect. It is the right way to register a node with something outside React: an IntersectionObserver, a focus manager, or managing a list of refs in a Map keyed by id.

Manipulating the DOM with refs has two legitimate jobs, and they are the only two you should need often:

  • Focusing a text input, with input.current.focus(), because focus is browser state React does not model.
  • And scrolling to an element, with node.scrollIntoView(), for the same reason.

Anything that changes what is displayed should change state instead. A ref that sets style.display is a component fighting its own render.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: ref cleanup function, createRef(, forwardRef(, manipulating the DOM with refs, managing a list of refs, when react attaches the refs, focusing a text input and scrolling to an element.

7.4 useImperativeHandle

useImperativeHandle( customises what a parent receives through a ref: a small object of your choosing, instead of the DOM node.

import { useRef, useImperativeHandle, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Editor({ ref }) {
  const area = useRef(null);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    clear: () => { area.current.value = ''; },
    length: () => area.current.value.length,
  }), []);
  return <textarea ref={area} defaultValue="hello" />;
}
function App() {
  const api = useRef(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    globalThis.exposed = Object.keys(api.current).join(',');
    globalThis.before = api.current.length();
    api.current.clear();
    globalThis.after = api.current.length();
  }, []);
  return <Editor ref={api} />;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log('exposed:', globalThis.exposed, '| length before:', globalThis.before,
            '-> after clear:', globalThis.after);

exposed: clear,length | length before: 5 -> after clear: 0

The parent got exactly two methods, and no access to the <textarea>. That is an imperative handle. The reason to build one is the same as the reason to have a private field: the parent cannot reach in and set style, add a listener or read parentNode, so the component stays free to change its markup.

Use it sparingly. Most components should expose nothing imperative at all, and a handle with more than three methods is usually state that wants lifting (§3.7).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: useImperativeHandle( and imperative handle.

7.5 Removing Effect Dependencies

§6.3 said the array is derived, not chosen. This subsection is the practical result: when an Effect re-runs too often, removing effect dependencies means changing the code so the setup no longer reads the value.

Four moves cover nearly every case.

Move static objects outside the component. An object or function that never changes does not need to be recreated on each render. If it is defined at module level, it is not reactive and cannot be a dependency.

Move dynamic things into the Effect. If only one Effect uses a function, define it inside the setup. It is then not a reactive value of the component at all.

Read primitive values from objects. useEffect(…, [options]) re-runs whenever the caller passes a new object literal, which is every render. Writing const { url, room } = options in the body and [url, room] in the array makes it depend on the two strings instead, and strings compare by value.

Use an updater function. An Effect that reads state only to compute the next state does not need that state as a dependency: setCount(c => c + 1) reads nothing.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const runs = [];
function Bad({ options }) {                    // depends on an object identity
  useEffect(() => { runs.push('bad'); }, [options]);
  return null;
}
function Good({ options }) {                   // depends on two strings
  const { url, room } = options;
  useEffect(() => { runs.push('good'); }, [url, room]);
  return null;
}
function App({ tick }) {
  const options = { url: 'wss://x', room: 'general' };   // new object every render
  return <><Bad options={options} /><Good options={options} /></>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App tick={1} />); });
runs.length = 0;
await act(async () => { root.render(<App tick={2} />); });
await act(async () => { root.render(<App tick={3} />); });
console.log('two unrelated re-renders re-ran:', runs.join(', ') || '(neither)');

two unrelated re-renders re-ran: bad, bad

The Bad Effect synchronized again twice for no reason (a real WebSocket would have disconnected and reconnected twice), while Good did not run at all, because its two strings were unchanged.

Suppressing the dependency linter is the move that is never right. // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps does not remove the dependency. It removes the warning, and leaves you with a closure frozen at whatever render installed it (§6.7). Every time you want to suppress it, the real answer is one of the four moves above, or useEffectEvent.

To have in hand before moving on: suppressing the dependency linter, move static objects outside the component and read primitive values from objects.

7.6 useEffectEvent

There is one case the four moves do not cover: the Effect really needs the latest value of something, but must not synchronize again when it changes. Examples: logging the current theme when a chat connects, reading the current user in an analytics call, using the current callback in a subscription.

useEffectEvent( creates an effect event: a function that always sees the latest props and state, and that is not a reactive dependency.

import { useState, useEffect, useEffectEvent, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Chat({ room, theme }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => { log.push(`connected ${room} theme=${theme}`); });
  useEffect(() => {
    log.push(`connect ${room}`);
    onConnected();
    return () => { log.push(`disconnect ${room}`); };
  }, [room]);                                  // theme is NOT here, and that is correct
  return <b>{room}/{theme}</b>;
}
function App() {
  const [room, setRoom] = useState('general');
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  globalThis.setRoom = setRoom; globalThis.setTheme = setTheme;
  return <Chat room={room} theme={theme} />;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log('mount      :', log.join(' | ')); log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setTheme('dark'); });
console.log('theme only :', log.join(' | ') || '(the Effect did not re-run)'); log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setRoom('random'); });
console.log('room change:', log.join(' | '));

mount      : connect general | connected general theme=light
theme only : (the Effect did not re-run)
room change: disconnect general | connect random | connected random theme=dark

Both properties show up in one measurement. Changing the theme did not reconnect. Putting theme in the array would have done that, tearing down a live connection because a colour changed. And when the room really changed, the event saw theme=dark: the current value, not the one captured at mount.

Separating events from effects is the idea the API is named for. Code inside an Effect is reactive: it re-runs when its inputs change. Code inside an event handler is not: it runs once, when something happened, with whatever the values are at that moment. An Effect Event is a piece of non-reactive logic that you can call from a reactive place.

The limitations are real and deliberate:

Call it only from Effects
Not during render. The lint says "… is a function created with useEffectEvent, and can only be called from Effects".
Never pass it anywhere
Not to a child, not to addEventListener, not into a dependency array. It is declared and called in the same component.
It is not a general escape from deps
Wrapping everything in Effect Events gives an Effect that never re-synchronizes — which is [] with extra ceremony. Use it for the specific values that should not cause re-synchronization.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: reactive dependency, useEffectEvent(, non-reactive logic and separating events from effects.

7.7 useSyncExternalStore

State that lives outside React (a store, a browser API, a module-level variable) cannot be read directly during render, because of tearing (§12.8): different parts of the screen showing different versions of the same value. useSyncExternalStore( is the supported way to subscribe to it.

import { useSyncExternalStore, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let value = 0;
const listeners = new Set();
const store = {
  subscribe(cb) { listeners.add(cb); return () => listeners.delete(cb); },
  getSnapshot() { return value; },
  set(v) { value = v; listeners.forEach(cb => cb()); },
};

function Widget() {
  const n = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getSnapshot, () => 0);
  return <b>{n}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Widget />); });
console.log('initial:', box.textContent, '| listeners:', listeners.size);
await act(async () => { store.set(7); });
console.log('after set:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { root.unmount(); });
console.log('after unmount, listeners:', listeners.size);

initial: 0 | listeners: 1
after set: 7
after unmount, listeners: 0

It takes three arguments.

  • The subscribe function takes a callback and returns an unsubscribe function. It must be stable, because React subscribes again whenever its identity changes. Defining it inside the component is the usual cause of "my subscribe function gets called after every re-render".
  • getSnapshot( returns the current value, and must return a cached value. Returning a new object on each call makes React see a change on every render and loop forever, which is what "The result of getSnapshot should be cached" means.
  • And getServerSnapshot supplies a value during server rendering and hydration, where there is no store to read.

This is the hook to reach for when connecting a store. It is also the one that correctly reads window.matchMedia, navigator.onLine, document.visibilityState and similar browser state.

In summary, the vocabulary here is useSyncExternalStore( and getServerSnapshot.

7.8 useLayoutEffect and useInsertionEffect

Two more Effects, distinguished only by when they run.

import { useEffect, useLayoutEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const order = [];
function Order() {
  useLayoutEffect(() => { order.push('layout'); });
  useEffect(() => { order.push('passive'); });
  return <i>o</i>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Order />); });
console.log(order.join(' -> '));

layout -> passive

useLayoutEffect( runs right after the DOM is updated and before the browser paints, and nothing else runs until it finishes. That is its entire reason to exist and its entire cost: whatever it does, the user waits for it. Use it for measuring layout before the browser repaints, such as reading a node's height to decide whether a tooltip goes above or below it. Doing that work in useEffect would let the user see one frame with the tooltip in the wrong place. That visible frame is the flicker that sends people here.

It does not run on the server, and React warns if you use it in a server-rendered component without guarding it, because on the server there is no layout to measure.

useInsertionEffect( runs even earlier, before any change to the DOM. It exists for exactly one audience: CSS-in-JS libraries that must add a <style> rule before the elements using it are laid out. It cannot read layout and cannot access refs. If you are not writing a styling library, you do not need it.

The decision comes down to one question: Does the user see the wrong thing if this runs after the paint? Yes, for a measurement that repositions something: use useLayoutEffect. No, for everything else: use useEffect.

What to carry forward from this subsection: useLayoutEffect(, useInsertionEffect(, measuring layout before the browser repaints and flicker.

7.9 Fragment Refs

§7.3's refs point at one DOM node. A component that wraps other people's children — a toolbar that handles clicks for whatever buttons it is given, a list that reports which of its items are on screen — has no single node to point at, and the traditional fix is to wrap the children in a <div> and put the ref on that. The <div> is the problem: it breaks a flex or grid layout the children were written for, it is invalid inside a <ul> or a <tr>, and it exists only to hold a ref.

React 19.3 lets a <Fragment> take a ref. What arrives in ref.current is not a DOM node, since a fragment renders none. It is a FragmentInstance: an object with the DOM methods you would have called on a wrapper element, applied to the fragment's children instead.

import { Fragment, useRef, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const clicks = [];
function Toolbar({ children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    const fragment = ref.current;
    const onClick = e => clicks.push(`${e.target.textContent}@${e.currentTarget.tagName.toLowerCase()}`);
    fragment.addEventListener('click', onClick);
    return () => fragment.removeEventListener('click', onClick);
  }, []);
  globalThis.fragment = ref;
  return <Fragment ref={ref}>{children}</Fragment>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => {
  createRoot(box).render(
    <Toolbar>
      <p>no focusable here</p>
      <button>Bold</button>
      <span><button>Nested</button></span>
      <button>Italic</button>
    </Toolbar>);
});

console.log('instance:', globalThis.fragment.current.constructor.name);
for (const b of box.querySelectorAll('button')) b.click();
console.log('clicks  :', clicks.join(', '));

globalThis.fragment.current.focus();
console.log('focus() :', document.activeElement.textContent);
globalThis.fragment.current.focusLast();
console.log('focusLast():', document.activeElement.textContent);
console.log('the DOM :', box.innerHTML);

instance: FragmentInstance
clicks  : Bold@button, Nested@span, Italic@button
focus() : Bold
focusLast(): Italic
the DOM : <p>no focusable here</p><button>Bold</button><span><button>Nested</button></span><button>Italic</button>

Four things to read in that output.

There is no wrapper. The rendered DOM is the four children and nothing else, which is the whole point.

addEventListener attaches to every first-level child. All three clicks were caught, but look at currentTarget. The Nested button's click was handled at the <span>, because the <span> is the first-level child and the listener lives there; the button inside it reached it by ordinary bubbling. Methods that act on children (addEventListener, removeEventListener, observeUsing, getClientRects) work on the fragment's first-level host children, not on everything beneath them.

focus() searches depth-first. It skipped the <p> and focused the first element that can take focus, and focusLast() found the last one. Unlike the event methods, focus looks through nested children. That makes a fragment ref the natural way to build "focus the first field in this group", or a focus trap that wraps around.

The syntax must be the long form. <>…</> cannot take props, so a ref needs <Fragment ref={ref}>, with Fragment imported from react.

The second half of the API is observers, and here a fragment ref does something a hand-written wrapper cannot do cheaply. jsdom has no IntersectionObserver, but observeUsing accepts anything with observe and unobserve methods, so a recorder shows exactly what React passes over:

import { Fragment, useRef, useLayoutEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

// Anything with observe/unobserve will do: record what the fragment hands over.
const log = [];
const recorder = { observe: el => log.push(`observe ${el.textContent}`),
                   unobserve: el => log.push(`unobserve ${el.textContent}`) };

function TrackVisibility({ children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const fragment = ref.current;
    fragment.observeUsing(recorder);
    return () => fragment.unobserveUsing(recorder);
  }, []);
  return <Fragment ref={ref}>{children}</Fragment>;
}
const Feed = ({ items }) =>
  <TrackVisibility>{items.map(i => <article key={i}>{i}</article>)}tail text</TrackVisibility>;

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
for (const items of [['a', 'b'], ['a', 'b', 'c'], ['b', 'c']]) {
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Feed items={items} />); });
  console.log(JSON.stringify(items).padEnd(15), log.splice(0).join(', '));
}
console.log('reactFragments on <article>:', document.querySelector('article').reactFragments.size);

["a","b"]       observe a, observe b
["a","b","c"]   observe c
["b","c"]       unobserve a
reactFragments on <article>: 1

React keeps the observer in sync with the children. When c was inserted, React called observe on it; when a was removed, it called unobserve. The component never re-ran its layout effect, because the dependency array is empty. A version written with querySelectorAll on a wrapper would have observed a and b forever, missed c, and kept a reference to the removed a. The text node was never observed, because an observer cannot watch text. A fragment with nothing but text gets a development warning, measured as "observeUsing() was called on a FragmentInstance with only text children. Observers do not work on text nodes.". Event listeners added with addEventListener are kept in sync the same way.

Each child records which fragments own it. reactFragments is a Set of FragmentInstances on every first-level child. It exists for libraries that share one observer across many fragments: the observer's callback receives an element, and reactFragments maps it back to the fragments that asked.

The full method list uses the DOM names, so code written for an element reads the same:

  • addEventListener, removeEventListener and dispatchEvent;
  • focus, focusLast and blur (which only removes focus when the focused element is inside the fragment);
  • observeUsing and unobserveUsing, for an IntersectionObserver or ResizeObserver;
  • getClientRects, which returns one rectangle per first-level child;
  • getRootNode and compareDocumentPosition;
  • and scrollIntoView(alignToTop), which takes only the boolean form. Passing the options object that Element.scrollIntoView accepts throws an error.

Listeners added through a fragment are not applied inside a hidden <Activity> tree (§12.9), and are attached automatically when it becomes visible.

When to reach for it: when the component's job is to add behaviour to children it does not render itself. When the component renders its own markup, a ref on its own element (§7.3) is simpler, and remains the answer. The react.dev page for <Fragment> still labels the ref prop canary (preview-only); the 19.3.0 package exports it, and the examples above ran against that package.

One line each, for reference: Fragment refs, FragmentInstance, observeUsing( and focusLast(.

What This Section Established

The largest escape hatch is not needing one. Derived values are computed during render; things caused by an interaction go in the handler; state that resets with a prop gets a key. Adjusting state during render is legitimate and narrow — measured, two render calls and one commit, so the wrong frame is never painted.

useRef is a mutable box that does not re-render — measured, three writes and zero renders. It may not be read or written during render, with lazy initialisation the one sanctioned exception.

A ref to a DOM node is null during the first render and populated at commit — measured. ref is a plain prop in React 19 and forwardRef is deprecated. A ref callback may return a cleanup that runs on detach — measured, attach B | detach.

useImperativeHandle narrows what a parent can reach to methods you name — measured, clear,length and nothing else.

Dependencies are removed by changing the code: hoist static values out, move single-use functions in, destructure primitives out of objects, use updater functions. Measured, an object dependency re-ran an Effect on two unrelated re-renders while the destructured version ran on neither. Suppressing the linter is never the fix.

useEffectEvent gives non-reactive access to the latest values — measured, a theme change did not reconnect the chat, and the next genuine reconnection saw the new theme. Call it only from Effects, and never pass it anywhere.

useSyncExternalStore subscribes safely to state outside React: a stable subscribe, a cached getSnapshot, and a server snapshot. Measured, one listener on mount and zero after unmount.

useLayoutEffect runs before the paint — measured, layout -> passive — and is for measurements that would otherwise flicker. useInsertionEffect is for CSS-in-JS libraries only.

A ref on <Fragment> (React 19.3) gives a FragmentInstance that applies DOM methods to the fragment's children without a wrapper element — measured, events on every first-level child, focus() searching depth-first, and an observer kept in sync as children are inserted and removed.

Exercises

1. Delete four Effects. Take a component with four Effects — deriving a filtered list, resetting a form when the record changes, POSTing on submit, and notifying a parent of a state change — and rewrite it with none. For each, name the replacement and say how many renders you removed.

2. Prove refs are not reactive. Instrument a component with a render counter, write to a ref ten times, and show the count does not move. Then read the ref during render and describe two ways the result can be wrong, one of them specific to transitions.

3. Two ref callbacks. Register a list of DOM nodes in a Map, first with the pre-19 node => { if (node) … else … } form and then with the cleanup form. Show that both work, then delete an item from the middle of the list and say which form leaves a stale entry and why.

4. Remove three dependencies. Start with an Effect depending on an options object, a callback prop and a piece of state used only to compute the next state. Remove all three without suppressing the linter, and for each say which of the four moves you used.

5. Effect Event or dependency? For each value used by a chat-connection Effect, decide whether it belongs in the dependency array or inside a useEffectEvent: the room id, the server URL, the current theme, an onMessage callback prop, and the user's display name shown in a "connected" toast. Justify each in one sentence.

Solution

1. Four deletions.

filtered list        compute during render                       -1 render, -1 state
reset on record      <Form key={recordId} />                     -1 render, no flash
POST on submit       the submit handler / an Action              -1 state flag
notify the parent    call onChange in the handler that set state -1 render

Four Effects, four extra renders, and three pieces of state that existed only to trigger them. The reset case also removes a visible frame in which the old values were shown against the new record.

2. Refs are not reactive. Measured in §7.2: ten writes, zero renders.

Reading a ref during render can be wrong in two ways. It can be stale or null: on the first render the DOM ref is null, and on later ones it holds the node from the previous commit. And under a transition it can be inconsistent: React may render the component, abandon that render, and render again — the two passes can read different values, and the one that commits is not necessarily the one whose value you reasoned about. That is why react-hooks/refs treats a render-phase read as an error rather than a warning.

3. Two ref callbacks.

const map = useRef(new Map());

// pre-19: one function, two jobs
<li ref={node => { if (node) map.current.set(id, node); else map.current.delete(id); }} />

// 19: setup and cleanup, symmetric with useEffect
<li ref={node => { map.current.set(id, node); return () => map.current.delete(id); }} />

Both work for a simple mount and unmount. The pre-19 form leaves a stale entry when the same callback identity is reused across a list reorder: React calls it with null and then with the new node, but if the callback closes over an id that has moved, the delete and the set can target different keys and one entry is never removed. The cleanup form cannot make that mistake, because the cleanup is the closure created by the setup that added the entry — it deletes exactly what it added.

4. Three removals.

function Chat({ options, onMessage }) {
  const { url, room } = options;                      // 3. primitives out of the object
  const onMessageEvent = useEffectEvent(onMessage);   // 4. non-reactive callback
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = connect(url, room);
    c.on('message', m => { onMessageEvent(m); setCount(n => n + 1); });  // 2. updater
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [url, room]);
  return <b>{count}</b>;
}

The moves: read primitive values from objects for options; an updater function for count, which is now read by nobody; and useEffectEvent for onMessage, because the Effect wants the latest callback and must not reconnect when the parent re-renders with a new one. The connection survives every re-render that does not change the URL or the room, which is the goal.

5. Dependency or event.

room id           dependency   changing it must reconnect — that is the synchronization
server URL        dependency   same: a different server is a different connection
current theme     event        a colour must never drop a live connection
onMessage prop    event        the latest handler is wanted; its identity changes every render
display name      event        read when the toast fires, not a reason to reconnect

The test is one question: would you want to disconnect and reconnect when this changes? Yes means dependency. No, but I still want the current value, means Effect Event.

SECTION 8

Custom Hooks and Hook API Design

A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks (hooks are React's built-in functions such as useState and useEffect). That is the entire definition. There is no registration and no base class. React treats it exactly like any other function it calls during a render.

What makes them worth a section is what they are for, because the obvious answer is wrong. Custom hooks are not mainly a way to avoid repeating code: a repeated three-line effect is rarely worth pulling out. They are a way to give a piece of stateful behaviour a name. Then the component reads as a description of what it shows, rather than a description of how it stays up to date.

The test of a good custom hook is how much it improves the component that uses it. If useChatRoom(roomId) replaces twelve lines of connection management with one line that says what those lines were for, it has earned its place. If useNumber() replaces useState(0), it has not.

8.1 Extracting One

Start with a component doing two unrelated things, and pull one of them out.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

// the extracted hook: it owns the state AND the synchronization
function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => {
    const on = () => setIsOnline(true), off = () => setIsOnline(false);
    window.addEventListener('online', on);
    window.addEventListener('offline', off);
    return () => { window.removeEventListener('online', on); window.removeEventListener('offline', off); };
  }, []);
  return isOnline;
}

function StatusBar() { return <b>{useOnlineStatus() ? 'Online' : 'Offline'}</b>; }
function SaveButton() { return <i>{useOnlineStatus() ? 'Save' : 'Reconnecting…'}</i>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<><StatusBar /><SaveButton /></>); });
console.log('initial:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { window.dispatchEvent(new window.Event('offline')); });
console.log('offline:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { window.dispatchEvent(new window.Event('online')); });
console.log('online :', box.textContent);

initial: OnlineSave
offline: OfflineReconnecting…
online : OnlineSave

Two components, one behaviour, and neither component contains an addEventListener. The extraction moved the entire concern (state, effect and cleanup), not just the effect. Moving only the effect is the usual mistake: a hook that returns a setter for the caller to connect up has kept the two pieces tied together, and added a layer.

Hook names always start with use. This is not decoration. It is how the linter knows to apply the Rules of Hooks to the function, and how the compiler decides whether to treat it as a hook (§11.3, measured: a use-prefixed function that calls no hooks is not compiled as one). A function that calls no hooks should not be named use…, precisely so that a reader knows it can be called anywhere.

8.2 Sharing Logic, Not State

Sharing stateful logic is what a custom hook does. The property people get wrong most often follows from the word logic: custom hooks do not share state. Each place that calls the hook gets its own.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function useCounter(start) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(start);
  return [n, () => setN(v => v + 1)];
}
function Pair() {
  const [a, incA] = useCounter(0);
  const [b, incB] = useCounter(100);
  globalThis.incA = incA; globalThis.incB = incB;
  return <b>{a}/{b}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Pair />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.incA(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.incA(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.incB(); });
console.log(box.textContent);

2/101

Two calls to the same hook in the same component give two completely independent counters. A custom hook is inlined at each call site, as if its body were pasted there. The useState inside it takes a slot on the calling component's fiber (§5.4), and two calls take two slots. Nothing is shared except the code.

That has a direct consequence for design. If two components must see the same value, a custom hook will not do it. You need lifted state (§3.7), a context (§4.4) or an external store (§7.7). A hook that reads a context is the standard way to package that. From the outside it looks the same as any other hook, which is why you have to understand the difference rather than guess it.

The terms above, gathered: external store, sharing stateful logic and custom hooks do not share state.

8.3 Passing Reactive Values Between Hooks

A custom hook is called during render, so it receives fresh values every time. That means passing reactive values between hooks works exactly like passing props, and the hook stays synchronized automatically.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
