function useConnection(url, room) {          // takes reactive values as arguments
  useEffect(() => {
    log.push(`connect ${room}@${url}`);
    return () => { log.push(`disconnect ${room}`); };
  }, [url, room]);
}
function Chat() {
  const [url, setUrl] = useState('wss://a');
  const [room, setRoom] = useState('general');
  globalThis.setUrl = setUrl; globalThis.setRoom = setRoom;
  useConnection(url, room);
  return <b>{room}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Chat />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.setRoom('random'); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.setUrl('wss://b'); });
console.log(log.join(' | '));

connect general@wss://a | disconnect general | connect random@wss://a | disconnect random | connect random@wss://b

The hook synchronized again when either argument changed, and the caller wrote no dependency array at all. That is the real gain in convenience: the dependency management moved inside the hook, where it is written once and reviewed once, and the call site is a single line that names the intent.

Passing event handlers to custom hooks needs one more step. A handler prop is a new function on every render, so it would make the hook synchronize again constantly. Wrap it in useEffectEvent inside the hook (§7.6), so callers can pass an inline arrow function without thinking about it:

function useConnection(url, room, onMessage) {
  const onMessageEvent = useEffectEvent(onMessage);
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = connect(url, room);
    c.on('message', m => onMessageEvent(m));
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [url, room]);                      // the handler is deliberately not here
}

That is a hook doing its job: the awkward part is inside it, written once, and the caller writes useConnection(url, room, m => setMessages(ms => [...ms, m])).

One line each, for reference: passing props and passing event handlers to custom hooks.

8.4 What Makes a Good Hook

Concrete, high-level use case
useChatRoom, useOnlineStatus, useMediaQuery. The name describes what the application needs, not which React API it happens to use.
Not a lifecycle wrapper
useMount, useUpdateEffect, useEffectOnce are hooks that hide which values an effect depends on — they take the linter's input away and reintroduce the class-component model React deliberately left.
Owns a whole concern
State plus synchronization plus cleanup. A hook that returns a setter for the caller to wire up has not removed the coupling.
Returns the smallest useful thing
A value, or a pair, or a small object. A hook returning eleven fields is a component that has not been split.

The return shape follows one convention worth adopting:

  • a tuple when the caller will rename the values: const [n, setN] = useCounter(), because the names are the caller's choice, as with useState;
  • an object when the caller will destructure some of it: const { data, error } = useQuery(url), because any order would be arbitrary, and callers rarely want all of it.

Two hooks help the developer rather than changing behaviour.

  • useDebugValue( attaches a label to a custom hook in DevTools, for example useDebugValue(isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Offline'). It takes an optional formatter that is only called when someone actually inspects the value, so an expensive formatting step costs nothing in normal running.
  • And useId( generates an id that is the same on the server and in the browser, which is the one job Math.random() cannot do:
import { useId, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Field({ label }) {
  const id = useId();
  return <><label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label><input id={id} /></>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<><Field label="a" /><Field label="b" /></>); });
const ids = [...box.querySelectorAll('input')].map(i => i.id);
const fors = [...box.querySelectorAll('label')].map(l => l.htmlFor);
console.log('ids are distinct :', ids[0] !== ids[1]);
console.log('labels match     :', JSON.stringify(ids) === JSON.stringify(fors));

ids are distinct : true
labels match     : true

Generating ids for accessibility attributes is the whole use case: htmlFor/id, aria-describedby, aria-labelledby. useId is not for list keys. It produces one id per component instance, not one per item, and §1.8's rules still apply there. When one component needs several ids, derive them from one call: `${id}-hint`, `${id}-error`. identifierPrefix on createRoot and hydrateRoot adds a prefix to them, which matters when two React roots share a page.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: useId(, identifierPrefix and generating ids for accessibility attributes.

8.5 Hooks the Compiler and Linter Care About

Three rules from §5 apply specifically to custom hooks. They are worth repeating here, because a hook is where they are broken most often.

A hook must be called unconditionally, like any other. Wrapping a useEffect in an if inside a custom hook is the same violation as doing it in a component. The hook is inlined, so the caller's list of slots shifts.

Do not create hooks dynamically. react-hooks/component-hook-factories exists for functions that build a hook or a component during render. A factory that returns a fresh function on each render produces a new identity every time (§2.4), and the compiler cannot analyse it.

A hook that is not a hook should not be named like one. Measured in §11.3: a use-prefixed function that calls no hooks and reads no reactive values is not compiled as a hook. Naming a pure helper useFormat gives it the restrictions of the Rules of Hooks with none of the benefits, and stops callers from using it in a loop or a condition for no reason.

The other side is worth stating too: a function called during render that calls no hooks does not need the prefix. formatPrice(cents) is a plain function. You can call it anywhere and test it trivially, and the use prefix would be a lie about what it does.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the use prefix and react-hooks/component-hook-factories.

8.6 Building a Small Library

The last thing worth knowing is what a set of hooks looks like, because that is where design decisions add up. Here is a two-hook library where one hook is built on the other, which is the standard shape.

import { useState, useEffect, useCallback, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

// low-level: one concern, no opinion about what it is used for
function useInterval(callback, delay) {
  useEffect(() => {
    if (delay === null) return;               // null means paused
    const id = setInterval(callback, delay);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [callback, delay]);
}
// high-level: built on the first, and names an application concern
function useStopwatch(tickMs) {
  const [ms, setMs] = useState(0);
  const [running, setRunning] = useState(false);
  const tick = useCallback(() => setMs(v => v + tickMs), [tickMs]);
  useInterval(tick, running ? tickMs : null);
  return { ms, running, start: () => setRunning(true), stop: () => setRunning(false),
           reset: () => setMs(0) };
}

function Timer() {
  const w = useStopwatch(10);
  globalThis.w = w;
  return <b>{w.ms}ms {w.running ? 'running' : 'stopped'}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Timer />); });
console.log('initial :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.w.start(); });
console.log('started :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.w.stop(); globalThis.w.reset(); });
console.log('reset   :', box.textContent);

initial : 0ms stopped
started : 0ms running
reset   : 0ms stopped

Four things in that design are deliberate, and each is a decision you will make again.

useInterval takes null to mean paused, instead of offering a separate pause(). A single argument that can say "not running" keeps the hook declarative: the caller describes the state it wants, not the step to get there. It is the same principle as §3.6's declarative UI, applied to a hook's API.

tick is wrapped in useCallback because it is a dependency of useInterval's effect. Without it, every render of Timer would restart the interval. This is the ugly detail that belongs inside the library rather than at every call site. It is also the detail the compiler removes entirely (§11.11).

useStopwatch returns an object, because callers want ms and one or two of the controls, not all five in a fixed order.

The controls are recreated each render and that is fine: they are used in event handlers, not in dependency arrays. If a caller needed them stable, that is the moment to memoise. Not before, and not just in case.

What This Section Established

A custom hook is a use-prefixed function that calls hooks. Its purpose is to name a stateful behaviour, and its value is measured by what the calling component reads like afterwards.

Custom hooks share logic, not state — measured, two calls to useCounter in one component produced two independent counters, because the hook is inlined and each call takes its own slot on the caller's fiber. Shared state needs lifting, context or an external store.

Reactive values pass in as arguments and the hook re-synchronizes on its own — measured, a connection hook reconnected when either the room or the URL changed, with no dependency array at the call site. Handler arguments are wrapped in useEffectEvent inside the hook so callers can pass inline arrows.

Good hooks name a concrete concern and own it completely — state, effect and cleanup. Lifecycle wrappers like useMount are the anti-pattern, because they hide which values the effect depends on.

useId produces server-and-client-stable ids for accessibility attributes — measured, distinct per instance and matching between htmlFor and id — and is not for list keys. useDebugValue labels a hook in DevTools, with a formatter that only runs when inspected.

And the prefix is a contract in both directions: a function with hooks in it must have it, and a function without them must not.

Exercises

1. Extract a whole concern. Take a component that subscribes to matchMedia, holds the result in state, and cleans up. Extract useMediaQuery(query) so that the component contains no addEventListener and no useEffect. Then use it twice in one component with different queries and show that the two are independent.

2. Prove the inlining. Call the same custom hook three times in one component, each with a different initial value, and show all three states independently. Then explain, in terms of the fiber's hook list, why a conditional call to that hook would break the component rather than the hook.

3. Fix a re-synchronizing hook. Write useConnection(url, room, onMessage) where onMessage is passed as an inline arrow. Show it reconnecting on every parent render. Fix it inside the hook, and say why fixing it at the call site with useCallback is worse.

4. Design two return shapes. Write the same hook twice, returning a tuple and returning an object. Give one caller for which each is clearly better, and state the rule you would put in a style guide.

5. Spot the bad hooks. For each of useMount, useToggle, usePrevious, useUpdateEffect, useDebounce and useFetch, say whether you would allow it in a codebase and why. For the ones you reject, give the thing to write instead.

Solution

1. useMediaQuery.

function useMediaQuery(query) {
  const [matches, setMatches] = useState(() => window.matchMedia(query).matches);
  useEffect(() => {
    const mql = window.matchMedia(query);
    const on = e => setMatches(e.matches);
    setMatches(mql.matches);            // re-sync in case it changed before we subscribed
    mql.addEventListener('change', on);
    return () => mql.removeEventListener('change', on);
  }, [query]);
  return matches;
}

Two calls with different queries give two independent booleans, for the §8.2 reason. Note the lazy initialiser (§3.3) and the re-sync inside the effect: between the first render and the effect running, the media query can already have changed.

useSyncExternalStore (§7.7) is arguably the better implementation of this exact hook, because matchMedia is an external store — worth writing both and comparing.

2. The inlining. Measured in §8.2: 2/101 from two independent counters.

A conditional call breaks the component, not the hook, because the hook has no hook list of its own — its useState occupies a slot on the calling component's fiber. Skipping the call removes that slot, so every hook declared after it in the component shifts up by one and React reports the previous-versus-next table from §5.4. The hook is fine; the caller's list is corrupted.

3. The re-synchronizing hook.

// inside the hook — correct
function useConnection(url, room, onMessage) {
  const onMessageEvent = useEffectEvent(onMessage);
  useEffect(() => {
    const c = connect(url, room);
    c.on('message', onMessageEvent);
    return () => c.disconnect();
  }, [url, room]);
}

Fixing it at the call site with useCallback is worse for three reasons: every caller has to know to do it, every caller has to get the dependency array right, and a single caller who forgets reintroduces the bug for everyone. The hook's contract should be "pass any function"; making that true is the hook author's job.

4. Return shapes.

const [open, setOpen] = useDisclosure(false);       // tuple: caller renames freely
const { data, error, isLoading } = useQuery(url);   // object: caller takes a subset

The style-guide rule: return a tuple when there are at most two values and the caller will always want both under their own names; return an object otherwise. The failure mode of a tuple with four entries is const [, , , reset] = useThing(), which is unreadable and breaks silently when the order changes.

5. Six hooks.

useMount        REJECT   hides the dependency array; write useEffect(..., []) and mean it
useToggle       ALLOW    tiny but names a real thing, and cannot hide a dependency
usePrevious     ALLOW    with care: a legitimate ref pattern that is easy to get wrong once
useUpdateEffect REJECT   "skip the first run" is a lifecycle wrapper; usually the sign of
                         derived state that belongs in render (§7.1)
useDebounce     ALLOW    a real concern with an external resource (a timer) and a cleanup
useFetch        DEPENDS  fine as a thin wrapper you own; a poor substitute for a data
                         library, since it will not have caching, de-duplication,
                         retries or the race guard from §6.6 unless you write them

The pattern in the rejections: both hide which values an effect depends on, which is the one thing the dependency array exists to make visible and the one thing the linter needs in order to help.

SECTION 9

Events and DOM Components

React's host components are the built-in tags such as <div> and <input>. They look like HTML, and they are not HTML. <input> in JSX is a React component named input that renders an <input> element. This section is about the differences between the two: how it handles events, how it manages its value, and what its attributes are called.

The differences exist for one reason. React owns the DOM (§2.3). Anything that lets the DOM hold state React does not know about creates a second source of truth, two places that can disagree about the same value. So React:

  • intercepts events;
  • takes over form values;
  • renames attributes to their DOM-property spellings;
  • and hoists document-level elements (moves them into the page's <head>).

Each of those is a small surprise the first time, and a consequence of the same principle every time.

This section deliberately does not re-teach two things. The DOM API itself, and event propagation (how an event travels up through parent elements) in general, are covered in the JavaScript course. HTML semantics and ARIA are covered in the HTML course. What is here is what React does differently, and where that difference will surprise someone who knows the platform well.

9.1 Handlers Are Props

Adding event handlers means passing a function as a prop whose name is on followed by the capitalised event name.

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const seen = [];
function Toolbar({ onAction }) {
  return <button onClick={() => onAction('saved')}>Save</button>;
}
function App() { return <Toolbar onAction={what => seen.push('handled: ' + what)} />; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('button').dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log(seen.join(', '));

handled: saved

Two naming conventions carry real information.

  • Props that are handlers on host elements are onClick, onChange, onSubmit: the DOM event name, in camelCase.
  • Props that a component accepts and calls are named for what happened in that component's own terms: onAction, onSelect, onDismiss.

A <Toolbar onClick={…}> is ambiguous. Is it a click on the toolbar, or on the toolbar's one button? onAction says which.

Reading props in event handlers works because the handler is defined during render and captures that render's props (§2.12). That is also why an inline arrow function is the normal style rather than a bad habit: it captures the values the user is looking at right now, which is nearly always what you want.

One syntax trap costs people an afternoon. onClick={handleClick} passes the function; onClick={handleClick()} calls it during render and passes the result. The second one runs on every render, usually sets state, and produces "Too many re-renders". The rule is that the value after = must be a function. So if you need to pass arguments, wrap it: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}.

To have in hand before moving on: too many re-renders.

9.2 The Synthetic Event

React does not hand your handler the browser's event object. It hands you a react event object, a wrapper with the same interface that behaves the same in every browser.

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const seen = [];
function App() {
  return <button onClick={e => {
    seen.push('wrapper: ' + e.constructor.name);
    seen.push('native: ' + e.nativeEvent.constructor.name);
    seen.push('currentTarget: ' + e.currentTarget.tagName);
    seen.push('target: ' + e.target.tagName);
  }}>go</button>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('button').dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log(seen.join(' | '));

wrapper: SyntheticBaseEvent | native: MouseEvent | currentTarget: BUTTON | target: BUTTON

A synthetic event implements the standard interface (type, target, currentTarget, preventDefault, stopPropagation, bubbles, and the properties for each kind of event, like clientX or key) and smooths over the differences between browsers. nativeEvent is the real underlying event, for when you need something React does not expose.

target versus currentTarget is the distinction to keep clear. target is where the event started. currentTarget is the element whose handler is running. In a list with one handler on the parent, target is the row that was clicked, and currentTarget is the <ul>.

One historical note, worth knowing because old advice lingers. React used to pool synthetic events: it reused the object and emptied its properties after the handler returned. So reading e.target inside a setTimeout gave null, and the fix was e.persist(). Pooling was removed in React 17. The event object is now an ordinary object you may keep, and e.persist() still exists but does nothing. Any code calling it can drop the call.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: React event object.

9.3 Delegation at the Root

React does not attach a listener to your <button>. It attaches listeners to the root container (the element you passed to createRoot), and works out which component's handler to run from the event's target. That is event delegation at the root container, and you can observe it:

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const seen = [];
globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => {
  createRoot(box).render(<button onClick={() => seen.push('react handler')}>go</button>);
});
const btn = box.querySelector('button');
btn.addEventListener('click', () => seen.push('direct listener'));

await act(async () => { btn.dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true })); });
console.log('bubbling click    :', seen.join(', ')); seen.length = 0;
await act(async () => { btn.dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: false })); });
console.log('non-bubbling click:', seen.join(', ') || 'nothing');

bubbling click    : direct listener, react handler
non-bubbling click: direct listener

The second line is the proof. A click that does not bubble reached the element's own listener and never reached React's handler, because the event never travelled up to the root container, where React is listening. Nothing is attached to the button itself.

Three practical consequences.

Rendering into multiple roots isolates their events. Two createRoot calls have two places that listen, so stopPropagation in one cannot affect the other.

Mixing React with non-React listeners needs care about order. A listener added directly to an element runs when the event is at that element. React's runs when the event reaches the root, which is later. So stopPropagation in the direct listener stops React's handler from running at all. That is the usual explanation for "my onClick stopped working after I added a third-party library".

React sets a no-op onclick property on elements with handlers. It is a workaround for older iOS Safari, which does not fire click events for elements that are not normally clickable and have no onclick. It is harmless, and worth recognising if you inspect an element and wonder what noop is doing there.

In summary, the vocabulary here is event delegation at the root container.

9.4 Propagation, Capture and Default

By default, handlers receive events during the bubble phase (on the way back up from the target). A prop ending in Capture receives them during the capture phase (on the way down).

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const order = [];
function App() {
  return (
    <div onClickCapture={() => order.push('div capture')}
         onClick={() => order.push('div bubble')}>
      <button onClickCapture={() => order.push('button capture')}
              onClick={() => order.push('button bubble')}>go</button>
    </div>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('button').dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log(order.join(' -> '));

div capture -> button capture -> button bubble -> div bubble

Down through the ancestors, then back up: the standard DOM order, reproduced faithfully by the synthetic system even though only the root has a real listener.

Event propagation (the event travelling through the tree) in the synthetic system matches the DOM's, and the two methods that interrupt it behave as they do in the DOM.

  • stopPropagation( stops the event travelling any further, so an inner handler can prevent an outer one from running.
  • preventDefault( cancels the browser's own behaviour (submitting a form, following a link, ticking a checkbox), and does not stop propagation.

The two are independent, and often confused: a submit handler that only calls stopPropagation still navigates away.

onClickCapture and the other capture props are for when an ancestor must see the event first. Examples: closing a menu before an inner button acts, or an analytics layer recording every click, whatever stops propagation later.

React's preferred alternative is worth naming, because it avoids the question entirely: pass a handler down rather than intercepting on the way up. If a parent needs to know about a child's click, give the child an onSelect prop. The parent then hears about exactly the events it asked for, and no unrelated click inside the child can trigger it.

What to carry forward from this subsection: stopPropagation(, preventDefault( and capture phase.

The terms above, gathered: event propagation.

9.5 The style Prop

The style prop takes an object, not a string, and React writes it to the element's style property.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <div style={{ marginTop: 10, zIndex: 3, opacity: 0.5, width: '3em', backgroundColor: 'red' }} />
));

<div style="margin-top:10px;z-index:3;opacity:0.5;width:3em;background-color:red"></div>

Three behaviours in one line of output. Keys are camelCased, and converted to their dashed CSS names. A number is given px: marginTop: 10 became 10px. But a number for a unitless property is not: zIndex and opacity came out bare, because React knows the list of properties that take plain numbers (zIndex, opacity, flex, lineHeight, fontWeight, order and about forty others).

style is for values that really are dynamic and different for each instance: a computed position, a progress width, a colour from data. Everything static belongs in a stylesheet or a class, for the reasons the CSS course covers. An inline style cannot be overridden without !important, does not take part in the cascade, and is repeated in the HTML for every instance.

Custom properties (CSS variables) work, and they are the escape hatch that keeps everything else in CSS. style={{ '--progress': pct }} sets a variable a stylesheet can use, so the dynamic value crosses over without the styling coming with it.

9.6 dangerouslySetInnerHTML

React escapes every string it renders, turning characters like < into harmless text. That is what makes <p>{userInput}</p> safe by default. dangerouslySetInnerHTML is the deliberate exception.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

const untrusted = '<img src=x onerror="steal()">';
console.log('escaped :', renderToStaticMarkup(<p>{untrusted}</p>));
console.log('raw     :', renderToStaticMarkup(<p dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: untrusted }} />));

escaped : <p>&lt;img src=x onerror=&quot;steal()&quot;&gt;</p>
raw     : <p><img src=x onerror="steal()"></p>

The first is harmless text. The second is a live <img> with an event handler. If untrusted came from a user, that is a cross-site scripting vulnerability: someone else's script running in your page.

The API is awkward on purpose: the long name, and the { __html: … } wrapper, which means you cannot pass a string by accident. Its legitimate uses are narrow: rendering HTML from a content pipeline you trust, or from Markdown you converted yourself. Every one of them should pass through a sanitiser such as DOMPurify at the point where the HTML enters your system, not at the point of rendering.

suppressContentEditableWarning and suppressHydrationWarning (§16.9) are the two other opt-outs in the same family. They are named to stand out, and they are correct only when you can say exactly why you need them.

One line each, for reference: suppressContentEditableWarning.

9.7 Form Elements

Form controls are where React differs from HTML the most, because they are the elements that hold their own state.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Form() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('a');
  const [choice, setChoice] = useState('two');
  const [agreed, setAgreed] = useState(true);
  globalThis.setText = setText;
  return (
    <form>
      <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
      <textarea value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
      <select value={choice} onChange={e => setChoice(e.target.value)}>
        <option value="one">One</option><option value="two">Two</option>
      </select>
      <input type="checkbox" checked={agreed} onChange={e => setAgreed(e.target.checked)} />
      <progress value={0.4} />
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Form />); });
console.log('select value:', box.querySelector('select').value);
console.log('textarea    :', box.querySelector('textarea').value);
console.log('checkbox    :', box.querySelector('input[type=checkbox]').checked);
console.log('server html :', renderToStaticMarkup(<textarea defaultValue="hi" />));

select value: two
textarea    : a
checkbox    : true
server html : <textarea>hi</textarea>

Four divergences from HTML in that one component.

<textarea> takes a value prop, instead of having its content as children. That is why the second line of that output reads a and not hi: it is the component's textarea, driven by text, not the standalone one on the last line. HTML puts the initial text between the tags; React would have to treat that as both content and value, so it does not. Note that the server output on the last line does render it as a child, because that is what HTML requires.

<select> takes value, and <option> does not take selected. HTML marks the chosen option; React sets the value on the parent, which gives one source of truth instead of n. For select multiple, add the multiple attribute. With multiple, the value is an array: value={['a','b']}.

A checkbox uses checked, not value, and defaultChecked is the uncontrolled form. value on a checkbox is the string submitted when it is ticked, which is a different thing entirely. The handler reads e.target.checked.

<progress value> is not controlled at all. It is a display element that the user cannot change, so React writes the attribute and there is nothing to control.

The one warning everyone meets, "A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled", comes from value={x} where x starts as undefined. React sees no value prop on the first render, decides the input is uncontrolled, and then sees one later. The fix is value={x ?? ''}.

One more difference, in behaviour rather than naming: onChange fires on every keystroke, not when the field loses focus. React's onChange is connected to the DOM's input event, not to the DOM's change event, and that is deliberate: a controlled input needs to hear every character. React also offers onInput itself, which fires at the same moment. It exists so that code moving over from plain DOM handlers can keep the name it had. If you really want the DOM's change behaviour, onBlur is what you mean. Between the two, prefer onChange: onInput exists for compatibility and has no advantage in new code.

The jumping-caret bug is worth knowing before it happens to you. If onChange transforms the value (upper-casing it, removing characters, formatting a phone number), React re-renders with a value whose length differs from what the user typed, and the browser moves the caret (the text cursor) to the end. The two answers are formatting when the field loses focus, or managing selectionStart yourself.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: onChange fires on every keystroke, defaultChecked and select multiple.

9.8 Custom Elements

A custom html element, one whose tag name contains a hyphen, is passed through by React instead of being treated as unknown.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <my-widget data-id="7" aria-label="Widget" some-attr="x" />
));

<my-widget data-id="7" aria-label="Widget" some-attr="x"></my-widget>

Every attribute went through with the spelling given, including one that is not a valid DOM property. React 19 improved this a lot. It now checks whether the custom element has a matching property, and sets that if so, falling back to an attribute otherwise. So an object or an array can be passed to a custom element that declares a property for it, instead of being turned into the string [object Object].

Two things still do not cross over.

  • Custom events do not become on* props, so listening for a <my-widget>'s own event needs a ref and addEventListener.
  • React's synthetic system does not see events that a custom element sends inside its shadow root (its private internal DOM), unless they are composed and bubbling.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: custom HTML element.

9.9 Portals

createPortal( renders children into a different DOM node, while keeping them in the same React tree.

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';

const seen = [];
globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const app = document.getElementById('app');
const elsewhere = document.createElement('div');
elsewhere.id = 'elsewhere';
document.body.appendChild(elsewhere);

function App() {
  return (
    <div onClick={() => seen.push('caught by the React parent')}>
      inline
      {createPortal(<button>in the portal</button>, elsewhere)}
    </div>
  );
}
await act(async () => { createRoot(app).render(<App />); });
console.log('app       :', app.innerHTML);
console.log('elsewhere :', elsewhere.innerHTML);
await act(async () => {
  elsewhere.querySelector('button').dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log('click     :', seen.join(', '));

app       : <div>inline</div>
elsewhere : <button>in the portal</button>
click     : caught by the React parent

The button is in a different part of the document — outside the <div> entirely — and clicking it still ran the <div>'s onClick. Event bubbling through a portal follows the React tree, not the DOM tree, because propagation is computed from the component hierarchy (§9.3).

That combination is exactly what a modal dialog needs. The DOM position escapes the parent's overflow: hidden, its z-index stacking context and its transform, so the dialog can cover the page. And the React position keeps context, state and event handling intact, so the dialog is still a child of the component that opened it.

The same mechanism renders React into markup React does not own, such as a widget mounted into a page produced by a server-side template, without a second root and without losing the shared tree.

Portals do not change accessibility. Focus management, role="dialog", aria-modal and returning focus on close are all still your job. <dialog> with showModal() handles several of them natively, and §7.3's ref patterns are how you drive it.

To have in hand before moving on: createPortal(, modal dialog and event bubbling through a portal.

What This Section Established

Handlers are props: onClick on a host element, and a name describing what happened for a component's own callback. onClick={f()} calls during render — the value must be a function.

The event object is a synthetic wrapper with nativeEvent underneath it, and pooling was removed in React 17, so e.persist() is a no-op that old code can drop.

React attaches nothing to your elements; it listens at the root container. Measured: a non-bubbling click ran the element's own listener and never reached React's handler. Capture and bubble ordering is faithful — div capture -> button capture -> button bubble -> div bubble — and a third-party listener that stops propagation stops React entirely.

style takes an object, camelCases the keys, adds px to numbers and does not add it to unitless properties — measured, margin-top:10px beside z-index:3 and opacity:0.5.

dangerouslySetInnerHTML is the one place React does not escape — measured, the same string rendered as inert text and as a live <img onerror>.

Form controls diverge from HTML in four ways: <textarea value>, <select value> with no selected on options, checked for checkboxes, and <progress> not being controlled at all. value={x ?? ''} prevents the uncontrolled-to-controlled warning.

Portals put children elsewhere in the DOM and leave them where they were in the React tree — measured, a click on a button outside the parent's DOM subtree still ran the parent's onClick.

Exercises

1. Prove the delegation. Attach a direct listener and a React handler to the same button, then dispatch a bubbling and a non-bubbling click. Explain the difference. Then add a direct listener that calls stopPropagation and show React's handler never running.

2. Order the phases. Nest three elements with both capture and bubble handlers and predict the six-entry order before running it. Then add stopPropagation at the middle element's capture handler and predict again.

3. Break a controlled input three ways. Produce the uncontrolled-to-controlled warning, the caret-jumping bug, and an input that ignores typing entirely. Give the fix for each in one line.

4. Style versus class. Render the same component with a computed width as an inline style and as a CSS custom property consumed by a class. Show the markup for both, and give two things the second can do that the first cannot.

5. Portal a dialog. Render a dialog through a portal from inside a container with overflow: hidden. Show that it escapes the container in the DOM, that a click inside it reaches the React parent's handler, and name three accessibility responsibilities the portal did not take care of.

Solution

1. Delegation. Measured in §9.3: the bubbling click ran both handlers, the non-bubbling one ran only the direct listener.

Adding btn.addEventListener('click', e => e.stopPropagation()) stops React's handler completely, because the event is halted at the button and never reaches the root container. This is the exact failure mode when a chart library, a drag-and-drop library or an analytics snippet attaches its own listeners — and the symptom is "onClick works everywhere except inside this widget", which points at the widget rather than at the mechanism.

2. Six entries.

outer capture -> middle capture -> inner capture ->
inner bubble  -> middle bubble  -> outer bubble

With stopPropagation in the middle element's capture handler:

outer capture -> middle capture

Two entries. Stopping during capture prevents the event ever reaching the target, so the inner element's own handler never runs — which is what makes capture the right phase for a "swallow all clicks while this overlay is open" guard, and the wrong phase for almost everything else.

3. Three broken inputs.

<input value={maybeUndefined} onChange={onChange} />   // uncontrolled -> controlled
<input value={v} onChange={e => setV(e.target.value.toUpperCase())} />   // caret jumps
<input value={v} />                                    // read-only: no onChange at all

Fixes: value={maybeUndefined ?? ''}; format on blur rather than on change (or set selectionStart after the update); and add an onChange, or say you meant it with readOnly.

The third is worth dwelling on: React logs "You provided a value prop to a form field without an onChange handler", and the input genuinely will not accept typing — the DOM value changes and React overwrites it on the next render.

4. Style versus class.

inline    <div style="width:37%"></div>
variable  <div class="bar" style="--pct:37%"></div>   + .bar { width: var(--pct) }

Two things the second can do: respond to media and container queries, because the width now lives in a stylesheet where @media and @container can override it; and be themed or overridden by a later rule, because an inline style loses only to !important while a class participates in the cascade normally. A third, in practice: the value appears once in the CSS instead of once per instance in the HTML.

5. The dialog.

The measurement is §9.9's: the button lives in a different DOM subtree and its click still reaches the React parent. Placed inside overflow: hidden, an inline dialog would be clipped and a portalled one is not.

Three things the portal did not do: focus management (moving focus into the dialog on open and returning it to the trigger on close), a focus trap (Tab must not escape to the page behind), and the semantics — role="dialog", aria-modal="true", a labelled title, and Escape to close. Native <dialog> with showModal() provides the trap, the backdrop and Escape; the labelling and the focus return are still yours.

SECTION 10

Performance: What Re-renders, and Measuring It

React applications are usually fast without any effort. The ones that are not are usually slow for a reason that no amount of memo will fix. So this section starts with the diagnosis and only then reaches the tools. Doing it the other way round is how codebases end up with two hundred useCallback calls and the same frame rate they had before.

There are exactly three reasons a React application feels slow, and they need different fixes.

Too much work per render
One component does something genuinely expensive — parsing, sorting fifty thousand rows, a synchronous layout read. Fix the work: useMemo, a better algorithm, or move it out of render.
Too many components rendering
Each render is cheap and there are three thousand of them. Fix the fan-out: move state down, pass children, memo, or the compiler (§11).
The work is at the wrong time
The total is fine but it lands in the frame where the user pressed a key. Fix the priority: transitions and deferred values (§12).

Applying the wrong fix is worse than doing nothing, because each fix has a real cost. memo adds a comparison to every render, useMemo adds a cache to every render, and a transition adds a render. Measure first is not a platitude here. Measuring is how you tell which of the three problems you have.

10.1 What Re-renders

Here is the default from §2.2 again, because everything else builds on it: when a component re-renders, React re-renders its entire subtree, whether or not props changed. There is no automatic comparison.

That gives you one useful rule for diagnosis. When something re-renders more than you expect, the cause is always one of four things. Check them in this order:

Its state changed. Look at the component itself.

Its parent re-rendered. Look upward. This is the common case, and the one people forget.

A context it reads changed (§4.7). Note that memo does not stop this.

Its key changed, so it did not re-render at all: it remounted, starting from scratch (§2.6).

10.2 memo

react.memo wraps a component and skips calling it when its props are shallow-equal to last time (each prop the same as before).

import { useState, memo, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let plain = 0, memoed = 0;
function Plain({ n }) { plain++; return <b>{n}</b>; }
const Memoed = memo(function Memoed({ n }) { memoed++; return <i>{n}</i>; });

function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  const [other, setOther] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bumpOther = () => setOther(v => v + 1);
  globalThis.bumpN = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <><Plain n={n} /><Memoed n={n} /><u>{other}</u></>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
plain = memoed = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpOther(); });
console.log('unrelated state changed -> Plain:', plain, '| Memoed:', memoed);
plain = memoed = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpN(); });
console.log('n changed               -> Plain:', plain, '| Memoed:', memoed);

unrelated state changed -> Plain: 1 | Memoed: 0
n changed               -> Plain: 1 | Memoed: 1

That is the whole behaviour. When n was unchanged, memo skipped the call; when it changed, it did not.

The comparison is shallow: each prop is compared with Object.is, by identity rather than by contents. That one fact decides when memo works and when it is just decoration, and it leads straight to §10.4.

arePropsEqual is an optional second argument for a custom comparison. It is almost always a mistake. A deep comparison can cost more than the render it saves. And returning true wrongly produces a component that never updates: a bug with no error and no obvious cause. If you need it, the props are probably wrong.

Skipping re-rendering of components is what it buys. It is worth it when all of these hold:

  • the component is expensive, or it sits at the top of a large subtree;
  • its props really stay the same across most of its parent's re-renders;
  • and you have a measurement.

When it is not. It is not worth it when its props change every time anyway (then the comparison is pure cost), or when it is a leaf rendering three DOM nodes. And if its parent passes it a fresh object or callback on every render, memo is doing nothing at all: minimizing props changes with useMemo and useCallback comes first, which is §10.4.

And if the React Compiler is on, most of this is already handled (§11.11). A cached element is equal by reference, and the reconciler skips the subtree without any wrapper.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: React.memo, arePropsEqual, skipping re-rendering of components and minimizing props changes.

10.3 Move State Down, and Pass children Up

Here are two fixes to the structure that need no memoisation at all. Both are better than memo when they apply.

Move state down. If only one leaf uses a piece of state, the state belongs in that leaf, or in a small component wrapping it. It does not belong in the parent that renders everything else.

Pass content as children. Elements created by a parent stay the same objects across that component's re-renders, so React skips them. §4.8 measured this: a provider whose subtree came in as children re-rendered twice for its own state, and re-rendered its children zero times.

import { useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let heavy = 0;
function Heavy() { heavy++; return <b>heavy</b>; }

function Inline() {                            // renders Heavy itself
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bumpInline = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <div>{n}<Heavy /></div>;
}
function Wrapper({ children }) {               // receives Heavy from above
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bumpWrapper = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <div>{n}{children}</div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const r1 = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { r1.render(<Inline />); });
heavy = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpInline(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpInline(); });
console.log('rendered inline   -> Heavy rendered', heavy, 'time(s)');

const r2 = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { r2.render(<Wrapper><Heavy /></Wrapper>); });
heavy = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpWrapper(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.bumpWrapper(); });
console.log('passed as children -> Heavy rendered', heavy, 'time(s)');

rendered inline   -> Heavy rendered 2 time(s)
passed as children -> Heavy rendered 0 time(s)

Two state changes, two re-renders of the wrapper, and zero re-renders of the expensive child, with no memo, no useMemo and no comparison function. The <Heavy /> element was created once, outside Wrapper. So on each re-render Wrapper returned the identical element object, and React's reconciler saw nothing to do.

This is the highest-value performance technique in React. It is a design change rather than an optimisation, and components that take children are more reusable anyway. Reach for it before reaching for memo.

10.4 useMemo, useCallback and Referential Equality

useMemo( caches a computed value between renders; useCallback( caches a function. They are the same mechanism (useCallback(fn, deps) is useMemo(() => fn, deps)), and they have two separate jobs worth keeping apart.

Job one: skip an expensive calculation. This is what useMemo is named for, and it is the rarer case. "Expensive" means milliseconds, measured. Sorting fifty items is not expensive; parsing a megabyte of Markdown is.

Job two: keep a reference stable so that something downstream can compare it. This is the common case, and it is the one that makes memo work at all.

Referential equality (being the very same object) is the reason. Every render creates new objects, arrays and functions, and Object.is compares them by identity. So a prop that holds "the same data" is a different value every time:

import { useState, useMemo, useCallback, memo, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let renders = 0;
const Child = memo(function Child({ config, onPick }) { renders++; return <b>.</b>; });

function App({ stable }) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bump = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  const fresh = { rows: 10 };
  const freshFn = () => {};
  const cached = useMemo(() => ({ rows: 10 }), []);
  const cachedFn = useCallback(() => {}, []);
  return <><i>{n}</i>
    <Child config={stable ? cached : fresh} onPick={stable ? cachedFn : freshFn} /></>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const stable of [false, true]) {
  const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
  await act(async () => { root.render(<App stable={stable} />); });
  renders = 0;
  await act(async () => { globalThis.bump(); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.bump(); });
  console.log(stable ? 'memoised props:' : 'fresh props   :', renders, 'child render(s)');
}

fresh props   : 2 child render(s)
memoised props: 0 child render(s)

The memo on Child did nothing at all in the first run. A new config object and a new onPick function on every render meant the shallow comparison failed every time, so the wrapper cost a comparison and saved nothing. That is the most common way memo ends up as decoration, and it is why the three tools work as a set or not at all: memo on the child, useMemo on the object props, useCallback on the function props. One without the others is overhead.

That is exactly the argument for the React Compiler (§11.11). It does all three, correctly, with no dependency arrays to maintain, and §11 measured its output as byte-identical to the hand-written version.

In summary, the vocabulary here is an expensive calculation.

10.5 The Profiler Component

<profiler> measures a subtree programmatically, in any build, without opening DevTools.

import { Profiler, useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const records = [];
function onRender(id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime) {
  records.push({ id, phase,
    types: [actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime].map(v => typeof v).join(', ') });
}
function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bump = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  return <Profiler id="app" onRender={onRender}><b>{n}</b></Profiler>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.bump(); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.bump(); });
console.log('phases   :', records.map(r => r.phase).join(', '));
console.log('id       :', records[0].id);
console.log('arg types:', records[0].types);

phases   : mount, update, update
id       : app
arg types: number, number, number, number

The onRender callback receives six arguments, and the four numeric ones are the measurement:

actualDuration
Milliseconds spent rendering this subtree this time. Should fall towards zero on repeat renders as memoisation takes effect — if it does not, nothing is being skipped.
baseDuration
What it would cost with no memoisation at all. The ratio actual / base is how much your optimisations are actually buying.
startTime
When React began this render.
commit time
commitTime: when it committed. Renders that commit together share it, which is how you group a batch.

phase is 'mount', 'update' or 'nested-update', and the third is worth watching for on its own. It means a component set state during the commit, forcing another render before the browser could paint. That is a cascade, and it is usually §7.1's derived-state mistake.

Profilers can be nested, and id tells them apart. So wrapping several regions with different ids gives you a breakdown per region from one callback. Note that <Profiler> adds real overhead: use it to answer a question and then take it out, or switch it on only behind a flag.

What to carry forward from this subsection: onRender callback.

10.6 DevTools

The React Developer Tools browser extension is where everyday performance work happens, and three of its features are worth knowing by name.

The Components tab shows the render tree (§1.12) with each component's props, state and hooks. Its "highlight updates when components render" option is the fastest possible answer to "what is re-rendering?": you type one character and watch half the screen flash.

The Profiler tab records a session and gives a flame graph for each commit. Each component is coloured by how long it took and labelled with why it rendered: changed props, changed state, changed context, or parent rendered. That last label settles most arguments, because "parent rendered" points somewhere other than where you were looking.

React Performance tracks are the newer feature. With a profiling build, React writes its own rows into the browser's normal performance timeline, next to the network and main-thread rows.

  • The Scheduler track shows what React was working on, and at what priority.
  • The Components track shows individual renders.
  • And there is a special marker for a cascading update: a render set off by a commit.

Seeing React's work in the same timeline as the browser's is what lets you say whether a long frame was React's fault or a layout thrash. Between the flame graph's labels and these tracks, why did this render stops being a question you reason about and becomes one you look up.

react-devtools also has a standalone package for React Native and for environments that are not a browser. It is also what shows the "Memo ✨" badge on components the compiler optimised (§11.9).

The terms above, gathered: React Developer Tools, Profiler tab, React Performance tracks, cascading update and changed props.

One line each, for reference: why did this render.

10.7 What Optimisation Cannot Fix

A component that is slow on its own. React can pause between components, not inside one (§12.12). A component body that takes 200 ms blocks for 200 ms at every priority. Split it, or move the work out of render.

A bad algorithm. useMemo around an O(n²) calculation (one whose work grows with the square of the input) makes it run less often. The first render still pays for it, and so does every render where the input changed.

Too many DOM nodes. Rendering ten thousand rows is slow because ten thousand rows is slow. The answer is windowing, rendering only the fifty rows that are visible, and no React feature replaces it.

Network latency. No render optimisation makes a request faster. §13 and §16 change when the user sees things; they do not change how long the data takes.

Layout thrashing. Reading a layout property after writing to the DOM forces the browser to recalculate the layout immediately (a reflow). Doing that in a loop is quadratic. This is a browser cost, not a React one, and it shows up in the Profiler as time React did not spend rendering.

A last word on the order of work, because it is where most effort is wasted. Measure, fix the biggest thing, measure again. In practice the biggest thing is usually structural: state that sits too high in the tree, a context whose value changes on every keystroke, a list that is not windowed. Structural fixes cost nothing at runtime. Memoisation is the fix for what is left, and more and more it is the compiler's job rather than yours.

What This Section Established

Three causes of slowness, three different fixes: too much work in one render, too many components rendering, or the work landing at the wrong time. Applying the wrong one adds cost and changes nothing.

React re-renders the whole subtree by default. When something renders unexpectedly, check in order: its own state, its parent, a context it reads, or a changed key.

memo skips a component whose props are shallow-equal — measured, zero renders on an unrelated state change and one when the prop actually changed. arePropsEqual is almost always a mistake.

Passing content as children beats memo where it applies: measured, two state changes in a wrapper re-rendered an expensive child zero times, with no memoisation anywhere, because the element was created outside and was reference-equal.

memo without stable props is pure overhead — measured, a memo'd child re-rendered on both updates because its object and function props were fresh each time, and dropped to zero when they were memoised. The three tools work as a set, which is the argument for letting the compiler do all three.

<Profiler> reports actualDuration against baseDuration, and their ratio is what your optimisations bought. A nested-update phase means a render caused by a commit.

And the limits are real: a slow component, a bad algorithm, too many DOM nodes, network latency and layout thrashing are all outside what memoisation can reach.

Exercises

1. Find the fan-out. Build a tree where a state change at the top re-renders forty components, instrument every one with a counter, then fix it three ways — moving state down, passing children, and memo — and report the counts for each. Say which fix you would ship and why.

2. Make memo useless. Wrap a child in memo and pass it an inline object and an inline arrow. Show that it re-renders every time. Fix it with useMemo and useCallback, show it drop to zero, then delete the memo and show that the two caches now buy nothing. Explain the dependency between the three.

3. Read the ratio. Wrap a subtree in <Profiler> and record actualDuration and baseDuration for a mount and five updates, with and without memoisation. State what a ratio near 1 tells you, and what a ratio near 0 tells you about the last update.

4. Catch a cascade. Write a component that sets state in an effect from a prop, and show <Profiler> reporting a nested-update phase. Then remove the effect per §7.1 and show the phase disappearing along with one render.

5. Optimise the wrong thing. Take a list of five thousand rows that is slow. Apply memo to the row component and measure. Apply windowing and measure. Report both numbers and say what the first one taught you about where the time was going.

Solution

1. The fan-out.

baseline                 40 renders per keystroke
move state down          1  (only the component that owns it)
pass children            1  for the wrapper, 0 for the passed subtree
memo on every child      40 comparisons, then 0 renders — if props are stable

Ship moving the state down, if the state genuinely belongs to one leaf. It is the only fix with no runtime cost at all, it makes the data flow easier to read, and it cannot be undone by someone later passing a fresh object. memo everywhere is the most expensive of the three and the most fragile.

2. Making memo useless. Measured in §10.4: 2 renders with fresh props, 0 with memoised props.

Deleting the memo while keeping the two caches gives 2 renders again, because nothing is comparing the props any more. The dependency is symmetric: memo is the only thing that reads the stability, and useMemo/useCallback are the only things that provide it. Either alone is overhead — a comparison that always fails, or a cache nobody consults.

3. The ratio.

actual / base near 1 means nothing is being skipped: every child re-rendered, and whatever memoisation is present is not engaging. Near 0 means almost the whole subtree was skipped and only a small part actually re-rendered.

The useful reading is the trend across updates. A mount necessarily has actual ≈ base; if update five still does, the optimisation is not working, and the Profiler tab's "why did this render" annotation is the next thing to look at.

4. The cascade.

useEffect(() => { setDerived(compute(prop)); }, [prop]);   // nested-update
const derived = compute(prop);                             // no extra render at all

The Effect version commits, then sets state, then commits again — <Profiler> reports update followed by nested-update, and the user briefly saw the pre-update value. Computing during render removes the second commit and the phase along with it.

5. Optimising the wrong thing.

memo on the row typically changes very little: the rows are re-rendering because the list re-rendered, and each row is cheap. The cost is five thousand Object.is comparisons instead of five thousand cheap renders — a saving that is real but small, on top of a DOM that still has five thousand rows in it.

Windowing changes the number of rows rendered and the number of DOM nodes, which is where the time actually was. The lesson from measuring the first attempt is that "many cheap renders" and "many DOM nodes" look identical from the outside and have completely different fixes — which is why §10 opens with the diagnosis rather than the tools.

SECTION 11

The React Compiler

Every optimisation in §10 has the same shape. You notice that something is recomputed or re-rendered when it did not need to be. You work out what it depends on. Then you write that dependency list down by hand in a useMemo, a useCallback or a memo. It works, but it is tedious, and the dependency lists rot: a refactor adds a variable, nobody updates the array, and the memo silently returns an out-of-date value or stops helping.

The React Compiler does that work at build time, before your code ever runs. It reads your components, works out what each value depends on, and produces code that caches each value in an array that belongs to the component. The auto-memoization it performs is that same work, done by machine. It is a Babel plugin (Babel is a tool that rewrites JavaScript during the build), it ships as babel-plugin-react-compiler, and it reached 1.0 in 2025. The version measured throughout this section is 1.0.0, against React 19.2.8.

This section is unusually concrete, because the compiler's output is readable, and reading it settles arguments that are otherwise had entirely on faith. Every listing below is the actual output of running the plugin on the code above it. If you take one thing from the section, take the measurement in §11.13: a component written with useMemo and useCallback, and the same component written with neither, compile to byte-identical output.

11.1 What Problem It Solves

By default React re-renders a subtree whenever an ancestor renders (§2.2), and rebuilds every object and function in a component body on every render. Most of the time that is fine. When it is not, the fix is memoisation (caching), and memoising by hand has three costs that have nothing to do with speed at runtime.

It is verbose. A component with four derived values and three callbacks gains seven wrappers and seven dependency arrays. The code that says what the component does is now a minority of the lines.

It is fragile. A dependency array repeats, by hand, something the compiler already knows. When the two disagree, which happens whenever anyone edits the body without re-reading the array, the result is a stale closure. That is the hardest kind of React bug to see, because nothing throws an error.

It is applied where people guess, not where it pays. Machine auto-memoization has no such bias: it memoises everything that can be memoised, and nothing else. Memoising a component whose props change on every render costs a comparison and saves nothing. Failing to memoise the one object that flows into a heavy memo subtree costs a whole re-render. People are poor at telling these apart, and nothing tells them when they got it wrong.

The compiler removes all three costs by doing the analysis mechanically. What it cannot do is fix a component that breaks the Rules of React. That limit is the reason §5 comes before this section rather than after it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: auto-memoization.

11.2 What It Emits

Start with the smallest possible example, and read the output line by line.

function Greeting({ name, items }) {
  const upper = name.toUpperCase();
  const visible = items.filter(i => i.done);
  return <ul title={upper}>{visible.map(i => <li key={i.id}>{i.text}</li>)}</ul>;
}

Running babel --plugins babel-plugin-react-compiler over that produces:

import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
function Greeting(t0) {
  const $ = _c(9);
  const { name, items } = t0;
  let t1;
  if ($[0] !== name) {
    t1 = name.toUpperCase();
    $[0] = name;
    $[1] = t1;
  } else {
    t1 = $[1];
  }
  const upper = t1;
  let t2;
  let t3;
  if ($[2] !== items || $[3] !== upper) {
    const visible = items.filter(_temp);
    t2 = upper;
    t3 = visible.map(_temp2);
    $[2] = items;
    $[3] = upper;
    $[4] = t2;
    $[5] = t3;
  } else {
    t2 = $[4];
    t3 = $[5];
  }
  let t4;
  if ($[6] !== t2 || $[7] !== t3) {
    t4 = <ul title={t2}>{t3}</ul>;
    $[6] = t2;
    $[7] = t3;
    $[8] = t4;
  } else {
    t4 = $[8];
  }
  return t4;
}
function _temp2(i_0) { return <li key={i_0.id}>{i_0.text}</li>; }
function _temp(i) { return i.done; }

Five things are going on, and none of them is magic.

_c(9) allocates a cache. c comes from react/compiler-runtime, and it is a hook. It returns an array of nine slots attached to this component's fiber (§2.11), which persists across renders exactly as useState does. Nine is the number of slots the compiler decided it needed: one for each cached value, plus one for each dependency it must remember.

Each computation is guarded by a comparison. if ($[0] !== name) is Object.is written as !==: recompute only when the input changed, otherwise read the cached result. This is useMemo, generated for you.

Values are grouped by shared dependencies. visible and upper are computed in one block, because the JSX needs both and the compiler found that recomputing them together is cheaper than two separate guards. Nobody does that kind of grouping by hand.

The JSX element itself is cached. t4 is the <ul> element. This is the part that matters most, and the part manual memoisation almost never does. When the element object is the very same one as last render's, React's reconciler can skip the entire subtree, without a memo wrapper anywhere.

The inner callbacks are hoisted out. _temp and _temp2 are now functions at module level, created once for the life of the program instead of once per render. A closure that captures nothing does not need to be a closure.

11.3 It Compiles Components and Hooks, Not Everything

By default the compiler runs in infer mode: it decides for itself what is a component and what is a hook. It is cautious, and the exact line it draws is worth knowing.

function helper(xs) { return xs.map(x => x * 2); }
function Widget({ xs }) { return <b>{helper(xs).join(',')}</b>; }
function useThing(a) { return { a }; }

Compiled with the default configuration, only one of the three changes:

import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
function helper(xs) {
  return xs.map(x => x * 2);
}
function Widget(t0) {
  const $ = _c(4);
  const { xs } = t0;
  let t1;
  if ($[0] !== xs) {
    t1 = helper(xs).join(",");
    $[0] = xs;
    $[1] = t1;
  } else {
    t1 = $[1];
  }
  let t2;
  if ($[2] !== t1) {
    t2 = <b>{t1}</b>;
    $[2] = t1;
    $[3] = t2;
  } else {
    t2 = $[3];
  }
  return t2;
}
function useThing(a) {
  return { a };
}

helper was left alone, correctly. It is a plain function, React does not call it, and caching its result across renders would change its meaning rather than optimise it. Widget was compiled: it is capitalised and returns JSX.

useThing is the interesting one: it has the use prefix, and was not compiled. The compiler needs evidence that a function really is a hook. A use name on a function that calls no hooks and reads no reactive values is not enough. Add a real hook call, and it compiles:

import { useState } from 'react';
function useCart(items) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0);
  return { open, setOpen, total };
}

Which becomes:

import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
import { useState } from 'react';
function useCart(items) {
  const $ = _c(5);
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  let t0;
  if ($[0] !== items) {
    t0 = items.reduce(_temp, 0);
    $[0] = items;
    $[1] = t0;
  } else {
    t0 = $[1];
  }
  const total = t0;
  let t1;
  if ($[2] !== open || $[3] !== total) {
    t1 = { open, setOpen, total };
    $[2] = open;
    $[3] = total;
    $[4] = t1;
  } else {
    t1 = $[4];
  }
  return t1;
}

Note that the returned object is cached. A custom hook that returns a fresh object on every call defeats every memo below it (§10.6). The compiler fixed that without being asked, and this is the most common real-world gain from adopting it.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: infer mode.

11.4 The Directives

Two directives override the compiler's decision for one function. They have the same shape as 'use strict': a string literal as the first statement in a function body, or at the top of a module to apply to everything in it.

"use no memo" opts a function out. The compiler leaves it exactly as written:

function A({ x }) { "use no memo"; return <b>{x * 2}</b>; }
function B({ x }) { return <b>{x * 2}</b>; }

Compiled, A is untouched and B is not:

import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
function A({ x }) {
  "use no memo";

  return <b>{x * 2}</b>;
}
function B(t0) {
  const $ = _c(2);
  const { x } = t0;
  const t1 = x * 2;
  let t2;
  if ($[0] !== t1) {
    t2 = <b>{t1}</b>;
    $[0] = t1;
    $[1] = t2;
  } else {
    t2 = $[1];
  }
  return t2;
}

"use no memo" is a debugging tool with a shelf life, not a configuration option. Its legitimate use is narrowing down a problem. A component misbehaves after you adopt the compiler; you add the directive; the misbehaviour stops. Now you know the Rules-of-React violation is in that component. Then you fix the violation and delete the directive. A "use no memo" that has been in the codebase for six months is a component nobody went back to, and it is silently left out of every future improvement.

"use memo" is the opposite: it opts a function in. It only means anything in annotation mode (§11.5), where nothing is compiled unless it asks to be.

function C({ x }) { "use memo"; return <b>{x * 2}</b>; }
function D({ x }) { return <b>{x * 2}</b>; }

Under compilationMode: "annotation":

import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
function C(t0) {
  "use memo";

  const $ = _c(2);
  const { x } = t0;
  const t1 = x * 2;
  let t2;
  if ($[0] !== t1) {
    t2 = <b>{t1}</b>;
    $[0] = t1;
    $[1] = t2;
  } else {
    t2 = $[1];
  }
  return t2;
}
function D({ x }) {
  return <b>{x * 2}</b>;
}

The directive stays in the output in both cases. That is harmless (it is just a string on its own line) and occasionally useful when reading a bundle.

To have in hand before moving on: annotation mode.

11.5 compilationMode

compilationMode decides which functions are candidates at all. It takes four values, and the choice is a strategy for rolling the compiler out, not a performance setting.

infer
The default. Components and hooks the compiler can identify — a capitalised function returning JSX, or a use-prefixed function that genuinely behaves like a hook. Everything else is left alone.
annotation
Nothing is compiled unless it carries "use memo". The opt-in mode for adopting the compiler one file at a time in a codebase you do not yet trust it with.
all
Every top-level function. Almost always wrong: it will try to compile utilities that are not components, and their caching semantics are not React's.
syntax
Flow-annotated code, for codebases using Flow's component syntax rather than plain functions.

The practical advice is short: use infer, which is the default, and reach for annotation only as a temporary stage of adoption, with an end date attached.

11.6 When It Refuses

This is the property that makes the compiler safe to adopt, and the one most worth remembering: when the compiler cannot prove a function is safe to optimise, it skips that function and compiles the rest of the file. It does not fail the build, and it does not compile something it is unsure about.

import { useState, useRef } from 'react';
function CondHook({ on }) {
  if (on) { const [a] = useState(0); return <b>{a}</b>; }
  return <i>off</i>;
}
function RefInRender() {
  const r = useRef(0);
  r.current += 1;
  return <b>{r.current}</b>;
}
function Evil({ code }) {
  const v = eval(code);
  return <b>{v}</b>;
}
function Fine({ x }) { return <b>{x + 1}</b>; }

With the default configuration, exactly one of those four gets a _c(…) call: Fine. The other three (a conditional hook, a ref written during render, and eval) are output unchanged. The build succeeds, and the application runs. Three components lost an optimisation; nothing broke.

The logger option is how you see that happening, since by default the compiler says nothing. It takes an object with a logEvent(filename, event) method:

// babel.config.js
export default {
  plugins: [['babel-plugin-react-compiler', {
    logger: {
      logEvent(filename, event) {
        console.error(`[${event.kind}] ${event.fnLoc ? 'fn@' + event.fnLoc.start.line : ''}`);
      },
    },
  }]],
};

Run against the four-component file above, that prints one line per decision:

[CompileError] fn@2
[CompileError] fn@6
[CompileError] fn@6
[CompileError] fn@6
[CompileError] fn@11
[CompileSuccess] fn@15

CompileError here means "skipped", not "build failed". The naming is unfortunate, and worth knowing so that a CI log does not cause a panic. Three entries point at line 6 because RefInRender produced three separate diagnostics. Counting these lines is how you measure adoption: the ratio of CompileSuccess to CompileError across your codebase is the number that should go up over time.

panicThreshold turns the skip into a failure. Its default is 'none' (never throw), and the only other value worth using is 'all_errors', which turns every skipped function into a build error:

_CompilerError [ReactCompilerError]: Found 1 error:

Error: Hooks must always be called in a consistent order, and may not be called conditionally. See the Rules of Hooks (https://react.dev/warnings/invalid-hook-call-warning)

  1 | import { useState, useRef } from 'react';
  2 | function CondHook({ on }) {
> 3 |   if (on) { const [a] = useState(0); return <b>{a}</b>; }
    |                         ^^^^^^^^ Hooks must always be called in a consistent order, and may not be called conditionally.

Leave it at 'none' in production builds. A component that stopped compiling because someone added a try/catch should fall back to running without memoisation, not break the deploy. 'all_errors' belongs in a local debugging session. The lasting place to enforce the same thing is the lint plugin (§5.7), which reports the identical diagnostics without holding the build hostage.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: panicThreshold and the logger option.

11.7 target: Running the Compiler Against React 17 and 18

The generated code calls c from react/compiler-runtime, and that module only exists in React 19. The target option is how an older application can use the compiler anyway.

// babel.config.json — for a React 18 app
{ "plugins": [["babel-plugin-react-compiler", { "target": "18" }]] }

The emitted import changes:

import { c as _c } from "react-compiler-runtime";

One hyphen instead of a slash, and it is a different thing entirely. react-compiler-runtime is a separate npm package that recreates c on top of the hooks React 17/18 already has, and you must install it alongside. Forgetting it produces a module-not-found error when the app runs rather than when it builds, which is a bad way to find out.

target accepts '19' (the default, which uses React's built-in runtime), '18' and '17'. It is the only compiler option where a wrong value causes a crash at runtime rather than a missed optimisation. So it is the one to check first when a compiled build crashes on startup.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the target option.

11.8 gating: Shipping Both Versions at Once

The gating option compiles each component twice, and a feature flag picks between the two versions while the app runs. It exists so that a large application can turn the compiler on for a fraction of its users and compare, instead of betting the whole deploy on it.

// babel.config.json
{ "plugins": [["babel-plugin-react-compiler", {
    "gating": { "source": "./flags", "importSpecifierName": "isCompilerEnabled" } }]] }

Given a component C, the output becomes:

import { isCompilerEnabled } from "./flags";
import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
const C = isCompilerEnabled() ? function C(t0) {
  const $ = _c(2);
  const { x } = t0;
  const t1 = x * 2;
  let t2;
  if ($[0] !== t1) {
    t2 = <b>{t1}</b>;
    $[0] = t1;
    $[1] = t2;
  } else {
    t2 = $[1];
  }
  return t2;
} : function C({ x }) {
  return <b>{x * 2}</b>;
};

Both versions are in the bundle, and that is the cost: gating roughly doubles the size of every compiled component. That makes it a migration tool with an exit date, not a permanent configuration.

Two constraints are easy to get wrong.

  • The flag function is called during module evaluation (while the file is first loaded), so it must be synchronous and available immediately. Reading it from configuration you fetch over the network will not work.
  • It must return the same value for the whole session. Flipping it part-way through swaps the function identity of every component at once, which unmounts and remounts your whole tree.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the gating option.

11.9 Installing It

The compiler is a Babel plugin, and every toolchain has a place to put one. It must run first in the plugin list, before any transform that rewrites JSX or hooks, because it analyses code that still looks like your source.

// babel.config.js — the plugin on its own
export default { plugins: [['babel-plugin-react-compiler', {}]] };

Vite passes Babel options through its React plugin:

// vite.config.js
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
export default {
  plugins: [react({ babel: { plugins: [['babel-plugin-react-compiler', {}]] } })],
};

Next.js wires it up itself, given a flag:

// next.config.js
export default { experimental: { reactCompiler: true } };

Webpack and Rspack take it through babel-loader. React Router and Expo both accept a babel.config.js and need no special handling. Metro reads the same config for React Native. In every case the way to check that it worked is the same, and worth doing rather than assuming: build once, then search the output for compiler-runtime.

grep -rc "compiler-runtime" dist/assets/*.js | head
