The other confirmation is visual: React DevTools shows a small "Memo ✨" badge next to compiled components in the Components tab. If neither the search nor the badge shows anything, the plugin is configured but not running. That is usually because it was added to a Babel config the bundler is not reading.

The terms above, gathered: Metro.

11.10 Incremental Adoption

Turning the compiler on across a large codebase in one commit is possible, and sometimes right. When it is not, there are three strategies, from least to most cautious.

Directory-based adoption uses Babel's own overrides to limit the plugin to part of the tree. It is the best of the three, because the code inside the directory needs no annotation, so nothing has to be undone later.

// babel.config.js
export default {
  overrides: [
    { test: './src/modern/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}',
      plugins: [['babel-plugin-react-compiler', {}]] },
  ],
};

Annotation mode (§11.5) reverses the default, so that files opt in with "use memo". Use it when the risky code is scattered rather than grouped, and accept that every directive is a line someone will have to delete.

Runtime gating (§11.8) is the heaviest, and the only one that lets you compare compiled and uncompiled behaviour on real users. Reach for it when the application is large enough that "we think it is fine" is not a good enough answer.

Whichever you pick, the order of steps is the same. Turn on eslint-plugin-react-hooks first and fix what it reports. That is the same analysis the compiler runs, delivered as a lint error you can fix in your own time rather than as a silently skipped component. Then enable the compiler. Then watch the logger counts move.

One line each, for reference: directory-based adoption.

11.11 What It Means for useMemo, useCallback and memo

This is the question everyone asks, and it has a measured answer. Take a component written with careful manual memoisation:

import { useMemo, useCallback } from 'react';
function Q({ xs, n, onPick }) {
  const sorted = useMemo(() => [...xs].sort(), [xs]);
  const pick = useCallback(i => onPick(sorted[i]), [onPick, sorted]);
  return <ul onClick={pick}>{sorted.length}{n}</ul>;
}

And the same component with all of it deleted:

function R({ xs, n, onPick }) {
  const sorted = [...xs].sort();
  const pick = i => onPick(sorted[i]);
  return <ul onClick={pick}>{sorted.length}{n}</ul>;
}

Compile both. After making only the function name and the now-unused import the same, the two outputs are identical, line for line: 40 lines each, the same nine cache slots, the same guards in the same order:

import { c as _c } from "react/compiler-runtime";
function X(t0) {
  const $ = _c(9);
  const { xs, n, onPick } = t0;
  let t1;
  if ($[0] !== xs) {
    t1 = [...xs].sort();
    $[0] = xs;
    $[1] = t1;
  } else {
    t1 = $[1];
  }
  const sorted = t1;
  let t2;
  if ($[2] !== onPick || $[3] !== sorted) {
    t2 = i => onPick(sorted[i]);
    $[2] = onPick;
    $[3] = sorted;
    $[4] = t2;
  } else {
    t2 = $[4];
  }
  const pick = t2;
  let t3;
  if ($[5] !== n || $[6] !== pick || $[7] !== sorted.length) {
    t3 = <ul onClick={pick}>{sorted.length}{n}</ul>;
    $[5] = n;
    $[6] = pick;
    $[7] = sorted.length;
    $[8] = t3;
  } else {
    t3 = $[8];
  }
  return t3;
}

That is the whole argument. In a compiled codebase the two files behave the same, so the useMemo and the useCallback are pure cost: three extra lines, two dependency arrays to keep correct, and one more thing for a reviewer to check.

Three qualifications keep this honest.

Existing memoisation is preserved, not just tolerated. The compiler must keep the meaning of a useMemo you wrote. The react-hooks/preserve-manual-memoization lint rule reports the cases where it cannot, usually because the dependency array is wrong in a way that makes the two readings disagree. When that rule fires, the array is what to fix.

It does not always keep the mechanism. Take const total = useMemo(() => xs.reduce(...), [xs]), where the only thing using it is total + n. The compiler outputs a bare xs.reduce(...) with no cache slot at all. It worked out that the reduce feeds a value that changes with n anyway, so caching it gains nothing. What the user sees is the same; the number of times your reducer runs is not. If a useMemo guards something truly expensive and important to the program's meaning, measure it after compiling rather than assuming the slot survived.

memo is a different thing. React.memo decides whether React calls a component at all, which is a decision at the call site. The compiler's element caching mostly makes it unnecessary: a cached element is equal by reference, so the reconciler skips the subtree without any wrapper. Mostly, not always. A component that receives a prop from code that was not compiled, or from a third-party library that rebuilds objects, can still benefit. Delete memo when you can show it is doing nothing; keep it where a profile says otherwise.

The migration advice that follows: do not delete existing memoisation as a project. It is not hurting anything. A mass deletion is a large diff with no visible benefit, and a real chance of touching one of the cases above. Stop writing new memoisation, delete what you touch for other reasons, and let the code gradually come into line.

11.12 Compiling a Library

Compiling libraries is a different decision from compiling an application, because you do not choose which React version your users run.

The gain is real. Your components are optimised for every user of the library, including those who have not adopted the compiler themselves, and they cannot accidentally undo your optimisation. The cost is a hard dependency on a runtime that must be present.

If your library's peerDependencies allow React 17 or 18, you must set target to match and add react-compiler-runtime to your own dependencies. Not to peers, because it is your generated code that imports it. Ship a build for the lowest React you support: code compiled for target: '18' runs fine on 19, while code compiled for 19 crashes on 18.

Test the compiled output, not the source. A test suite that imports src/ is testing code your users never receive. Point it at the build directory, and run it against the oldest React version in your peer range as well as the newest.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: compiling libraries.

11.13 What It Does Not Do

The compiler is an optimiser, and an optimiser promises to keep the meaning of correct programs unchanged. So everything below is still your job.

It does not fix a Rules-of-React violation — it declines to optimise around it. A component that changes props or writes a ref during render is skipped (§11.6), and keeps running exactly as badly as before. The compiler is a reason to obey the rules, not a substitute for obeying them.

It catches less than the linter does. Measured on this machine: props.title = 'x' is reported by react-hooks/immutability, but items.push('x') and items.sort() on a destructured array prop are reported by none of the seventeen rules, and the compiler compiles both without complaint. Property assignment is analysed; a method call that changes a prop in place is not. That is a real hole. It is the most common way a prop actually gets changed in production code, and nothing in the toolchain will tell you about it. Copy before you sort (§3.4).

It does not reduce the number of renders React performs. It reduces the work inside a render, and makes elements equal by reference so the reconciler can skip subtrees. If your problem is that a context value changes on every keystroke and half the app re-renders, the compiler will make each of those renders cheaper, and will not stop them happening. §10 and §12 are still the tools for that.

It does not memoise across component instances or across mounts. The cache lives on the fiber. Unmount the component, and the cache goes with it.

It does not help with a slow algorithm. A cached O(n²) is an O(n²) that runs less often. The first render still pays for it, and so does every render where the input changed.

What This Section Established

The React Compiler is a Babel plugin that generates the memoisation you would otherwise write by hand. Its output is a per-component cache array from react/compiler-runtime, allocated with _c(n), with each value guarded by an Object.is comparison against the dependency it was computed from — including the returned JSX element, which manual memoisation almost never caches and which is what lets the reconciler prune whole subtrees.

It compiles components and hooks and leaves plain functions alone, and it is conservative about what counts as a hook: a use-prefixed function that calls no hooks is not compiled. "use memo" and "use no memo" override the decision for one function; compilationMode sets the default policy, and infer is the right one.

When it cannot prove a function is safe it skips that function and compiles the rest — measured, three of four components skipped with no build failure. logger is how you see that, panicThreshold: 'all_errors' turns it into a build error for local debugging only, and the lint plugin is the durable place to enforce it.

target: '18' retargets the emitted import to the separate react-compiler-runtime package, which must be installed; gating ships both versions behind a synchronous flag at roughly double the code size.

And the headline measurement: a component written with useMemo and useCallback compiles to byte-identical output to the same component written with neither. Stop writing new manual memoisation; do not launch a project to delete the old.

Exercises

1. Predict the cache size. For each of these, predict the integer in _c(n) before compiling, then check: a component with one prop and no derived values; one that derives two values from the same prop; one that derives two values from two different props; and one with a useState plus a callback closing over it. State the rule you inferred for how slots are counted.

2. Find the skip. Write four components that the compiler will skip, each for a different reason, and confirm with a logger that counts CompileSuccess against CompileError. Then fix two of them so they compile, and say for each fix which Rule of React the original was breaking.

3. Delete the memoisation. Take a component with at least two useMemos and one useCallback, compile it, then delete all three and compile again. Diff the two outputs. If they differ, work out which of the three the compiler did not reproduce and why — and decide whether that one should stay.

4. Gate it. Configure gating against a flag module, compile a two-component file, and measure the size of the output with and without gating. Then explain what breaks if the flag function reads from localStorage asynchronously, and what breaks if it returns a different value on the second call.

5. The hole. Write a component that mutates a prop in a way neither the compiler nor any of the seventeen lint rules reports. Show that both are silent. Then write the version that would be caught, name the rule that catches it, and give the one-line rewrite that makes the original correct.

Solution

1. Cache sizes.

one prop, no derived values        _c(2)   one slot for the dep, one for the element
two values from the same prop      _c(4)   dep + value, then dep + element (grouped)
two values from two props          _c(6)   two guarded blocks plus the element block
useState + a callback over it      _c(4)   dep + callback, then dep + element

The rule: one slot per remembered dependency plus one slot per cached result, with values sharing a guard when they share all their dependencies. A component with no props and no derived values still gets _c(1) — the element alone.

2. Four skips.

import { useState, useRef } from 'react';

function S1({ on }) {                      // conditional hook
  if (on) { const [a] = useState(0); return <b>{a}</b>; }
  return <i>off</i>;
}
function S2() {                            // ref written during render
  const r = useRef(0);
  r.current += 1;
  return <b>{r.current}</b>;
}
function S3({ code }) { return <b>{eval(code)}</b>; }        // unsupported syntax
function S4() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); setN(n + 1); return <b>{n}</b>; }

S1 breaks the Rules of Hooks; S2 and S4 break "components must be pure" — a ref write and a setState are both side effects during render. S3 is not a rule violation at all, it is syntax the analysis cannot follow.

The two easiest fixes: S1 moves the useState above the if; S2 moves the increment into an effect, or uses state if the value is meant to be rendered. Both then compile.

3. Deleting memoisation.

Run the two through the plugin and diff. Where the outputs match, the manual memoisation was pure overhead. Where they differ, the usual cause is a useMemo whose result feeds a value that changes anyway — the compiler drops the slot because caching it saves nothing downstream.

That one is worth keeping only if the computation itself is what costs, rather than the identity of its result: a parse, a large sort, a synchronous layout read. In that case it is genuinely expensive and the honest fix is to measure it after compiling, not to argue from the diff.

4. Gating.

without gating   40 lines   one implementation per component
with gating      74 lines   both implementations, plus the flag import

An asynchronous flag breaks because the ternary is evaluated when the module is first imported — before any await could resolve — so the flag reads undefined and every component takes the uncompiled branch, silently.

A flag that changes value between calls is worse: C is chosen once per module evaluation, but a flag read again after a hot reload or a second bundle chunk can pick the other branch, and the two Cs are different function identities. React sees a different type at the same position and remounts the entire subtree (§2.4), losing all its state.

5. The hole.

function Silent({ items }) {          // reported by nothing
  items.sort();
  return <b>{items[0]}</b>;
}
function Caught(props) {              // react-hooks/immutability: "This value cannot be modified"
  props.title = 'x';
  return <b>{props.title}</b>;
}

Silent produces zero lint findings and compiles without complaint; Caught is reported at the assignment. The difference is that the analysis tracks property assignment and not mutating method calls through a destructured binding.

The one-line fix for Silent is to copy first:

function Fixed({ items }) {
  const sorted = [...items].sort();
  return <b>{sorted[0]}</b>;
}

toSorted() is the modern equivalent and says the same thing in one call. Either way the prop is untouched, which is what the rule wanted and what neither tool was able to check.

SECTION 12

Concurrent React: Transitions, Actions and Activity

Up to here, an update has been one indivisible thing: state changes, React re-renders, React commits (applies the result to the page). That model is true of every example so far. It is not true of React.

The missing piece is priority. Not every update is equally urgent, and treating them all as urgent produces the worst interface:

  • a search box that stutters because each keystroke re-renders ten thousand rows;
  • a tab that freezes for 300 ms when you click it;
  • a list that cannot be scrolled while it filters.

The user's typing is urgent: it must appear in the next frame, or the input feels broken. The results below it are not urgent. They can arrive a moment later and nobody notices.

React's answer is that you say which updates are not urgent, and React does the rest. It renders those at a lower priority, in a render pass it is willing to abandon, while keeping the urgent ones fast. That is what "concurrent" means here. It does not mean threads or parallelism. It means a render phase that can be interrupted (§2.11's fiber tree, React's internal record of the components, is what makes that possible), plus a scheduler that decides what to work on next.

This section covers the four tools that let you use it:

  • transitions, which mark an update as non-urgent;
  • Actions, which extend that across an await;
  • useDeferredValue, which does the same for a value rather than an update;
  • and <Activity>, which keeps a part of the tree alive without rendering it.

Everything below was measured by counting renders in a real root (the place where a React app is attached to the page).

12.1 Two Kinds of Update

Urgent
Typing, clicking, dragging, pressing a key. The result must be visible immediately or the control feels broken. This is the default for every setState.
Non-urgent
Showing the results of what was typed, switching to a tab whose content is expensive, navigating. A short delay is invisible; a frozen input is not.

Every update is urgent unless you say otherwise. That is the right default: an interface that quietly lowers the priority of something important is worse than one that is sometimes slow. So marking an update as non-urgent is always something you do explicitly, and there are exactly two ways to do it: useTransition and startTransition.

12.2 useTransition

useTransition() returns a pending flag, and a function to wrap updates in. What it produces is a non-blocking transition: the update happens, and nothing about it blocks the frame the user is typing into.

import { useState, useTransition, useDeferredValue, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Search() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState('');
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  log.push(`render q=${q || '-'} pending=${isPending}`);
  globalThis.urgent = v => setQ(v);
  globalThis.slow = v => startTransition(() => setQ(v));
  return <span>{q}|{String(isPending)}</span>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Search />); });

log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.urgent('a'); });
console.log('urgent    :', log.join(' ; '));
log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.slow('ab'); });
console.log('transition:', log.join(' ; '));

urgent    : render q=a pending=false
transition: render q=a pending=true ; render q=ab pending=false

Read the second line carefully, because it is the whole mechanism.

The transition produced two renders. The first still shows the old value q='a', with isPending=true. React re-rendered straight away so that you can show a pending indicator, but it did not apply the state change yet. The second render has the new value and isPending=false.

That is what a transition buys you: the old UI stays on screen, fully interactive, while the new one is prepared. No spinner replacing content that was already there, no blank frame. And most importantly, the input the user is typing into keeps working, because the expensive results are being rendered at a priority the browser is allowed to interrupt.

isPending is what you render during that window: dimming the out-of-date results, showing a small spinner beside the control, disabling a submit button. Anything except removing the content, which would throw away the very thing the transition was protecting.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: useTransition( and non-blocking transition.

12.3 What a Transition Actually Changes

A transition changes three specific things. All three are worth knowing, because two of them are often credited to the wrong cause.

The update is interruptible. If another update arrives while React is rendering the transition, React can abandon the work in progress and start again with the newer state. Nothing half-rendered is ever committed, so an abandoned render is invisible: it costs CPU time and nothing else.

Suspense behaves differently inside one. A component that suspends (waits for something) during a transition does not replace content that is already visible with a fallback. React keeps showing the old UI until the new one is ready. This is the most useful consequence, and §13.7 covers it in detail. Without a transition, navigating to a route whose data is not loaded blanks the page. With one, the old page stays until the new one can be shown.

That second property is worth measuring rather than taking on trust, because it is the one that changes how routers are written. Watch the DOM during a navigation whose data is not ready, with and without a transition:

import { useState, useTransition, Suspense, use, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const useTx of [false, true]) {
  const pages = { home: Promise.resolve('HOME'),
                  about: new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('ABOUT'), 15)) };
  function Page({ url }) { return <b>{use(pages[url])}</b>; }
  function Router() {
    const [url, setUrl] = useState('home');
    const [isPending, start] = useTransition();
    globalThis.go = u => (useTx ? start(() => setUrl(u)) : setUrl(u));
    return <div>{isPending ? '[pending]' : ''}
      <Suspense fallback={<i>FALLBACK</i>}><Page url={url} /></Suspense></div>;
  }
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Router />); });

  let sawFallback = false, sawPending = false;
  new window.MutationObserver(() => {
    if (box.textContent.includes('FALLBACK')) sawFallback = true;
    if (box.textContent.includes('[pending]')) sawPending = true;
  }).observe(box, { subtree: true, childList: true, characterData: true });

  await act(async () => { globalThis.go('about'); });
  await act(async () => { await pages.about; });    // the slow page arrives, then React commits
  console.log((useTx ? 'in a transition:' : 'plain setState :'),
              'fallback shown:', sawFallback, '| pending shown:', sawPending,
              '| final:', box.textContent.trim());
}

plain setState : fallback shown: true | pending shown: false | final: ABOUT
in a transition: fallback shown: false | pending shown: true | final: ABOUT

Same components, same data, same final state. The plain update tore down the visible page and showed a spinner for fifteen milliseconds. The transition left the page alone and offered a pending indicator instead. On a real navigation those fifteen milliseconds are two hundred, and it is the difference between an application and a website that blinks.

This is why a suspense-enabled router is built on transitions rather than on loading state. The router marks the URL change as a transition, the route component suspends while its data loads, and the previous page stays until the next one is ready. That is the behaviour users already expect from a browser, reproduced without a full page load. It is also why "wrap navigations in startTransition" is the first advice given to anyone writing routing by hand.

Nothing about the work gets faster. A transition does not make your component cheaper, and it does not move the work off the main thread. If rendering the results takes 400 ms of JavaScript, it still takes 400 ms. It is spread across frames instead of blocking one: that is the difference between a stutter and a freeze, not the difference between slow and fast. When the profiler says a component takes 400 ms, §10 is the section that helps.

To have in hand before moving on: suspense-enabled router.

12.4 startTransition Without the Hook

startTransition( is also exported directly from react, for the same purpose without the pending flag. You use it outside a component, where you cannot call a hook: in a store, a router, or an event handler that lives in a module.

import { startTransition } from 'react';
// in a router, far from any component
export function navigate(url) {
  startTransition(() => { history.pushState({}, '', url); notifySubscribers(url); });
}

The trade-off is exactly the missing isPending. If you need to show that something is happening, you need the hook, and it must live in a component that renders during the transition.

One rule about the callback catches people: the function you pass runs synchronously and immediately. startTransition is not setTimeout. It runs your callback right there, and marks every setState performed during that call as non-urgent. That leads straight to the next two subsections.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: startTransition(.

12.5 Actions: Transitions That Span an await

React 19 extends transitions across asynchronous work (work that waits, such as a network request). An async action is an async function passed to startTransition, and the pending state now covers the whole operation, not just the part before the first await.

import { useState, useTransition, startTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const seen = [];
function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  const [isPending, start] = useTransition();
  seen.push(`n=${n} pending=${isPending}`);
  globalThis.goodAsync = () => start(async () => {
    await Promise.resolve();
    setN(v => v + 1);                              // inside the action
  });
  globalThis.badAsync = async () => {
    await Promise.resolve();
    startTransition(() => setN(v => v + 100));     // started AFTER the await
  };
  return <span>{n}</span>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });

seen.length = 0;
await act(async () => { await globalThis.goodAsync(); });
console.log('async action   :', seen.join(' ; '));
seen.length = 0;
await act(async () => { await globalThis.badAsync(); });
console.log('after the await:', seen.join(' ; '));

async action   : n=0 pending=true ; n=1 pending=true ; n=1 pending=false
after the await: n=101 pending=false

The first case is what you want. isPending became true the moment the action started, stayed true across the await, and became false only when the update it eventually made had committed. Three renders, one continuous pending window, and you never wrote a setLoading(true) / setLoading(false) pair. That pair is the one that leaves a spinner stuck forever when the code in the middle throws.

The second case is the trap, and it is worth being able to spot on sight. Calling startTransition after an await produced one render with pending=false. React tracks a transition only while the function you handed it is running synchronously. Once you have awaited, that context is gone, and a startTransition started later is a new transition that nothing is watching.

The rule is short: await inside the action, never before startTransition. If the code you are calling is already async, wrap the call, not what comes after it.

This is also the mechanism behind useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic, which are covered in §15. An Action is the basic building block, and those three make it convenient to use.

In summary, the vocabulary here is an async action.

12.6 useDeferredValue

useDeferredValue( solves the same problem from the other end, and its typical behaviour is showing stale content while fresh content is prepared. Instead of marking an update as non-urgent, it takes a value and gives you back a version that lags behind: the previous value during the render that changed it, and the new one on a later, low-priority render.

Both mechanisms appear in the same measurement:

import { useState, useTransition, useDeferredValue, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Box() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState('');
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(q);
  log.push(`q=${q || '-'} deferred=${deferred || '-'}`);
  globalThis.type = v => setQ(v);
  return <span>{q}|{deferred}</span>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Box />); });
log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.type('a'); });
console.log(log.join(' ; '));

q=a deferred=- ; q=a deferred=a

Two renders from one keystroke (the mount was cleared from the log first). The first has the new q and the old deferred. That render is urgent and cheap, so the input updates in the next frame. The second has both, and it is the low-priority render that does the expensive work.

The pattern that follows: pass q to the input and deferred to the expensive list. The input is always current; the list is at most one render behind.

Which to reach for.

  • Use useTransition when you control the update: you are calling setState and can wrap it.
  • Use useDeferredValue when you do not: the value arrives as a prop, from a context or from a store, and there is no setState of yours to wrap.

The second is also the only option when a single value feeds both an urgent and a non-urgent part of the tree, since you need both versions at once.

useDeferredValue also takes an initialValue, used for the first render only. Without it, the first render has nothing old to show and must do the expensive work immediately. With it, the mount is cheap too.

What to carry forward from this subsection: useDeferredValue( and showing stale content.

12.7 Deferring Is Not Debouncing

These look alike and are not, and the difference decides which one is correct.

Debounce / throttle
  • Waits a fixed time you chose by guessing
  • Delays the work even on a fast machine where it was never needed
  • Cannot be interrupted once it starts — it is a normal render
  • Right for things with an external cost: network requests, analytics
Transition / deferred value
  • Waits for the machine: as fast as this device allows
  • No delay at all when the render is cheap
  • Interruptible — a newer keystroke abandons the in-flight render
  • Right for rendering cost, which is the only thing React can schedule

The two work together rather than competing. Debounce the fetch (wait until the typing pauses), because each request costs the server money. Defer the render, because that cost is local and React can measure it. Replacing a debounce with a transition around a network call removes the rate limiting, and is a common mistake.

12.8 Interruption, and Why Purity Is Not Optional

A transition render can be abandoned. React starts rendering, a newer update arrives, and the half-built tree is thrown away: never committed, never seen.

This is where §5's purity rule stops being a style preference and becomes a requirement for correct behaviour. A component that increments a module-level counter during render, pushes to an array, or writes to a ref will do so on renders that are discarded. The count will then be wrong by an amount that depends on the user's typing speed and their CPU. You cannot debug that from the symptom, and it will not reproduce on your machine.

<StrictMode>'s double render (§2.13) exists precisely to bring this kind of bug out early, and the react-hooks/purity lint rule (§5.7) catches the common shapes without running the code. A codebase that is going to use transitions should turn both on first.

The same reasoning explains why useSyncExternalStore exists (§7.7). A render that can be interrupted may read an external value at two different moments within one render pass, and see two different values. Different parts of the UI then show inconsistent data, which is called tearing. useSyncExternalStore gives React a way to notice that the store changed during the render, and start again. Reading a changeable external value directly during render does not, and concurrency is what turns that from a theoretical problem into one you can see.

12.9 Activity

<Activity> renders a subtree in one of two modes: visible, which behaves normally, or hidden, which keeps the state and the DOM, but stops rendering updates and removes the effects.

import { useState, useEffect, act, Activity } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function Panel() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.bump = () => setN(v => v + 1);
  useEffect(() => { log.push('effect mounted'); return () => { log.push('effect cleaned'); }; }, []);
  return <b>panel:{n}</b>;
}
function App() {
  const [mode, setMode] = useState('visible');
  globalThis.setMode = setMode;
  return <div><Activity mode={mode}><Panel /></Activity></div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.bump(); globalThis.bump(); });
console.log('visible:', JSON.stringify(box.innerHTML), '|', log.join(','));
log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setMode('hidden'); });
console.log('hidden :', JSON.stringify(box.innerHTML), '|', log.join(','));
log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.setMode('visible'); });
console.log('back   :', JSON.stringify(box.innerHTML), '|', log.join(','));

visible: "<div><b>panel:2</b></div>" | effect mounted
hidden : "<div><b style=\"display: none;\">panel:2</b></div>" | effect cleaned
back   : "<div><b style=\"\">panel:2</b></div>" | effect mounted

Every part of that is worth naming.

The DOM stayed. React set display: none instead of removing the node. Scroll positions, media playback, canvas contents and iframe state all survive.

The state stayed. panel:2 is still panel:2 when it comes back. This is the answer §2.7 promised for "preserve state for a component that is currently hidden", and it does not require lifting the state or paying to keep rendering it.

The effects were cleaned up. A hidden <Activity> removes its effects: a subscription closes, an interval stops, a WebSocket disconnects. That is the crucial difference from applying display: none by hand. Hiding with CSS leaves every effect running, so the hidden panel keeps polling your server forever.

<Activity> is also useful the other way round: pre-rendering content that is likely to become visible. A hidden subtree that has never been shown is rendered at low priority, so the content of a tab the user has not clicked yet is ready before they click it. The cost is real (it is still rendering work), so it is a tool for the two or three places you can predict the user will go next, not for every route.

<Activity> is exported from the stable React package, and has been since 19.2.

The terms above, gathered: pre-rendering content that is likely to become visible.

12.10 ViewTransition and Transition Types

The browser's View Transition API animates between two states of a page. It takes a snapshot of the page, lets you change the DOM, takes a second snapshot, and then cross-fades or morphs between the two using CSS animations you control. React's <ViewTransition> component connects that API to React's own transitions. Wrap a subtree in it, and when a transition changes that subtree, React asks the browser to animate the change instead of jumping to it.

<ViewTransition> and addTransitionType( are exported by the stable React 19.3.0 package. They shipped in 19.3; until then they were canary-only, and the 19.2.8 package does not export them. The export check at the end of this subsection shows how to confirm that for any API, in ten seconds, against the version you actually installed.

The first thing to establish is when it animates, because that is where most confusion comes from. jsdom has no View Transition API, so the example below replaces the browser with a recording stand-in, letting us see exactly what React asks for:

import { useState, startTransition, addTransitionType, ViewTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

// jsdom has no View Transition API, so these lines stand in for the browser: they
// record what React asks for, then run the DOM update React hands over, as a browser would.
globalThis.CSS = { escape: s => s };
document.fonts = { status: 'loaded' };
document.documentElement.getAnimations = () => [];
document.documentElement.animate = () => ({ cancel() {} });
const calls = [];
document.startViewTransition = ({ update, types }) => {
  const img = document.querySelector('img');
  calls.push(`types=${JSON.stringify(types)} name=${img.style.viewTransitionName}`);
  const done = Promise.resolve().then(update);
  return { ready: done, finished: done, updateCallbackDone: done, skipTransition() {} };
};

function Photo() {
  const [big, setBig] = useState(false);
  globalThis.urgent = () => setBig(b => !b);
  globalThis.animated = type => startTransition(() => {
    if (type) addTransitionType(type);
    setBig(b => !b);
  });
  return <ViewTransition><img alt="" className={big ? 'big' : 'small'} /></ViewTransition>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
await act(async () => { root.render(<Photo />); });

await act(async () => { globalThis.urgent(); });
console.log('plain setState :', calls.splice(0).join(' ; ') || 'no view transition');
await act(async () => { globalThis.animated(); });
console.log('startTransition:', calls.splice(0).join(' ; ') || 'no view transition');
await act(async () => { globalThis.animated('zoom-in'); });
console.log('with a type    :', calls.splice(0).join(' ; ') || 'no view transition');
console.log('afterwards     :', document.getElementById('app').innerHTML);

plain setState : no view transition
startTransition: types=null name=_t_0_
with a type    : types=["zoom-in"] name=_t_0_
afterwards     : <img alt="" class="big" style="">

Four facts, each of which decides how you write the code.

A plain setState does not animate. The urgent update changed the same <img> inside the same <ViewTransition>, and React never called startViewTransition. The component takes part only when the update that changed its contents was a transition: startTransition, a useTransition start function, an Action, useDeferredValue, or a <Suspense> boundary revealing its content. That rule ties the browser API to §12.2's priority. An animation says the UI is moving from one settled state to another, and an urgent update is by definition not waiting to settle.

React names the element for you. The browser matches elements across the two snapshots by their CSS view-transition-name. React gave the <img> a generated one (_t_0_) for the length of the transition, and the last line shows it removed afterwards (style=""). You never write view-transition-name yourself. If you write it by hand next to a <ViewTransition>, you create a conflict you will lose.

Transition types travel to the browser. addTransitionType('zoom-in'), called inside the startTransition callback, arrived as types: ["zoom-in"] in the browser call. Types describe why a transition happened ('nav-forward', 'nav-back', 'open-detail'), so one piece of UI can animate differently depending on the cause. They are collected for each transition and cleared after each commit; with none, React passed null.

Only the DOM nodes directly inside it are affected. The <ViewTransition> renders no element of its own: the output is a bare <img>. It applies to the nearest DOM nodes below it. That is why it must sit above any wrapper element rather than inside one, a point the shared-element example below measures.

Enter, exit, update and share

What the browser animates depends on what happened to the <ViewTransition> in the commit. React sorts every change into one of four animation triggers:

enter
The <ViewTransition> was inserted by this transition, and it is the outermost one inserted.
exit
It was deleted, and it is the outermost one deleted.
update
It stayed, and the DOM inside it mutated — or it was resized because a sibling moved it.
share
A named one was deleted and another with the same name was inserted in the same transition.

Each animation trigger has a prop of the same name (enter, exit, update, share), plus default for any trigger you do not list. The value of each is a View Transition Class:

  • "auto", for the browser's default cross-fade;
  • "none", to switch that trigger off;
  • or a class name of your own, which React gives to the browser as the element's view-transition-class, so your CSS can target it.

The value may also be an object keyed by transition type, which is where addTransitionType pays off:

import { useState, startTransition, addTransitionType, ViewTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.CSS = { escape: s => s };
document.fonts = { status: 'loaded' };
document.documentElement.getAnimations = () => [];
document.documentElement.animate = () => ({ cancel() {} });
const tagged = () => [...document.querySelectorAll('#app *')]
  .filter(el => el.style.viewTransitionName)
  .map(el => `<${el.tagName.toLowerCase()}> class=${el.style.viewTransitionClass ?? '-'}`).join(' ') || 'nothing';
document.startViewTransition = ({ update, types }) => {
  const before = tagged();
  const done = Promise.resolve().then(update).then(() =>
    console.log(`types=${JSON.stringify(types)}  old: ${before}  new: ${tagged()}`));
  return { ready: done, finished: done, updateCallbackDone: done, skipTransition() {} };
};

function Panel() {
  const [shown, setShown] = useState(false);
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  globalThis.toggle = type => startTransition(() => { addTransitionType(type); setShown(s => !s); });
  globalThis.bump = () => startTransition(() => setN(v => v + 1));
  return <section>{shown &&
    <ViewTransition enter={{ forward: 'slide-in', default: 'fade' }} exit="fade" update="pulse" default="none">
      <aside>item {n}</aside>
    </ViewTransition>}</section>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
await act(async () => { createRoot(document.getElementById('app')).render(<Panel />); });
for (const [label, go] of [['enter, forward', () => globalThis.toggle('forward')],
                           ['update        ', () => globalThis.bump()],
                           ['exit          ', () => globalThis.toggle('back')],
                           ['enter, back   ', () => globalThis.toggle('back')]]) {
  process.stdout.write(label + '  ');
  await act(async () => { go(); });
}

enter, forward  types=["forward"]  old: nothing  new: <aside> class=slide-in
update          types=null  old: <aside> class=pulse  new: <aside> class=pulse
exit            types=["back"]  old: <aside> class=fade  new: nothing
enter, back     types=["back"]  old: nothing  new: <aside> class=fade

Read it row by row. The enter caused by a 'forward' transition got slide-in, from the object's forward key. The enter caused by 'back' fell through to the object's default, fade. The update, a text change inside the <aside>, used update="pulse", and appeared in both snapshots because the element existed on both sides. The exit is visible only in the old snapshot, and the enter only in the new one, which is exactly what the browser needs to animate something appearing or disappearing.

default="none" is the pattern to copy. Without it, every trigger you did not mention falls back to "auto", so a component written to fade in on mount also cross-fades on every unrelated layout change. Opting in one trigger at a time keeps animations where you meant them.

The classes are then plain CSS, written against the four view-transition pseudo-elements:

  • ::view-transition-group(.x) animates the element's position and size;
  • ::view-transition-old(.x) and ::view-transition-new(.x) are the two snapshots;
  • and ::view-transition-image-pair(.x) holds the pair:
::view-transition-old(.slide-in) {
  animation: 250ms ease-out both slide-out-left;
}
::view-transition-new(.slide-in) {
  animation: 250ms ease-out both slide-in-right;
}
::view-transition-group(.fade) {
  animation-duration: 150ms;
}
@keyframes slide-in-right { from { translate: 40px 0; opacity: 0; } }
@keyframes slide-out-left { to { translate: -40px 0; opacity: 0; } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-group(*),
  ::view-transition-old(*),
  ::view-transition-new(*) {
    animation: none;
  }
}

The @media block at the end is not optional polish. React does not respect prefers-reduced-motion for you: a user who asked their operating system for less motion gets every animation you wrote, unless your CSS switches them off. Treat those six lines as part of the feature.

Shared elements, and the top-level rule

The name prop gives a <ViewTransition> a fixed identity instead of a generated one. When a transition deletes one named <ViewTransition> and inserts another with the same name, the pair triggers the fourth kind of animation, share. The browser morphs the old element into the new one: the thumbnail that seems to grow into the full image. This is a shared element transition, and it is the one effect that is hard to build any other way. Names must be unique among what is mounted at one time. Mounting two with the same name makes React log, in development, that this "is not supported and will cause View Transitions to error".

Where a <ViewTransition> sits decides whether it takes part at all, and the rule is different for shared and unshared ones. The event callbacks from the next subsection make this visible, since each trigger calls its own:

import { useState, startTransition, ViewTransition } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.CSS = { escape: s => s };                     // the same stand-in as above
document.fonts = { status: 'loaded' };
document.documentElement.getAnimations = () => [];
document.documentElement.animate = () => ({ cancel() {} });
document.startViewTransition = ({ update }) => {
  const done = Promise.resolve().then(update);
  return { ready: done, finished: done, updateCallbackDone: done, skipTransition() {} };
};

const fired = [];
const report = side => ({ onShare: () => { fired.push(`${side}: share`); },
                          onEnter: () => { fired.push(`${side}: enter`); },
                          onExit: () => { fired.push(`${side}: exit`); } });
const Thumb = ({ name }) => <ViewTransition name={name} {...report('thumb')}><img alt="" /></ViewTransition>;
const Full = ({ name }) => <ViewTransition name={name} {...report('full')}><img alt="" /></ViewTransition>;
const layouts = {
  'named, top level  ': open => open ? <Full name="photo-3" /> : <Thumb name="photo-3" />,
  'named, nested     ': open => open ? <Full name="photo-3" /> : <ul><li><Thumb name="photo-3" /></li></ul>,
  'unnamed, top level': open => open ? <Full /> : <Thumb />,
  'unnamed, nested   ': open => open ? <div><Full /></div> : <ul><li><Thumb /></li></ul>,
};

const settle = () => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));   // no act(): see below
for (const [label, layout] of Object.entries(layouts)) {
  let open;
  function Gallery() { const [isOpen, setOpen] = useState(false); open = setOpen; return layout(isOpen); }
  const root = createRoot(document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('div')));
  root.render(<Gallery />);
  await settle();
  fired.length = 0;
  startTransition(() => open(true));
  await settle();
  console.log(label, '→', fired.join(', ') || 'nothing animates');
  root.unmount();
}

named, top level   → thumb: share
named, nested      → thumb: share
unnamed, top level → thumb: exit, full: enter
unnamed, nested    → nothing animates

Four layouts, one transition each, and the rule falls out of the table:

An unnamed <ViewTransition> enters or exits only if it is the top-level one in the subtree being inserted or removed. In the last row the thumbnail sits inside a <ul> that is removed, and the full image inside a <div> that is inserted, and nothing animates at all: each <ViewTransition> has a DOM node above it inside the changing subtree. That is deliberate — if every nested boundary animated on its own, removing one list would launch a hundred animations — and it is the reason to put a <ViewTransition> above any wrapper element in the component that is conditionally rendered, never inside it.

A named pair shares wherever it is. That is the rule that makes a shared element transition practical in real layouts. The second row is the thumbnail nested two elements deep in the removed <ul>, and it still shared. React's documentation says it directly: unlike enter and exit, a shared pair "can be deeply inside the deleted/mounted tree". And when a boundary would qualify for both, share wins, which is why the first row reports one share rather than an exit and an enter. The callback fires on the removed side, because the animation runs from the old element to the new one.

The reference adds two more conditions. A shared element does not animate when either side is outside the viewport (the visible area of the page), since there is nothing visible to morph from. And no share happens if the transition shows a <Suspense> fallback between removing one side and mounting the other.

This block deliberately does not use act(). Every other example in the course does. Under act() the same program reports thumb: exit, full: enter for the first row and only full: enter for the second (measured). act() commits synchronously, and skips the pass in which React collects the named boundaries that are about to appear, so it never forms the pair. The results above, with plain timers, are identical to the same components run in Chromium 151 against the real View Transition API. So a test that checks a shared-element animation through Testing Library, which wraps everything in act(), will see an exit and an enter. Test the share in a real browser (§18).

Animating a Suspense reveal

The list of things that start an animation, at the top of this subsection, included <Suspense>. It deserves its own measurement, because it is the one that needs no startTransition at all. Wrap a boundary in a <ViewTransition>, and the swap from fallback to content is itself the animated change. Animating a Suspense reveal needs nothing else:

import { Suspense, ViewTransition, use } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.CSS = { escape: s => s };                     // the same stand-in as above
document.fonts = { status: 'loaded' };
document.documentElement.getAnimations = () => [];
document.documentElement.animate = () => ({ cancel() {} });
document.startViewTransition = ({ update }) => {
  const done = Promise.resolve().then(update);
  return { ready: done, finished: done, updateCallbackDone: done, skipTransition() {} };
};

const fired = [];
const report = { onEnter: () => { fired.push('enter'); }, onExit: () => { fired.push('exit'); },
                 onUpdate: () => { fired.push('update'); } };
const settle = () => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));

for (const wrapped of [true, false]) {
  let arrive;
  const profile = new Promise(r => { arrive = r; });
  const Profile = () => <p>{use(profile)}</p>;
  const boundary = <Suspense fallback={<p>skeleton</p>}><Profile /></Suspense>;
  const box = document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('div'));
  createRoot(box).render(wrapped ? <ViewTransition {...report}>{boundary}</ViewTransition> : boundary);
  await settle();
  const before = box.textContent;
  fired.length = 0;
  arrive('Ada Lovelace');
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 400));          // reveals are throttled to one per 300 ms
  console.log(wrapped ? 'wrapped  :' : 'unwrapped:', before, '->', box.textContent, '|',
              fired.join(', ') || 'no view transition');
}

wrapped  : skeleton -> Ada Lovelace | update
unwrapped: skeleton -> Ada Lovelace | no view transition

The reveal happened on its own, when a promise resolved, and the wrapped boundary reported an update. React treats the switch from fallback to content as the boundary's contents changing. So the default is a cross-fade from the skeleton (the grey placeholder) to the real card, and update="…" is where a custom reveal goes. Without the wrapper, the content simply replaced the skeleton. (The 400 ms wait is not arbitrary. React reveals Suspense content at most once every 300 ms, so that boundaries finishing close together appear together, and any test of a reveal that depends on timing has to allow for that.)

During that animated reveal, React also waits briefly for resources the new content needs, so that it animates in complete. Reading 19.3.0's react-dom shows how. Inside the update it hands to startViewTransition, React builds a list of promises to wait for:

  • document.fonts.ready, if the new content started loading a font;
  • every visible image that has not finished loading, up to a byte budget estimated from the connection's bandwidth.

It then races that list against a 500 ms timeout before letting the browser take the new snapshot. Stylesheets with a precedence (§16.14) already suspend the boundary itself. Fonts and images are waited for only during a <ViewTransition> update. That is why a reveal that is not wrapped shows text in a fallback font for a moment, and images popping in. An <img> with its own onLoad handler opts out of the wait, on the reasoning that you are handling its arrival yourself.

View Transition Events

For animation that CSS cannot express, such as a spring or a value computed from the element's size and position, each trigger also has a callback, a View Transition Event: onEnter, onExit, onUpdate and onShare. Each receives the view transition instance and the transition's types, and may return a cleanup function:

import { useState, startTransition, addTransitionType, ViewTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.CSS = { escape: s => s };
document.fonts = { status: 'loaded' };
document.documentElement.getAnimations = () => [];
document.documentElement.animate = () => ({ cancel() {} });
document.startViewTransition = ({ update }) => {
  const done = Promise.resolve().then(update);
  return { ready: done, finished: done, updateCallbackDone: done, skipTransition() {} };
};

function Panel() {
  const [shown, setShown] = useState(false);
  globalThis.toggle = type => startTransition(() => { addTransitionType(type); setShown(s => !s); });
  return shown && <ViewTransition
      onEnter={(instance, types) => { console.log('onEnter', instance.name, types); return () => console.log('enter cleanup'); }}
      onExit={(instance, types) => { console.log('onExit', instance.name, types); }}>
      <aside>hi</aside></ViewTransition>;
}
globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
await act(async () => { createRoot(document.getElementById('app')).render(<Panel />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.toggle('forward'); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.toggle('back'); });

onEnter _t_0_ [ 'forward' ]
enter cleanup
onExit _t_0_ [ 'back' ]

The instance exposes the pseudo-elements as objects you can animate from JavaScript (instance.old, instance.new, instance.group, instance.imagePair), plus the name React assigned. The usual body is const a = instance.new.animate(keyframes, options); return () => a.cancel();. The cleanup is not decoration. It runs when the transition finishes or is interrupted by the next one, and an animation left running on a pseudo-element of a finished transition is a leak.

The reference lists three more constraints, and each explains a bug report you would otherwise file.

  • flushSync inside a <ViewTransition> cancels the animation, because it forces an immediate commit that cannot wait for a snapshot.
  • Animations are of images: the browser animates snapshots, so content that moves on its own inside the element (a playing video, a spinner) freezes for the length of the animation.
  • It does nothing outside the DOM: React Native does not implement it.

Checking what your release exports

Every one of these APIs was documented on react.dev for months before a stable release exported it, and some documented APIs still are not exported. The canary channel publishes what is headed for the next stable release; the experimental channel carries APIs that may never ship. Asking the installed package is a ten-second habit that saves an afternoon of wondering why an import is undefined:

import * as React from 'react';
const wanted = ['Activity', 'useEffectEvent', 'cacheSignal', 'ViewTransition', 'addTransitionType',
                'experimental_taintUniqueValue'];
for (const n of wanted) console.log(n.padEnd(29), typeof React[n] === 'undefined' ? 'not in this build' : 'available');

Activity                      available
useEffectEvent                available
cacheSignal                   available
ViewTransition                available
addTransitionType             available
experimental_taintUniqueValue not in this build

Against 19.2.8, the same check reported ViewTransition and addTransitionType missing. The taint APIs are still absent from 19.3.0, and are not on canary either. Measured: only a 0.0.0-experimental build exports them, and only under the react-server condition (§17.10). The symptom is an import that type-checks against @types/react and is undefined when the code runs; the channel is the explanation.

One line each, for reference: , addTransitionType(, View Transition Class, View Transition Event, shared element transition and canary channel.

12.11 Transitions Render Independently

Before React 19.3, every transition in progress was rendered together. React tied them into a single render (it entangled them), so a slow transition held up unrelated ones that were ready. React 19.3 renders each transition on its own. It is a change of behaviour in a minor release, it affects any interface where two transitions can overlap, and it is easy to measure:

import { useState, useTransition, Suspense, use, act, version } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let arrive;
const report = new Promise(r => { arrive = r; });          // a slow request
function Report({ open }) { return open ? <b>{use(report)}</b> : <b>-</b>; }

function Dashboard() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
  const [reportPending, startReport] = useTransition();
  const [pagePending, startPage] = useTransition();
  globalThis.openReport = () => startReport(() => setOpen(true));
  globalThis.nextPage = () => startPage(() => setPage(p => p + 1));
  return <div>
    <Suspense fallback="loading"><Report open={open} /></Suspense>
    {` page=${page}`}{reportPending ? ' [report…]' : ''}{pagePending ? ' [page…]' : ''}
  </div>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => { createRoot(box).render(<Dashboard />); });
console.log('React', version);
await act(async () => { globalThis.openReport(); });
console.log('slow transition started:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.nextPage(); });
console.log('fast transition started:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { arrive('REPORT'); await report; });
console.log('slow one finishes      :', box.textContent);

React 19.3.0
slow transition started: - page=1 [report…]
fast transition started: - page=2 [report…]
slow one finishes      : REPORT page=2

The report's transition suspends on a request that has not arrived. The page change is a second, unrelated transition, started while the first is waiting. In 19.3.0 the page change committed immediately (page=2), while the report kept its pending indicator and its old content. When the report finally arrived, it committed on its own.

The same program under React 19.2.8 printed a different middle line:

fast transition started: - page=1 [report…] [page…]

In 19.2 the page change also waited, page=1 [page…], until the slow report resolved, and then both committed in one render. The page transition was ready all along; it was tied to one that was not.

What this changes in practice:

Independent work is no longer held hostage. A tab switch, a filter or a pagination click wrapped in a transition now commits as soon as it is ready, even while a navigation elsewhere on the page is waiting for data. That was the most common reason people removed a transition that "made the button slow".

Each useTransition reports its own pending state honestly. In 19.2 the page's isPending stayed true until the report finished, because its update was stuck in the same render. Code that treated "any transition pending" as one global busy state was relying on that tying-together. In 19.3 two indicators can be in different states, which is correct, and may surprise a test that assumed otherwise.

Queued work is still queued. Independence applies to unrelated transitions; it is not permission to run everything at once. useActionState still runs its queued actions one after another, each receiving the previous result, identically in 19.2.8 and 19.3.0, and §15.2 measures it. The react.dev pages for useTransition and startTransition still carry a caveat that multiple ongoing transitions are batched together. That describes 19.2; the measurement above is what 19.3 does.

12.12 What Concurrency Does Not Fix

Being precise about the limits is what stops transitions from becoming a superstition applied to every setState.

It does not make rendering faster. This is repeated because it is repeatedly forgotten. Priority changes when work happens, not how much work there is.

It does not help a single slow component. React can pause between components, not inside one. A component whose body takes 200 ms blocks the main thread for 200 ms whatever its priority, because the smallest unit React can pause after is one fiber. Splitting that component, or moving the work out of render, is the only fix.

It does not make network requests faster or fewer. A transition around a fetch changes nothing about the fetch. Debouncing, caching and removing duplicate requests are separate tools (§17.12 for the server side).

It does not remove the need for memo or the compiler. A cheap render at low priority is still cheaper than an expensive one. §10 and §11 reduce the work; §12 schedules it.

And marking everything as a transition is worse than marking nothing. If the update that shows the typed character is non-urgent too, then nothing is urgent, and you have rebuilt an interface that lags everywhere, with extra steps. All the value is in the contrast between the two priorities.

What This Section Established

Updates have two priorities. Everything is urgent by default, and useTransition or startTransition is how you say an update is not.

A transition produces two renders — measured: the first keeps the old value with isPending true, the second applies the change. That is what lets the old UI stay interactive while the new one is prepared, and it is what stops Suspense from replacing visible content with a fallback.

An async function passed to startTransition is an Action: the pending window spans the await. Measured, calling startTransition after an await instead produces one render with pending=false — the transition context is gone. Await inside, never before.

useDeferredValue is the same idea applied to a value you did not create: measured, one render with the new value and the stale deferred one, then a low-priority render with both. It is not a debounce — it waits for the machine rather than for a clock, and it is interruptible.

Interruption is why purity is a correctness requirement rather than a style rule: an abandoned render really does run your component body, and a side effect in there will fire on renders nobody ever sees.

<Activity mode="hidden"> keeps DOM and state, sets display: none, and unmounts effects — measured — which is what distinguishes it from hiding a subtree with CSS by hand. <ViewTransition> animates only changes made by a transition — measured, a plain setState never reached the browser's startViewTransition — and only the top-level one in an inserted or removed subtree takes part in enter, exit or share. Since 19.3, transitions also render independently: measured, a ready transition committed while an unrelated one was still suspended, where 19.2.8 held both until the slow one finished.

Exercises

1. Count the renders. Instrument a component with a render log and record the exact sequence for: an urgent update; the same update wrapped in startTransition; and a value read through useDeferredValue. Write down for each render what the state was and what isPending was, then explain why the transition needs two renders and the urgent update needs one.

2. Break the pending state. Write an async operation two ways — start(async () => { await f(); setX(1); }) and async () => { await f(); startTransition(() => setX(1)); } — and log isPending throughout. Show that the second never reports pending, and explain what React lost track of.

3. Transition or debounce. For each of these, say which tool is right and why the other is wrong: filtering ten thousand rows already in memory; querying a paid search API; recomputing a chart from a slider; sending a "user is typing" notification over a WebSocket. One of them wants both — say which and in what order.

4. Hidden three ways. Implement a tab whose inactive panel keeps its scroll position and its typed input, using (a) display: none applied by hand, (b) lifting the state into the parent, and (c) <Activity mode="hidden">. For each, state what happens to the panel's useEffect subscription and what that costs.

5. Prove interruption is real. Write a component that increments a module-level counter in its body, wrap an update in a transition, and drive several updates in quick succession. Show that the counter exceeds the number of commits. Then fix the component and say which lint rule would have caught it.

6. Animate a list-to-detail navigation. A photo grid renders <ul> of thumbnails; clicking one navigates to a detail page showing the photo full size. Make the thumbnail morph into the full image on the way in and back again on the way out, slide the page left going forward and right going back, and do nothing at all for a user who has asked for reduced motion. Say where each <ViewTransition> goes, what calls addTransitionType, and why a plain setState for the navigation would silently produce no animation.

Solution

1. The render sequences.

urgent           1 render    q='a'          pending=false
transition       2 renders   q='' pending=true      <- old value, pending shown
                             q='a' pending=false    <- the change applied
useDeferredValue 2 renders   q='a' deferred=''      <- urgent, cheap
                             q='a' deferred='a'     <- low priority, expensive

The transition needs two because the pending state is itself information the UI must show, and it must be shown while the old content is still there. One render could not do both: it would either apply the change (losing the old content) or not render at all (losing the pending indicator).

2. Breaking the pending state.

Measured in §12.5: the good form logs pending=true across three renders and settles at false; the bad form logs a single render at pending=false.

What React lost track of is the transition context. startTransition marks updates made during the synchronous execution of its callback. An await ends that execution — the rest of the function runs later, from the microtask queue, with no transition in scope — so the startTransition that runs afterwards opens a brand-new transition that no useTransition hook is observing.

3. Which tool.

filter 10k in-memory rows     transition / deferred value
                              the cost is rendering, which is what React schedules;
                              a debounce would add delay on a fast machine

query a paid search API       debounce
                              the cost is per request and external; a transition
                              would send one request per keystroke

recompute a chart from        deferred value on the slider's value
a slider                      the slider must stay at the user's finger; the chart
                              may lag one render

"user is typing" over a       throttle
WebSocket                     a rate limit on an external channel, not a render cost

The first one wants both if the rows are fetched rather than in memory: debounce the fetch, defer the render. In that order — the debounce decides whether a request happens at all, the deferral decides when its result is drawn.

4. Hidden three ways.

(a) display:none by hand   scroll ✓  input ✓  effects KEEP RUNNING
                           the subscription stays open forever; the hidden panel
                           keeps polling. Also still re-renders on every update.

(b) lift the state up      scroll ✗  input ✓  effects unmount with the component
                           DOM is destroyed, so scroll position is lost unless you
                           store that too. Cheapest to render.

(c) <Activity mode=hidden> scroll ✓  input ✓  effects UNMOUNT
                           DOM and state kept, subscription closed, no update
                           rendering while hidden.

(c) is what (a) was trying to be. The cost it does carry is memory: the DOM nodes stay allocated, so hiding fifty large panels this way is not free.

5. Proving interruption.

let bodyRuns = 0;
function Impure({ q }) {
  bodyRuns++;                      // a side effect during render
  return <b>{q}</b>;
}

Driving several transition updates in quick succession makes bodyRuns exceed the number of committed renders, because React starts rendering with one value, is interrupted by a newer one, and discards the partial tree — the body ran, nothing was committed. The exact excess depends on timing, which is the point: it is not reproducible.

The fix is to move the counter out of render — into an effect if it should count commits, or out of the component entirely if it is instrumentation. react-hooks/purity reports the mutation of a variable declared outside the component with "Cannot reassign variables declared outside of the component/hook", and <StrictMode> would have made the double-count visible on the very first render.

6. List to detail.

Three placements, and a run that proves each does what it is for (the same browser stand-in as §12.10, and no act(), for the reason §12.10 measured):

import { useState, ViewTransition, startTransition, addTransitionType } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.CSS = { escape: s => s };
document.fonts = { status: 'loaded' };
document.documentElement.getAnimations = () => [];
document.documentElement.animate = () => ({ cancel() {} });
const fired = [];
document.startViewTransition = ({ update, types }) => {
  const done = Promise.resolve().then(update).then(() => fired.unshift(`types=${JSON.stringify(types)}`));
  return { ready: done, finished: done, updateCallbackDone: done, skipTransition() {} };
};
const on = who => ({ onShare: () => { fired.push(`${who} share`); }, onEnter: () => { fired.push(`${who} enter`); },
                     onExit: () => { fired.push(`${who} exit`); } });

const photos = [{ id: 1, alt: 'one' }, { id: 2, alt: 'two' }];

function navigate(setRoute, to, direction) {
  startTransition(() => {                    // a plain setState would never animate
    addTransitionType(direction);            // 'forward' or 'back'
    setRoute(to);
  });
}

function Grid({ open }) {
  return <ul>{photos.map(p =>
    <li key={p.id} onClick={() => open(p.id)}>
      <ViewTransition name={`photo-${p.id}`} {...on(`thumb ${p.id}`)}><img alt={p.alt} /></ViewTransition>
    </li>)}</ul>;
}

function Detail({ id }) {
  return <ViewTransition name={`photo-${id}`} {...on(`full ${id}`)}><img alt="full size" /></ViewTransition>;
}

function Page({ children, id }) {
  return <ViewTransition default="none" {...on(id)}
                         enter={{ forward: 'slide-from-right', back: 'slide-from-left' }}
                         exit={{ forward: 'slide-to-left', back: 'slide-to-right' }}>
    <main>{children}</main>
  </ViewTransition>;
}

function App() {
  const [route, setRoute] = useState('grid');
  globalThis.go = (to, dir) => navigate(setRoute, to, dir);
  return route === 'grid'
    ? <Page key="grid" id="grid page"><Grid open={id => globalThis.go(id, 'forward')} /></Page>
    : <Page key={route} id="detail page"><Detail id={route} /></Page>;
}

const settle = () => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
root.render(<App />);
await settle();
for (const [to, dir] of [[2, 'forward'], ['grid', 'back']]) {
  fired.length = 0;
  globalThis.go(to, dir);
  await settle();
  console.log(`${dir.padEnd(7)}:`, fired.join(', '));
}

forward: types=["forward"], grid page exit, thumb 2 share, detail page enter
back   : types=["back"], detail page exit, full 2 share, grid page enter

The page slide is enter and exit on <Page>. Each route renders its own <Page> with its own key, so a navigation removes one and inserts another, and each is the top-level <ViewTransition> of its subtree. Without the key, React would keep the same <Page> and report an update, and the enter/exit maps would never apply. The maps are keyed by the type navigate added, and default="none" stops a re-layout inside a page from cross-fading.

The photo morph is a named pair. photo-2 is deleted from inside the grid's <ul> and inserted in the detail page, and it shares in both directions even though the thumbnail is nested — named pairs are exempt from the top-level rule, and share takes precedence over the enter or exit the boundary would otherwise get.

Why a plain setState would do nothing: a <ViewTransition> only animates changes made by a transition. §12.10 measured startViewTransition never being called for an urgent update. Reduced motion is the @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block from §12.10, setting animation: none on the three pseudo-elements — React will not do it for you.

SECTION 13

Suspense, lazy and Code Splitting

<Suspense> is one component with one prop, and it is the hardest thing in React to describe accurately. That is not because the mechanism is complicated. It is because almost everything written about it describes a use case rather than the thing itself.

Here is the thing itself. A Suspense boundary is a placeholder in the tree for content that is not ready yet. Sometimes a component below it cannot render yet, because a module is still downloading, or because a promise it needs has not resolved. When that happens, React does not throw an error and does not render half a tree. It walks up to the nearest boundary, shows that boundary's fallback (for example a spinner) instead of everything below it, and comes back when the missing thing arrives.

That is the whole contract. Three things follow from it that are worth stating before any example.

Suspense does not fetch anything. It has no opinion about data loading, no cache and no request logic. It is the way something else says "not yet", and that something else is lazy, use, a framework's data layer, or a server component (§17).

A boundary is a unit of reveal, not a unit of loading. Everything inside one boundary appears together, at the moment the last part of it is ready. So where you put boundaries is a design decision about what the user sees, and in what order. §13.5 is entirely about it.

It is not an error boundary. A Suspense boundary catches "not ready"; §14's error boundaries catch "went wrong". They are often placed together, but they are different components with different props.

13.1 What Activates a Boundary

What activates suspense is a short, fixed list, and knowing it prevents most of the confusion.

lazy()
A component whose module has not finished downloading. The original use case, and still the most common.
use(promise)
Reading a promise that has not resolved. §13.8.
An async Server Component
Its await has not finished. §17.6.
A framework's data hook
Anything built on the same primitive — a router's loader, a Suspense-enabled query library.
A stylesheet with precedence
Waiting for a stylesheet to load before revealing the content it belongs to, so nothing paints unstyled. §16.14.
NOT: fetching in an effect
A useEffect that fetches and calls setState never suspends. The component rendered successfully with no data; that is a state you must render yourself.
NOT: a promise in an event handler
Suspending is something that happens during render. An await in an onClick is ordinary asynchronous JavaScript.

The two "does not" entries are where the disappointment comes from. Wrapping a component that fetches in an effect in a <Suspense> boundary does nothing at all. There is no error and no warning, and the fallback never appears. The mechanism was never engaged.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: what activates suspense and waiting for a stylesheet to load.

13.2 lazy and Code Splitting

lazy( takes a function that returns a promise for a module, and gives back a component that suspends until that module arrives.

import { Suspense, lazy, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const Late = lazy(() => Promise.resolve({ default: () => <b>LOADED</b> }));

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => {
  root.render(<Suspense fallback={<i>loading…</i>}><Late /></Suspense>);
});
console.log(box.innerHTML);

<b>LOADED</b>

In a real application the loader is () => import('./Chart.jsx'). That dynamic import is what a bundler recognises: it stops following imports at that point, and outputs the module and its dependencies as a separate file, called a chunk. That is code splitting: the module tree from §1.12 cut into pieces, with lazy marking the cuts.

Four rules make the difference between a split that helps and one that does nothing.

Declare the lazy component outside the component that renders it. Calling lazy() during render produces a new component type on every render. React treats that as a different type at that position (§2.4), and remounts it every time. This is the most common lazy bug, and it shows up as "my lazy component's state gets reset".

The loader must be a literal import() the bundler can see. lazy(() => import(path)) with a computed path defeats the bundler's analysis. Most bundlers will then bundle either everything matching a pattern, or nothing at all.

Split at meaningful boundaries. A route, a modal that most users never open, a heavy editor, a charting library. Splitting off a 2 kB component adds a network round trip and saves nothing.

Preload before you need it. The point of splitting is a smaller first download, not a slower interaction. Call the same loader function on hover or on focus, or use preload() from §16.15. That starts the download before the click, so the chunk is usually there by the time it is needed.

lazy is also the reason <Suspense> was introduced in the first place, and the two must be used together: a lazy component with no boundary above it throws an error.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: dynamic import and preload(.

13.3 The fallback, and What It Costs

The fallback prop takes an element to render in place of the whole subtree. It is not a slot for a spinner; it is a replacement tree. The two design questions about it are its size and its shape.

A fallback that is smaller than the content it replaces makes the layout jump when the content arrives. A fallback with a different shape makes the change feel like a page change. Skeleton screens (grey placeholders shaped like the content) beat spinners for a reason that is not about looks: a skeleton takes up the same space, so nothing moves when the real content lands.
