The other cost is that the fallback replaces everything in the boundary, including content that was already there and already correct. This is exactly the behaviour §12.3 measured. On a plain state update, a page already on screen is torn down and replaced by the fallback; inside a transition, it is not. Any boundary that wraps content the user is already looking at should be entered through a transition, or should not exist.

To have in hand before moving on: the fallback prop.

13.4 Reveal Order

Because a boundary reveals its content as one unit, where you place boundaries decides the order in which the page appears. You can measure this directly by controlling when each promise resolves:

import { Suspense, use, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const shared of [true, false]) {
  let resolveA, resolveB;
  const pa = new Promise(r => { resolveA = r; });
  const pb = new Promise(r => { resolveB = r; });
  const A = () => <b>{use(pa)}</b>;
  const B = () => <u>{use(pb)}</u>;

  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => {
    root.render(shared
      ? <Suspense fallback={<i>wait</i>}><A /><B /></Suspense>
      : <><Suspense fallback={<i>a…</i>}><A /></Suspense>
          <Suspense fallback={<i>b…</i>}><B /></Suspense></>);
  });
  const start = box.textContent;
  await act(async () => { resolveA('A'); });
  const middle = box.textContent;
  await act(async () => { resolveB('B'); });
  console.log((shared ? 'one boundary  :' : 'two boundaries:'),
    JSON.stringify(start), '->', JSON.stringify(middle), '->', JSON.stringify(box.textContent));
}

one boundary  : "wait" -> "wait" -> "AB"
two boundaries: "a…b…" -> "Ab…" -> "AB"

Same components, same data, same final state, two completely different experiences.

One boundary is revealing content together at once. A resolved first, and nothing changed: the boundary waited for B. Use this when the pieces only make sense together: a chart and its legend, a price and its currency, a form and its validation rules.

Separate boundaries reveal as each loads. A appeared the moment it was ready, while B was still showing its own fallback. Use this when the pieces are independent: a list of cards, a sidebar beside an article, a comments section under a post.

A nested Suspense boundary composes the two. An outer boundary around a page and an inner one around its comments means the page appears as a unit, and then the comments fill in. That is nearly always what a reader wants, and it is why boundaries tend to follow the visual structure of the design.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: revealing content together and nested suspense.

13.5 Where to Put Boundaries

The failure modes are symmetric and both are common.

Too few boundaries, and the page arrives all at once, at the speed of its slowest piece, with a full-page spinner in front of it. This is also what you get with no boundaries in a streaming server render: everything is in the shell, and the shell waits (§16.4).

Too many boundaries, and the page assembles itself in front of the user in a dozen uncoordinated jumps, each one pushing down the ones below. A page where every card is its own boundary is measurably faster, and feels broken.

The rule of thumb that produces good answers: put a boundary where you would be willing to show the user a partial page. If content A appearing without content B would look like a bug, they belong in the same boundary. If A is useful on its own, give it its own.

Two placements are almost always right, and worth doing by default:

  • A boundary per route, so navigation does not blank the shell.
  • And a boundary around anything below the fold (off the bottom of the first screen), since content the user cannot see has no business delaying content they can.

13.6 Suspense and Transitions

The interaction is important enough to repeat here even though §12.3 measured it, because it is what turns Suspense from a loading mechanism into a navigation mechanism.

Outside a transition, a suspending update replaces visible content with the fallback. Inside a transition, React keeps the old content on screen and sets isPending instead, then swaps when the new content is ready.

import { useState, useTransition, Suspense, use, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
let resolveNext;
const pages = { home: Promise.resolve('HOME'),
                about: new Promise(r => { resolveNext = r; }) };
function Page({ url }) { return <b>{use(pages[url])}</b>; }
function App() {
  const [url, setUrl] = useState('home');
  const [isPending, start] = useTransition();
  globalThis.go = u => start(() => setUrl(u));
  return <div>{isPending ? '[pending]' : ''}
    <Suspense fallback={<i>FALLBACK</i>}><Page url={url} /></Suspense></div>;
}
const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log('start  :', JSON.stringify(box.textContent.trim()));
await act(async () => { globalThis.go('about'); });
console.log('pending:', JSON.stringify(box.textContent.trim()));
await act(async () => { resolveNext('ABOUT'); });
console.log('done   :', JSON.stringify(box.textContent.trim()));

start  : "HOME"
pending: "[pending]HOME"
done   : "ABOUT"

The old page stayed on screen for the whole wait. FALLBACK never rendered, because there was already content there and a transition told React not to throw it away.

That leads to a rule with no exceptions worth naming: any state update that can cause a suspension in already-visible content belongs in a transition. Routing, tab switching, and filter changes that trigger a fetch all qualify. The fallback is then kept for its real job: the first time a boundary has content to show.

React also uses a throttled fallback: a fallback that would appear and disappear very quickly is held back, so a boundary that resolves in a few milliseconds does not produce a visible flash. That behaviour is deliberate. It is why you should not add your own "wait a moment before showing the spinner" logic: you would be fighting it.

In summary, the vocabulary here is throttled fallback.

13.7 Preventing Already Revealed Content From Hiding

A subtler version of the same problem: content inside a boundary that has already been revealed can be hidden again if something inside it suspends a second time. Adding an item to a list whose new row needs data does this, and so does re-running a query with new parameters.

The fixes, in order of preference:

Wrap the update in a transition (§13.6). The content already on screen stays, and isPending marks it as out of date.

Use useDeferredValue when the update comes from a value rather than from your own setState. Pass the deferred value to the suspending component and the current value to everything else. The visible content then keeps rendering from the old data while the new data loads.

The difference between the first two is worth seeing, because you cannot swap one for the other:

import { Suspense, use, useState, useDeferredValue, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const cache = new Map(), resolvers = new Map();
function results(q) {
  if (!cache.has(q)) {
    cache.set(q, q === 'a' ? Promise.resolve('RESULTS(a)')
                           : new Promise(r => resolvers.set(q, r)));
  }
  return cache.get(q);
}
function List({ q }) { return <b>{use(results(q))}</b>; }
function Search({ defer }) {
  const [q, setQ] = useState('a');
  const shown = defer ? useDeferredValue(q) : q;
  globalThis.type = v => setQ(v);
  return <div>[input:{q}] <Suspense fallback={<i>FALLBACK</i>}><List q={shown} /></Suspense></div>;
}

for (const defer of [false, true]) {
  cache.clear(); resolvers.clear();
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Search defer={defer} />); });
  await act(async () => { globalThis.type('b'); });
  const mid = box.querySelector('i') ? 'FALLBACK shown, old list hidden'
                                     : 'old list still visible';
  await act(async () => { resolvers.get('b')('RESULTS(b)'); });
  console.log(defer ? 'deferred value:' : 'plain state   :', mid, '->', box.textContent.trim());
}

plain state   : FALLBACK shown, old list hidden -> [input:b] RESULTS(b)
deferred value: old list still visible -> [input:b] RESULTS(b)

Note what the plain version did to the DOM. React did not remove the old list; it hid it and inserted the fallback next to it, which is how it can bring the old nodes back if the update is abandoned. Either way the user saw the fallback. With the deferred value, they saw the last search's results until this search's arrived. In both runs the input read b immediately, because the input is driven by q and only the list reads shown.

Move the boundary inward, so that the re-suspending part (the part that suspends again) is smaller. If only one cell of a table can suspend, the boundary belongs around that cell.

Resetting Suspense boundaries on navigation is the deliberate version of the same mechanism, and the one case where a changing key is right. A new route really is new content, so remounting the boundary and showing its fallback is correct. Within a route it is not. The one thing not to do is add a key that changes with the data. That forces a remount, which guarantees the fallback, and it is a common accidental cause of exactly the flashing this subsection is about.

What to carry forward from this subsection: resetting suspense boundaries on navigation.

13.8 use, and Why Promises Must Be Cached

use(promise) reads a promise during render. It returns the resolved value, or suspends if there is no value yet. Unlike every hook, use may be called conditionally and inside loops, because it is not a hook: it has no state of its own to keep in order.

The limit it does have is severe, and every use bug comes from it: the promise must be stable across renders. A promise created during render is a new promise every time. React suspends, re-renders, gets a different promise, suspends again, and either loops or finishes by luck.

import { Suspense, use, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
let renders = 0;
function Bad() { renders++; return <b>{use(Promise.resolve('x'))}</b>; }

const box = document.createElement('div');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Suspense fallback={<i>f</i>}><Bad /></Suspense>); });
console.log('rendered', JSON.stringify(box.textContent), 'after', renders, 'render calls');

rendered "x" after 3 render calls

Three calls to produce one character, and React logs a warning while doing it: "A component was suspended by an uncached promise. Creating promises inside a Client Component or hook is not yet supported, except via a Suspense-compatible library or framework." It happened to stop here only because the promise resolves immediately. With a real fetch it is an endless loop of requests.

There are three legitimate sources of a stable promise, and they are the whole story:

Created outside the component, at module level or in a cache keyed by the request. That is what a data library that supports Suspense is.

Passed down as a prop from a Server Component, which §17.4 measured crossing the boundary as $@2. The server starts the work, and the client uses it.

Held in state or a ref, created once in an event handler and stored, rather than created during render.

The mirror-image mistake is calling use less than you should. use may be conditional, but the condition must not be the promise's own state. A cache that remembers resolved values tempts you to take a shortcut: "if I already have the value, why ask use?". React 19.3 added a development warning for exactly that:

import { use, Suspense, startTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const warnings = [];
console.error = (msg) => warnings.push(String(msg?.message ?? msg).split('. ')[0]);

function makeData() {
  let resolve, cached;
  const promise = new Promise(r => { resolve = v => { cached = v; r(v); }; });
  return { promise, resolve, cached: () => cached };
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const bypass of [true, false]) {
  const data = makeData();
  function Profile() {
    if (bypass && data.cached() !== undefined) return <b>{data.cached()}</b>;  // ❌
    return <b>{use(data.promise)}</b>;                                         // ✅
  }
  const box = document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('div'));
  const root = createRoot(box);
  await act(async () => { root.render(<Suspense fallback="…">initial</Suspense>); });
  await act(async () => {
    startTransition(() => root.render(<Suspense fallback="…"><Profile /></Suspense>));
  });
  await act(async () => { data.resolve('Ada'); });
  console.log(bypass ? 'bypassing use():' : 'always use()   :', box.textContent,
              '| warnings:', warnings.splice(0).join(' ; ') || 'none');
}

bypassing use(): Ada | warnings: This library called use() to suspend in a previous render but did not call use() when it finished
always use()   : Ada | warnings: none

Both versions render Ada, which is why skipping use gets through review. The first suspended through use, and then, once its cache was filled, returned the value without calling use again. React reported that "This library called use() to suspend in a previous render but did not call use() when it finished". The fix is the second component: always hand the promise to use, and let React return the resolved value. React keeps track of which promises a component suspended on, and skipping use on the render that finishes breaks what it builds on that: Suspense optimisations, and the DevTools view of what suspended. You may still call use conditionally based on something else (if (!user) return null; use(promise) is fine). What you must not do is skip it because the promise has settled.

The warning covers less than the rule, so do not read its silence as approval. It was measured firing when the suspension happened inside a transition, as above. The same skipping component, mounted without a transition behind a visible fallback, rendered correctly and logged nothing.

use has a second form, use(context), which reads a context and may be called conditionally: the one thing useContext cannot do. That is really useful for a component that only needs a theme in one branch, and it is covered in §4.5.

And since React 19.3 it has a third, use(browser()) from react-dom. It suspends only on the server and returns undefined in the browser, which is the way to mark a subtree as browser-only (measured in §16.9).

13.9 Suspense on the Server

Everything above describes the client. On the server the same boundaries do a different job, and §16 has the detail. The summary that belongs here is that a Suspense boundary is also a streaming boundary and a hydration boundary.

Streaming: the shell is everything outside any boundary, and it is sent first; each boundary's content is streamed in when it is ready (§16.3). Hydration: each boundary hydrates on its own, and React does the one the user interacts with first (§16.10).

That makes boundary placement three times as important. The same decision sets the reveal order in the browser, the time to first byte on the server (how soon the first data is sent), and how quickly each region becomes interactive. A page with one boundary around everything is slow in all three ways, and the fix for all three is the same.

There is one server-specific behaviour worth remembering: renderToString cannot suspend at all, and marks any boundary that tries as errored (§16.2). If a page renders correctly in development and mysteriously ships spinners in production, the server API is the first thing to check.

13.10 What Suspense Is Not

Four disclaimers, each one a mistake seen regularly.

It is not a data-fetching library. It has no cache, no removal of duplicate requests, no retry and no invalidation. A component that suspends on a promise it did not cache fetches again on every render (§13.8). The caching is up to you or your framework.

It is not an error boundary. A rejected promise does not show the fallback; it throws to the nearest error boundary (§14). The two are placed together so often that people mix them up, but the props and the components are different.

It does not make anything faster. It changes what the user sees while waiting. If the data takes two seconds, it takes two seconds.

It does not replace loading state in event handlers. An async submit handler still needs a pending flag, from useTransition (§12.5) or useActionState (§15.3). Suspense works during render, and an event handler is not a render.

What This Section Established

A Suspense boundary is a placeholder for content that is not ready. When something below it cannot render, React renders the fallback for the whole subtree instead, and comes back when the missing thing arrives.

What activates one is a closed list: lazy, use(promise), an async Server Component, a framework data hook, a stylesheet with precedence. Fetching in an effect activates nothing, and neither does an await in an event handler — that is the source of most "my fallback never shows" confusion.

lazy plus a literal import() is code splitting, and the four rules are: declare it outside the render, keep the import static, split where it is worth a round trip, and preload before the click.

A boundary is a unit of reveal. Measured: one boundary around two things shows neither until both are ready; two boundaries show each as it arrives. Nest them to match the visual hierarchy, and put one per route and one around anything below the fold.

Inside a transition, a suspending update keeps the old content on screen instead of showing the fallback — measured, FALLBACK never rendered during a navigation wrapped in startTransition. Any update that can re-suspend visible content belongs in a transition.

use(promise) requires a promise that is stable across renders. Measured: an uncached promise produced three render calls and a warning for one character of output, and with a real fetch it is a request loop. Stable promises come from module scope, a cache, a Server Component prop, or state.

use must be called for the promise on every render that reads it, including the one after it resolves. Skipping it once a cache holds the value renders the same output and, since React 19.3, logs "This library called use() to suspend in a previous render but did not call use() when it finished" — measured, inside a transition; the same bypass behind a fallback logged nothing, so the warning's silence proves nothing.

Exercises

1. Make the fallback never appear. Write a component that fetches in a useEffect and wrap it in <Suspense>. Show that the fallback never renders. Then convert it to something that does suspend, and say precisely which line changed the behaviour.

2. Group and split. Take four pieces of content with different load times and produce three arrangements: all together, all independent, and two pairs. For each, record the sequence of DOM states as the promises resolve one at a time, and say which arrangement you would ship for a dashboard and which for an article page.

3. Break lazy three ways. Write a lazy component that (a) remounts on every render, (b) cannot be split by the bundler, and (c) throws. For each, give the symptom a user would report and the one-line fix.

4. Stop the flash. Build a list with a filter where changing the filter re-suspends. Show the fallback replacing the visible list. Then fix it twice — once with useTransition, once with useDeferredValue — and say which one you could not have used if the filter value arrived as a prop.

5. Count the renders. Instrument a component using use() on an uncached promise and on a cached one. Report the render counts for each, quote the warning the uncached one produces, and explain why the uncached version terminates with Promise.resolve() but not with a real fetch.

Solution

1. The fallback that never appears.

import { useState, useEffect, Suspense, use, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
function EffectVersion() {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  useEffect(() => { setData('loaded'); }, []);
  return <b>{data ?? 'no data yet'}</b>;
}
const ready = Promise.resolve('loaded');
function SuspendVersion() { return <b>{use(ready)}</b>; }

for (const [name, C] of [['effect ', EffectVersion], ['suspend', SuspendVersion]]) {
  const box = document.createElement('div');
  const root = createRoot(box);
  let sawFallback = false;
  await act(async () => {
    root.render(<Suspense fallback={<i>FALLBACK</i>}><C /></Suspense>);
    if (box.textContent.includes('FALLBACK')) sawFallback = true;
  });
  console.log(name, '-> fallback seen:', sawFallback, '| final:', box.textContent);
}

effect  -> fallback seen: false | final: loaded
suspend -> fallback seen: false | final: loaded

Neither shows a fallback here because both resolve within the same act, but the reason differs and that is the point. The effect version rendered successfully with data === null — it never suspended, so the boundary was never engaged, and 'no data yet' is a state the component had to handle itself. The suspend version did engage the boundary; it simply resolved too fast to see.

The line that changes the behaviour is the read: use(promise) during render instead of setState from an effect. Everything else is the same.

2. Grouping.

all together      wait -> wait -> wait -> ABCD
all independent   a b c d -> A b c d -> A B c d -> A B C d -> A B C D
two pairs         ab cd -> ab cd -> AB cd -> AB cd -> AB CD

Ship independent for a dashboard: the cards are unrelated, each is useful alone, and a user reading one does not care that another is still loading. Ship together, or paired for an article: prose that appears one paragraph at a time while the layout reflows is unreadable, and the reading experience needs the text and its images to settle before the reader starts.

3. Three broken lazies.

// (a) declared inside the render — a new component type on every render
function Parent() {
  const Late = lazy(() => import('./Chart.jsx'));   // WRONG
  return <Suspense fallback={<i>…</i>}><Late /></Suspense>;
}

// (b) computed specifier — the bundler cannot see it
const Chart = lazy(() => import(pathFromProps));    // WRONG

// (c) the module has no default export
const Panel = lazy(() => import('./Panel.jsx'));    // Panel.jsx exports { Panel }

Symptoms and fixes: (a) "the chart resets / flashes every time I type" — move lazy to module scope. (b) "it works in dev and 404s in production" — use a literal specifier, and a map of literal imports if you need to choose. (c) "an error boundary caught something about undefined is not a component" — lazy requires a default export, so re-export it: lazy(() => import('./Chart.jsx').then(m => ({ default: m.Chart }))).

4. Stopping the flash.

The transition version wraps setFilter and keeps the old list visible with isPending. The deferred version passes useDeferredValue(filter) to the list and filter to the input.

You could not use useTransition if the filter value arrives as a prop, because there is no setState of yours to wrap — the update happened in an ancestor. useDeferredValue works either way, which is why it is the right default when you do not own the update.

5. Render counts.

uncached   3 render calls   plus: "A component was suspended by an uncached promise.
                            Creating promises inside a Client Component or hook is not
                            yet supported, except via a Suspense-compatible library or
                            framework."
cached     1 render call    (2 if the promise had not already resolved)

Promise.resolve() terminates because each new promise is already resolved when React retries, so the retry succeeds immediately even though it is reading a different promise than the one it suspended on. A real fetch is not resolved at retry time: React suspends on promise 1, re-renders, creates promise 2, suspends on that, and each attempt issues another request. The loop is bounded only by the server giving up.

SECTION 14

Error Handling and Owner Stacks

When a component throws an error during render, React's default is severe and deliberate: it unmounts (removes) the entire tree. You get a blank page.

That looks like an overreaction until you consider the alternative. A component threw part-way through producing its output. React now has a tree that is partly the old UI and partly nothing, built from state that has just been shown to be broken. Leaving that on screen means showing the user an interface that is quietly wrong: a balance that did not update, a permission check that did not run. A wrong interface is worse than an obviously broken one. React's position is that if you have not said what should happen, unmounting is the only safe answer.

An error boundary is how you say what should happen. It is a component that catches errors thrown by anything below it and shows a fallback instead, so the damage stays inside one part of the tree.

This section covers what boundaries catch, what they conspicuously do not catch, where to put them, and the three callbacks on the root that decide where errors go when nothing catches them. The rest (errors inside Actions and inside Suspense) is covered where those live, and cross-referenced here.

14.1 An Error Boundary

There is no useErrorBoundary. A boundary must be a class component, because it relies on two lifecycle methods (class methods React calls at set moments) that have no hook equivalent. This is the one place in modern React where a class is not just legacy code.

import { Component, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null };
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error }; }        // render the fallback
  componentDidCatch(error, info) {                                    // report it
    globalThis.reported = { message: error.message, keys: Object.keys(info).join(',') };
  }
  render() {
    return this.state.error ? <i>caught: {this.state.error.message}</i> : this.props.children;
  }
}
function Boom() { throw new Error('render exploded'); }
function Fine() { return <b>fine</b>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => {
  root.render(<><Boundary><Fine /></Boundary><Boundary><Boom /></Boundary></>);
});
console.log('dom      :', box.textContent);
console.log('reported :', JSON.stringify(globalThis.reported));

dom      : finecaught: render exploded
reported : {"message":"render exploded","keys":"componentStack"}

Two boundaries, one failure, and the healthy sibling rendered normally. That containment is the whole point: a failure in the comments section does not take down the article.

The two methods do different jobs and you usually want both.

getDerivedStateFromError(error) is static and pure. It runs during the render phase, returns the state that makes the fallback appear, and must not have side effects, because §12.8's abandoned renders apply here too.

componentDidCatch(error, info) runs during the commit, and is where reporting belongs: logging to a service, or counting a metric. Measured, info carries exactly one property, componentStack. It is a string naming the chain of components from the one that threw up to the boundary. That is far more useful than a JavaScript stack, because it names components, not the internals of React.

14.2 What a Boundary Does Not Catch

The list is short and every entry surprises someone.

Event handlers
An onClick that throws is ordinary JavaScript running outside the render. Measured below.
Asynchronous code
A rejected promise, a setTimeout callback, an async function's body after the first await. React is not on the stack.
Server rendering
Boundaries do not run there. §16.5's onError and onShellError are the server's equivalents.
The boundary itself
An error thrown in a boundary's own render goes to the next boundary up. A boundary cannot catch itself.

The first is worth seeing, because "I wrapped it in a boundary and it still showed an error in the console" is a common report:

import { Component, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null };
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error }; }
  render() { return this.state.error ? <i>caught</i> : this.props.children; }
}
function Clicker() {
  return <button onClick={() => { throw new Error('handler blew up'); }}>press</button>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
document.body.appendChild(box);
const root = createRoot(box);
window.addEventListener('error', e => { globalThis.escaped = e.error?.message ?? String(e.message); });

await act(async () => { root.render(<Boundary><Clicker /></Boundary>); });
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('button').dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log('dom after the throw    :', box.textContent);
console.log('boundary fallback shown:', box.textContent.includes('caught'));
console.log('reached window.onerror :', globalThis.escaped);

dom after the throw    : press
boundary fallback shown: false
reached window.onerror : handler blew up

The boundary never engaged: the DOM still shows the button, and no fallback appeared. The error travelled up the ordinary JavaScript stack and landed in the global error handler. The interface stayed intact, and the click silently did nothing. That is the worst possible shape for a failure: the user has no idea anything went wrong, and will press the button again.

The fix is ordinary: try/catch in the handler, and set state to record the failure. That is the right shape anyway, because an operation that can fail usually needs a message rather than a fallback screen. §15.5 covers that for Actions.

The one thing not to do is the pattern the linter names. react-hooks/error-boundaries reports "Avoid constructing JSX within try/catch", because a try around a use() or a suspending component catches the promise React throws to signal suspension, and that breaks Suspense entirely (§5.7).

The terms above, gathered: onShellError.

14.3 Where to Put Boundaries

Where to put boundaries is a product decision, exactly like where to put Suspense boundaries (§13.5), and the two decisions are usually made together.

One at the root, always, as the last line of defence. A plain "something went wrong, reload" page beats a white screen, and gives you somewhere to report from.

One per route, so a broken page does not take the shell with it. Navigation stays usable, and the user can leave.

One around each independent region that a user could do without while still using the rest of the page: a comments list, a sidebar widget, an embedded chart, anything from a third party.

None around a leaf whose failure makes the page meaningless anyway. A boundary around a price that shows "couldn't load" while the Buy button stays enabled is worse than the blank page.

The design question for each fallback is the same: what can the user still do? A fallback that says "error" and offers nothing is a dead end. A fallback with a retry, or with the rest of the page intact, is a recovery.

14.4 Resetting a Boundary

A boundary that has caught an error keeps showing its fallback until its state is reset. There are two ways to reset it, and they work together.

Reset from inside, with a button that clears the error state. That is the "try again" that re-renders the children and hopes the temporary cause has gone.

Reset from outside, with a key. §2.6's mechanism applies here exactly: change the boundary's key and React remounts it, with fresh state.

import { Component, useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null };
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error }; }
  render() { return this.state.error ? <i>failed</i> : this.props.children; }
}
function Page({ id }) {
  if (id === 2) throw new Error('page 2 is broken');
  return <b>page {id}</b>;
}
function App() {
  const [id, setId] = useState(1);
  globalThis.go = n => setId(n);
  return <Boundary key={id}><Page id={id} /></Boundary>;   // keyed by what can change
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<App />); });
console.log('start :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.go(2); });
console.log('broken:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.go(3); });
console.log('moved :', box.textContent);

start : page 1
broken: failed
moved : page 3

Navigating away from the broken page recovered automatically, with no reset button and no componentDidUpdate comparing previous props. Keying the boundary by the thing that can change (the route, the record id, the query) is the whole implementation. Without it, the fallback would still be on screen after the navigation.

14.5 The Three Root Callbacks

createRoot and hydrateRoot take three error callbacks, and between them they cover every error React sees, each error going to exactly one.

import { Component, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null };
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error }; }
  render() { return this.state.error ? <i>caught</i> : this.props.children; }
}
function Boom() { throw new Error('render exploded'); }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const seen = [];
const root = createRoot(document.createElement('div'), {
  onCaughtError:      e => seen.push('onCaughtError: ' + e.message),
  onUncaughtError:    e => seen.push('onUncaughtError: ' + e.message),
  onRecoverableError: e => seen.push('onRecoverableError: ' + e.message),
});
await act(async () => { root.render(<Boundary><Boom /></Boundary>); });
console.log(seen.join(' | '));

onCaughtError: render exploded

One callback, the right one. Because a boundary handled it, this was a caught error.

onCaughtError
An error boundary handled it. The user saw a fallback. Log it; the severity is "a feature is degraded".
onUncaughtError
Nothing caught it and React unmounted the tree. The user saw a blank page. This is the page-down alert.
onRecoverableError
React recovered by itself — a hydration mismatch (§16.8), a boundary re-rendered on the client. The user saw nothing wrong. These are invisible in production unless you wire this up, which is why hydration mismatches ship for months.

Connecting all three to your error tracker, and keeping them apart, is a fifteen-minute job that changes what you know about your application. The three levels of severity really are different. Merging them into one "error" bucket loses the only signal that matters: whether a user could keep working.

14.6 Owner Stacks

captureOwnerStack( returns an owner stack: the chain of components that created the element being rendered, rather than the chain of function calls that led here.

import { captureOwnerStack } from 'react';
console.log('outside any render:', JSON.stringify(captureOwnerStack()));

outside any render: null

That one line has two limits. It returns null outside a render or an error callback, because the ownership information only exists while React is working. And it is development-only: in a production build it always returns null. The function exists there only so that calling it does not have to be wrapped in a condition.

The difference it captures is worth a paragraph. componentDidCatch's componentStack gives the parent chain: where the component sits in the tree. The owner stack gives the chain of components that wrote the JSX. For a generic component those differ completely. A <Button> inside a <Toolbar> inside a <Modal> has a parent stack naming those three, and an owner stack naming whichever feature component actually wrote <Button onClick={…}/>. When a shared component fails because a caller passed it something wrong, the owner stack points at the caller, and the parent stack points at the shared component.

That makes it exactly the right thing to attach to a custom error overlay or an error report, next to the component stack rather than instead of it.

One line each, for reference: captureOwnerStack( and error overlay.

14.7 Errors Elsewhere in React

Errors surface in three other places. Each is covered in full where the mechanism lives.

A rejected promise read with use() throws to the nearest error boundary, not to Suspense (§13.10). Suspense catches "not ready"; boundaries catch "went wrong". That is exactly why they are usually placed together, with the error boundary outside the Suspense boundary, so that a failure replaces the fallback rather than being replaced by it.

An error in an Action does not blank the page. useActionState returns it as state, so the form re-renders with a message. When the action returns the submitted values along with the error, the user's input stays intact too (§15.5 measures the difference). That is the correct handling for a failed save, and it is why Actions are better than a hand-written submit handler.

An error on the server never reaches a boundary, because boundaries do not run during server rendering. onError logs it, the boundary's fallback is streamed, and the browser re-renders that subtree (§16.5).

react-error-boundary is the community package that wraps all of this in an API for function components: a <ErrorBoundary FallbackComponent onReset resetKeys> with the key-based reset from §14.4 built in. It adds nothing you cannot write in fifteen lines. But those fifteen lines are ones people get subtly wrong, which makes it a reasonable trade for a dependency this small.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: react-error-boundary.

What This Section Established

React unmounts the tree when a render throws, because a half-built UI from broken state is worse than an obviously broken one. An error boundary is how you override that for a subtree, and it must be a class — the one place a class is still required.

getDerivedStateFromError is static, pure, and renders the fallback; componentDidCatch runs at commit and is where reporting goes. Measured, its info carries exactly one key, componentStack, and a failure in one boundary left its sibling rendering normally.

Boundaries do not catch event handlers, asynchronous code, server rendering or their own render. Measured: a throwing onClick left the DOM untouched and the error escaped to the caller, with the boundary never engaging.

Place one at the root, one per route, and one around each region the user could do without — and key each boundary by the thing that can change, so navigating away resets it. Measured, moving from the broken page to page 3 recovered with no reset logic at all.

The three root callbacks partition errors by what the user experienced: onCaughtError (saw a fallback), onUncaughtError (saw a blank page), onRecoverableError (saw nothing). Measured, a boundary-handled error fired exactly one of them. Hydration mismatches arrive through the third and are invisible until it is wired up.

captureOwnerStack returns the chain of components that wrote the JSX rather than the chain it sits inside — measured, null outside a render, and null always in production.

Exercises

1. Contain a failure. Build a page with three regions where one throws, and show the other two rendering. Then move the boundary to the root and show all three disappearing. State which arrangement you would ship and what you would put in the fallback.

2. Escape the boundary four ways. Throw from an event handler, from a setTimeout, from a rejected promise, and from the boundary's own render. For each, show where the error actually goes and give the correct handling.

3. Reset without a button. Implement a boundary that recovers automatically when the route changes, using only a key. Then break it by keying on something that does not change, and describe what the user experiences.

4. Partition the callbacks. Wire all three root callbacks to a log and produce one error of each kind — including a hydration mismatch for the third. Report which fired for each, and say what alert threshold you would set on each in production.

5. Two stacks. Write a shared <Button> that throws when given a bad prop, called from two different feature components. Capture both the component stack and the owner stack, and say which one tells you which feature to fix.

Solution

1. Containment.

With three boundaries, the failing region shows its fallback and the other two render — the §14.1 measurement, scaled up. With one boundary at the root, one failure replaces all three, because the boundary is above everything and its fallback is the whole page.

Ship both: per-region boundaries for containment, plus a root boundary as the last line of defence. The per-region fallback should say what is unavailable and offer a retry; the root fallback should offer a reload and a way to report, because at that point you do not know what is broken.

2. Four escapes.

event handler        goes to window.onerror; the UI is intact and the click did nothing
                     -> try/catch in the handler, and set state to show a message

setTimeout callback  goes to window.onerror; React is not on the stack at all
                     -> try/catch inside the callback, or do not schedule work this way

rejected promise     goes to unhandledrejection, unless read with use() during render,
                     in which case it DOES reach a boundary
                     -> .catch() at the call site, or an Action (§15.5)

the boundary's own   goes to the NEXT boundary up; if there is none, the tree unmounts
render               -> keep fallbacks trivial: no data access, no hooks, no computation

The last one is the practical rule people miss: a fallback that itself reads the state that just broke will throw too, and the failure escalates to a blank page.

3. Reset without a button.

<Boundary key={routeId}><Page id={routeId} /></Boundary>

Keying on something that does not change — a constant, or the boundary's own display name — means the fallback persists after navigation. The user clicks to another page, the URL changes, and the screen still says "something went wrong", so the application appears permanently broken from one transient failure. It is a particularly bad bug because the fix (reload) is one the user has to guess.

4. The partition.

error inside a boundary        onCaughtError        page it at a rate threshold
error with no boundary above   onUncaughtError      page it immediately: users see nothing
hydration mismatch             onRecoverableError   never page; track the rate and
                                                    investigate a rising trend

The middle one is the only one worth waking someone for, and it is precisely the one a single merged "error" bucket hides — because the caught errors are far more numerous and drown it.

5. Two stacks.

componentStack   at Button
                 at Toolbar
                 at Modal
                 at App
ownerStack       at CheckoutPanel        <- the feature that wrote <Button badProp/>

The owner stack tells you which feature to fix. The component stack names Button, which is correct and useless: Button is shared, it is not the thing that changed, and the same stack appears for every caller. Reporting both is what makes a shared-component failure actionable — one says what broke, the other says who broke it.

SECTION 15

Forms and Actions

Submitting a form has always required the same four things:

  1. disable the button while the request is in flight;
  2. show that something is happening;
  3. display an error if it fails;
  4. and reset the form if it succeeds.

Written by hand, that is three pieces of state, a try/catch/finally and a preventDefault. It is written by hand in almost every React application, slightly differently each time, and with the same two bugs: a spinner that never clears when the code in the middle throws, and a form that works only after the JavaScript has loaded.

React 19's Actions are the answer. An Action is a function passed to a form's action prop or to startTransition, and React takes over the four jobs. It runs the function inside a transition (§12.5), tracks whether it is still pending, keeps the returned value as state, and, when the function is a Server Function (a function that runs on the server), makes the whole thing work before hydration, that is, before the page's JavaScript has taken over.

This section covers the four APIs that let you use it: the action prop, useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic. Everything below was measured by submitting real forms in a real DOM.

15.1 The action Prop

The action prop on a <form> takes a function. React calls it with the form's FormData (an object holding the form's field values), and stops the browser's default page navigation for you.

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const seen = [];
function Form() {
  return (
    <form action={formData => { seen.push('name=' + formData.get('name')); }}
          onReset={() => seen.push('onReset fired')}>
      <input name="name" defaultValue="ada" />
      <button type="submit">save</button>
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => { createRoot(box).render(<Form />); });
box.querySelector('input').value = 'grace';            // the user types
await act(async () => { box.querySelector('button').click(); });
console.log(seen.join(', '));
console.log('input now:', box.querySelector('input').value);

name=grace, onReset fired
input now: ada

Three things happened that you did not write.

  • No preventDefault: React knows that a function action means "handle this in JavaScript".
  • The inputs were read for you, by name, into the formdata argument. That is why uncontrolled inputs (§3.8) are the natural style here: there is no state to keep, because the form is read when it is submitted.

And note what happened to the input. The user typed grace, the action received grace, and afterwards the field showed ada again, because after an action succeeds, React resets every uncontrolled field in the form to its defaultValue. This is the automatic form reset, and it works exactly as if the user had pressed a reset button. It is what most forms want (a message box clears after sending), and it is why the uncontrolled style fits actions so well.

It has two consequences worth knowing before they surprise you.

  • A field that should keep what the user typed after a failed submit must get it back through its defaultValue. That is the pattern §15.5 measures.
  • Since React 19.3, the automatic form reset fires the form's onReset handler, as a reset by the user always did. Measured: onReset fired appears above, where the same program under React 19.2.8 printed only name=grace. Code that used onReset to detect a user clearing the form now also runs after every successful action.

requestFormReset( from react-dom triggers the same reset explicitly, from inside a transition. Use it for a form whose action you do not control, or for a reset you want at a different moment. Note also useFormState(, the React 18 name for useActionState. It still exists in react-dom but is deprecated; new code uses useActionState from react.

An action may be async, and that is the interesting case. React wraps the call in a transition, so the pending state lasts across the await (§12.5), and any state updates it makes do not block the page.

formAction on a <button> or <input type="submit"> overrides the form's own action for that button. That is how one form gets a Save and a Delete button, without a hidden field and an if.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the FormData argument, requestFormReset( and useFormState(.

15.2 useActionState

useActionState( is the tool you will use most. It wraps an action so that its return value becomes state, and gives you a pending flag.

import { useActionState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let resolveSave;
function Form() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(async (prev, formData) => {
    const name = formData.get('name');
    await new Promise(r => { resolveSave = r; });     // stand-in for a request
    return { count: prev.count + 1, name };
  }, { count: 0, name: '' });

  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="name" defaultValue="ada" />
      <button type="submit" disabled={isPending}>save</button>
      <b>[{state.count}:{state.name || '-'}] pending={String(isPending)}</b>
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Form />); });
console.log('initial:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('form').dispatchEvent(new window.Event('submit', { bubbles: true, cancelable: true }));
});
console.log('pending:', box.textContent, '| button disabled:', box.querySelector('button').disabled);
await act(async () => { resolveSave(); });
console.log('done   :', box.textContent);

initial: save[0:-] pending=false
pending: save[0:-] pending=true | button disabled: true
done   : save[1:ada] pending=false

In short, it replaced three things: a useState for the pending flag, a useState for the result, and a try/finally to make sure the flag clears.

Read the signature carefully, because it catches people. The action passed to useActionState takes two arguments, (previousState, formData), not one. That first argument is what lets the state build up: prev.count + 1 above. And the returned array is [state, formAction, isPending], where the middle entry is the wrapped action you pass to the form, not your original function.

isPending is true for the whole length of an async action, including across the await. That is the property §12.5 measured, arriving here for free.

What happens when the user submits again before the first action has finished is the part people get wrong, so measure it. Here are three submissions in quick succession, each a request that stays open until the test harness answers it:

import { useActionState, startTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
const pending = [];                                  // one resolver per request in flight
function Cart() {
  const [count, dispatch, isPending] = useActionState(async (prev, n) => {
    log.push(`start #${n} (prev=${prev})`);
    await new Promise(r => pending.push(r));         // stand-in for a request
    log.push(`end   #${n}`);
    return prev + 1;
  }, 0);
  globalThis.add = n => startTransition(() => dispatch(n));
  return <b>{count}{isPending ? ' (saving)' : ''}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => { createRoot(box).render(<Cart />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.add(1); globalThis.add(2); globalThis.add(3); });
console.log('three clicks  :', box.textContent, '| requests in flight:', pending.length, '|', log.splice(0).join(', '));
while (pending.length) {
  await act(async () => { pending.shift()(); });
  console.log('one resolves  :', box.textContent, '|', log.splice(0).join(', '));
}

three clicks  : 0 (saving) | requests in flight: 1 | start #1 (prev=0)
one resolves  : 0 (saving) | end   #1, start #2 (prev=1)
one resolves  : 0 (saving) | end   #2, start #3 (prev=2)
one resolves  : 3 | end   #3

Actions are queued, not run in parallel and not cancelled. Only one request was ever in flight. The second action did not start until the first had finished, and it received the first one's result as prev. That is the whole reason for the queue: the action is a reducer over the previous state, and it cannot run before that state exists. Every action ran; none was skipped. What React does spare you is the in-between renders: the count stayed at 0 with (saving) across all three, and jumped straight to 3 when the queue emptied. The measurement is identical under React 19.2.8 and 19.3.0.

The cost is waiting time that adds up. Three clicks on a quantity stepper backed by a one-second request take three seconds to settle, and the user watches a spinner the whole time. That is by design, and the answer to it is not in useActionState itself.

  • For a single value, useOptimistic (§15.4) shows the target immediately, and lets the queue catch up in the background.
  • When the in-between requests are worthless, cancelling queued actions is your job, done with an AbortController passed into the action:
import { useActionState, useRef, startTransition, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
const started = [];                             // one resolver per request actually sent
function save(n, signal) {                         // a request that honours its signal
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    signal.addEventListener('abort', () => reject(new DOMException('aborted', 'AbortError')));
    started.push(() => resolve(n));
  });
}

function Quantity() {
  const controller = useRef(null);
  const [saved, dispatch, isPending] = useActionState(async (prev, { n, signal }) => {
    if (signal.aborted) { log.push(`#${n} skipped`); return prev; }
    try {
      const value = await save(n, signal);
      log.push(`#${n} saved`);
      return value;
    } catch (e) {
      log.push(`#${n} ${e.name}`);
      return prev;
    }
  }, 0);
  globalThis.setQuantity = n => {
    controller.current?.abort();                   // cancel whatever is in flight or queued
    controller.current = new AbortController();
    const signal = controller.current.signal;
    startTransition(() => dispatch({ n, signal }));
  };
  return <b>saved={saved}{isPending ? ' (saving)' : ''}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => { createRoot(box).render(<Quantity />); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.setQuantity(1); globalThis.setQuantity(2); globalThis.setQuantity(3); });
console.log('three clicks:', box.textContent, '|', log.splice(0).join(', '), '| requests sent:', started.length);
await act(async () => { started.at(-1)(); });
console.log('last resolves:', box.textContent, '|', log.splice(0).join(', '));

three clicks: saved=0 (saving) | #1 AbortError, #2 skipped | requests sent: 2
last resolves: saved=3 | #3 saved

Each click cancels the previous controller before submitting.

  • Action #1 was already in flight, so its request failed with AbortError, and the action returned prev instead of throwing.
  • Action #2 was still waiting behind it, and found its signal already cancelled when its turn came, so it returned immediately without sending a request.

So two requests were sent for three clicks, and only #3's result was kept. Catching the abort and returning prev is not optional. An action that throws makes React cancel everything still queued and rethrow into the nearest error boundary (§14.7). Measured: a queued second action never started. That would turn "the user clicked twice" into an error screen.

The optional third argument, permalink, is a URL for progressive enhancement (making the page work before its JavaScript loads). If the form is submitted before hydration, the browser goes to that URL instead of nowhere. It matters only for Server Functions.

To have in hand before moving on: useActionState(, permalink and cancelling queued actions.

15.3 useFormStatus

useFormStatus( reads the status of the nearest <form> above the component that calls it. It exists so that a button from a shared design system can show a spinner without every form passing a prop down.

import { useActionState, act } from 'react';
import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let resolveSave;
function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending, method, data } = useFormStatus();
  globalThis.status = { pending, method, hasData: !!data };
  return <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'saving…' : 'save'}</button>;
}
function Form() {
  const [, formAction] = useActionState(async () => {
    await new Promise(r => { resolveSave = r; });
    return null;
  }, null);
  return <form action={formAction}><input name="n" defaultValue="x" /><SubmitButton /></form>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Form />); });
console.log('idle   :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('form').dispatchEvent(new window.Event('submit', { bubbles: true, cancelable: true }));
});
console.log('pending:', box.textContent, '|', JSON.stringify(globalThis.status));
await act(async () => { resolveSave(); });
console.log('done   :', box.textContent);

idle   : save
pending: saving… | {"pending":true,"method":"get","hasData":true}
done   : save

The button knew the form was submitting, and nothing was passed to it. That is the whole point, and it makes a shared <SubmitButton> possible for the first time.

The rule is strict, and it is the one thing to remember: useFormStatus must be called from a component rendered inside the form, not from the component that renders the form. Calling it in Form above would report pending: false forever. The hook looks upward for a form and finds none, because the <form> is in that component's own output, not above it. status.pending is never true is the documented symptom, and this is always the cause.

Besides pending, it gives data (the FormData being submitted, so a button can show what is being saved), plus method and action.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: useFormStatus(.

15.4 useOptimistic

useOptimistic( shows the result of an action before it has finished, and undoes it automatically if the action fails.

import { useOptimistic, useActionState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let resolveSend, failNext = false;
function Chat() {
  const [messages, formAction] = useActionState(async (prev, formData) => {
    const text = formData.get('text');
    await new Promise((res, rej) => { resolveSend = failNext ? () => rej(new Error('x')) : () => res(); });
    return [...prev, text];
  }, ['hello']);
  const [shown, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(messages, (state, text) => [...state, text + '…']);

  return (
    <form action={async formData => { addOptimistic(formData.get('text')); await formAction(formData); }}>
      <input name="text" defaultValue="hi" />
      <b>{shown.join(',')}</b>
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Chat />); });
console.log('initial  :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('form').dispatchEvent(new window.Event('submit', { bubbles: true, cancelable: true }));
});
console.log('optimistic:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { resolveSend(); });
console.log('confirmed :', box.textContent);

initial  : hello
optimistic: hello,hi…
confirmed : hello,hi

The message appeared immediately with its "sending" marker, and was replaced by the real value when the action returned. No temporary array in state, no matching of the optimistic entry against the real one, no cleanup.

How it works: useOptimistic(actualState, reducer) returns the state to display, and a function to apply an optimistic update (one shown before the server confirms it). The optimistic value exists only while an action is pending. The moment the action settles, React throws it away and shows actualState again. That is what makes failure handling automatic. If the action throws, there is no optimistic value left over to clean up, and the UI is back to the truth without a line of code.

Two rules. addOptimistic must be called inside an action. Outside one, there is no pending window for the value to live in, and React reports "An optimistic state update occurred outside a Transition or Action". And the reducer must be pure, like every other reducer (§4.2).

15.5 Errors in Actions

An action that throws does not blank the page. The usual way to handle an error is to return it as state rather than throw it:

import { useActionState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Form({ echo }) {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(async (prev, formData) => {
    const email = String(formData.get('email'));
    if (!email.includes('@')) return echo ? { error: 'That is not an email address', email }
                                          : { error: 'That is not an email address' };
    return { ok: true, email };
  }, {});
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="email" defaultValue={state.email ?? ''} />
      <button type="submit" disabled={isPending}>submit</button>
      <b>{state.error ? `error: ${state.error}` : state.ok ? `saved ${state.email}` : 'ready'}</b>
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
for (const echo of [true, false]) {
  const box = document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('div'));
  await act(async () => { createRoot(box).render(<Form echo={echo} />); });
  const input = box.querySelector('input');
  const submit = () => act(async () => { box.querySelector('button').click(); });
  console.log(echo ? 'echoing the value back:' : 'returning only the error:');
  input.value = 'ada.example.com';                     // the user types a mistake
  await submit();
  console.log('  invalid:', box.querySelector('b').textContent, '| input:', JSON.stringify(input.value));
  input.value = 'ada@example.com';
  await submit();
  console.log('  valid  :', box.querySelector('b').textContent, '| input:', JSON.stringify(input.value));
}

echoing the value back:
  invalid: error: That is not an email address | input: "ada.example.com"
  valid  : saved ada@example.com | input: "ada@example.com"
returning only the error:
  invalid: error: That is not an email address | input: ""
  valid  : saved ada@example.com | input: "ada@example.com"

Handling form submission errors this way produced a message beside the form, and a second attempt that succeeded, in both versions. What differs is the input, and it is the reason the pattern is written the way it is. §15.1 measured that React resets the form's uncontrolled fields after an action finishes. And an action that returns an error has, as far as React is concerned, finished successfully.

  • Returning only the error wiped what the user typed (""), so they must type it all again to fix one character.
  • Returning { error, email } and rendering defaultValue={state.email} makes the reset put their text back instead ("ada.example.com").

The state carries both the problem and enough to re-render the form with what the user typed. That is what makes a failed submit harmless.

Throwing from an action is still possible, and goes to the nearest error boundary (§14.7). Keep that for failures that really make the page unusable, such as an expired session, and return everything else as state.

In summary, the vocabulary here is handling form submission errors.

15.6 Progressive Enhancement

The property that justifies the whole design: a form whose action is a Server Function works before any JavaScript has loaded.

The browser submits the form natively, as forms have done since 1993, and React's server handler runs the function and returns the next page. Once hydration finishes, React takes over the same form and handles it without a page load. Same code, two mechanisms, and the user cannot tell which one ran.

Keeps it working
Uncontrolled inputs with name attributes; a real <button type="submit">; a Server Function as the action; useActionState with a permalink.
Breaks it
An onSubmit with preventDefault; a button disabled until hydration; an action that reads client state; controlled inputs whose value lives only in React; a <div onClick> instead of a submit button.

useFormStatus and useOptimistic are designed to add the pending and optimistic behaviour without taking the no-JavaScript path away. Without JavaScript they simply do nothing, rather than breaking.

Whether this matters is a judgement about your users, and it is worth making on purpose rather than by default. It is not only about JavaScript being switched off. It covers the gap between the HTML arriving and hydration finishing, which on a slow connection is several seconds. During that gap, a form that needs JavaScript silently does nothing when pressed.

15.7 Calling an Action Outside a Form

Actions are not tied to forms. A function passed to startTransition is an Action, with the same pending behaviour (§12.5).

import { useTransition, useState, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let resolveDelete;
function Row({ id }) {
  const [gone, setGone] = useState(false);
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  globalThis.remove = () => startTransition(async () => {
    await new Promise(r => { resolveDelete = r; });
    setGone(true);
  });
  return <b>{gone ? 'deleted' : isPending ? 'deleting…' : `row ${id}`}</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<Row id={7} />); });
console.log('idle   :', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { globalThis.remove(); });
console.log('pending:', box.textContent);
await act(async () => { resolveDelete(); });
console.log('done   :', box.textContent);

idle   : row 7
pending: deleting…
done   : deleted

Same three states, and no form involved. The reason to use a transition rather than a bare async handler is the one from §12.5: the pending flag is managed for you across the await, and the resulting update does not block the page.

Handling multiple submission types in one form is the related pattern, and there are two clean ways to do it:

  • formAction on each button, which overrides the form's action for that button;
  • or a single action that checks which button submitted the form.

The second works because a submit button's own name and value are part of the form data, for the button that was clicked and only that one:

import { act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const seen = [];
function Draft() {
  async function action(formData) {
    seen.push(`intent=${formData.get('intent')} title=${formData.get('title')}`);
  }
  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="title" defaultValue="Notes" />
      <button name="intent" value="save">Save</button>
      <button name="intent" value="delete">Delete</button>
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
await act(async () => { createRoot(box).render(<Draft />); });
for (const button of box.querySelectorAll('button')) {
  await act(async () => { button.click(); });
}
console.log(seen.join('\n'));

intent=save title=Notes
intent=delete title=Notes

Both buttons share name="intent", and each submission carried exactly one intent: the clicked button's. The action branches on formData.get('intent'). The same form still works as a plain HTML form before hydration, because this is how browsers have always built form data. Prefer formAction when the two buttons do unrelated work. Prefer the shared action when they are variations of one operation that share validation.

What to carry forward from this subsection: multiple submission types.

What This Section Established

An action is a function passed to <form action> or to startTransition. React prevents the default, reads the form into FormData, runs the function in a transition, and tracks the pending state — measured, no preventDefault and the inputs read by name with nothing written.

useActionState(action, initial) makes the action's return value into state and gives a pending flag. The action takes (previousState, formData) — two arguments — and the hook returns [state, formAction, isPending]. Measured, a full submit cycle with the button disabled throughout and no try/finally anywhere. Submitting again while an action runs queues the next one rather than cancelling anything — measured, three dispatches ran one after another, each receiving the previous result, with one render at the end — and cancelling is done with an AbortController the action checks.

useFormStatus reads the nearest form above the calling component, which is why it must live in a child — measured, {"pending":true,"method":"get","hasData":true} inside the submit button. Calling it in the component that renders the form reports false forever.

useOptimistic shows a value only while an action is pending and discards it when the action settles — measured, hello,hi… during and hello,hi after — which is what makes failure handling free.

A successful action resets the form's uncontrolled fields — measured, a typed grace went back to its defaultValue, and since 19.3 onReset fires when it happens. Errors are therefore returned as state together with the submitted values, which the fields read back through defaultValue — measured, returning only the error wiped the user's input to "", returning { error, email } kept it.

And a form whose action is a Server Function submits natively before hydration; onSubmit with preventDefault, a button disabled until hydration, or an action reading client state each take that away.

Exercises

1. Replace the boilerplate. Take a submit handler with isLoading, error and result state plus a try/catch/finally, and rewrite it with useActionState. Count the lines and the pieces of state removed, then name the specific bug the finally was there to prevent.

2. Break useFormStatus. Call it in the component that renders the <form> and show that pending is always false. Move it into a child and show it working. Explain the lookup in terms of the render tree.

3. Optimistic with a failure. Add an item optimistically, then make the action reject, and record the displayed list at three moments: before, during and after. Show that no cleanup code was needed, and say what would have been required with a plain useState.

4. Two buttons, one form. Implement Save and Delete on one form, twice: with formAction on each button, and with one action that inspects the submitter. Give one advantage of each.

5. Audit the enhancement. Take a form and list every change that would break its no-JavaScript path. For each, say whether you would accept the break and what you would lose.

Solution

1. The replacement.

// before: 3 state variables, ~18 lines
const [isLoading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [error, setError] = useState(null);
const [result, setResult] = useState(null);
async function onSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  setLoading(true); setError(null);
  try { setResult(await save(new FormData(e.target))); }
  catch (err) { setError(err.message); }
  finally { setLoading(false); }
}

// after: 0 state variables, 4 lines
const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(async (prev, formData) => {
  try { return { result: await save(formData) }; }
  catch (err) { return { error: err.message }; }
}, {});

The finally existed to prevent a spinner that never clears: without it, a throw skips setLoading(false) and the form is disabled forever with no indication why. useActionState cannot have that bug, because the pending window is React's and it ends when the promise settles either way.

2. Breaking useFormStatus.

Called in the component that renders the <form>, it reports pending: false permanently. The hook walks up the render tree looking for a form context, and the <form> element is in that component's returned output — below it, not above it. Moving the call into a child that the form renders puts the form between the hook and the root, and the lookup finds it.

The same reasoning explains why it works from arbitrarily deep: any descendant of the form is below it, however many components intervene.

3. Optimistic failure.

before : hello
during : hello,hi…          the optimistic entry
after  : hello              the action rejected; the optimistic value is simply gone

No cleanup, because the optimistic value never lived in state — it exists only for the duration of the pending action and is discarded when the action settles.

With a plain useState you would have to append a placeholder with a temporary id, remember that id, and remove exactly that entry in a catch — while handling the case where two submissions are in flight and the ids must not collide. That last case is where hand-rolled optimistic UI usually breaks.

4. Two buttons.

// A: formAction per button
<button formAction={saveAction}>Save</button>
<button formAction={deleteAction}>Delete</button>

// B: one action, inspect the submitter
<button name="intent" value="save">Save</button>
<button name="intent" value="delete">Delete</button>
// ... action: switch (formData.get('intent')) { ... }

A keeps the two operations completely separate — separate functions, separate types, separate tests — and each button's action is visible where the button is. B submits through one endpoint, which matters for a Server Function: one action id, one authorisation check, one place to validate, and the intent travels as ordinary form data so it survives the no-JavaScript path unchanged.

5. The audit.

onSubmit + preventDefault        breaks it   accept only if there is no server action anyway
controlled inputs, no name       breaks it   never accept: add name= even when controlled
disabled until hydrated          breaks it   rarely accept; use useFormStatus instead
<div onClick> as the submitter   breaks it   never accept: it also breaks the keyboard
action reads client state        breaks it   accept if the feature is genuinely client-only
useOptimistic / useFormStatus    fine        these degrade to nothing, by design

What you lose in each case is the same thing: the window between the HTML arriving and hydration completing. On a fast connection that is invisible; on a slow one it is several seconds during which the form looks ready and does nothing.

SECTION 16

Server Rendering, Hydration and Streaming

Everything so far has assumed that React owns a DOM node in a browser and builds the page from nothing. Server-side rendering changes that starting point. The page's HTML is produced somewhere else (a Node process, an edge worker, a build step) and sent to the browser as text. Only then does React attach to it.

The reasons for server-side rendering are worth stating precisely, because "SSR is faster" is not one of them, and believing it leads to the wrong architecture. Server-side rendering changes when the user sees content, not how much work happens: the browser shows meaningful HTML before any JavaScript has downloaded, parsed or run. It has two other benefits:

  • crawlers and link previewers get something to read without running a script;
  • data fetching can happen next to the database, instead of over a round trip from the browser.

The costs are just as concrete:

  • a server that must run your component code;
  • a class of bug that only exists at the seam between the two renders (the server's and the browser's);
  • and a page that looks interactive before it is.

This section is the mechanism at that seam. It covers four server APIs and which to use; what the streamed HTML (HTML sent in pieces as it becomes ready) literally contains; what hydration does, and what happens when it fails; and the three document-level features (metadata, stylesheets, preloading) that only make sense once you know a server render is involved.

Every listing is the real output of React 19.3.0's server renderers, printed rather than described. The markers in that output look cryptic and are not: by the end of §16.5 you will be able to read a streamed React page by eye.

16.1 Four Server APIs

React ships four ways to turn an element tree into HTML, in two modules. Choosing the wrong one is the most common structural mistake in a React server setup.

renderToStaticMarkup
A string, with no hydration markers. For HTML that will never become interactive: an email, an RSS body, a static fragment. Hydrating its output is not supported.
renderToString(
A string, synchronously, with hydration markers. Does not support Suspense — §16.3 shows exactly what it does instead. Legacy; kept for environments that cannot stream.
renderToPipeableStream(
renderToReadableStream(
The real answer. A stream, sent as it is produced, with Suspense boundaries filled in later. The first is for Node streams, the second for Web streams (edge runtimes, Deno, Bun). Identical semantics, different plumbing.
prerender(reactNode, options?)
prerenderToNodeStream(
From react-dom/static. Waits for all data before producing anything, so the output is a complete page suitable for writing to a file or a CDN. Static generation, not request handling.

None of that list is optional plumbing. Choosing one of them is choosing how server-side rendering behaves for your application. And the choice is hard to undo once you have designed where your boundaries go (§16.4) around it.

The rule that follows: stream for a request, prerender for a build, renderToStaticMarkup for output that will not hydrate, and renderToString only when you have no other option.

For a tree with no Suspense and no data, the first two produce the same thing:

import { renderToString, renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function App() {
  return <div><h1>Title</h1><input defaultValue="v" readOnly disabled /></div>;
}
console.log('static:', renderToStaticMarkup(<App />));
console.log('string:', renderToString(<App />));

static: <div><h1>Title</h1><input readOnly="" disabled="" value="v"/></div>
string: <div><h1>Title</h1><input readOnly="" disabled="" value="v"/></div>

Two details in that output are worth pausing on, because they surprise people writing snapshot tests (tests that compare output with a saved copy).

  • defaultValue is emitted as value: it is React's name for "the initial value of an uncontrolled input", and the DOM's name for that is the value attribute.
  • readOnly is emitted with its React casing, not lowercased: React writes readOnly="" rather than readonly="". HTML attribute names ignore case, so browsers do not care, but a test comparing strings does.

The terms above, gathered: renderToPipeableStream(, renderToReadableStream(, prerender(reactNode and prerenderToNodeStream(.

One line each, for reference: server-side rendering.

16.2 renderToString Does Not Support Suspense

This is the most important limitation to know, because the failure is silent: nothing throws. It just quietly gives up on part of your page.

import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server';
