import { Suspense, use } from 'react';

const never = new Promise(() => {});                 // never resolves
function Slow() { return <b>{use(never)}</b>; }
function Page() {
  return <main><p>shell</p><Suspense fallback={<i>loading</i>}><Slow /></Suspense></main>;
}

const html = renderToString(<Page />);
const msg = html.match(/data-msg="([^"]*)"/)[1].split('\n')[0];
console.log('boundary marker:', html.includes('<!--$!-->') ? '<!--$!-->  (errored)' : 'none');
console.log('what rendered  :', html.includes('<i>loading</i>') ? 'the fallback' : 'the content');
console.log('message        :', msg);

boundary marker: <!--$!-->  (errored)
what rendered  : the fallback
message        : Switched to client rendering because the server rendering aborted due to:

React marks that boundary as errored, with <!--$!--> instead of the healthy <!--$-->. It outputs the fallback, and embeds a <template data-msg=…> explaining that it switched to rendering in the browser. The result is that the subtree is not rendered on the server at all. The user gets the spinner in the HTML and waits for JavaScript to produce the real content, which is exactly what server rendering was supposed to avoid.

So renderToString is only suitable for trees with no Suspense anywhere: no lazy, no use(promise), no data-fetching boundary. In a modern application that condition is hard to keep and easy to break by accident. That is why the streaming APIs are the default recommendation, not just a performance upgrade.

16.3 Streaming: the Shell and the Rest

renderToReadableStream returns a stream that starts with the shell (everything outside any Suspense boundary), and then delivers each boundary's content as its data arrives.

import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';
import { Suspense, use } from 'react';

const slow = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('LATE'), 10));
function Slow() { return <b>{use(slow)}</b>; }
function Page() {
  return <main><p>shell</p><Suspense fallback={<i>loading</i>}><Slow /></Suspense></main>;
}

const stream = await renderToReadableStream(<Page />, { bootstrapScripts: ['/app.js'] });
const chunks = [];
for await (const c of stream) chunks.push(new TextDecoder().decode(c));

console.log('chunks delivered:', chunks.length);
console.log('shell begins    :', JSON.stringify(chunks[0].slice(0, 74)));
console.log('main begins     :', JSON.stringify(
  chunks[0].slice(chunks[0].indexOf('<main>'), chunks[0].indexOf('</main>') + 7)));
console.log('shell has the fallback:', chunks[0].includes('<i>loading</i>'));
console.log('shell has the content :', chunks[0].includes('LATE'));
console.log('later chunk has it    :', chunks[1].includes('<b>LATE</b>'));

chunks delivered: 2
shell begins    : "<link rel=\"preload\" as=\"script\" fetchPriority=\"low\" href=\"/app.js\"/><main>"
main begins     : "<main><p>shell</p><!--$?--><template id=\"B:0\"></template><i>loading</i><!--/$--></main>"
shell has the fallback: true
shell has the content : false
later chunk has it    : true

Two things to notice.

  • bootstrapScripts emitted a preload link as well as the script tag, at the very front of the stream and at low fetch priority. React is telling the browser to start downloading your bundle while it reads the rest, without letting that download compete with the HTML itself.
  • The rest of that chunk is a complete, valid piece of HTML that a browser can read and paint immediately.

Read the markers:

<!--$-->
A resolved Suspense boundary. Its content follows.
<!--$?-->
A pending boundary: the fallback is here now and real content will arrive later. The <template id="B:0"> beside it is the placeholder React will replace.
<!--$!-->
An errored boundary. The client will re-render this subtree from scratch.
<!--/$-->
The end of a boundary, whatever its state.

The later chunk contains the resolved content wrapped in a hidden element, plus a small script that moves it into place:

…/app.js" id="_R_" async=""></script><div hidden id="S:0"><b>LATE</b></div><script>$RB=[]…

That is the entire mechanism behind streaming HTML and it needs no framework to understand: content is appended at the bottom of the document inside <div hidden>, and an inline script swaps it for the placeholder. It works with JavaScript disabled up to the shell, and it works before React itself has loaded, because the swap script is plain DOM manipulation.

bootstrapScripts is how your browser bundle gets into that output. React inserts the <script> tags itself, at the right point, with async. Its sibling bootstrapModules does the same with type="module". Adding the script tag by hand in your JSX instead is a common mistake: React will not know it is the entry point for hydration, and cannot place it correctly relative to the streamed chunks.

Modules bring one more option. A type="module" script that imports react by its bare name only works if the browser has an import map saying where react lives, and the map must appear before the first module script. The importMap option makes React output it in the right place. The nonce option, the value your Content-Security-Policy allows scripts to carry, goes on everything React writes:

import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';

const stream = await renderToReadableStream(<html><body><h1>Hi</h1></body></html>, {
  bootstrapModules: ['/client.js'],
  importMap: { imports: { react: '/vendor/react.js' } },
  nonce: 'r4nd0m',
});
await stream.allReady;
const html = await new Response(stream).text();
for (const tag of html.match(/<script[^>]*>[^<]*<\/script>|<link[^>]*>/g)) console.log(tag);

<script type="importmap" nonce="r4nd0m">{"imports":{"react":"/vendor/react.js"}}</script>
<link rel="modulepreload" fetchPriority="low" nonce="r4nd0m" href="/client.js"/>
<script type="module" src="/client.js" nonce="r4nd0m" id="_R_" async=""></script>

Three tags that carry scripts, one nonce on each, and the import map first. The first line is the 19.3 change. Under React 19.2.8 the same program output <script type="importmap"> without the nonce (measured). So a page with a strict script-src 'nonce-…' policy had its import map blocked, and every bare import failed, while the module script next to it was allowed. If you pinned an older React and wrote the map into the page by hand to work around that, 19.3 is the release where the option does it correctly.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: bootstrapModules, importMap and streaming HTML.

16.4 Choosing What Goes Into the Shell

The shell is everything not inside a Suspense boundary, and its size is the biggest single factor in how fast the page feels. React will not send anything until the shell is complete, because the shell is what makes the document readable.

That gives a design rule with real teeth: anything slow must be inside a Suspense boundary, or it delays the entire page. A layout component that waits for the user's session before rendering the header holds up the navigation, the footer and every other boundary, even the ones whose data was ready immediately.

It follows that boundary placement is a product decision rather than a technical one. Each boundary is a promise to the user: this part will appear later, and here is what it looks like while you wait. Too few boundaries, and the page arrives all at once, late. Too many, and the page flickers into existence in a dozen uncoordinated pieces. §13.6 covers the controls over reveal order that make the middle ground possible.

onShellReady (in renderToPipeableStream) and the promise returned by renderToReadableStream both fire at the same moment: the shell is done, and you may start sending bytes. That is where a status code of 200 is decided, and it is also the last moment at which you can decide something else.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: onShellReady.

16.5 Errors on the Server

Server rendering has two kinds of error region, and they need different responses. That is why React gives you two callbacks rather than one.

An error inside the shell is fatal. There is no HTML to send, so the request must become an error response. An error inside a Suspense boundary is not fatal. The shell has already been sent and the status code has already gone out, so React can simply stream that boundary's fallback and let the browser try again.

import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';
import { Suspense } from 'react';

function Boom() { throw new Error('data source down'); }
function Page() {
  return <main><p>shell</p><Suspense fallback={<i>unavailable</i>}><Boom /></Suspense></main>;
}

const logged = [];
const stream = await renderToReadableStream(<Page />, {
  onError(error) { logged.push(error.message); },
});
let html = '';
for await (const c of stream) html += new TextDecoder().decode(c);

console.log('onError saw   :', logged);
console.log('boundary state:', html.includes('<!--$!-->') ? 'errored' : 'ok');
console.log('user sees     :', html.includes('<i>unavailable</i>') ? 'the fallback' : 'nothing');

onError saw   : [ 'data source down' ]
boundary state: errored
user sees     : the fallback

The shell survived, the boundary is marked errored, and the fallback was sent. onError fired so that the failure reaches your logs, and that is its whole job: onError is for logging, not for recovery. Returning a value from it does not change what is rendered.

For the fatal case, renderToReadableStream rejects its promise and renderToPipeableStream calls onShellError. The correct response there is to give up on the React render entirely and send a static error page with a 500, because whatever went wrong comes before everything else.

Setting the status code follows from this split: decide it when the shell resolves, never later. Once the first byte is out the status is fixed, and an error in a boundary can only be reported inside the page.

16.6 Aborting Server Rendering

Aborting server rendering is not an error path; it is a deadline. A server render that never finishes is a request that never ends. Both streaming APIs take a signal, and both offer an abort() on the returned object.

Aborting does not cut the HTML short. React finishes the document by outputting the fallback for every boundary that has not resolved yet, and marking them to be rendered in the browser. So the user gets a complete page whose slow parts will fill in from the browser. That is graceful degradation: the page falls back from streaming server rendering to browser rendering, one boundary at a time.

The practical setup is a timeout that fires well before your infrastructure's own. Abort at, say, five seconds, so that the user gets a shell plus fallbacks rather than a gateway timeout with nothing at all. onAllReady is the opposite policy: the callback that fires only when every boundary has resolved. That is what a crawler or a static build wants, and it is what prerender is for (§16.11).

To have in hand before moving on: onAllReady.

16.7 Hydration

Hydrating server-rendered html is the browser half. hydrateRoot( walks through the existing DOM instead of creating it. It attaches React's internal state to nodes that are already there, connects event handlers, and runs effects.

import { act } from 'react';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function App({ label }) { return <div><span>{label}</span></div>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
box.innerHTML = renderToStaticMarkup(<App label="server" />);

const errors = [];
await act(async () => {
  hydrateRoot(box, <App label="server" />, {
    onRecoverableError(e) { errors.push(String(e.message).split('.')[0]); },
  });
});
console.log('recoverable errors:', errors.length);
console.log('dom after hydration:', box.innerHTML);

recoverable errors: 0
dom after hydration: <div><span>server</span></div>

Nothing changed in the DOM, and that is the point: React found the markup it expected and took it over. The nodes were never recreated, so no image reloaded, no scroll position moved, and no CSS transition restarted.

A hydrated root has the same two methods as one created in the browser.

  • root.render( re-renders it with a new element. The second and later renders behave normally, with no hydration involved.
  • root.unmount() tears the whole tree down and detaches React from the container. A host application calls it when it removes the region React was mounted into. Calling root.unmount() on a hydrated root is the same operation as on one created in the browser: React detaches, effects clean up, and the container's contents are removed.

The mental model that keeps hydration straight: the server render decides the HTML, and the first client render must agree with it. During hydration React does not compare and patch in the usual way; it expects a match. From the second render in the browser onwards, it is business as usual.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: hydrating server-rendered HTML.

16.8 Hydration Mismatches

When the first render in the browser disagrees with the server's HTML, React reports a hydration mismatch, and rebuilds the subtree that disagrees in the browser.

import { act } from 'react';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function App({ label }) { return <div><span>{label}</span></div>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
document.body.appendChild(box);
box.innerHTML = renderToStaticMarkup(<App label="server" />);

const errors = [];
await act(async () => {
  hydrateRoot(box, <App label="client" />, {
    onRecoverableError(e) { errors.push(String(e.message).split('.')[0]); },
  });
});
console.log('recoverable errors:', errors.length);
console.log('message           :', JSON.stringify(errors[0]));
console.log('who won           :', JSON.stringify(box.innerHTML));

recoverable errors: 1
message           : "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client"
who won           : "<div><span>client</span></div>"

Three facts to take from that.

  • The client wins: React throws away the server's markup for that subtree and re-renders it.
  • It is recoverable, not fatal: the page works, which is exactly why mismatches ship to production unnoticed.
  • And it is reported through onRecoverableError, which is the callback to connect to your error tracking. Without it, the only signal is a console message nobody reads in production.

The causes are a short list, and every mismatch is one of them:

Time and randomness
Date.now(), new Date().toLocaleString(), Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID(). The server ran them at a different moment, in a different timezone.
Browser-only data
window, localStorage, navigator, media queries, the user's theme preference. The server has none of it.
Invalid nesting
A <div> inside a <p>, a stray node inside a <table>. The browser's parser silently restructures the server's HTML, so the DOM no longer matches what React sent.
Third-party mutation
An extension or an analytics snippet that edits the DOM before React attaches.

The third one is worth dwelling on because it is invisible in the source: the HTML you sent and the DOM the browser built are not always the same document. <p><div/></p> becomes three siblings. React compares against the DOM, so a nesting error that HTML tolerates becomes a hydration error that React does not.

16.9 Deliberate Differences

Some differences between server and browser are correct, and there are three supported ways to say so: switch off the check for one value, render twice, or declare that a subtree renders only in the browser.

suppressHydrationWarning switches off the check for one element's text content. It applies to one level only and is not inherited by children. The right use is a value that is truly allowed to differ, and truly does not matter:

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Stamp({ at }) {
  return <time suppressHydrationWarning dateTime={at}>{new Date(at).toISOString()}</time>;
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Stamp at="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z" />));

<time dateTime="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z">2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z</time>

Note that suppressHydrationWarning does not appear in the output: it is an instruction to the hydration check, not HTML. Note too that dateTime came out as dateTime, the second example of the casing quirk from §16.1. React lowercases the attributes it has a mapping for (tabIndex → tabindex, htmlFor → for), and writes the rest with the spelling you used. Browsers do not care; tests that compare strings do. Use suppression sparingly. It suppresses the warning, not the mismatch, and a suppressed subtree can still look wrong.

A two-pass render is the honest answer when the browser really knows something the server cannot. That is the general shape of displaying different content on the server and the client. Render the version that is safe on the server first, then switch after mounting.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Local({ iso }) {
  const [onClient, setOnClient] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => { setOnClient(true); }, []);
  return <time dateTime={iso}>{onClient ? 'local time' : iso}</time>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const iso = '2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z';
const box = document.createElement('div');
document.body.appendChild(box);
box.innerHTML = renderToStaticMarkup(<Local iso={iso} />);
console.log('server html:', box.innerHTML);   // read back through the DOM

const errors = [];
await act(async () => {
  hydrateRoot(box, <Local iso={iso} />, { onRecoverableError: e => errors.push(e.message) });
});
console.log('after hydration:', box.innerHTML, '| errors:', errors.length);

server html: <time datetime="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z">2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z</time>
after hydration: <time datetime="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z">local time</time> | errors: 0

(The attribute reads back as datetime here rather than dateTime, because it has been through the browser's parser, which normalises attribute names. The casing quirk above is in the string React produces, not in the DOM the browser builds from it.)

Zero errors, because the first render in the browser matched the server exactly, and the difference arrived in an effect, which runs after hydration is complete. This costs an extra render and a brief flash of the server's value, and it is the correct trade for anything the user can see. Using suppressHydrationWarning here instead would hide the mismatch and keep the wrong markup.

Browser-only subtrees with browser(). Some components cannot render on the server at all: an editor restoring a draft from localStorage, a chart that measures the window, anything that reads the user's time zone. The two-pass render works for them, but forces you to write a pointless server version. The old alternative was to throw during server rendering and let the nearest <Suspense> show its fallback. That works, and records an error every time. React 19.3 adds browser() to react-dom for exactly this case. use(browser(reason)) stops server rendering at that component, shows the nearest <Suspense> fallback in the HTML, and lets the browser render the real thing.

import { use, Suspense } from 'react';
import { browser } from 'react-dom';
import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';

function SavedDraft() {
  use(browser('The draft lives in localStorage.'));
  return <textarea defaultValue={localStorage.getItem('draft') ?? ''} />;
}
function OldWay() {             // the pre-19.3 idiom: throw while rendering on the server
  throw new Error('needs the browser');
}

async function serve(Component, label) {
  const log = [];
  const stream = await renderToReadableStream(
    <main><Suspense fallback={<p>Loading draft…</p>}><Component /></Suspense></main>, {
      onBrowserBailout(error) { log.push(`onBrowserBailout (cause: ${error.cause})`); },
      onError(error) { log.push(`onError: ${error.message}`); },
    });
  await stream.allReady;
  const html = (await new Response(stream).text()).replace(/<template[^>]*><\/template>/, '');
  console.log(label.padEnd(10), html, '|', log.join(' ; '));
}
await serve(SavedDraft, 'browser()');
await serve(OldWay, 'throwing');

try {
  await renderToReadableStream(<main><SavedDraft /></main>, { onError() {} });
} catch (e) { console.log('no Suspense:', e.message.split('\n')[0]); }

browser()  <main><!--$!--><p>Loading draft…</p><!--/$--></main> | onBrowserBailout (cause: The draft lives in localStorage.)
throwing   <main><!--$!--><p>Loading draft…</p><!--/$--></main> | onError: needs the browser
no Suspense: The server render could not complete because client rendering was requested outside a Suspense boundary. See this error's cause for additional details.

(The printout leaves out the <template> React outputs to carry the reason to the browser, because in development it contains a component stack with file paths in it.)

Both components produced the same HTML: the fallback, inside a boundary marked <!--$!--> ("render this in the browser", the marker from §16.2). What differs is how the server was told.

  • The throwing component went to onError, where production code sends errors to monitoring. Every page view of that editor is now an error in your dashboard, and a real error thrown by the same component looks exactly like the deliberate one.
  • browser() went to onBrowserBailout, a separate channel whose only purpose is to observe these deferrals, with the reason you wrote as the error's cause.

And without a <Suspense> boundary there is no fallback to show, so the server render fails outright, the same requirement as for any other suspension.

The browser half is where the difference is larger:

import { use, Suspense, act } from 'react';
import { browser } from 'react-dom';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';

let onServer = true;
function SavedDraft() {
  const value = use(browser('The draft lives in localStorage.'));
  return <textarea defaultValue={`use() gave ${value}; draft=${localStorage.getItem('draft')}`} />;
}
function OldWay() {
  if (onServer) throw new Error('needs the browser');
  return <textarea defaultValue="rendered in the browser" />;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
localStorage.setItem('draft', 'hello');
for (const Component of [SavedDraft, OldWay]) {
  const page = <main><Suspense fallback={<p>Loading draft…</p>}><Component /></Suspense></main>;
  onServer = true;
  const stream = await renderToReadableStream(page, { onError() {} });
  await stream.allReady;
  const box = document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('div'));
  box.innerHTML = await new Response(stream).text();

  onServer = false;
  const recoverable = [];
  await act(async () => {
    hydrateRoot(box, page, { onRecoverableError: e => recoverable.push(e.message.replace(/\s+/g, ' ')) });
  });
  console.log(Component.name.padEnd(10), box.querySelector('textarea').value,
              '| recoverable:', recoverable.join(' ') || 'none');
}

SavedDraft use() gave undefined; draft=hello | recoverable: none
OldWay     rendered in the browser | recoverable: Switched to client rendering because the server rendering errored: needs the browser

In the browser, use(browser()) returns undefined and the component renders normally: it read the draft. Hydration then finished without complaint. The throwing version rendered too, but only after React raised a recoverable error, "Switched to client rendering because the server rendering errored". By default that is logged to the console of every user, and goes to onRecoverableError (§16.8). browser() declares that this is intended, and React treats it that way on both sides.

The reference gives three rules, and the examples above already follow each of them.

  • use(browser()) belongs in a Client Component: a Server Component has no browser to hand the work to.
  • Calling browser() without passing the result to use() does nothing, and throwing it is wrong.
  • reason may be a function instead of a string. React calls it only on the server, so an expensive explanation costs nothing in the browser.

browser() can also be passed to abort(), the deadline from §16.6. Measured with renderToPipeableStream and a boundary that never resolves: abort(browser('the server render timed out')) reported the boundary to onBrowserBailout, while abort(new Error('timed out')) reported it to onError, and the HTML was the same fallback either way. A render deadline is a policy, not a failure, and this is how to stop it filling the error dashboard.

Use it for what it says: a subtree that really needs the browser. It does not replace the two-pass render when the server can render something useful, because the server's version is what a reader sees first and what a crawler indexes. A fallback is a worse first screen than a server-rendered timestamp.

In summary, the vocabulary here is displaying different content on the server and the client, browser() and onBrowserBailout.

16.10 Selective Hydration

Hydration is not one indivisible operation. React hydrates each Suspense boundary separately, which produces two behaviours worth knowing by name.

Selective hydration means a boundary whose HTML has arrived can be hydrated while another is still streaming. The page becomes interactive in pieces, rather than all at once.

Progressive hydration is the prioritising on top of that. If the user clicks inside a boundary that has not been hydrated yet, React hydrates that one first, ahead of whatever it was working on. The click is replayed once hydration completes, so the interaction is not lost, only delayed.

The consequence for design is the same as in §16.4: Suspense boundaries are hydration boundaries too. Splitting a page into boundaries improves both when content appears and when it becomes interactive. A page with a single boundary around everything gets neither benefit.

The gap between "painted" and "interactive" is real, and it is the honest cost of server rendering. A button that is visible but not yet connected is worse than no button at all, if the user cannot tell the difference. Disabling a button until hydration is a pattern worth considering for destructive actions. And useFormStatus (§15.5) plus a <form> action gives you a submit that works before hydration, because the browser handles it.

What to carry forward from this subsection: progressive hydration.

16.11 Static Prerendering

react-dom/static has the same shape as the streaming API, with one difference in behaviour: it waits for everything.

import { prerender } from 'react-dom/static';
import { Suspense, use } from 'react';

const slow = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('LATE'), 10));
function Slow() { return <b>{use(slow)}</b>; }
function Page() {
  return <main><p>shell</p><Suspense fallback={<i>loading</i>}><Slow /></Suspense></main>;
}

const { prelude } = await prerender(<Page />);
let html = '';
for await (const c of prelude) html += new TextDecoder().decode(c);
console.log('contains the content :', html.includes('<b>LATE</b>'));
console.log('contains the fallback:', html.includes('<i>loading</i>'));

contains the content : true
contains the fallback: false

No fallback appears at all: every boundary resolved before a single byte was produced. That is exactly what you want when writing a file to disk or to a CDN. It is exactly what you do not want when handling a live request, because the slowest query decides the time to first byte.

prerenderToNodeStream( is the same thing for Node streams. You choose between them by your runtime, not by what you want to do. The pair is what static site generation is built on: run the prerender at build time, write the bytes to a file, and serve them from a CDN.

The terms above, gathered: static site generation.

16.12 Resuming a Prerender

The two APIs above are the two ends of a range, and React 19 fills in the middle. prerender( can produce a page with some boundaries deliberately left unfinished, along with a postponed state describing what remains. Later, resume( and resumeToPipeableStream( take that state and a fresh render, and complete the missing parts when a request comes in.

This is the mechanism behind partial prerendering. The page's shell and its static regions are built once, cached at the edge (on servers close to the user), and served instantly to everyone. The personalised boundaries are rendered for each request, and streamed into the same document. resumeAndPrerender( and resumeAndPrerenderToNodeStream are the static counterparts, for completing a prerender at a later build step rather than at request time.

To be honest about it, these are framework-facing APIs. Producing and storing the postponed state, sending a request to the right cached first part, and deciding what to postpone are not things you set up by hand in an application. Next.js and similar frameworks are the intended callers. Know that the layer exists and what it buys, so that "partial prerendering" is a mechanism to you rather than a slogan, and use it through a framework.

One line each, for reference: resume(, resumeToPipeableStream( and resumeAndPrerender(.

16.13 Hoisting Document Metadata

Hoisting document metadata is new in React 19. Render <title>, <meta> and <link> anywhere in the tree, and React moves them into the document's head. Before this, every React application needed a library for the job.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Article({ title }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <title>{title}</title>
      <meta name="description" content="a measured example" />
      <p>body</p>
    </article>
  );
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Article title="My page" />));

<title>My page</title><meta name="description" content="a measured example"/><article><p>body</p></article>

The two tags came out before the <article> that contained them. In a browser they are moved into <head>. In the server output they are moved to the front of the stream, so the browser's parser sees them early.

What makes this really useful, not just convenient, is that it composes: metadata can be declared by whichever component actually knows it. A blog post component owns its own title, a product page owns its own Open Graph tags (the tags that control link previews), and neither has to pass anything upward through a context or some other side channel. It also works inside Suspense boundaries, so a title that depends on fetched data is a normal thing to write.

Two constraints. There is no automatic removal of duplicate <meta> tags by name: render two descriptions and you get two. And <title> accepts a single string child only, so <title>Hello {name}</title> is an error; build the string first.

16.14 Stylesheet Precedence

Stylesheet precedence is the second half of the same feature. A <link rel="stylesheet"> with a precedence prop gets special treatment. React moves it to the head, removes duplicates, orders it against other stylesheets by precedence, and (this is the part that matters) suspends until it has loaded, so content never appears unstyled.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Widget() {
  return (
    <article>
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="/theme.css" precedence="default" />
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="/reset.css" precedence="low" />
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="/theme.css" precedence="default" />
      <p>content</p>
    </article>
  );
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Widget />));

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/theme.css" data-precedence="default"/><link rel="stylesheet" href="/reset.css" data-precedence="low"/><article><p>content</p></article>

/theme.css was declared twice and appears once. That is the deduplicated stylesheet rendering that makes it safe for every component to declare the stylesheets it needs, without coordinating with the others. precedence became data-precedence in the output. That is how React finds and orders these links in the browser when a later component adds another one.

Precedence values are any strings you like, ordered by convention; the common scheme is reset, low, default, high. What they buy is a guarantee CSS cannot otherwise give in an application split into chunks. A stylesheet loaded later by a lazily rendered component is still inserted at the right position in the cascade, rather than at the end, so it does not silently override a base stylesheet.

<style> works the same way, with a required href acting as its key for removing duplicates. And async script deduplication does the same for <script async src>: rendering an external script from two different components loads it once.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: deduplicated stylesheet rendering, async script deduplication and rendering an external script.

16.15 Preloading Resources

React exposes the browser's resource hints (tags that tell the browser to fetch or connect early) as functions you can call from anywhere in a render or an event handler. Like metadata, it moves the resulting tags to the front.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';
import { preload, preinit, preconnect, prefetchDNS } from 'react-dom';

function Deep() {
  preinit('/critical.js', { as: 'script' });
  preload('/hero.avif', { as: 'image' });
  preconnect('https://cdn.example.com');
  prefetchDNS('https://analytics.example.com');
  return <p>deep</p>;
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<article><Deep /></article>));

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com"/><link href="https://analytics.example.com" rel="dns-prefetch"/><script src="/critical.js" async=""></script><link rel="preload" href="/hero.avif" as="image"/><article><p>deep</p></article>

Every hint was output ahead of the <article>, even though all four calls happen inside a component nested within it. That move to the front is the whole value. The browser's preload scanner sees the hints while it is still reading the top of the document, which is the only moment at which a hint is worth anything.

The four differ in how much they commit to. The two cheapest, prefetchDNS( and preconnect(, are the ones worth calling on a guess, because being wrong about them costs almost nothing:

prefetchDNS(
Resolve this hostname. Cheapest; use for a domain you might need.
preconnect(
Resolve, connect and complete the TLS handshake. Use for a domain you will certainly hit but whose URL you do not know yet.
preload
Download this exact URL now, at the priority its as implies, but do not execute or apply it.
preinit(
Download and evaluate: a script runs, a stylesheet applies. The strongest commitment, and the one to be careful with.

preloadModule( and preinitModule( are the ES-module forms of the last two. All six are safe to call repeatedly, because React removes duplicates. That is what makes calling them from inside a component reasonable rather than reckless.

React also calls preload for you in one case: every <img src> the server renderer emits gets a matching <link rel="preload" as="image"> hoisted ahead of it. That was measured, with no request from you. It is worth knowing because it shows up in snapshot tests as an unexplained extra element, and because it means hand-writing a preload for an image you are already rendering is redundant.

The one that earns its keep most often is preload in an event handler: preloading the code and data for a route when the user's pointer moves over the link, so the navigation has nothing left to fetch.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: preloadModule( and preinitModule(.

What This Section Established

There are four server APIs and the choice is structural. Stream (renderToPipeableStream for Node, renderToReadableStream for Web) for requests; prerender for builds; renderToStaticMarkup for HTML that will never hydrate; renderToString only where nothing else is possible — measured, it marks a suspended boundary as errored, ships the fallback, and hands the subtree to the client.

Streamed HTML is readable by eye once you know four markers: <!--$--> resolved, <!--$?--> pending, <!--$!--> errored, <!--/$--> end. Content that arrives late is appended in a <div hidden> and moved into place by a plain inline script, which is why streaming works before React has loaded.

The shell is everything outside a Suspense boundary and nothing ships until it is done, so anything slow belongs inside a boundary. onError logs boundary failures and cannot recover from them; onShellError is the fatal case and the only one that should change the status code.

Hydration asserts rather than diffs: the first client render must match the server's HTML. A mismatch is recoverable — measured, one onRecoverableError and the client's markup wins — which is why these reach production unnoticed. Wire onRecoverableError to your error tracker. The causes are time, randomness, browser-only data, invalid nesting and third-party mutation, and the honest fix for a genuine difference is a two-pass render, not suppressHydrationWarning.

A subtree that genuinely needs the browser declares it with use(browser(reason)) (React 19.3) inside a <Suspense> boundary. Measured against the old idiom of throwing on the server: the HTML is the same fallback, but the deferral goes to onBrowserBailout instead of onError, and hydration raises no recoverable error — so an intended behaviour stops being reported as a failure on both sides.

React 19 hoists <title>, <meta> and <link> from anywhere in the tree; stylesheets with a precedence are deduplicated and ordered against the cascade; and the six preloading functions are hoisted to the front of the document even when called from a deeply nested component.

Exercises

1. Read a stream by hand. Render a page with two Suspense boundaries whose data resolves at different times, collect the chunks, and annotate the output: mark every <!--$…--> marker with its meaning, find each <template id="B:n"> and the <div hidden id="S:n"> that later replaces it, and say why the hidden div appears at the end of the document rather than in place.

2. Move the boundary. Take a page where a slow component sits in the shell. Measure the time to the first chunk. Wrap it in a Suspense boundary and measure again. Then explain, in terms of §16.4, why the total time to a complete page did not improve.

3. Three mismatches. Write one component that mismatches because of time, one because of browser-only data, and one because of invalid nesting. For each, capture the onRecoverableError message and say which of the three is not fixable with suppressHydrationWarning and why.

4. Two passes versus suppression. Implement "show the user's local timezone" twice — once with suppressHydrationWarning, once with the two-pass pattern. Show the hydration error count for each and the DOM after hydration. Then state which one a user would notice and what they would see.

5. Precedence in a code-split app. Two lazily-loaded components each declare a stylesheet, one with precedence="low" and one with precedence="high", and they load in the opposite order. Predict the order of the <link> elements in the head, then say what would happen without the precedence prop and why that is a correctness problem rather than a tidiness one.

Solution

1. Reading a stream.

<main>
  <p>shell</p>                     shell content: sent immediately
  <!--$?-->                        boundary 0 is PENDING
  <template id="B:0"></template>     the placeholder React will replace
  <i>loading</i>                     the fallback, visible now
  <!--/$-->                        end of boundary 0
  <!--$?--><template id="B:1"></template><i>loading</i><!--/$-->
</main>
<script src="/app.js" async></script>

… later, as each resolves …
<div hidden id="S:0"><b>FIRST</b></div><script>$RC("B:0","S:0")</script>
<div hidden id="S:1"><b>SECOND</b></div><script>$RC("B:1","S:1")</script>

The hidden div is appended at the end because HTML is a stream that can only grow at the bottom — a server cannot go back and edit bytes it has already sent. Appending plus a script that moves the node is the only way to fill a hole in a document that is still being parsed.

2. Moving the boundary.

Time to first chunk drops from "as slow as the slowest thing in the shell" to "as fast as the fastest render", because React can complete the shell without waiting. Total time to a complete page does not improve: the slow data still takes as long as it took, and it is still the last thing to arrive. Streaming changes when the user sees something, never how long the work takes — the same distinction the section opened with.

3. Three mismatches.

import { act } from 'react';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Nested() { return <p><span>ok</span></p>; }
function NestedBad() { return <p><div>moved</div></p>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.createElement('div');
document.body.appendChild(box);
box.innerHTML = renderToStaticMarkup(<NestedBad />);
console.log('what the server sent :', '<p><div>moved</div></p>');
console.log('what the browser built:', box.innerHTML);

what the server sent : <p><div>moved</div></p>
what the browser built: <p></p><div>moved</div><p></p>

The nesting case is the one suppressHydrationWarning cannot fix. The other two are differences in content at a node React can identify, and suppression tells React to accept the difference. Here the node structure itself is different — the browser turned one <p> containing a <div> into three siblings — so there is no single element on which to put the attribute, and the tree React is asserting against does not exist. The only fix is valid HTML.

4. Two passes versus suppression.

The suppressed version reports zero hydration errors and leaves the server's value in the DOM — React accepts the mismatch rather than repairing it, so the user sees UTC forever, or until something else re-renders that subtree. The two-pass version also reports zero errors but shows the server value for one frame and then the correct local value.

A user notices the first one: it is simply wrong, permanently, and silently. The flash in the second is the visible cost of being correct, and it is why the pattern is usually paired with a placeholder that does not look like a wrong answer — a dash or a skeleton rather than the UTC time.

5. Precedence in a code-split app.

With precedence, the links are ordered low then high in the head regardless of which component loaded first, because React inserts each one into its precedence group rather than appending it. Without the prop, each <link> is appended when its component renders, so the head order follows load order — which in a code-split app depends on network timing.

That is a correctness problem, not tidiness: CSS specificity ties are broken by document order, so two rules of equal specificity resolve differently depending on which chunk happened to arrive first. The same page then renders differently on a fast and a slow connection, and the bug is unreproducible locally.

SECTION 17

Server Components and Server Functions

§16 was about running the components you already had in a second place. Server Components are a different idea: components that run only on the server. Their code is never sent to the browser, so they can do things a component has never been able to do: read a file, query a database, hold a secret.

The idea is easy to state and easy to get wrong, so it is worth being exact. A Server Component is not a component that runs on the server and then again in the browser; that is server-side rendering, which is §16. A Server Component runs once, on the server. What the browser receives is not its code but its output: a description of the tree it produced, serialised (turned into text) in a format designed for streaming. The component itself never crosses over.

That single fact produces every rule in this section:

  • A Server Component cannot use state or effects, because there is no second render to hold state for.
  • Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component must be serialisable, because they travel as data.
  • A Server Component can hold an API key, because the code holding it is never shipped.
  • And the boundary between the two kinds is marked explicitly, rather than worked out automatically.

Server Components need a bundler (the build tool that packages code for the browser) that understands them. That is why they arrive through a framework rather than through npm install react. It does not make them magic, and this section makes a point of showing the actual bytes. Everything below was produced by running React 19.2.8's reference implementation, react-server-dom-webpack, directly.

17.1 Two Environments, One Tree

React now has two places where components can run, and they can do different things. Keeping them apart is the whole skill.

Server Component — the default
Runs once, on the server or at build time. Its code stays there.
  • Can: async/await, read the filesystem, query a database, use secrets, import heavy libraries at no client cost
  • Cannot: useState, useEffect, event handlers, browser APIs, any hook that implies a second render
Client Component — opted in with 'use client'
Ships to the browser. Rendered on the server too (that is SSR), then hydrated.
  • Can: everything in §1–§15 — state, effects, refs, events, context
  • Cannot: await at the top level of the component, touch the filesystem, hold a secret

The word "client" in client component means available to the client, not only on the client. A Client Component still renders on the server during server-side rendering. The difference is that its code is also in the bundle, so it can render again in the browser and become interactive.

Note also that "Server Component" and "server rendering" are separate ideas. A Client Component is rendered on the server. A Server Component is not "rendered on the server" in the §16 sense at all: it is executed on the server, and never rendered in the browser.

17.2 The Payload

The best way to understand the model is to look at what actually travels over the network. Take two components, one of which is async:

async function Author({ id }) {
  const name = await Promise.resolve('Ada');
  return <span className="author">{name} (#{id})</span>;
}
function Post() {
  return <article><h1>Title</h1><Author id={7} /></article>;
}

Render them with the reference server implementation:

cat > rsc.mjs <<'EOF'
import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-server-dom-webpack/server.edge';
import { createElement as h } from 'react';
async function Author({ id }) {
  const name = await Promise.resolve('Ada');
  return h('span', { className: 'author' }, name, ' (#', id, ')');
}
const Post = () => h('article', null, h('h1', null, 'Title'), h(Author, { id: 7 }));
for await (const c of renderToReadableStream(h(Post), {})) {
  process.stdout.write(new TextDecoder().decode(c));
}
EOF
NODE_ENV=production node --conditions react-server rsc.mjs

0:["$","article",null,{"children":[["$","h1",null,{"children":"Title"}],"$L1"]}]
1:["$","span",null,{"className":"author","children":["Ada"," (#",7,")"]}]

That is the rsc payload (RSC stands for React Server Components), complete. It rewards a slow read.

It is a line-oriented stream of numbered rows. Row 0 is the root. Each row is JSON, and the format is designed so that the browser can start building the tree before the stream has finished.

["$","article",null,{…}] is an element: the same {type, key, props} from §1.4, in array form. It holds the "$" marker, the type, the key and the props.

"$L1" is a lazy reference to row 1. When Post rendered, Author had not finished waiting, so React output a placeholder and carried on. Row 1 arrived afterwards. That is streaming at the data level rather than the HTML level, and it is why a slow Server Component does not block the rest of the page.

Author does not appear anywhere. Not its name, not its code, not the promise it waited for: only the <span> it produced. The browser has no way to know a component was involved, and that is exactly the point: the size of a Server Component's implementation is not a cost the user pays. Import a 300 kB Markdown renderer in a Server Component, and the bundle does not grow.

To have in hand before moving on: RSC payload.

17.3 'use client': Where the Boundary Is

'use client' is a directive at the top of a file. It marks that file, and everything it imports, as belonging to the browser bundle, and it creates the boundary between the two environments.

// LikeButton.jsx
'use client';
import { useState } from 'react';

export function LikeButton({ initial }) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(initial);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>♥ {n}</button>;
}

Two things about that directive that are commonly misunderstood.

It marks an entry point, not a component. You do not put 'use client' on every interactive file. You put it at the boundary, and everything below it is client code automatically. A 'use client' file that imports three helpers pulls those helpers into the bundle without them needing the directive.

There is no 'use server' counterpart for components. Server is the default. A file with no directive is a Server Component in a framework that supports RSC. 'use server' means something else entirely (§17.7). That mistake is worth knowing about, because writing 'use server' at the top of a component file turns every export into an endpoint anyone can call.

In the payload, a Client Component appears as an import row rather than as its output:

1:I[null,null,"Button"]
0:["$","div",null,{"children":["$","$L1",null,{"label":"Save","n":1}]}]

Row 1 is an I: an instruction to the browser runtime to load the module for Button and render it with these props. The tree refers to it as $L1, exactly as it referred to the async component's output. The browser runtime resolves the reference by loading that chunk.

That is the whole architecture in two rows. Server Components turn into data; Client Components turn into code plus data.

17.4 What Crosses the Boundary

Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component are serialised (turned into text) in the payload. So serializable props is a real constraint with a precise definition, and the definition is broader than "JSON".

Measured against React 19.3.0's reference serialiser, passing each of these to a Client Component:

string, number,
boolean, null
crosses
Written literally: {"a":"x","b":1,"c":true,"d":null}
plain object, array
crosses
Recursively, with the same rules applied to every value inside.
Date
crosses
"$D1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z" — a real Date arrives on the client.
Map, Set
crosses
"$Q2" and "$W2", with the entries in row 2. Wider than JSON allows.
BigInt, TypedArray
crosses
"$n10"; typed arrays get a binary row.
Promise
crosses
"$@2", and its resolved value streams in later as row 2. This is what makes use(promise) across the boundary work.
function
error
"Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components unless you explicitly expose it by marking it with "use server"." The same rule governs serializable arguments going the other way, into a Server Function.
class instance
error
Only plain objects. Methods and the prototype cannot travel, so React refuses rather than silently sending a stripped object.
Symbol
error
Except the well-known symbols, which have stable global identity.

Two of those rows change how you design.

  • A Promise crosses: a Server Component can start a fetch and hand the unresolved promise to a Client Component, which then reads it with use() and suspends. The request begins on the server and the waiting happens in the browser, with no extra round trip to start it.
  • And a class instance does not, which is why a database library's model object cannot be a prop. Convert it to a plain object at the boundary, on purpose. That is also the moment to drop the fields the browser has no business seeing.

Elements cross too, which is the basis of the next subsection.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: serializable props and serializable arguments.

17.5 Composing Across the Boundary

The rule "a Server Component cannot be imported by a Client Component" sounds as if it forbids mixing them. It does not, and the pattern that makes it work is one you already know from §1.10: pass the Server Component's output as children.

// Sidebar.jsx  — a Client Component: it needs state for the collapse toggle
'use client';
import { useState } from 'react';

export function Sidebar({ children }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(true);
  return (
    <aside>
      <button onClick={() => setOpen(o => !o)}>{open ? 'Hide' : 'Show'}</button>
      {open && children}
    </aside>
  );
}

// Page.jsx  — a Server Component: no directive, so it stays on the server
export function Page() {
  return (
    <Sidebar>
      <ServerOnlyTree />
    </Sidebar>
  );
}
async function ServerOnlyTree() {
  const rows = await Promise.resolve(['a', 'b']);
  return <ul>{rows.map(r => <li key={r}>{r}</li>)}</ul>;
}

Sidebar is a Client Component and ServerOnlyTree runs only on the server, yet the second renders inside the first. There is no contradiction. Sidebar never imports ServerOnlyTree. It receives an already-rendered element in children, which is data, and data serialises like any other prop.

This is the most important RSC pattern, and it turns the usual advice about layout upside down. Keep 'use client' as low in the tree as possible, and let interactive shells accept children. A 'use client' at the top of your layout file makes the entire application a client bundle. That mistake has no error message: everything still works, and none of the benefit arrives.

17.6 Async Components

An async function component is legal in the server environment, and works exactly as it reads: await at the top, use the value below.

import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function Data() {
  const v = await Promise.resolve('from await');
  return <b>{v}</b>;
}
function Page() {
  return <main><Suspense fallback={<i>loading</i>}><Data /></Suspense></main>;
}

const stream = await renderToReadableStream(<Page />);
let html = '';
for await (const c of stream) html += new TextDecoder().decode(c);
console.log('async component rendered:', html.includes('from await'));
console.log('fallback also shipped   :', html.includes('<i>loading</i>'));

async component rendered: true
fallback also shipped   : true

Both are true, and that is the streaming behaviour from §16.3: the fallback goes out in the shell and the content follows. An async component is a suspending component, so it needs a Suspense boundary above it. Without one, the suspension travels up to the nearest boundary, and if there is none, the whole page waits.

The restriction that catches people: async works in the server environment only. An async Client Component is not supported, and there is no await in a Client Component's body. When a Client Component needs to wait for something, it uses use(promise) (§13.9) on a promise created outside the render, often one handed to it by a Server Component, as in §17.4.

17.7 Server Functions and 'use server'

'use server' marks a function as callable from the browser. It points the other way from 'use client'. It does not mean "this code ships to the browser", but "the browser may ask the server to run this".

// actions.js
'use server';

export async function renameItem(id, name) {
  // runs on the server, always
  return { id, name: String(name).trim() };
}

The bundler replaces the export with a server function reference. When a Client Component imports and calls it, what actually happens is an HTTP request carrying the arguments, sent by React's runtime. The return value is serialised back, with the same rules as §17.4.

Two placements, both valid:

Module-level, as above: the directive is the first statement in the file, and every export becomes a server function. Importing an action into client code is exactly this form: a Client Component imports it like any other module and calls it like any other async function.

Function-level, inside a Server Component: the directive is the first statement in the function body. This lets the action capture values from the server, which is often exactly what you want.

// a Server Component defining an inline action
export function EditForm({ id }) {
  async function save(formData) {
    'use server';
    const name = formData.get('name');
    return { id, name };            // `id` is closed over — it never went to the client
  }
  return (
    <form action={save}>
      <input name="name" defaultValue="untitled" />
      <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}

The captured id is worth understanding rather than just accepting. It does not travel to the browser as a value the user can see or change. React serialises it into an opaque bundle of bound arguments, encrypted by the framework, which the browser sends back with the call. That is convenient, and it is not a security boundary, for the reason in §17.9.

In summary, the vocabulary here is importing an action into client code.

17.8 Actions, Forms and Progressive Enhancement

Server functions and <form action> were designed together for progressive enhancement: a form whose action is a server function submits and works before any JavaScript has loaded.

The browser does the submission natively, as forms always have, and React's server handler recognises it, runs the function and returns the next page. Once hydration completes, React takes over the same form and handles it without a page load instead. Same code, two mechanisms, and the user cannot tell which one ran.

This is the strongest argument for the whole architecture, and it comes with a condition that is easy to break: the enhancement only holds while the form works without JavaScript. An onSubmit handler that calls preventDefault, a submit button that is disabled until hydration, or an action that depends on browser state all take it away. §15 covers useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic, which are designed to add pending states and optimistic updates without breaking the no-JavaScript path.

You can also call a server function outside a form, from an event handler or from a transition. It is an ordinary async call:

'use client';
import { useTransition } from 'react';

export function DeleteButton({ id, remove }) {     // `remove` is a server function
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  return (
    <button disabled={isPending} onClick={() => startTransition(async () => {
      await remove(id);
    })}>
      {isPending ? 'Deleting…' : 'Delete'}
    </button>
  );
}

Wrapping it in startTransition is not decoration. It is what makes the pending state and the resulting re-render non-blocking, and §12 explains why that matters.

17.9 Every Server Function Is a Public Endpoint

This is the most important sentence in the section, and the one most often skipped.

Treat an action as a public endpoint, because a server function is a URL. The bundler gives it an id, React's runtime sends requests to it, and anyone else can send requests to it too: with any arguments, in any order, at any time, whatever your UI would have sent. The fact that your only call site passes a checked id from a component the user cannot reach is worth nothing.

Three consequences that must be in every server function you write:

Authenticate and authorise inside the function. Check who the user is and what they may do inside the function itself. Not in the component that renders the form, not in a layout above it, not in middleware you hope runs. Inside. The check that the current user may delete this item belongs in the function that deletes it.

Validate every argument. Arguments arrive rebuilt from a request body. Type annotations are erased (§1 of the TypeScript course), so a number parameter can receive a string, an object or undefined. Parse the input rather than assume its shape.

Treat closed-over values as inputs, not as constants. The bound id from §17.7 is signed and encrypted by the framework, so the browser cannot read or forge it. But it was still chosen at render time, by a request you may not have checked as carefully as this one. Check again.

The mental substitution that gets this right: read every 'use server' function as though it began with app.post('/some-random-id', ...), because that is what it is. The syntax looking like an import does not change who can reach it.

What to carry forward from this subsection: treat an action as a public endpoint.

17.10 Tainting

React provides two APIs for one specific failure: accidentally serialising something secret into the payload. They are a safety net, not the security model.

taintUniqueValue marks a specific string or bigint (a token, a password hash, a private key), so that passing it to a Client Component throws an error instead of sending it.

taintObjectReference marks an object, so that passing that object throws. Note the limitation carefully: it marks the reference, not the contents. A user object marked this way still lets user.email through, because that is a different value.

Both are exported as experimental_taintObjectReference and experimental_taintUniqueValue. Measured: neither is present in the stable React 19.3.0 package, nor in the 19.3 canary. Only a 0.0.0-experimental build exports them, which is the experimental channel, where APIs are published that may change or never ship. And even there, only under the react-server condition that a Server Components bundler uses. 19.3 promoted <ViewTransition> and browser() to stable, and left these behind. Know that they exist and what they cover; do not plan your security around them.

The lasting version of the same discipline needs no API: construct the object you send. A Server Component that fetches a user row and passes user to a client component is one database change away from leaking a column that did not exist when the code was written. Passing { name: user.name, avatar: user.avatar } cannot leak a field nobody added to that literal, and it documents the contract at the same time.

The terms above, gathered: experimental channel.

17.11 What a Server Component Cannot Do

The things a Server Component cannot do are all one rule in different forms: a Server Component runs once and is never re-rendered, so anything whose meaning depends on a second render is unavailable.

State and effects
useState, useReducer, useEffect, useLayoutEffect, useRef. There is no later render to hold a value for and no commit to run an effect after.
Event handlers
An onClick is a function prop, and functions do not serialise (§17.4). The error you get names exactly that.
Browser APIs
window, document, localStorage. Not present, and not shimmed.
Context
useContext is unavailable in a Server Component. Pass props, or put the provider in a Client Component near the top of the tree.
Custom hooks that use any of the above
Transitively. A hook is server-safe only if everything it calls is.

The context restriction is the one that changes existing applications most. A theme, a locale, a set of feature flags: all of these used to be context. In an RSC application they are either props passed down from the top, or a Client Component provider wrapping the interactive parts. The second is usually right, and it is the children pattern from §17.5 again.

17.12 cache and cacheSignal

Two Server Component APIs deal with the fact that a request's work is spread across a tree whose parts fetch data independently.

cache(fn) memoises a function for the length of a single request. Both preloading data early and sharing a snapshot of data across a tree are this same mechanism, used at different moments. Two components asking for the same user get one query.

The scope is the part to get right, and it is worth measuring rather than assuming. Called outside a render, cache does nothing at all:

import { cache } from 'react';

let calls = 0;
const getUser = cache(id => { calls++; return { id, name: 'Ada' }; });

console.log(getUser(1), getUser(1), getUser(2));
console.log('underlying calls outside a render:', calls);

{ id: 1, name: 'Ada' } { id: 1, name: 'Ada' } { id: 2, name: 'Ada' }
underlying calls outside a render: 3

Three lookups, three executions. The saved results are stored per render, and outside one there is nowhere to put them, so cache simply passes the call through. Move the same three lookups into an actual server render, and the picture changes:

cat > cache.mjs <<'EOF'
import { cache, createElement as h } from 'react';
import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-server-dom-webpack/server.edge';
let calls = 0;
const getUser = cache(id => { calls++; return { id, name: 'Ada' }; });
const A = () => h('b', null, getUser(1).name);
const B = () => h('i', null, getUser(1).name);
const C = () => h('u', null, getUser(2).name);
const Page = () => h('div', null, h(A), h(B), h(C));
for await (const _ of renderToReadableStream(h(Page), {})) {}
console.log('inside one RSC render, three lookups ->', calls, 'underlying call(s)');
EOF
NODE_ENV=production node --conditions react-server cache.mjs

inside one RSC render, three lookups -> 2 underlying call(s)

Two, not three. The two lookups of user 1 collapsed into one, and user 2 was fetched separately, because the cache is keyed on the arguments.

That scoping is the whole design: it is a de-duplicator, not a data cache. Its lifetime is one render, and nothing survives to the next request. So there is no problem of clearing out old entries, and no out-of-date data to reason about. It also sets a trap worth stating: a unit test that calls a cached function directly and expects one execution will see every call go through, because there is no render around it.

This is what makes "fetch the data where you need it" a workable rule rather than an N+1 disaster (one query per item instead of one in total). A layout, a header and three cards can all call getUser(id) without coordinating, and one query happens.

cacheSignal() returns an AbortSignal that fires when React has finished rendering: because the request was aborted, the user navigated away, or the render errored. Passing it to fetch means a request in flight whose result nobody will ever read gets cancelled, instead of running to completion and being thrown away. On a busy server that is real capacity saved.

Both are exported by the stable React 19.3.0 package, and both mean something only in the server environment.

One line each, for reference: preloading data and sharing a snapshot of data.

17.13 Where This Actually Runs

Server Components need a bundler that can find 'use client' boundaries, output a chunk per boundary, and produce the module map that turns an I row into a URL. React ships the reference implementations (react-server-dom-webpack, and equivalents for other bundlers), and they are reference implementations, not products.

In practice that means a framework: Next.js's App Router, React Router in framework mode, or another stack that supports RSC. This is not temporary. The bundler integration really is part of the architecture, in the same way that you cannot understand a 'use client' file without knowing which chunk it lands in.

RSC without a server is worth naming, because it removes a common objection. The "server" in the name is about where the code runs, not when. A build step is a perfectly good place to run Server Components, and the output is a payload written to a file and served from a CDN. A site exported as static files can use Server Components fully. What it cannot do is run server functions, because those are, by definition, a live endpoint.

The migration path for an existing browser-only application is the one §17.5 implies, and it is step by step rather than a rewrite. Put 'use client' at the top of what you have and check nothing changed. Then move the boundary down one component at a time, converting data loading to async components as you go. Each step is small and correct on its own, and the benefit grows with how far down the boundary has moved.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: RSC without a server.

What This Section Established

A Server Component runs once, on the server or at build time, and its code never reaches the browser — only its output does. That is why it cannot have state, effects, event handlers, context or browser APIs, and why importing a large library in one costs the user nothing.

The payload is a numbered stream of JSON rows. ["$","article",null,{…}] is an element; "$L1" is a lazy reference to a row that arrives later; 1:I[…] is a Client Component to load. Measured, an async Server Component appears in the payload only as the markup it returned — its name and its awaited promise are absent.

'use client' marks a boundary, not a component: everything the marked file imports joins the client bundle. Keep it low in the tree and let interactive shells take children, which is how a Server Component renders inside a Client Component without being imported by it.

What crosses the boundary is wider than JSON — measured: Date, Map, Set, BigInt, typed arrays and promises all serialise, while functions, class instances and symbols throw. A promise crossing is what lets a Server Component start a fetch and a Client Component use() it.

'use server' is the other direction: a function the browser may ask the server to run. It is a public HTTP endpoint with an unusual calling convention, so it authenticates, authorises and validates inside itself, closed-over arguments included. <form action> plus a server function works before hydration, which is the architecture's best property and the one easiest to break.

cache() de-duplicates within one request so that components can fetch independently; cacheSignal() cancels work nobody will read. The taint APIs are a net rather than a model, and are not in the stable package — constructing the object you send is the durable discipline.

Exercises

1. Read a payload. Render a Server Component containing a static header, an async child and a Client Component, and print the payload. Annotate every row: which is the root, which is a lazy reference, which is an import, and which row resolves which reference. Then say what a reader of the payload alone could learn about your server code.

2. Move the boundary. Take a page with 'use client' at the top and one interactive button at the bottom. Move the directive down to the button. List everything that changes: which modules are in the bundle, which components can be async, and what has to change about how the button gets its data.

3. Serialise the matrix. For each of Date, Map, Set, a promise, a class instance and an arrow function, predict whether it crosses to a Client Component and, if it does, what the payload encoding looks like. Verify. Then explain why a class instance is refused rather than sent as a plain object.

4. Attack your own action. Write a server function deleteNote(id) whose only call site passes an id from a component that renders solely for the note's owner. Then write the curl that deletes someone else's note. Fix it, and state which of the three rules in §17.9 the original violated.

5. Prove the de-duplication. Build a tree where three components each need the same record. Implement it once with a plain function and once with cache(), counting the underlying calls each way. Then say what would happen if the same code ran for two different requests concurrently, and why that is not a cache-invalidation problem.

Solution

1. Reading a payload.

2:I[null,null,"Button"]            an IMPORT row: load the Button chunk
0:["$","article",null,{"children":[
     ["$","h1",null,{"children":"Header"}],   inline, resolved immediately
     "$L1",                                   lazy -> row 1 (the async child)
     ["$","$L2",null,{"label":"Save"}]        the client component, with its props
   ]}]
1:["$","span",null,{"children":"Ada"}]        row 1 arrives when the await resolved

From the payload alone a reader learns: the shape of the rendered markup, the props passed to every Client Component, and the module name of each Client Component. They learn nothing about the Server Components — not their names, not their source, not what they queried. That asymmetry is the security property the architecture provides, and it is also why props to Client Components must be treated as public.

2. Moving the boundary.

Before: every module reachable from the page's imports is in the client bundle, no component in the file can be async, and data must be fetched from an effect or a use() on the client.

After: only the button's module and its imports are in the bundle. Everything above it may be async and may query directly. The button now gets its data as props from a Server Component — and those props must satisfy §17.4, so an ORM row has to become a plain object at the boundary.

The one thing that must change structurally: if the button previously read a context, that context provider is now above it in Server-Component territory where context does not exist. Either thread the value as a prop, or make a small 'use client' provider that wraps the interactive region.

3. The matrix.

Date            crosses    "$D1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"
Map             crosses    "$Q2"   with 2:[["k",1]]
Set             crosses    "$W2"   with 2:[1,2]
Promise         crosses    "$@2"   with the resolved value arriving as row 2
class instance  refused    an error row
arrow function  refused    "Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components
                            unless you explicitly expose it by marking it with
                            "use server"."

A class instance is refused rather than flattened because flattening would be a silent lie: the object that arrived would have the data but none of the methods, and the first user.fullName() on the client would fail at a place with no connection to the boundary that caused it. Refusing at the boundary puts the error where the mistake is.

4. Attacking your own action.

// actions.js — the vulnerable version
'use server';
export async function deleteNote(id) {
  return db.notes.delete(id);          // no auth check anywhere
}

curl -X POST https://example.com/ \
  -H 'Next-Action: <the action id from the page source>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '[42]'

The action id is in the HTML of any page that renders the form, so it is not a secret. The fixed version:

'use server';
export async function deleteNote(id) {
  const user = await requireSession();                 // authenticate
  const note = await db.notes.find(Number(id));        // validate the argument
  if (!note || note.ownerId !== user.id) throw new Error('not found');   // authorise
  return db.notes.delete(note.id);
}

The original violated all three rules, but the load-bearing one is authorise inside the function: the check existed, in the component that decided whether to render the form. That check protects the UI and protects nothing else.

5. De-duplication.

cat > dedupe.mjs <<'EOF'
import { cache, createElement as h } from 'react';
import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-server-dom-webpack/server.edge';
let plainCalls = 0, cachedCalls = 0;
const plain = id => { plainCalls++; return { id }; };
const cached = cache(id => { cachedCalls++; return { id }; });
const P = () => h('b', null, String(plain(1).id));
const Q = () => h('i', null, String(cached(1).id));
const Page = () => h('div', null, h(P), h(P), h(P), h(Q), h(Q), h(Q));
for await (const _ of renderToReadableStream(h(Page), {})) {}
console.log('plain:', plainCalls, '| cached:', cachedCalls);
EOF
NODE_ENV=production node --conditions react-server dedupe.mjs

plain: 3 | cached: 1

Two concurrent requests each get their own cache, because the lifetime is the render, not the process. And the same code outside a render de-duplicates nothing at all — measured in §17.12 — which is the detail that makes a naive unit test of a cached function misleading. Nothing is shared between them and nothing survives either of them.

That is why there is no invalidation problem: invalidation exists when a cache outlives the data's ability to change. This one is discarded before the response is finished, so the worst staleness possible is "two components in the same render saw the same snapshot" — which is the desired behaviour, not a hazard.

SECTION 18

TypeScript, Testing and Class Components

This section has three subjects that do not obviously belong together. What they share is that each is about the code around your components, rather than the components themselves:

  • types are how a component's contract (what it accepts and returns) is stated;
  • tests are how that contract is checked;
  • and class components, the older way of writing components, are where a large amount of existing React code still lives.

The TypeScript half deliberately does not re-teach the type system: the TypeScript course covers generics, narrowing, conditional types and JSX typing. What is here is the React-specific vocabulary: which types to reach for, which to avoid, and the handful of places where React's type definitions do something you would not predict.

The testing half is not a survey of test runners either. It covers the two things React itself provides, act and the rules about what makes a component testable, plus the principle that decides what to test at all.

18.1 Typing Props

TypeScript with React needs almost nothing beyond the language itself. React adds no special syntax and no decorators, and a component is just a function whose parameter happens to be a props object. What follows is the vocabulary: the types worth knowing by name, and the handful of places where React's type definitions behave unexpectedly.

Props are an object type, so an interface or a type alias is all you need.

interface BadgeProps {
  label: string;
  tone?: 'neutral' | 'warn' | 'error';       // a union, not a string
  count?: number;
  onDismiss?: () => void;
}

function Badge({ label, tone = 'neutral', count, onDismiss }: BadgeProps) {
  return <span className={`badge badge--${tone}`}>
    {label}{count !== undefined ? ` (${count})` : ''}
    {onDismiss ? <button onClick={onDismiss}>×</button> : null}
  </span>;
}

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Badge label="new" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Badge label="late" tone="warn" count={3} />));

<span class="badge badge--neutral">new</span>
<span class="badge badge--warn">late (3)</span>

Two habits are worth adopting from the start.

  • Prefer a union to string for anything with a fixed set of values. tone: 'neutral' | 'warn' | 'error' gives you autocomplete, catches typos, and makes an exhaustive switch (one that handles every case) possible.
  • And React.FC is not needed and is best avoided: it adds nothing that annotating the props parameter does not. It once silently added children to every component, a behaviour removed in React 18's types, which broke code that relied on it. And it gets in the way of generic components (§18.5).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: TypeScript with React.

18.2 children and the Node Types
