children is typed with react.reactnode, which is the type of anything React can render: an element, a string, a number, null, undefined, a boolean, an array of those, or a promise of one.

import type { ReactNode, ReactElement } from 'react';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

function Panel({ title, children }: { title: string; children: ReactNode }) {
  return <section><h2>{title}</h2><div>{children}</div></section>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Panel title="a">text</Panel>));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Panel title="b">{[1, 2]}{null}<i>x</i></Panel>));

<section><h2>a</h2><div>text</div></section>
<section><h2>b</h2><div>12<i>x</i></div></section>

Both are legal ReactNodes, which is exactly why the type is the right default. It matches §1.6's rendering rules precisely, including that null and booleans render nothing.

react.reactelement is the narrower type — specifically a JSX element, not a string or a number. Use it only when you genuinely need to restrict a prop to an element, and know that it does not let you constrain which element: ReactElement cannot express "a <Tab>, not a <div>", because JSX's type does not carry that information usefully. Attempts to enforce "only these children" through types produce a lot of machinery and a poor error message; a runtime check, or a slots API (§1.10), is the honest answer.

propswithchildren wraps a props type to add an optional children: PropsWithChildren<{ title: string }>. It saves one line, and is mostly a matter of taste. Writing children: ReactNode yourself says whether children are required, which the helper cannot.

To have in hand before moving on: React.ReactNode and React.ReactElement.

18.3 Deriving Props from the DOM

The most useful React type in everyday work is the one that saves you from re-declaring what an element already accepts.

import type { ComponentProps } from 'react';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

// every prop a real <button> takes, plus one of ours
type ButtonProps = ComponentProps<'button'> & { variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost' };

function Button({ variant = 'primary', className, ...rest }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button className={`btn btn--${variant} ${className ?? ''}`.trim()} {...rest} />;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Button>Save</Button>));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <Button variant="ghost" type="submit" disabled aria-label="Save" className="wide">S</Button>));

<button class="btn btn--primary">Save</button>
<button class="btn btn--ghost wide" type="submit" disabled="" aria-label="Save">S</button>

type, disabled and aria-label were all accepted and correctly typed without being declared, because componentprops reads them from the DOM element's own definition. The alternative, listing the props you think a button needs, is wrong the day someone needs formAction.

componentpropswithoutref is the same thing with ref removed, for a component that manages its own ref internally. In React 19 the difference matters less than it did, because ref is an ordinary prop (§7.3) and ComponentProps includes it. But the type is still what you want when you deliberately do not pass a ref through.

ComponentProps also works on your own components, as ComponentProps<typeof Button>. That is how a wrapper stays in step with what it wraps.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: ComponentPropsWithoutRef.

18.4 Typing Hooks

Most hooks infer their types correctly and need no annotation. The four that do not are worth knowing exactly, because each goes wrong in a different way.

import { useState, useRef, useReducer, createContext } from 'react';

// 3. useReducer: annotate the reducer, and the rest follows
type State = { step: number };
type Action = { type: 'next' } | { type: 'reset' };
function reducer(state: State, action: Action): State {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'next': return { step: state.step + 1 };
    case 'reset': return { step: 0 };
  }
}
// 4. useContext: the default value determines the type
const ThemeContext = createContext<'light' | 'dark'>('light');

function Annotated() {
  // 1. useState: inferred from the initial value; annotate when it starts null or empty
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);                          // number — no annotation
  const [user, setUser] = useState<{ id: number } | null>(null);  // else it is `null` forever
  const [tags, setTags] = useState<string[]>([]);                 // else it is `never[]`

  // 2. useRef: two distinct shapes
  const box = useRef<HTMLDivElement | null>(null);   // a DOM ref: starts null
  const timer = useRef<number>(0);                   // a mutable value: starts set

  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { step: 0 });

  void count; void setCount; void user; void setUser; void tags; void setTags;
  void box; void timer; void state; void dispatch;
  return null;
}
void Annotated; void ThemeContext;
export {};

Typing usestate is only necessary when the initial value does not represent the real type. useState(null) infers null, and rejects everything you assign later; useState([]) infers never[]. Both are the same mistake (inferring the type from a placeholder), and both are fixed by passing the type explicitly.

useRef has two shapes that behave differently, and it is worth choosing deliberately.

  • A DOM ref is useRef<HTMLDivElement | null>(null), and .current can be null, because it is null until the commit attaches the node (§7.3, measured).
  • A ref holding a changeable value is useRef<number>(0), and .current cannot be null, because you always have a value.

Typing usereducer needs only the reducer annotated: useReducer infers the state and the dispatch from it. Note that the reducer above has no default branch and still compiles, because every member of the Action union is handled. That is the payoff of a discriminated union (a union whose members share a label field), and the reason to write actions as one.

Typing usecontext is decided by createContext's argument. When there is no sensible default, the honest pattern is createContext<T | null>(null), plus a custom hook that throws:

import { createContext, useContext } from 'react';

type Auth = { userId: number };
const AuthContext = createContext<Auth | null>(null);

function useAuth(): Auth {
  const value = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (value === null) throw new Error('useAuth must be used inside <AuthProvider>');
  return value;                          // narrowed to Auth — callers never see null
}
void useAuth; void AuthContext;
export {};

The throw is what makes the return type non-nullable. Every consumer is spared a null check, and a missing provider becomes a named error, instead of a Cannot read properties of null twelve frames away.

In summary, the vocabulary here is typing useState, typing useReducer and typing useContext.

18.5 Events, Styles and Generic Components

Typing a dom event handler is a matter of picking the right event type. The reliable way to find it is to let ComponentProps tell you, rather than guessing:

import type { ChangeEvent, MouseEvent, FormEvent, KeyboardEvent, CSSProperties } from 'react';

function Field() {
  const onChange = (e: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => e.target.value.trim();
  const onClick = (e: MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => e.currentTarget.disabled;
  const onSubmit = (e: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) => e.preventDefault();
  const onKey = (e: KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => e.key === 'Enter';
  const style: CSSProperties = { marginTop: 8, zIndex: 2 };   // number, not string
  return <form onSubmit={onSubmit} style={style}>
    <input onChange={onChange} onKeyDown={onKey} />
    <button onClick={onClick}>go</button>
  </form>;
}
void Field;
export {};

Two details in there earn their place.

  • The type parameter is the element the handler is attached to, which is what makes e.currentTarget correctly typed. e.target is only EventTarget in general, because an event can start anywhere.
  • And the style props type is CSSProperties, which accepts a number for the properties that take one (§9.5), and rejects a misspelled property outright.

When the handler is written inline, React infers all of this, so annotate only when the function is defined separately.

A generic component (one that works for many item types) is the one place where React's typing gets really involved. It is worth one example, because the pattern comes back in every table, list and select:

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

interface ListProps<T> {
  items: readonly T[];
  keyOf: (item: T) => string;
  render: (item: T) => React.ReactNode;
}
function List<T>({ items, keyOf, render }: ListProps<T>) {
  return <ul>{items.map(item => <li key={keyOf(item)}>{render(item)}</li>)}</ul>;
}

const users = [{ id: 'a', name: 'Ada' }, { id: 'b', name: 'Grace' }];
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <List items={users} keyOf={u => u.id} render={u => <b>{u.name}</b>} />
));

<ul><li><b>Ada</b></li><li><b>Grace</b></li></ul>

T was inferred from items, so u is fully typed in both callbacks, with nothing written at the call site. This is also the concrete reason to avoid React.FC: it is not generic, so a component annotated with it cannot infer a type parameter this way.

A tsconfig for a React project needs one option beyond the usual: "jsx": "react-jsx", which selects the automatic runtime from §1.3. "jsx": "preserve" is the right value when a bundler will do the JSX transform instead. The TypeScript course covers the rest of the file.

What to carry forward from this subsection: typing a DOM event handler and style props type.

18.6 Testing: act

await act( is React's own testing tool, and it does one thing. It runs the callback, and then finishes everything React has queued (renders, effects, and the microtasks they scheduled) before returning.

import { useState, useEffect, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => { globalThis.effectRan = true; }, []);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(v => v + 1)}>count {n}</button>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);

await act(async () => { root.render(<Counter />); });
console.log('after mount    :', box.innerHTML, '| effect ran:', globalThis.effectRan);
await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('button').dispatchEvent(new window.MouseEvent('click', { bubbles: true }));
});
console.log('after one click:', box.innerHTML);

after mount    : <button>count 0</button> | effect ran: true
after one click: <button>count 1</button>

Testing components in this course always has that shape, and dispatching events in tests uses the same dispatchEvent you have seen throughout: a real event on a real node, wrapped in act so that React has finished responding before the assertion runs. Every assertion in this course's DOM examples has that shape, and the reason is the warning you get without it: "An update to Counter inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)". Outside act, React's work is scheduled rather than immediate, so an assertion made straight after render sees an empty container.

Two mechanics to know.

  • globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true tells React it is in a test, which is what makes act finish the work synchronously. Test frameworks usually set it for you.
  • And prefer await act(async () => …) to the synchronous form. The async version also waits for promises, so an effect that awaits, or an Action, settles before your assertion.

act is also the tool for the awkward cases the earlier sections used: resolving a promise inside act so that a Suspense boundary re-renders (§13.4), and driving an Action to completion (§15.2).

The terms above, gathered: testing components and dispatching events in tests.

18.7 What to Test

React Testing Library is the standard layer on top of the above. Its value is a principle rather than an API: query the DOM the way a user finds things, and assert on what a user can see.

getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })    what a user (or a screen reader) perceives
getByLabelText('Email')                  a form field found through its label
getByText('3 items')                     visible content
getByTestId('cart')                      the escape hatch, when nothing else identifies it

Two consequences fall out and both are useful. Tests written this way survive refactors — changing a <div> to a <section>, renaming a class, splitting a component — because none of that changes what the user perceives. And they double as accessibility checks: if getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }) cannot find your button, a screen reader cannot either.

What to test, in order of value:

Behaviour a user performs
Fill the form, submit, see the result. One test covering a real path is worth ten covering render output.
Reducers and pure functions
No renderer needed at all (§4.2, measured). The cheapest tests you will write, and the ones that keep working.
Custom hooks, through a component
A hook is only meaningful inside a render, so test it by rendering a component that uses it — which is also how it will actually be used.
Not: implementation details
Which hooks were called, what state holds, how many times something rendered. Those change when you refactor and tell you nothing about whether the feature works.

The one exception to the last row is a performance test, where render counts are the thing being tested, and it should say so in its name.

One line each, for reference: React Testing Library.

18.8 The Application Around React

React renders. It does not route, fetch, bundle or build. Everything in that list is a decision you make separately, and React's own advice, honestly summarised, is that most applications should not make those decisions one at a time.

A full-stack framework is the recommended starting point, and the reason is not convenience. Routing, data fetching, code splitting and server rendering affect each other. §13.5's boundary placement is a reveal-order decision, a streaming decision and a hydration decision all at once, and §17's Server Components need a bundler that understands 'use client'. A framework has already made those decisions in a consistent way.

Next.js App Router
The most complete Server Components implementation, with file-based routing, Server Functions and partial prerendering (§16.12). Deploys as a static export too, so "needs a server" is a choice rather than a requirement.
React Router (v7)
A router that grew into a framework. Nested routes with per-route loaders and actions map directly onto §13 and §15, and it can be adopted a route at a time from an existing single-page app.
Expo (React Native)
The same component model rendering native views instead of DOM nodes. Everything in §1–§15 transfers unchanged; §9 and §16 do not, because there is no DOM and no HTML.

Building a React app from scratch is legitimate, and it means putting the pieces together yourself.

  • A build tool: Vite is the default answer, with Parcel (no configuration needed) and Rsbuild (based on Rspack, and fast on large codebases) as the alternatives, and Metro for React Native.
  • Then client-side routing, from React Router or a smaller library. Whatever you choose, wrap navigations in startTransition (§12.3), or the old page blanks on every link.
  • Then data fetching, which wants a library that supports Suspense rather than the Effect from §6.6.
  • Then code splitting per route with lazy (§13.2).

Create React App is deprecated, and should not be used for anything new. It was the standard starting template for years, so it is still what most tutorials show. It is unmaintained, its dependencies are old enough to produce security-audit warnings on install, and it has no path to Server Components. Moving to Vite usually takes an afternoon: replace the scripts, rename .js files containing JSX to .jsx, and move %PUBLIC_URL% references.

To add React to an existing project is the other direction, and it is well supported. React does not require owning the page: createRoot takes any DOM node, so a server-rendered template can mount React into one <div> and leave the rest alone. Several roots on one page are fine — note from §9.3 that each gets its own event delegation, so they are isolated. A portal (§9.9) renders React into a node the surrounding page owns without a second root.

Editor setup is two tools and one setting.

  • ESLint with eslint-plugin-react-hooks (§5.6). This is the single highest-value thing in this list, because it catches the kind of bug that produces no error.
  • Prettier, or your editor's built-in formatter, with formatting on save turned on, so that formatting stops being something anyone reviews.
  • And the TypeScript language service, which is what makes §18.3's ComponentProps pay off while you type, rather than at build time.

Add the React Developer Tools extension (§10.6) at the same time. Its highlight-updates option answers "what is re-rendering?" faster than any amount of reasoning, and its Components tab is the only place where you can see the render tree from §1.12 directly.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: Parcel, Rsbuild, Next.js App Router, Expo (React Native), full-stack framework, client-side routing, editor setup, formatting on save, add React to an existing project, Create React App and building a React app from scratch.

18.9 Class Components

React.Component is the base class, and classes are not deprecated: there is no plan to remove them. They are simply not how new React is written, and the reason is concrete. Every hook in §6–§8 exists because class lifecycle methods split one concern across three methods.

import { Component } from 'react';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

class Clock extends Component<{ tz: string }, { now: string }> {
  state = { now: 'start' };
  static defaultProps = { tz: 'UTC' };
  timer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | null = null;

  componentDidMount() { this.timer = setInterval(() => this.tick(), 1000); }
  componentDidUpdate(prev: { tz: string }) { if (prev.tz !== this.props.tz) this.tick(); }
  componentWillUnmount() { if (this.timer) clearInterval(this.timer); }
  tick() { this.setState({ now: 'tick' }); }
  render() { return <b>{this.props.tz}:{this.state.now}</b>; }
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Clock tz="CET" />));

<b>CET:start</b>

The timer's setup, its reaction to a prop change, and its teardown are in three separate methods, and nothing in the language connects them. §6.2's Effect does all three in one block, whose cleanup is returned from its own setup, which is why the two cannot fall out of step.

The API surface, for reading existing code:

setState(
Merges into state (unlike useState, which replaces) and takes an optional callback that runs after the commit.
render, and the render method's contract
The render method is the class equivalent of a function component's body, and it obeys the same purity rule (§5.1) for the same reasons.
componentDidMount / componentDidUpdate / componentWillUnmount
The three that became one useEffect.
shouldComponentUpdate / PureComponent
memo's ancestors. PureComponent is a shallow prop and state comparison.
getDerivedStateFromProps
Almost always the §7.1 mistake. A key or a render-time computation replaces it.
getSnapshotBeforeUpdate
Reads the DOM before it is mutated — a scroll position across an insertion. useLayoutEffect covers it.
UNSAFE_componentWillMount and friends
Renamed because they are unsafe under concurrent rendering — they can run on a render that is abandoned (§12.8).
static contextType / defaultProps / forceUpdate(
One context per class; default props (function components use default parameters); and a re-render with no state change, which is nearly always a mutation that should have been state.

getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch are the exception. They have no hook equivalent, and they are the reason error boundaries are still classes (§14.1).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: React.Component, setState(, shouldComponentUpdate, getSnapshotBeforeUpdate, getDerivedStateFromProps, static contextType, UNSAFE_componentWillMount and forceUpdate(.

18.10 Migrating a Class to a Function

Converting is mechanical, and doing it in this order keeps the component working at every step.

this.props.x
a destructured parameter
this.state (one object)
several useState calls, one per independent value (§3.5) — or one useReducer
setState({a: 1}) merging
separate setters, or setX(prev => ({...prev, a: 1})) — useState replaces, it does not merge
the three lifecycle methods
one useEffect per concern, not one per method
an instance field (this.timer)
useRef, or a local inside the Effect if only that Effect uses it
defaultProps
default parameter values
static contextType
useContext — and now you may read several

The step people get wrong is the fourth. Translating each lifecycle method into its own Effect recreates the split the hooks were designed to fix. Group by what is being synchronized, so that the subscription's setup and teardown land in one Effect, and the analytics call lands in another.

Two legacy APIs to recognise while you are in there. ReactDOM.render and unmountComponentAtNode are the entry points from before React 18, removed in React 19. createRoot replaces them, and their removal is the change that breaks a React 17 application on upgrade. And forwardRef (§7.3) is deprecated now that ref is a prop.

To have in hand before moving on: ReactDOM.render and unmountComponentAtNode.

What This Section Established

Props are an ordinary object type; prefer a union to string for fixed sets, and skip React.FC — it adds nothing and cannot be generic.

ReactNode is anything renderable and is the right type for children; ReactElement is narrower and cannot express which element. ComponentProps<'button'> gives you everything a real button accepts — measured, type, disabled and aria-label all worked without being declared.

Four hooks need help: useState when the initial value is a placeholder (null infers null, [] infers never[]), useRef in its two distinct shapes, useReducer through its reducer's annotation, and useContext through createContext's default. A createContext<T | null>(null) plus a hook that throws gives consumers a non-nullable type and a named error.

Event handler types are parameterised by the element they are attached to, which is what makes currentTarget typed. A generic component infers its parameter from a prop, at no cost to the call site.

await act() flushes React's queued work so an assertion can see it, and IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT is what makes it synchronous. Query by role and by label, assert on what a user perceives, and do not test which hooks ran.

Class components are supported and are not how new code is written, because their three lifecycle methods split one concern three ways. The migration is mechanical; the step to get right is grouping Effects by concern rather than by the method they came from. getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch remain the one class-only capability.

Exercises

1. Type a component from the DOM. Write an <Input> that accepts every prop a real <input> does plus a label, without listing any of them. Then show it accepting type="email", required and aria-describedby, and rejecting a misspelled prop.

2. Fix three inferences. Write useState(null), useState([]) and useState({}) and show the error each produces on the first assignment. Annotate each correctly and say what the annotation is protecting against.

3. A context that cannot be null. Build a provider and a useX hook so that consumers never see null and a missing provider throws a named error. Then show what a consumer's code looks like without the hook, and count the null checks removed.

4. Test a behaviour, not a render. Write two tests for the same form: one asserting on the rendered markup, one performing the user's actual path with act and asserting on the outcome. Then rename an element and change a class, and report which test broke.

5. Migrate a class. Convert a class with two pieces of state, three lifecycle methods and one instance field to a function component. Say how many Effects you ended up with and why that number is not three.

Solution

1. Typed from the DOM.

import type { ComponentProps } from 'react';
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server';

type InputProps = ComponentProps<'input'> & { label: string };
function Input({ label, id, ...rest }: InputProps) {
  return <><label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label><input id={id} {...rest} /></>;
}
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <Input label="Email" id="e" type="email" required aria-describedby="hint" />
));

<label for="e">Email</label><input id="e" type="email" required="" aria-describedby="hint"/>

A misspelled prop — requried — is rejected with "Property 'requried' does not exist on type 'InputProps'", because the intersection is a closed object type. That is the payoff over [key: string]: any.

2. Three inferences.

useState(null)   infers null      -> "Argument of type '{...}' is not assignable to
                                     parameter of type 'SetStateAction<null>'"
useState([])     infers never[]   -> "Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to
                                     parameter of type 'never'"
useState({})     infers {}        -> reading .name fails: "Property 'name' does not
                                     exist on type '{}'"

Annotate as useState<User | null>(null), useState<string[]>([]), useState<Partial<Form>>({}). What the annotation protects against is inference from a placeholder: the initial value is chosen for "nothing yet", and TypeScript quite reasonably concludes that "nothing" is the type.

3. A non-null context.

import { createContext, useContext } from 'react';
type Auth = { userId: number };
const AuthContext = createContext<Auth | null>(null);
export function useAuth(): Auth {
  const v = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (v === null) throw new Error('useAuth must be used inside <AuthProvider>');
  return v;
}

Without the hook, every consumer writes const auth = useContext(AuthContext); and then either auth?.userId at each use or an early return — so a component reading three fields removes three null checks, and a codebase with forty consumers removes forty-plus. The error message is the other half: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'userId') names nothing useful, while "must be used inside <AuthProvider>" names the fix.

4. Behaviour versus markup.

// markup test: asserts on structure
expect(container.innerHTML).toContain('<div class="form-row">');
// behaviour test: performs the path
await act(async () => { fireEvent.change(getByLabelText('Email'), { target: { value: 'a@b.com' } }); });
await act(async () => { fireEvent.click(getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })); });
expect(getByText('Saved')).toBeTruthy();

Renaming the <div> to a <section> and changing form-row to field breaks the first test and not the second — and neither change affects a single user. That is the whole argument: the first test is a snapshot of your implementation with a failing assertion attached.

5. The migration.

Two Effects, not three. componentDidMount and componentWillUnmount were the setup and teardown of one subscription, so they become one Effect with a cleanup; componentDidUpdate's prop comparison disappears entirely, because the dependency array does that comparison for you. The second Effect is whatever unrelated concern was also crammed into componentDidMount — usually an analytics call — and separating it is the point of the exercise: it has different dependencies and should not re-run when the subscription's do.

The instance field becomes a local const inside the Effect, because only that Effect used it. A useRef is needed only when something outside the Effect reads it.

SECTION 19

Capstone: A Complete Feature, Measured

Eighteen sections of mechanism are worth nothing until they meet a feature that has to work. This capstone is one build: a task board, carried from an empty file to something with:

  • a state shape that cannot go wrong;
  • effects that synchronize rather than set off a chain of updates;
  • a form that survives a failure;
  • and a set of measurements proving each claim.

Build it as you read. Every stage names the sections it draws on, so a stage that misbehaves gives you somewhere to go back to, instead of a search. Every block here runs: under node with jsdom (a simulated browser page) and the real react-dom, exactly as every other example in this course has. The numbers printed are the numbers this machine produced.

The last three stages are the ones usually skipped, and the ones that decide whether the code is any good: the measurements, an audit against what the earlier sections established, and an honest list of what is still wrong.

19.1 The Brief

State
A board of tasks, each in one of three columns. The state must not be able to represent a task in two columns, a selection pointing at a deleted task, or a filtered list that disagrees with the tasks.
Interaction
Add, move and delete. Every interaction is one dispatch, so no intermediate state is ever rendered.
Distribution
Columns read the tasks; the composer only dispatches. A change to the tasks must not re-render the composer.
Async
Saving goes through an Action: pending state managed, a failure returns a message beside the still-populated form, and the optimistic row disappears on its own.
Synchronization
One Effect, for one external system, with a cleanup that fully undoes its setup. Nothing derived lives in state.
Proof
Render counts, effect pairing and error containment measured rather than asserted.

19.2 The State Shape

Start with the state, because §3.5 is the decision everything else inherits. The board is normalised: one map from id to task, and one array of ids for each column. A task's column is not stored on the task. It is implied by which array holds its id, so "in two columns" cannot even be represented, rather than merely being discouraged.

const COLUMNS = ['todo', 'doing', 'done'];

function boardReducer(board, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added': {
      const task = { id: action.id, text: action.text };
      return { ...board,
        tasks: { ...board.tasks, [task.id]: task },
        order: { ...board.order, todo: [...board.order.todo, task.id] } };
    }
    case 'moved': {
      const from = COLUMNS.find(c => board.order[c].includes(action.id));
      if (!from || from === action.to) return board;
      return { ...board, order: { ...board.order,
        [from]: board.order[from].filter(id => id !== action.id),
        [action.to]: [...board.order[action.to], action.id] } };
    }
    case 'deleted': {
      const { [action.id]: _gone, ...tasks } = board.tasks;
      const order = Object.fromEntries(
        COLUMNS.map(c => [c, board.order[c].filter(id => id !== action.id)]));
      return { tasks, order };
    }
    default: throw new Error('unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}
const empty = { tasks: {}, order: { todo: [], doing: [], done: [] } };

// the reducer is a plain function: no renderer needed (§4.2)
let b = boardReducer(empty, { type: 'added', id: 't1', text: 'write' });
b = boardReducer(b, { type: 'added', id: 't2', text: 'test' });
b = boardReducer(b, { type: 'moved', id: 't1', to: 'doing' });
console.log('todo :', b.order.todo, '| doing:', b.order.doing);
b = boardReducer(b, { type: 'deleted', id: 't1' });
console.log('after delete -> tasks:', Object.keys(b.tasks), '| doing:', b.order.doing);
console.log('empty untouched:', JSON.stringify(empty.order.todo));
try { boardReducer(b, { type: 'typo' }); } catch (e) { console.log('caught:', e.message); }

todo : [ 't2' ] | doing: [ 't1' ]
after delete -> tasks: [ 't2' ] | doing: []
empty untouched: []
caught: unknown action: typo

Four properties are established before a single component exists.

  • Moving a task removed it from its old column in the same transition that added it to the new one, so no render can ever see it in both.
  • Deleting removed it from the map and from every column, so an id pointing at nothing is impossible.
  • The initial state was not mutated.
  • And an unknown action throws, instead of silently returning the old board (§4.2).

19.3 Distribution: Two Contexts

This is §4.8's shape, and the reason for it is the third line of the brief.

import { createContext, useContext, useReducer, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const COLUMNS = ['todo', 'doing', 'done'];
function boardReducer(board, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added': return { ...board,
      tasks: { ...board.tasks, [action.id]: { id: action.id, text: action.text } },
      order: { ...board.order, todo: [...board.order.todo, action.id] } };
    case 'moved': {
      const from = COLUMNS.find(c => board.order[c].includes(action.id));
      if (!from || from === action.to) return board;
      return { ...board, order: { ...board.order,
        [from]: board.order[from].filter(id => id !== action.id),
        [action.to]: [...board.order[action.to], action.id] } };
    }
    default: throw new Error('unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}
const BoardContext = createContext(null);
const DispatchContext = createContext(null);

function BoardProvider({ children }) {
  const [board, dispatch] = useReducer(boardReducer,
    { tasks: {}, order: { todo: [], doing: [], done: [] } });
  return <BoardContext value={board}><DispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</DispatchContext></BoardContext>;
}

let columnRenders = 0, composerRenders = 0;
function Column({ name }) {
  columnRenders++;
  const board = useContext(BoardContext);
  return <b>[{name}:{board.order[name].map(id => board.tasks[id].text).join(',') || '-'}]</b>;
}
function Composer() {
  composerRenders++;
  const dispatch = useContext(DispatchContext);
  globalThis.add = (id, text) => dispatch({ type: 'added', id, text });
  globalThis.move = (id, to) => dispatch({ type: 'moved', id, to });
  return <i>+</i>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => {
  root.render(<BoardProvider><Column name="todo" /><Column name="doing" /><Composer /></BoardProvider>);
});
columnRenders = composerRenders = 0;
await act(async () => { globalThis.add('t1', 'write'); });
await act(async () => { globalThis.move('t1', 'doing'); });
console.log(box.textContent);
console.log('two board changes -> Column renders:', columnRenders, '| Composer renders:', composerRenders);

[todo:-][doing:write]+
two board changes -> Column renders: 4 | Composer renders: 0

Two changes, four column renders (two columns × two changes) and zero composer renders. The composer (the form for adding a task) reads only DispatchContext, whose value never changes. And the children were created outside the provider, so the provider's own re-render did not spread down into them (§4.8, measured there for the same reason).

That is the brief's third requirement, met by the structure rather than by memoisation.

19.4 Saving Through an Action

§15's four jobs, none of them written by hand.

import { useActionState, useOptimistic, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

let settle;
function save(text) { return new Promise((res, rej) => { settle = { res, rej }; }); }

function Composer() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(async (prev, formData) => {
    const text = String(formData.get('text') ?? '').trim();
    if (!text) return { error: 'A task needs a name', text };
    try { await save(text); return { saved: [...(prev.saved ?? []), text] }; }
    catch (e) { return { error: e.message, text }; }
  }, {});
  const [shown, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(state.saved ?? [], (list, t) => [...list, t + '…']);

  return (
    <form action={async fd => { addOptimistic(String(fd.get('text'))); await formAction(fd); }}>
      <input name="text" defaultValue={state.text ?? 'write'} />
      <button type="submit" disabled={isPending}>add</button>
      <b>[{shown.join(',') || '-'}]{state.error ? ' ERR:' + state.error : ''}</b>
    </form>
  );
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
const submit = async () => { await act(async () => {
  box.querySelector('form').dispatchEvent(new window.Event('submit', { bubbles: true, cancelable: true }));
}); };

await act(async () => { root.render(<Composer />); });
console.log('idle      :', box.textContent);
box.querySelector('input').value = 'buy milk';           // the user types
await submit();
console.log('optimistic:', box.textContent, '| disabled:', box.querySelector('button').disabled);
await act(async () => { settle.rej(new Error('network down')); });
console.log('failed    :', box.textContent, '| input:', box.querySelector('input').value);
await submit();
await act(async () => { settle.res(); });
console.log('succeeded :', box.textContent, '| input:', box.querySelector('input').value);

idle      : add[-]
optimistic: add[buy milk…] | disabled: true
failed    : add[-] ERR:network down | input: buy milk
succeeded : add[buy milk] | input: write

Every line of the brief's fourth requirement, measured. The optimistic row appeared with its marker, and the button disabled itself. The failure removed the optimistic row automatically (there is no cleanup code anywhere in that component), and returned a message beside a form that still held the user's text: buy milk, restored through defaultValue={state.text} after React's reset that follows an action (§15.1, §15.5). The retry succeeded, the real value replaced the optimistic one, and the reset cleared the composer back to its default, which is what a composer should do after sending.

Written by hand, this is three useState calls, a try/catch/finally, and a scheme of temporary ids for matching the optimistic entry to the real one. None of it is here.

19.5 One Effect, One External System

The board needs to show whether the user is online. That is a real external system (§6.5), so it is a real Effect, and it is the only one in the application.

import { useState, useEffect, act, StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const log = [];
function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => {
    const on = () => setOnline(true), off = () => setOnline(false);
    log.push('subscribe');
    window.addEventListener('online', on);
    window.addEventListener('offline', off);
    return () => {
      log.push('unsubscribe');
      window.removeEventListener('online', on);
      window.removeEventListener('offline', off);
    };
  }, []);
  return online;
}
function Banner() { return <b>{useOnlineStatus() ? 'online' : 'offline'}</b>; }

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box);
await act(async () => { root.render(<StrictMode><Banner /></StrictMode>); });
console.log('mount under StrictMode:', log.join(', '));
await act(async () => { window.dispatchEvent(new window.Event('offline')); });
console.log('after going offline   :', box.textContent);
log.length = 0;
await act(async () => { root.unmount(); });
console.log('after unmount         :', log.join(', '));

mount under StrictMode: subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribe
after going offline   : offline
after unmount         : unsubscribe

subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribe is StrictMode's double run (§6.4), and it is the proof that the cleanup is correct. Had the listener not been removed, this component would now hold two of them, and every later offline event would run the handler twice. Every subscribe is matched, including the one at unmount.

Note what is not here. No Effect derives anything from props. No Effect calls setState from another Effect's result. The board's filtered views, its counts and its labels are all computed during render (§7.1). That is why one Effect is the feature's entire contact with the outside world.

19.6 Containment

Here is §14, applied per region, so that one broken column does not take down the board.

import { Component, act } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null };
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error }; }
  componentDidCatch(error) { globalThis.reported = error.message; }
  render() { return this.state.error ? <i>[{this.props.name} unavailable]</i> : this.props.children; }
}
function Column({ name, broken }) {
  if (broken) throw new Error(`${name} column failed`);
  return <b>[{name}]</b>;
}

globalThis.IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true;
const seen = [];
const box = document.getElementById('app');
const root = createRoot(box, { onCaughtError: e => seen.push('caught: ' + e.message) });
await act(async () => {
  root.render(<>
    <Boundary name="todo"><Column name="todo" /></Boundary>
    <Boundary name="doing"><Column name="doing" broken /></Boundary>
    <Boundary name="done"><Column name="done" /></Boundary>
  </>);
});
console.log('board  :', box.textContent);
console.log('root cb:', seen.join(', '));
console.log('report :', globalThis.reported);

board  : [todo][doing unavailable][done]
root cb: caught: doing column failed
report : doing column failed

Two of the three columns still work, the failure is named where it happened, and onCaughtError fired rather than onUncaughtError. So a monitoring system can tell "a region stopped working" apart from "the page is blank" (§14.5).

19.7 The Measurements

Everything the brief claimed, in one place, with the number this machine produced.

A task in two columns
Unrepresentable — a task's column is which array holds its id. §19.2.
A dangling selection
Deleting removed the id from the map and every column, measured.
One dispatch per interaction
moved is one action, so no render sees the intermediate state.
Composer isolated from the board
0 composer renders across two board changes, with no memo. §19.3.
Failure leaves no residue
The optimistic row vanished with zero cleanup code; the form kept its text. §19.4.
Cleanup undoes setup
subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribe under StrictMode, and one unsubscribe at unmount. §19.5.
One region's failure is contained
Two of three columns rendered; onCaughtError, not onUncaughtError. §19.6.

19.8 The Audit

Go back through the course and check the feature against it. This is the pass that finds what the gates cannot.

§2.6 — is anything keyed by index? The columns map over ids from the order arrays, and the ids are the keys. A list that can be reordered must not use the index, and this one is reordered by design.

§3.5 — is anything in state that could be computed? Counts, filtered views and the "is this column empty" flag are all derived during render. If any of them had been stored, §3.5's measured drift (stored values falling out of step) would apply.

§5.9 — is any prop mutated by a method call? The reducer builds new objects at every level, and never calls sort, push or splice on anything it received. Nothing in the toolchain would have told us otherwise.

§7.1 — is any Effect doing work that belongs in render or a handler? One Effect, one external system. Anything else would be on the §7.1 list.

§13.6 — would a suspending update blank the board? Any navigation or filter that can suspend must go through a transition, or the fallback replaces content the user is looking at.

§16.8 — could the first client render disagree with the server's? Nothing here reads the clock, Math.random, localStorage or window during render. useOnlineStatus starts as true and corrects itself in an Effect, which is §16.9's two-pass pattern.

§17.9 — if any of this became a Server Function, is it authorised inside itself? save is a browser-side stand-in here. As a Server Function it would need authentication, authorisation and argument validation in its own body: the checks in the component protect nothing.

19.9 What Is Still Wrong

Here is the honest list, because a capstone that claims to be finished is teaching the wrong lesson.

There is no persistence. Reloading loses the board. Adding it means deciding where the truth lives (on a server, in localStorage, or in a URL), and that decision changes the state shape, not just the storage call.

There is no routing. A board with a selected task should be linkable. That means the selection belongs in the URL rather than in useState, and the router's navigation belongs in a transition (§12.3).

The optimistic update is optimistic about the wrong thing. It shows the text, not the task's position in a column. A real optimistic update would insert into the target column's order array, which needs a temporary id, and a way to swap it for the server's id when that arrives.

Nothing is windowed. A board with five thousand tasks renders five thousand rows, and §10.7 says no amount of memoisation fixes that.

There is no server rendering. The whole feature runs only in the browser. Adding §16 means deciding where boundaries go. Adding §17 means deciding which parts are Server Components, which would remove the reducer from the browser bundle entirely and change the shape of the composer.

The tests are the measurements above and nothing else. They prove the mechanisms work; they do not prove that a user can complete a task. §18.7's behaviour tests are what would.

Each of those is work for another session, and each has a section that tells you how. That is the point of the course. Not that you now know React, but that when one of these problems lands on you, you know which measurement to take first.

What This Section Established

A feature built from the course's own rules, with every claim in the brief measured rather than asserted.

Normalised state made three bugs unrepresentable instead of merely avoidable, and the reducer was proven by calling it — no renderer, no DOM.

Splitting state from dispatch and passing children from above gave zero composer re-renders across two board changes, with no memoisation anywhere.

An Action handled the pending flag, the failure and the optimistic row with no useState, no finally and no cleanup code — the failed save left the form populated and the optimistic entry gone.

One Effect, one external system, and StrictMode's subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribe as the proof that its cleanup is complete.

Per-region error boundaries kept two of three columns alive and reported through onCaughtError rather than onUncaughtError.

And the last two subsections are the ones that matter most: an audit against the course, and a list of what is still wrong. Neither is something a gate can produce for you.

You started this course able to write React components. You now know what React is doing with them. That is the difference between guessing why something re-rendered and being able to say why.

What you can now do

  1. Hold the three stages apart. A component is a function. An element is the inert, frozen object it returns. A DOM node is what React eventually puts in the page. "The component rendered" and "the DOM changed" are different claims, and nearly every confusing bug lives in the gap between them.
  2. Read JSX as the function calls it becomes. Every odd-looking JSX rule follows from what JSX turns into, which you can print with one command:
    • children are a prop, so a single child is not an array;
    • key is a separate third argument, so it never reaches your component;
    • attributes are DOM property names, which is why they are camelCase.
  3. Predict what re-renders. By default React calls the whole subtree below a change again. Measured: a child with identical props re-rendered when unrelated state changed. Setting state to a value that is Object.is-equal to the old one calls nothing at all. When something renders unexpectedly, the cause is, in this order: its own state, its parent, a context it reads, or a changed key.
  4. Locate state by position, not by component. State belongs to a slot in the render tree. So wrapping a component in a <p> instead of a <div> resets its counter, two branches of a ternary share one state, and key is how you tell React the identity changed. key={index} hands one item's state to another item's data the moment a list is reordered.
  5. Choose a state shape that cannot go wrong. Group what changes together, refuse contradictions, compute anything you can derive, store ids rather than copies, and keep the structure flat. In one example a redundant fullName was showing a different person from its own first after a single rename, and nothing reported it.
  6. Write an Effect only for an external system. Think "start and stop", not "mount and unmount". Measured: on every dependency change React runs the cleanup with the old value, then the setup with the new one. The dependency array is derived from what the setup reads, and [] is a claim ("this reads nothing that changes"), not a schedule. In development, seeing subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribe is the proof your cleanup is complete.
  7. Not write the other Effects. Compute derived values during render. Put work caused by a user action in the event handler. Reset state on a prop change with a key. And remember that a chain of Effects is a chain of extra renders. That list is the single highest-value idea in the course after §2.5.
  8. Use the escape hatches deliberately. Refs (boxes that hold a value React does not track) are not reactive and are not read during render. A ref callback may now return a cleanup. useEffectEvent gives you the latest value without becoming a dependency. useSyncExternalStore is how you read state that lives outside React safely when rendering is concurrent.
  9. Schedule rather than only optimise. A transition keeps the old UI interactive, and stops Suspense from replacing content that is already visible. Measured: a navigation where FALLBACK never appeared. Put the await inside the action, never before startTransition, or the pending state is lost.
  10. Place Suspense boundaries as a design decision. A boundary is a unit of reveal: it is a streaming boundary and a hydration boundary at the same time. One boundary around two things showed neither until both were ready; two boundaries showed each as it arrived. And use() needs a promise that stays the same object across renders.
  11. Diagnose performance before treating it. A slow screen has one of three causes, each with a different fix: too much work, too many components, or work at the wrong time. Passing content as children gave zero re-renders of an expensive child with no memoisation at all. And memo without stable props is a comparison that always fails.
  12. Let the compiler do the memoising. A component with useMemo and useCallback, and the same component with neither, compile to byte-identical output. Stop writing new manual memoisation, but do not launch a project to delete the old.
  13. Obey the rules because they are the preconditions, not the etiquette. Purity (a render that only computes and changes nothing) is what makes it safe for React to throw a render away. The ordered list of hooks is why a conditional hook shifts every slot after it. And calling a component directly works, which is precisely why it is dangerous.
  14. Contain failures and know where they go. Put error boundaries around regions, keyed by what can change. Use the three root callbacks, which split errors by what the user actually experienced. And remember that an error thrown in an event handler reaches none of them.
  15. Let Actions do the four jobs. They keep a pending state across an await, hold the result as state, show an error beside a form that keeps its values, and show an optimistic row (one displayed before the server confirms it) that disappears on failure with no cleanup code. They also let a form submit before hydration, unless you take that away.
  16. Read a streamed page by eye. Look for <!--$-->, <!--$?-->, <!--$!--> and <!--/$-->, a <div hidden> at the bottom and a plain script that moves it into place. Hydration asserts rather than diffs: it expects the HTML to match instead of patching it. A mismatch is recoverable, which is why mismatches ship unnoticed unless onRecoverableError is wired up.
  17. Reason about the two environments. A Server Component's code never reaches the browser, only its output does. That is why it cannot hold state, and why importing a large library in one costs the user nothing. 'use client' marks a boundary, not a component, and belongs as low in the tree as it will go.
  18. Treat every server function as a public endpoint. Authenticate, authorise and validate inside the function, including the arguments it closed over. It is a URL with an unusual calling convention, and a check in the component that rendered the form protects nothing.

Where to go next

Some parts of React are still moving. Those are worth watching rather than learning once.

Transitions keep changing underneath the same API. React 19.3 made <ViewTransition>, addTransitionType and react-dom's browser() stable after a long run on the canary channel (React's preview builds). It also changed how overlapping transitions render without any change to the code you write: measured in §12.11, a ready transition no longer waits for an unrelated slow one. The taint APIs are still on the experimental channel only. Check what the installed package exports (§12.10) before planning around anything documented on react.dev, and re-measure concurrency claims, including this course's, on every minor release.

Server Components arrive through a framework. The bundler integration (the build tool splitting server code from client code) is genuinely part of the architecture, not a temporary inconvenience, and the reference implementations are only reference implementations. What is worth knowing is the payload format, the data the server sends to the browser. That is what makes the model concrete rather than magical, and it is two lines of JSON you can print.

The compiler changes what you write, gradually. Version 1.0 is stable, infer mode is the right default, and its lint plugin gives you the same analysis without adopting the compiler. The direction is clear: manual memoisation becomes something you read in old code rather than something you write.

The two habits that keep the knowledge current are smaller than they sound.

Ask the installed package what it exports before planning around a feature. Four lines answered it every time in this course, and they caught five APIs that the documentation presents without qualification. Object.keys(require('react')), and the same check for the lint preset, take thirty seconds and save an afternoon.

And measure React rather than quoting it. Nearly every number here came from running something, and several contradicted what is widely repeated:

  • $$typeof is Symbol(react.transitional.element), and production elements are not frozen;
  • a use-prefixed function that calls no hooks is not compiled as a hook;
  • cache() de-duplicates nothing outside a render;
  • Map, Set and promises cross the RSC boundary (the line between Server and Client Components), while class instances throw;
  • a mutating method call on a destructured array prop is caught by none of the seventeen lint rules, and compiled without complaint;
  • and React emits a preload link for every image it server-renders, whether or not you asked.

That last list is the habit in miniature. Each item is something a careful reader would have got wrong from the documentation alone, and each took under a minute to establish by running it. A component, a console.log and await act() are the whole method, and they will keep being right long after any particular fact here has changed.
